3.q: Lucia, 27, lacks capacity because of a severe learning disability and is 38 weeks pregnant. The team believes a planned caesarean is in her best interests, but she objects and her family disagree. There is no emergency. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask Lucia's GP to make the decision
Wait until labour starts and decide then
Apply to the Court of Protection for a decision
Proceed with the caesarean as a best interests decision
3.w: Where serious medical treatment is proposed for a person lacking capacity and there is disagreement or objection, the Court of Protection can decide what is in her best interests (MCA 2005). Planning ahead avoids an emergency decision.

n.0: A GP has no legal power to decide for an adult who lacks capacity.
n.1: Waiting for labour turns a plannable decision into an emergency with less time to safeguard her rights.
n.3: Proceeding with major surgery against objection and family disagreement, without the court, is not appropriate when time allows an application.

3.q: At a day 5 postnatal visit, the midwife notices a small bruise on the cheek of a 5-day-old baby. The parents say they do not know how it happened. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure the parents that bruising is common in newborns
Record the bruise in the notes and check it again at the next visit
Follow child protection procedures with urgent paediatric review
Ask the parents to take the baby to their GP within a week
3.w: NICE CG89 (child maltreatment): suspect maltreatment if there is bruising in a child who is not independently mobile. Follow local safeguarding procedures with urgent paediatric assessment (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Bruises in non-mobile babies are uncommon and must be investigated.
n.1: Bruising in a baby who is not mobile must not be left for review; it needs action now.
n.3: This delays assessment and leaves the baby at possible risk.

3.q: Funmi is leading the introduction of a new postnatal discharge checklist on her ward. Previous changes have failed because staff felt they were imposed. What should she do first?
o: Ask the ward manager to make use of the checklist mandatory from Monday
Introduce the checklist on night shifts first when the ward is quieter
Involve ward staff and women in identifying the problem and shaping the change
Issue the checklist by email with a start date and a compliance target
3.w: Effective change management engages the people affected early, builds shared understanding of the need for change and involves service users. This increases ownership and sustainability (SPM 5.11, 5.13.4).

n.0: Mandating use without engagement is likely to meet the same resistance.
n.1: Choosing a quieter shift does not address why previous changes were resisted.
n.3: Imposing change by email repeats the approach that has failed before.

3.q: Ruby, 32, took methyldopa for gestational hypertension during pregnancy. She gave birth yesterday and is breastfeeding. Her blood pressure remains raised and she still needs treatment. Which change to her medicines is recommended by NICE?
o: Stop all antihypertensives at birth and recheck her blood pressure at 2 weeks
Continue methyldopa unchanged until her 6 to 8 week GP review
Stop methyldopa within 2 days of birth and change to another antihypertensive
Increase the methyldopa dose, as blood pressure peaks on days 3 to 5
3.w: NICE NG133: if a woman has taken methyldopa in pregnancy, stop it within 2 days of birth and change to an alternative antihypertensive. Enalapril is the suggested first choice postnatally and is compatible with breastfeeding.

n.0: She still needs treatment, so stopping all medicines risks severe postnatal hypertension.
n.1: NG133 advises stopping methyldopa within 2 days of birth and changing to an alternative, not continuing it.
n.3: Methyldopa should be replaced, not increased, after the birth.

3.q: Baby Dev is 10 weeks old and has just moved to England from abroad. He has not had newborn blood spot screening. What should the health professional offer?
o: No screening, as blood spot screening ends at 8 weeks of age
Blood spot screening for the conditions except cystic fibrosis
Blood spot screening for all 10 conditions in the usual way
Cystic fibrosis screening, as the other tests are now too late
3.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: babies are eligible up to 1 year of age, except for cystic fibrosis screening, which is unreliable after 8 weeks. At 10 weeks Dev should be offered screening for the other conditions.

n.0: Eligibility continues to 1 year for the other conditions.
n.2: CF screening is unreliable after 8 weeks, so it is not offered at 10 weeks.
n.3: CF is the one test that is too late; the other conditions can still be screened.

3.q: Chloe, 26, is breastfeeding her 5-week-old baby in a café when a staff member asks her to feed in the toilets. She asks her midwife what her rights are. What should the midwife tell her?
o: Cafés may ask breastfeeding women to move to a private area
Businesses may refuse breastfeeding if they display a written policy
Her right to breastfeed in public applies until the baby is 6 months old
The Equality Act 2010 protects her right to breastfeed in any public space
3.w: NG194 1.5.5: inform women and partners that under the Equality Act 2010 women have the right to breastfeed in any public space. SPM 2.10 includes protection for women to breastfeed in all settings.

n.0: Asking her to move because she is breastfeeding is unlawful discrimination under the Equality Act 2010.
n.1: A written policy does not make discrimination lawful.
n.2: The protection for breastfeeding in public spaces is not limited to babies under 6 months.

3.q: Precious, 29, had an emergency caesarean birth. Her baby, born at 32 weeks, is in the neonatal unit. Precious wants to breastfeed. Which action best supports her and her baby together?
o: Arrange donor milk so that she does not need to express after surgery
Help her hand express colostrum as soon as possible after the birth
Advise her to start expressing once she can walk to the neonatal unit
Advise her to rest and plan breastfeeding when the baby is discharged
3.w: UNICEF UK Baby Friendly neonatal standards support mothers of babies in neonatal units to start expressing early after the birth and to express frequently, so the baby receives her own milk and her supply is established. Expressing can begin at the bedside after a caesarean. SPM 2.6 asks midwives to plan for mother and baby together even when they are cared for apart.

n.0: Donor milk may bridge a gap but does not replace support for her own milk, which she wants to give.
n.2: Delaying expression until she is mobile reduces milk supply; expressing can start at the bedside.
n.3: Early expression protects her supply and gives the preterm baby colostrum now.

3.q: Kerry, 34, had a caesarean in her first pregnancy and plans a vaginal birth at home with her second, against obstetric advice. What is the most appropriate action by the midwife?
o: Advise her to arrange private midwifery care for the birth
Document her plan and refer her to children's social care
Arrange a personalised care planning meeting with a consultant midwife
Tell Kerry midwives cannot attend a home birth after a caesarean
3.w: SPM 1.22: advocate for the woman when her decision is outside guidance, to minimise risk and maintain the relationship. A consultant midwife care planning meeting allows an honest discussion of risks and a plan that supports her choice (Code 2.5).

n.0: Sending her to private care withdraws NHS support instead of advocating for her.
n.1: Choosing a birth outside guidance is not a safeguarding concern.
n.3: The trust still provides midwifery care; a woman's choice of place of birth does not remove midwifery support.

3.q: Hannah, 27, has a BMI of 33 and no other medical history. She is planning a pregnancy and has read that women with a high BMI need a higher dose of folic acid. What is the current advice?
o: Take 5 mg daily, because a BMI of 30 or more needs the higher dose
Take 400 micrograms daily, as BMI alone does not need the higher dose
Take 5 mg daily, because a BMI of 30 or more raises pre-eclampsia risk
Take 400 micrograms daily, rising to 5 mg if her BMI rises above 35
3.w: NG247 1.1.6-1.1.7 (January 2025): women with a BMI of 25 or above, or at increased risk of pre-eclampsia, do not need more than 400 micrograms unless a 1.1.5 risk factor applies.

n.0: NG247 1.1.6 changed older teaching: BMI alone does not indicate the 5 mg dose.
n.2: Increased risk of pre-eclampsia does not, by itself, indicate 5 mg folic acid (NG247 1.1.7).
n.3: There is no BMI threshold for 5 mg in NG247; it depends on the listed risk factors.

3.q: Emily, 27, is booked for her 20-week scan. She asks the midwife whether a normal scan means her baby will definitely be healthy. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It screens for 11 specific physical conditions and cannot detect every problem
It is a diagnostic test, so any condition it does not find can be ruled out
It confirms or excludes Down's syndrome, which is the main condition it looks for
It checks for all physical and chromosomal conditions, so a normal scan is reassuring
3.w: The FASP 20-week scan (18+0 to 20+6 weeks) looks for 11 physical conditions, including spina bifida, anencephaly, cleft lip, congenital heart disease and Edwards' and Patau's syndromes. Some conditions are not detectable on scan, so a normal result cannot guarantee a healthy baby (FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.1: The anomaly scan is a screening test; a normal scan does not rule out every condition.
n.2: Down's syndrome is not one of the 11 conditions; it is screened for by the combined or quadruple test.
n.3: The scan looks for a defined list of conditions and many conditions cannot be seen on ultrasound.

3.q: Becky, 23, is breastfeeding her 3-day-old baby. She is tired and asks whether giving formula overnight would let her breasts 'fill up' so she has more milk in the morning. Which explanation by the midwife is accurate?
o: Frequent, effective milk removal signals the breasts to make more milk
Milk supply is fixed by breast size and is set by the third day
Supply depends mainly on how much water she drinks each day
Resting the breasts overnight builds a larger store for the next day
3.w: Breastfeeding works on supply and demand (NICE NG194 1.5.12): regular, effective milk removal, including at night, drives continued production. Replacing feeds with formula reduces stimulation and can lower supply (NG194 1.5.17).

n.1: Breast size does not determine supply; production responds to milk removal throughout lactation.
n.2: Drinking to thirst is enough; fluid intake does not drive milk supply.
n.3: Leaving milk in the breast signals the breast to slow production, so supply falls.

3.q: After a successful PDSA cycle reduced triage delays, the team leader wants the improvement to last when the project ends. Which step is most likely to sustain the change?
o: Thank the team and close the project now that the target has been reached
Build the new process into the guideline, training and data monitoring
Rely on the project champion to remind staff about the new process
Repeat the original baseline audit in two years to check progress
3.w: Sustaining improvement means embedding the change in standard processes (guidelines, induction, training) and continuing to monitor data so any slippage is noticed (SPM 5.11, 5.13.3).

n.0: Closing the project without embedding the change risks a return to old habits.
n.2: Dependence on one person is fragile; the process must not rely on an individual.
n.3: Waiting two years leaves any slippage unnoticed for too long.

3.q: Baby Zara's newborn hearing screen did not show a clear response in one ear, and she has been referred to audiology. Her mother is distressed and asks what this means. What is the most appropriate explanation?
o: It does not mean she has hearing loss; audiology within 4 weeks
The screen will be repeated at her 1-year health review
It confirms permanent hearing loss, so hearing aids will be fitted
Audiology will see her at 6 months if parents notice problems
3.w: Newborn hearing screening: no clear response can be due to fluid or debris in the ear, an unsettled baby or background noise, and does not mean the baby has hearing loss. Babies referred should have an audiology appointment within 4 weeks (Screening tests for you and your baby).

n.1: A referred baby needs audiology within 4 weeks, not a repeat screen at 1 year.
n.2: A screening result does not diagnose hearing loss; audiology assessment is needed.
n.3: Audiology follow-up is arranged now, not left to parental concern.

3.q: Rosie, 29, has a 3-month-old baby and has used the lactational amenorrhoea method so far. She has now started giving a formula feed at night so her partner can help. What should the midwife advise?
o: Continue LAM, adding condoms when the baby reaches 6 months
Continue LAM until her periods return
Start another method, as LAM is no longer reliable
Continue LAM, as her baby is under 6 months old
3.w: LAM is reliable only if the baby is under 6 months, the woman is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding and she has no periods. Giving formula, stopping night feeds or longer intervals between feeds mean another method should be used (NHS; FSRH).

n.0: She needs another method now because she is giving formula.
n.1: Return of periods is one trigger, but giving formula also ends LAM reliability.
n.3: LAM relies on exclusive or near-exclusive breastfeeding, which has stopped.

3.q: Ruby, 23, has a mild learning disability and is 12 weeks pregnant. She lives independently with some support. At booking, she seems confused by the information about screening tests. What should the midwife do first?
o: Ask how Ruby prefers to receive information and offer easy read
Record that she lacks capacity to decide about screening
Ask her support worker to make the screening decision for her
Book the screening tests and explain them at the next visit
3.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1(3): take all practicable steps to help a person decide before concluding they cannot. SPM 1.13 and Code 7.2: adapt communication, for example easy read and extra time, to strengthen her own ability to decide.

n.1: Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)) and cannot be judged lacking before steps have been taken to help her understand.
n.2: A support worker cannot make health decisions for an adult who has not been shown to lack capacity.
n.3: Booking tests before she understands them means there is no informed consent.

3.q: Kerry has been a registered midwife for 4 years and wants to prescribe medicines such as antibiotics for women with postnatal infections in her community caseload. What must happen before she can prescribe independently?
o: She must hold a patient group direction for each antibiotic she uses
She must complete an NMC-approved prescribing programme and have it recorded
She must complete 2 years of community practice and a local competency
She must be authorised in writing by her head of midwifery
3.w: Only nurses and midwives who have completed an NMC-approved prescribing qualification and had it recorded on the register can prescribe (Code 18, note to 18.5). SPM 3.19 expects the ability to progress to a prescribing qualification after registration.

n.0: A PGD allows supply or administration to a group; it is not prescribing.
n.2: Length of experience and a local competency do not confer prescribing rights.
n.3: A head of midwifery cannot authorise prescribing; it requires a recorded qualification.

3.q: Three weeks after discharge, the father of a baby Ruth cared for on the postnatal ward sends her a social media friend request and invites her for a drink to say thanks. Ruth had no previous relationship with the family. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the friend request but decline the invitation for a drink
Decline both, keeping a clear professional boundary with the family
Accept the drink if a colleague from the ward also attends
Accept both, as the family is no longer in her care
3.w: NMC Code 20.6: stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past, their families and carers. Ruth should politely decline both.

n.0: An online friendship with the family of a former patient still blurs the professional boundary that Code 20.6 protects.
n.2: A colleague's presence does not change the nature of a social relationship with a family recently in her care.
n.3: Code 20.6 expressly includes people who have been in your care in the past, so discharge does not end the boundary.

3.q: Ama, 32, is having a planned home birth and is pushing involuntarily. As the midwife watches the perineum, she sees fetal buttocks and genitalia rather than a head. No one has suspected breech before. What should the midwife do first?
o: Call for help, including a 999 ambulance and a second midwife
Carry Ama to the car for an immediate hospital transfer
Ask Ama to stop pushing until an ambulance arrives
Apply gentle traction to the buttocks to speed the birth
3.w: In an unexpected breech at advanced labour, call for help (999 ambulance, second midwife) and prepare for a vaginal breech birth. RCOG GTG 20b: women near or in the active second stage should not routinely be offered caesarean, and all midwives should be familiar with breech birth techniques.

n.1: Moving her during the active second stage risks the birth happening in transit without help.
n.2: Asking her to stop pushing will not halt the birth and wastes time needed to call help.
n.3: Traction risks extension of the arms and head; GTG 20b advises a hands-off approach.

3.q: A trial of a new antenatal education programme reports the risk of caesarean birth in the intervention group compared with usual care as a relative risk of 0.80 (95% confidence interval 0.65 to 0.98). Sophie, a student midwife, asks her practice supervisor how to interpret this. Which explanation is correct?
o: An 80% relative reduction that is statistically significant at the 5% level
A 20% relative reduction that is statistically significant at the 5% level
A 20% relative reduction that is not statistically significant
A 20% relative increase that is statistically significant at the 5% level
3.w: A relative risk of 0.80 means the risk is 80% of the comparison risk, a 20% relative reduction (1 minus 0.80). The 95% confidence interval (0.65 to 0.98) lies entirely below 1.0, the line of no effect, so the result is statistically significant at the 5% level.

n.0: An RR of 0.80 is a 20% reduction, not 80%; an 80% reduction would be an RR of 0.20.
n.2: The interval does not include 1.0 (its upper limit is 0.98), so the result is statistically significant.
n.3: A relative risk below 1.0 shows a reduction in risk, not an increase.

3.q: Ruth, 31, received oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM for active management of the third stage. On the delivery suite, 20 minutes after the placenta is delivered complete, she bleeds heavily from an atonic uterus despite massage and an empty bladder. She has no history of asthma. According to NICE NG235, which uterotonic is appropriate next?
o: Misoprostol 200 micrograms orally
A second dose of oxytocin with ergometrine IM
Carboprost intramuscularly
Ergometrine 500 micrograms intravenously
3.w: NICE NG235 table 12: after prophylaxis with oxytocin plus ergometrine, first-line treatment for atony is carboprost IM or an oxytocin infusion. Carboprost can be repeated at intervals of at least 15 minutes, up to 8 doses (NG235 1.10.34).

n.0: NG235 lists misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually or rectally, not 200 micrograms orally.
n.1: NG235 keeps a repeat of oxytocin with ergometrine for settings where other drugs are unavailable, such as a home birth; on the delivery suite carboprost or an oxytocin infusion is first line.
n.3: Ergometrine has already been given and IV ergometrine is not the NG235 next step.

3.q: Isla, 26, is in established labour. Her mother has told her to drink at least a litre of water every hour to keep her strength up. Which advice about drinking in labour is most accurate?
o: Avoid all fluids, as drinking increases the risk of aspiration
Drink plain water, as isotonic drinks raise the risk of hyponatraemia
Drink at least a litre an hour to prevent dehydration and ketosis
Drink when thirsty, as excess fluid can cause harm
3.w: NICE NG235 1.8.17 and 1.8.26 (updated 2025): drink when thirsty; isotonic drinks may be more beneficial than water; there is no benefit to drinking more than normal, and excessive oral or IV fluid can cause hyponatraemia (sodium under 130 mmol/L), with maternal and neonatal seizures or death.

n.0: Women should drink in labour when thirsty; fluid restriction is not advised.
n.1: Isotonic drinks may be more beneficial than water; excess water is the hyponatraemia risk.
n.2: Drinking a litre an hour risks fluid overload and hyponatraemia.

3.q: Grace, 19, comes to every antenatal appointment with her mother, who answers most questions for her. Grace says little. Which approach by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Ask her mother to wait outside for the rest of the pregnancy
Direct questions to her mother, who seems to know the history well
Continue as now, as Grace has not raised any concerns
Ask Grace privately how she would like her mother involved
3.w: SPM 1.10 asks midwives to involve partners and family in discussions on the woman's terms. Seeing Grace alone for part of the appointment lets her state her own wishes and allows routine enquiry about safety (NICE NG201).

n.0: Excluding her mother for the whole pregnancy may not be what Grace wants; her own preference should decide this.
n.1: Speaking through her mother bypasses Grace, who is the person receiving care and makes her own decisions.
n.2: A quiet young woman may not raise concerns while a relative is present, so the midwife should create the chance to speak privately.

3.q: Bernadette, 41, is booking at 8 weeks in her third pregnancy. Her previous pregnancies, 3 and 6 years ago, were normotensive. Her BMI is 27 and she has no medical conditions or family history of pre-eclampsia. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Aspirin from 12 weeks, as age 40 or over is a high-risk factor
Aspirin from 12 weeks, as any moderate risk factor qualifies
Weekly BP checks from booking, as her age needs closer surveillance
Routine BP and urine checks, with no aspirin indicated
3.w: Age 40 or over is a moderate risk factor. NICE advises aspirin when there is more than one moderate factor or any high-risk factor (NG133 1.1.2, 1.1.3). With a single moderate factor she continues routine BP and urine monitoring at every appointment (NG201 1.2.24, 1.2.28) and is reassessed in the second trimester (NG201 1.2.23).

n.0: Age 40 or over is classed as a moderate, not a high, risk factor.
n.1: One moderate factor alone does not meet the NICE threshold of more than one moderate factor.
n.2: There is no recommendation for weekly BP checks on the basis of age alone in an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy.

3.q: Baby Isla was born at 09:00 on Monday in a midwife-led unit and is well. Under the NHS NIPE screening programme, by when should her newborn physical examination be completed at the latest?
o: By 09:00 on Tuesday
By 09:00 on Wednesday
By 09:00 on Thursday
By 09:00 on Saturday
3.w: NIPE programme handbook: the newborn screening examination (eyes, heart, hips and testes) should be completed before, or at, 72 hours of age (KPI NP1). 72 hours after 09:00 Monday is 09:00 Thursday. NG194 1.3.3 also requires a complete examination within 72 hours.

n.0: Tuesday 09:00 is 24 hours, earlier than the latest permitted time.
n.1: Wednesday 09:00 is 48 hours; the standard is 72 hours.
n.3: Saturday 09:00 is 5 days, beyond the 72-hour standard.

3.q: Kayla, 17, is pregnant with her first baby and lives with her mother. She wants to continue the pregnancy and says she does not know anything about caring for a baby. Which additional service should the midwife offer to refer her to?
o: The Family Nurse Partnership programme
The specialist perinatal mental health team
The adult safeguarding team
The pregnancy options counselling service
3.w: The Family Nurse Partnership is an evidence-based home visiting programme for young first-time parents (usually 19 or under), running from pregnancy until the child is 2. It supports young parents who may find services hard to engage with (SPM 2.8, 2.9).

n.1: There is no indication of mental illness; this team is for moderate to severe perinatal mental health problems.
n.2: Kayla is under 18 and has no identified safeguarding concern; adult safeguarding does not apply.
n.3: She has decided to continue the pregnancy, so options counselling does not meet her needs.

3.q: Sophie, 33, has bipolar disorder and has decided with her psychiatrist to continue lithium through pregnancy. She is now 36 weeks. Which plan is most consistent with NICE CG192?
o: Check a lithium level once labour starts and continue her usual dose
Stop lithium at 36 weeks and restart it on the second postnatal day
Weekly plasma lithium levels from now, and plan birth in hospital
Lithium levels every 4 weeks until birth, with birth at home if she chooses
3.w: CG192 1.4.37: if lithium continues in pregnancy, check plasma levels every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks; maintain fluid balance; ensure she gives birth in hospital; monitor in labour; stop lithium during labour and check levels 12 hours after the last dose.

n.0: Lithium is stopped during labour because of dehydration and toxicity risk, with a level 12 hours after the last dose.
n.1: CG192 does not advise stopping lithium at 36 weeks; it is stopped during labour.
n.3: Levels become weekly from the 36th week, and CG192 advises birth in hospital.

3.q: Baby Noah is born at term in good condition and is in skin-to-skin contact with his mother. A colleague wants to weigh and dress him straight away to free the room. Which response by the midwife is best?
o: Agree to weigh him but let the mother dress him afterwards
Keep skin-to-skin and delay routine checks for the first hour
Weigh him now and return him for skin-to-skin to finish
Agree, as early weighing helps plan the first feed
3.w: NICE NG235: encourage skin-to-skin as soon as possible and avoid separating the woman and baby within the first hour for routine procedures, such as weighing, unless she asks or they are needed for the baby's immediate care. Best interests of woman and newborn guide the decision (SPM 1.14).

n.0: Weighing still separates them during the first hour without a clinical need.
n.2: Interrupting skin-to-skin for a routine weight goes against NG235's advice for the first hour.
n.3: Weighing is a routine procedure that NG235 advises delaying; feeding plans do not depend on weight in the first hour.

3.q: Before transfer home on day 1, Jo, 27, says breastfeeding is going well. The midwife has not yet observed a feed. What does NICE recommend before transfer?
o: Observe at least one effective feed as part of the feeding plan
Give a formula top-up so the baby is settled for the journey
Weigh the baby to confirm feeding is effective
Accept Jo's report and arrange a feed check on day 5
3.w: NG194 1.1.10: before transfer, make sure there is a plan for feeding the baby, including observing at least 1 effective feed; NG194 1.5.14 lists what to assess (SPM 3.6).

n.1: A top-up without clinical need can undermine breastfeeding.
n.2: Weight on day 1 does not show feeding effectiveness; normal weight loss occurs early.
n.3: NICE expects an effective feed to be observed before transfer.

3.q: The MBRRACE-UK 2022-24 maternal mortality data brief compares women living in the most and least deprived areas. What did it report?
o: Women in the most deprived areas had about twice the rate
Rates were similar across deprivation levels
Women in the most deprived areas had about five times the rate
Women in the least deprived areas had a higher rate
3.w: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: maternal mortality in the most deprived areas was about twice that in the least deprived. Midwives must understand health inequalities and their determinants (SPM 1.17.1).

n.1: The data show a clear gradient by deprivation.
n.2: The difference was about twice, not five times.
n.3: The gradient runs the other way: higher in the most deprived areas.

3.q: Mei, 29, is well and has an uncomplicated pregnancy. She asks about a birth centre in her town that is on a different site from the hospital and has no obstetricians or anaesthetists. Which setting is she describing?
o: An alongside midwifery unit
An obstetric unit
A freestanding midwifery unit
A midwife-led triage unit
3.w: NICE NG235 1.2.1 and 1.3.3 name four birth settings: home, freestanding midwifery unit (on a separate site from an obstetric unit), alongside midwifery unit (same site) and obstetric unit. A unit away from the hospital without obstetric or anaesthetic staff is freestanding (SPM 2.1).

n.0: An alongside midwifery unit is on the same site as an obstetric unit, so transfer does not need an ambulance.
n.1: An obstetric unit has obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal staff on site, which this birth centre lacks.
n.3: Triage assesses women who call or attend with concerns; it is not a place planned for giving birth.

3.q: The midwife gives 5 inflation breaths to Baby Tom, born at 41 weeks, but sees no chest rise and the heart rate is not increasing. What should she do next?
o: Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath
Give ventilation breaths at 30 per minute as planned
Reposition the head and use a two-person jaw thrust, then repeat
Increase the inflation pressure to 50 cm H2O and continue
3.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if there is no chest rise, check and correct head position, consider two-person jaw thrust or a supraglottic airway, then repeat the 5 inflation breaths. Compressions are not effective until the lungs are aerated.

n.0: Compressions are not started until the lungs have been effectively aerated.
n.1: Ventilation breaths will not work until airway obstruction is corrected and chest rise is seen.
n.3: Pressure may be increased cautiously after airway manoeuvres, not jumped to 50 cm H2O first.

3.q: Rhian, 27, is on continuous CTG in labour. The baseline is 135, variability is 10 beats per minute and contractions are 3 in 10. For the last 15 minutes there have been late decelerations with each contraction. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Pathological, needing urgent obstetric and senior midwife review
Suspicious, needing review if they continue for 30 minutes
Normal, as baseline and variability are reassuring
Suspicious, as the decelerations have lasted under 30 minutes
3.w: Late decelerations are a red feature regardless of how long they have been present (NICE NG229 1.4.24, amended 2025). Any red feature makes the CTG pathological (1.4.32), requiring urgent review by an obstetrician and senior midwife, exclusion of acute events and conservative measures (1.5.7).

n.1: Late decelerations are red at any duration, so the trace is already pathological.
n.2: Reassuring baseline and variability do not offset a red feature.
n.3: The 30-minute timing applies to variable decelerations with concerning characteristics, not late decelerations.

3.q: Grace, 34, smokes and had a previous baby below the 3rd centile. She has been placed on serial ultrasound surveillance for fetal growth starting at 28 weeks. At her 30-week community appointment, what should the midwife do about fundal height measurement?
o: Measure fundal height and refer for a scan if it falls below the 50th centile
Stop measuring fundal height, as serial scans have replaced it
Measure and plot fundal height at each visit alongside the scans
Measure fundal height weekly between her scan appointments
3.w: SBL v3 2.12: women on planned serial scan surveillance should stop having SFH measured once serial surveillance begins; growth is assessed by ultrasound.

n.0: SFH has been stopped for this pathway, and the 50th centile is not a referral trigger.
n.2: SBL v3 2.12 says SFH should cease once serial scan surveillance starts.
n.3: Weekly SFH is not part of any SBL v3 pathway and adds no information to serial scans.

3.q: Divya, 38, books at 10 weeks. She has chronic hypertension and her previous baby was growth restricted with pre-eclampsia. The FGR risk assessment places her in the high-risk category. In addition to aspirin, which surveillance does Saving Babies' Lives v3 recommend?
o: Uterine artery Doppler at 18+0 to 23+6 weeks, then serial growth scans
Fundal height measurement every 2 weeks from 24+0 weeks of pregnancy
Weekly computerised CTG from 28 weeks of pregnancy until birth
A single growth scan at 36 weeks to estimate the fetal weight
3.w: SBL v3 2.7 recommends uterine artery Doppler at 18+0 to 23+6 weeks for women at high risk of FGR, and 2.13 serial ultrasound surveillance of fetal growth (3 to 4 weekly) for women at increased risk.

n.1: SFH is the surveillance for low-risk women; high-risk women need ultrasound.
n.2: Routine weekly CTG is not the SBL v3 surveillance method; computerised CTG is used once FGR is suspected (2.14).
n.3: A single late scan would miss early-onset FGR in a high-risk pregnancy.

3.q: Sophie, 30, is booking at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her BMI is 37 and she has no medical conditions. Her sister and mother have never had pre-eclampsia. Should aspirin be advised to reduce her risk of pre-eclampsia?
o: Yes, because a BMI over 35 is a high-risk factor
Yes, because she has two moderate risk factors
No, because she has no high-risk factors
No, because a BMI of 37 is a single moderate risk factor
3.w: Nulliparity and a BMI of 35 or more at first visit are both moderate risk factors. More than one moderate risk factor means aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth is advised (NICE NG133 1.1.3).

n.0: BMI of 35 or more is a moderate, not a high, risk factor; the high-risk list is previous hypertensive disease, CKD, autoimmune disease, diabetes and chronic hypertension.
n.2: Aspirin is also advised for more than one moderate risk factor, even with no high-risk factor.
n.3: Being nulliparous is a second moderate factor, so she has two, not one.

3.q: After a one-week trial of a new triage call script, Ola collects data on call times and compares it with the previous month. Which stage of the PDSA cycle is she completing?
o: The Do stage
The Plan stage
The Study stage
The Act stage
3.w: In the Study stage the team analyses the data, compares results with predictions and reflects on what was learned. Act then decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change (SPM 5.1).

n.0: Do was the one-week trial itself.
n.1: Planning set out the change and predictions before the trial.
n.3: Act follows Study and decides what to do next with the change.

3.q: Ellie, 26, is having her first baby and has no risk factors. She is considering a home birth. Which information about her baby's safety is accurate according to NICE?
o: Planned home birth carries a lower risk than a midwife-led unit
Planned home birth carries a small increase in adverse outcomes for the baby
Planned home birth carries a large increase in risk and is advised against
Planned home birth carries no difference in outcome for the baby
3.w: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk nulliparous women, planning birth at home is associated with a small increase in the risk of an adverse outcome for the baby; the same recommendation says she may choose any setting and must be supported in her choice.

n.0: For nulliparous women the evidence shows a small increase at home, not a lower risk.
n.2: NG235 describes a small increase and supports her choice; it does not advise against home birth.
n.3: No difference applies to midwife-led units for nulliparous women and to home birth for multiparous women, not home birth for a first baby.

3.q: Jade, 29, is in the obstetric unit with suspected sepsis 3 days after birth. She meets high-risk criteria, her lactate is 4.6 mmol/L and her systolic blood pressure is 88 mmHg. The doctor asks the midwife to give an intravenous fluid bolus. What does NICE NG255 recommend?
o: 1000 mL of 5% glucose given over 1 hour
500 mL of crystalloid given over 4 hours
500 mL crystalloid over under 15 minutes
250 mL of colloid given over 30 minutes
3.w: NICE NG255 1.9.2: use crystalloids containing sodium 130-154 mmol/L as a 500 mL bolus over less than 15 minutes. With lactate over 4 or systolic 90 or less, give the bolus within 1 hour and refer to critical care (1.7.4); reassess, and give a second bolus if no improvement (1.9.4).

n.0: 5% glucose does not contain sodium in the recommended range and the volume and rate are wrong.
n.1: Giving the bolus over 4 hours is far slower than recommended.
n.3: NG255 recommends crystalloid in 500 mL boluses, not colloid.

3.q: Maya is the midwife at a freestanding birth centre when a woman has a sudden, heavy postpartum haemorrhage. One other midwife and a maternity support worker are on duty. What should Maya do first?
o: Phone the obstetric unit for advice before starting any treatment
Ask the support worker to estimate the blood loss before any other action
Call for help, request a 999 ambulance and give each colleague a clear role
Start the haemorrhage protocol herself and call for help once bleeding slows
3.w: In an unpredictable emergency, calling for help early, arranging transfer and allocating clear roles makes best use of a small team (SPM 5.13.6; NICE NG235 1.10.33: call for help, transfer to obstetric-led care).

n.0: Advice is useful but treatment and transfer must not wait for it.
n.1: Measuring blood loss matters, but it is not the first priority over summoning help.
n.3: Delaying the call for help until bleeding slows wastes time a small team cannot afford.

3.q: A woman at 22 weeks has a severe haemorrhage and the obstetric consultant believes immediate termination is needed to save her life. There is no time to obtain a second opinion. Under the Abortion Act 1967, is this lawful?
o: Yes, under the emergency provision in s1(4)
No, two practitioners must agree before any termination
No, termination must take place in an approved clinic
Yes, if a senior midwife also signs the certificate
3.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(4): the requirement for two opinions, and the place requirement, do not apply where a registered medical practitioner believes in good faith that termination is immediately necessary to save the life, or prevent grave permanent injury to the physical or mental health, of the pregnant woman.

n.1: Section 1(4) removes the two-opinion requirement in an emergency.
n.2: Section 1(4) also removes the requirement for an NHS hospital or approved place.
n.3: A midwife's signature is not part of the Act's requirements.

3.q: A baby born at term needs therapeutic cooling after a difficult labour in an NHS trust in England. The parents ask whether an independent body will look into the care. Which body carries out independent maternity safety investigations in England?
o: The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
Maternity and Newborn Safety Investigations (MNSI)
The Perinatal Mortality Review Tool (PMRT) team
The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC)
3.w: MNSI carries out independent investigations of certain maternity and newborn safety events reported by NHS trusts in England, working with families and staff and making safety recommendations without blaming individuals (MNSI).

n.0: The Ombudsman considers complaints after local processes are exhausted, not safety investigations.
n.2: The PMRT supports local hospital reviews of perinatal deaths; it is not an independent investigation body.
n.3: The NMC regulates individual registrants' fitness to practise; it does not investigate maternity safety events.

3.q: Ola, 33, is on continuous CTG in established labour. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes, the baseline is 140 beats per minute and there are no decelerations. Variability has been 3 to 4 beats per minute for the last 40 minutes. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Suspicious
Normal
Need for urgent intervention
Pathological
3.w: Variability under 5 beats per minute for 30 to 50 minutes is an amber feature (NICE NG229 1.4.18). Contractions, baseline and decelerations are white. One amber feature makes the CTG suspicious (NG229 1.4.32), prompting a full risk assessment and conservative measures.

n.1: A normal CTG has all four features white; reduced variability for 40 minutes is amber.
n.2: NG229 uses normal, suspicious and pathological; this is not one of its categories.
n.3: Pathological needs one red feature or two or more amber features; there is one amber feature.

3.q: A maternity governance meeting is discussing the East Kent report, "Reading the signals" (Kirkup, 2022). Which list matches the report's four areas for action?
o: Safe staffing, multidisciplinary training, complex antenatal care, bereavement care
Smoking, fetal growth, fetal movements, fetal monitoring, preterm birth, diabetes
Identifying poor performance, compassion and kindness, teamworking, responding with honesty
Listening to women, workforce, safety culture, standards and structures
3.w: East Kent (19 October 2022): identifying poorly performing units; giving care with compassion and kindness; teamworking with a common purpose; responding to challenge with honesty.

n.0: These are among the Ockenden immediate and essential action themes.
n.1: These are the six elements of Saving Babies' Lives v3.
n.3: These are the four themes of the NHS England three-year delivery plan (2023).

3.q: Zoe, 32, is 38 weeks pregnant and in early labour. Her membranes rupture spontaneously and there is a sudden fresh vaginal bleed of about 100 mL. Within minutes the fetal heart rate falls to 80 beats/min. Zoe is well, with a normal pulse and blood pressure. What should the midwife suspect?
o: Minor placental abruption
Cervical ectropion
A show from cervical change
Ruptured vasa praevia
3.w: RCOG GTG 63: if APH is associated with rupture of the membranes, bleeding from a ruptured vasa praevia should be considered. The bleeding is fetal blood, so the fetus is rapidly compromised while the mother stays well; this needs immediate obstetric help and urgent birth.

n.0: An abruption would usually cause pain and maternal signs; rapid fetal compromise with a well mother at membrane rupture suggests vasa praevia.
n.1: An ectropion does not cause sudden fetal bradycardia at membrane rupture.
n.2: A show is blood-stained mucus, not a 100 mL bleed with fetal bradycardia.

3.q: Alice, 29, is 34 weeks pregnant and attends for the second time in 10 days with reduced fetal movements. Her computerised CTG today meets criteria and her SFH is on her usual centile. Her last scan was at 20 weeks. What should be offered?
o: A repeat computerised CTG in 1 week, without an ultrasound scan
Reassurance, as a normal CTG excludes placental insufficiency
Induction of labour now because the episode is recurrent
A scan for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler
3.w: SBL v3 element 3 checklist: offer an ultrasound scan for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler to women presenting with recurrent RFM after 28+0 weeks, unless a growth scan was done in the previous 2 weeks.

n.0: A repeat CTG alone does not assess growth or placental function, which is the concern in recurrent RFM.
n.1: A normal CTG reflects current wellbeing and does not exclude placental insufficiency or FGR.
n.2: Birth for recurrent RFM is offered after 38+6 weeks; at 34 weeks the next step is a scan.

3.q: Freya, 29, collapses 20 minutes after a vaginal birth. She is pale and drowsy, with heart rate 142 beats/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg. There is blood on the bed and her uterus feels soft and high. What is the most likely cause and the immediate response?
o: Eclampsia: give magnesium sulfate 4 g IV
Vasovagal faint: lie her flat and raise her legs
Pulmonary embolism: give oxygen and wait for a CT scan
Haemorrhage: get help, massage, uterotonic, fluids
3.w: Collapse soon after birth with tachycardia, hypotension, visible bleeding and a soft uterus points to hypovolaemia from atonic PPH. Call for help, uterine massage, uterotonics and IV fluids (NICE NG235 1.10.33), within an ABC approach to maternal collapse.

n.0: There is no seizure or hypertension; she is hypotensive.
n.1: A faint does not cause a soft uterus with heavy bleeding and persistent shock.
n.2: A pulmonary embolism would not explain the bleeding and boggy uterus.

3.q: Ines gave birth to a baby boy at 39 weeks an hour ago. She has gestational diabetes treated with insulin. The baby is well, pink and alert, and has breastfed once 20 minutes after birth. When should the baby's first blood glucose be measured?
o: At 6 hours after birth if he is feeding well
At 24 hours, before transfer home
Within the first 30 minutes, before the first feed
At 2 to 4 hours after birth, before a feed
3.w: NG3 1.5.3 recommends routine blood glucose testing at 2 to 4 hours after birth in babies of women with diabetes. Babies feed within 30 minutes and then every 2 to 3 hours until pre-feed levels are at least 2.0 mmol/L (NG3 1.5.9).

n.0: Waiting 6 hours would miss the period when neonatal hypoglycaemia most commonly occurs.
n.1: Testing at 24 hours is far too late; NG3 sets 2 to 4 hours.
n.2: Testing before the first feed in a well baby is not recommended; the first feed should come within 30 minutes and the test at 2 to 4 hours.

3.q: Ellie, 26, is in her first labour with intact membranes. Four hours ago her cervix was 4 cm dilated; it is now 5 cm. Contractions are 2 in 10 minutes, she is well hydrated and the fetal heart is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Transfer her to obstetric-led care for confirmed delay
Start an oxytocin infusion to increase contraction frequency
Offer support and pain relief and re-examine in 2 hours
Perform an amniotomy now, as delay has been confirmed
3.w: Under 2 cm in 4 hours in a first labour means delay is suspected (NICE NG235 1.8.42). Discuss findings, offer support and pain relief (1.8.41, 1.8.43, 1.8.44) and advise a VE 2 hours later; delay is diagnosed if progress is under 1 cm (1.8.45). Amniotomy is then considered (1.8.46).

n.0: Delay has not yet been diagnosed, so transfer is not indicated on progress alone.
n.1: Oxytocin is considered by an obstetrician after confirmed delay, not as a first step for suspected delay.
n.3: Delay is suspected, not confirmed; amniotomy is considered once delay is diagnosed after the 2-hour re-examination.

3.q: Nadia, 29, was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 28 weeks and is learning to check her capillary blood glucose. She asks what fasting level she should aim for. Which target is correct?
o: 7.0 mmol/L
6.0 mmol/L
4.0 mmol/L
5.3 mmol/L
3.w: NG3 1.3.5 advises pregnant women with any form of diabetes to aim for a fasting plasma glucose of 5.3 mmol/L, and NG3 1.3.6 advises staying above 4 mmol/L if taking insulin.

n.0: 7.0 mmol/L at diagnosis is the level at which immediate insulin is offered (NG3 1.2.22), not the target.
n.1: 6.0 mmol/L is above the NG3 fasting target.
n.2: 4 mmol/L is the level to stay above if taking insulin, not the target to aim for.

3.q: Chloe, 30, is postnatal after a long labour. The midwife realises she has just given Chloe a dose of dihydrocodeine that was prescribed for the woman in the next bed. Chloe is sleepy but rousable and breathing normally. What is the midwife's first priority?
o: Assess Chloe and inform the doctor and coordinator now
Tell Chloe what happened at her discharge discussion
Refer herself to the NMC before the end of her shift
Complete an incident report before telling anyone else
3.w: Code 14.1 requires the midwife to act immediately to put right the situation where harm has or could have occurred: assess and monitor Chloe (including respiratory rate and sedation) and get medical review. She then explains and apologises (Code 14.2) and documents and reports the incident (Code 14.3).

n.1: Chloe must be told promptly, not at discharge (Code 14.2).
n.2: Self-referral to the NMC is not the immediate priority and is not required for every error.
n.3: Reporting matters, but Chloe's safety and medical review come first.

3.q: Hope, 19, attends the maternity unit for the first time at 24 weeks of pregnancy. She has not seen a midwife before and seems anxious when asked why. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make a child protection referral because late booking indicates neglect
Arrange a routine booking appointment with her community midwife in 4 weeks
Offer the combined screening test for Down's syndrome at this appointment
Complete her booking today and sensitively explore why she has booked late
3.w: Late booking is a recognised warning sign (for example of domestic abuse, concealed pregnancy or social difficulty). NG201 1.1.4-1.1.5 aims for booking by 10+0 weeks; a late booker should be booked promptly, with a sensitive exploration of reasons and safeguarding questions asked when she is alone (NG201 1.2.5; SPM 2.8).

n.0: Late booking is a warning sign to explore, not proof of harm; a referral is made if the assessment identifies risk.
n.1: She has already missed most of the antenatal schedule; delaying booking another month adds risk.
n.2: The combined test is offered up to 14+1 weeks, so it is no longer available at 24 weeks (FASP).

3.q: During the NIPE newborn examination of baby Leo, the midwife finds that the red reflex in his left eye is absent and the pupil looks white. The right eye is normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to a community optician for an eye test at 1 year
Refer urgently so he is seen by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks
Repeat the red reflex check at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
Refer for an ophthalmology appointment within 6 weeks
3.w: NIPE handbook 12.11: babies with screen positive (abnormal) red reflex results should be urgently referred and seen by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks of the newborn examination; an absent or white reflex may indicate congenital cataract or retinoblastoma.

n.0: An optician at 1 year is far too late; surgery for severe congenital cataract is time-critical.
n.2: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks delays assessment of a possible cataract or retinoblastoma.
n.3: The NIPE standard is assessment within 2 weeks, not 6.

3.q: Nadia, 4 days after birth, had pre-eclampsia and takes enalapril. Her blood pressure is 146/96 mmHg, she has no symptoms and her blood results are stable. She asks to go home. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Keep her in hospital until her blood pressure is below 130/80 mmHg
Transfer with no medical follow-up, as her BP is below 150/100 mmHg
Transfer home with a medical review 2 weeks after the birth
Keep her in hospital until the enalapril can be stopped completely
3.w: NICE NG133: transfer to community care is appropriate when there are no symptoms of pre-eclampsia, BP is 150/100 mmHg or less and blood results are stable or improving. Women still on antihypertensives need medical review at 2 weeks, plus the 6 to 8 week review.

n.0: 130/80 is a treatment target, not a requirement for transfer home.
n.1: Women discharged on antihypertensives need a review at 2 weeks and again at 6 to 8 weeks.
n.3: Treatment can be reduced in the community; it does not need to stop before transfer.

3.q: Priya, 31, has type 2 diabetes and is planning a pregnancy. Which folic acid regimen should be recommended?
o: 5 mg daily from before conception until 12 weeks
400 micrograms daily until 12 weeks, rising to 5 mg if her HbA1c is high
400 micrograms daily from before conception until 12 weeks
5 mg daily from confirmation of pregnancy until 12 weeks
3.w: NG247 1.1.5: high-dose 5 mg folic acid for women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes (and other specified risks), from before conception to 12 weeks. NG3 1.1.11 is consistent.

n.1: The 5 mg dose is indicated by type 1 or 2 diabetes itself, not by HbA1c level.
n.2: Diabetes is a high-risk factor, so the standard dose is not enough (NG247 1.1.5).
n.3: Supplementation should start before conception because the neural tube closes early in pregnancy.

3.q: Dani, 22, is formula feeding her baby and has no risk factors for blood clots. She would like to use the combined pill. When can she start it?
o: 6 weeks after the birth
Immediately after the birth
3 weeks after the birth
After her first period
3.w: Women who are not breastfeeding and have no VTE risk factors can start the combined pill, ring or patch 3 weeks after the birth (NHS; FSRH). VTE risk is raised in the early postnatal period.

n.0: The 6-week wait applies to women who are breastfeeding.
n.1: Combined methods are avoided in the first 3 weeks because of the raised VTE risk after birth.
n.3: Waiting for a period risks pregnancy, as ovulation comes first.

3.q: Ama, 27, is breastfeeding her 5-day-old baby. She tells the midwife that milk leaks from her breasts whenever she hears her baby cry, and asks why. Which hormone is mainly responsible for this response?
o: Progesterone from the placenta, causing milk secretion
Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, causing milk ejection
Oestrogen from the ovaries, causing alveolar growth
Prolactin from the anterior pituitary, causing milk synthesis
3.w: The let-down (milk ejection) reflex is mediated by oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli. It can be conditioned by the baby's cry or sight. Prolactin drives milk production (SPM 3.14 lactation physiology).

n.0: The fall in placental progesterone after birth allows copious milk production; progesterone does not cause let-down.
n.2: Oestrogen promotes breast development in pregnancy and high levels inhibit milk production.
n.3: Prolactin stimulates milk production in the alveoli; it does not eject milk.

3.q: Molly, 25, is 32 weeks pregnant and attends with her first episode of reduced fetal movements. The fetal heart is heard, the computerised CTG meets criteria, SFH is on her centile line and she has no risk factors. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Arrange induction of labour at 37 weeks because of the episode
Book an ultrasound scan for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler
Admit her for daily CTG monitoring until movements return to normal
Explain the results and advise her to return if movements reduce again
3.w: SBL v3 element 3: after a first episode of RFM with a normal cCTG and no other indication, a scan is not required; results are explained and she is encouraged to reattend with further concerns. A scan for growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler is offered for recurrent RFM after 28+0 weeks or if there is another indication.

n.0: Induction for RFM alone before 39+0 weeks is not recommended (SBL v3 element 3).
n.1: A scan is offered at a first presentation only when another indication exists, such as suspected SGA.
n.2: Admission for daily CTG is not indicated when assessment is normal and there are no risk factors.

3.q: Precious, 33, is giving birth on a midwife-led unit. The baby's head has been born but has retracted tightly against the perineum, and the shoulders have not delivered with the next contraction and routine axial traction. What is the midwife's first action?
o: Perform an episiotomy to make more room for the shoulders
Ask Precious to push harder with the next contraction
Call for help, stating that this is shoulder dystocia
Apply firm downward traction to the baby's head
3.w: Retraction of the head (turtle sign) and failure of routine axial traction to deliver the shoulders indicate shoulder dystocia. The first step is to call for help, clearly stating the emergency, so manoeuvres can begin with the right team present (RCOG GTG 42; SPM 4.7).

n.0: Shoulder dystocia is a bony problem; episiotomy is not the first action and is not needed in every case.
n.1: Maternal pushing alone will not release an impacted shoulder and can worsen the impaction.
n.3: Downward or excessive traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury and is avoided.

3.q: Hannah, a labour ward midwife, reads a small single-centre study suggesting a new upright birthing position reduces assisted births. She is keen to start using it with every woman she cares for from her next shift. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Appraise the study and weigh it against systematic reviews and guidance
Start offering the position to all women she cares for and record the outcomes
Email the study to all colleagues and recommend they adopt the position
Ask the next woman in labour whether she would like to try the new position
3.w: SPM 5.16 requires midwives to use research to inform decisions and develop practice, and Code 6.1 requires advice to be evidence-based. One small single-centre study should first be appraised for bias and weighed against the wider body of evidence (systematic reviews, NICE guidance) before any change is proposed through local governance.

n.1: Changing practice for all women on the basis of one unappraised small study bypasses appraisal and governance, and collecting outcomes informally is not a substitute.
n.2: Recommending adoption to colleagues spreads an unappraised finding before its quality and fit with wider evidence are known.
n.3: Offering the position before appraisal means the information given to the woman is not yet evidence-based, contrary to Code 6.1.

3.q: Dana is the labour ward coordinator. Four requests arrive at the same moment. Which should she attend to first?
o: A woman at 38 weeks with a mild headache whose blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg
A postnatal woman 2 hours after birth asking for her prescribed paracetamol
A woman in established labour whose fetal heart rate has been 85 bpm for 4 minutes
A woman booked for elective caesarean tomorrow who needs her bloods taken
3.w: SPM 5.19 requires safe prioritising. A prolonged fetal bradycardia lasting several minutes is an obstetric emergency needing immediate assessment and escalation; Code 25.1 asks leaders to identify priorities and deal with risk.

n.0: A mild headache with normal blood pressure needs review, but a prolonged fetal bradycardia is the more urgent threat.
n.1: Analgesia is important but can follow within minutes without risk to life.
n.3: Pre-operative bloods for tomorrow are routine and can be planned later in the shift.

3.q: Aoife, a midwife, is moving from a post in Belfast to a new post in Cardiff. She is checking which law on termination of pregnancy will apply to her new role. Which statement about the territorial extent of the Abortion Act 1967 is correct?
o: It extends to England and Wales, but not Scotland
It extends to England, Wales and Scotland
It extends to all four nations of the United Kingdom
It extends to England, Scotland and Northern Ireland
3.w: The Abortion Act 1967 extends to England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own separate legal framework, so the Act will apply in Cardiff but did not apply in Belfast. Midwives must differentiate between UK legislatures (SPM 1.2).

n.0: The Act also extends to Scotland.
n.2: The Act does not extend to Northern Ireland, which has its own framework.
n.3: The Act extends to Wales and does not extend to Northern Ireland.

3.q: Chen, 31, has been prescribed 10 days of low molecular weight heparin after her caesarean birth. She is breastfeeding and asks the midwife whether the injections will affect her baby. Which response is accurate?
o: She should express and discard milk for 4 hours after each dose
She should give formula until the 10-day course is finished
LMWH is considered safe to use while breastfeeding
A direct oral anticoagulant tablet is preferred while breastfeeding
3.w: RCOG GTG 37a: LMWH is safe in breastfeeding (warfarin is also safe). Use of direct oral anticoagulants (NOACs) is not recommended in women who are breastfeeding.

n.0: There is no need to discard milk; LMWH is safe in breastfeeding.
n.1: Interrupting breastfeeding is unnecessary and could undermine her milk supply.
n.3: GTG 37a advises that NOACs are not recommended in breastfeeding women.

3.q: Under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, what is needed for a midwife raising a concern about patient safety with her employer to be protected as a whistleblower?
o: She reasonably believes the disclosure is in the public interest
She raises the concern anonymously through a hotline
She has written evidence that proves the wrongdoing occurred
She has first raised the concern with the NMC
3.w: PIDA 1998 (inserting Part IVA into the Employment Rights Act 1996) protects a worker who makes a qualifying disclosure, which requires a reasonable belief that the information tends to show wrongdoing such as danger to health and safety, and that disclosure is in the public interest.

n.1: Anonymity is not a condition of protection; named concerns are protected too.
n.2: Proof is not required; a reasonable belief is enough.
n.3: Raising a concern with the employer first is the normal route; prior NMC contact is not a condition.

3.q: Rachel, 32, has bipolar disorder and is 6 days postnatal. Her partner phones the midwife: Rachel has not slept for 2 nights, is talking rapidly and believes strangers are watching the baby through the windows. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to specialist mental health services for assessment within 4 hours
Advise rest and sleep tonight and visit again early tomorrow morning
Ask Rachel the Whooley questions at her next routine visit
Book a routine GP appointment for her within the next 2 weeks
3.w: NICE CG192 1.5.11, 1.5.12: be alert for postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks in women with a history of severe mental illness such as bipolar disorder. If psychosis is suspected, refer to a secondary mental health service (preferably a specialist perinatal service) for assessment within 4 hours of referral.

n.1: Postpartum psychosis can deteriorate rapidly; delaying overnight puts Rachel and the baby at risk.
n.2: Screening questions are for identifying depression; she needs urgent assessment now.
n.3: 2 weeks is the CG192 timeframe for assessment after routine mental health referral, not suspected psychosis.

3.q: Lauren, 27, is 9 weeks pregnant and smokes about 10 cigarettes a day. At booking her carbon monoxide reading is 12 ppm. She says she would like to stop but has failed before. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to cut down to five cigarettes a day to protect the baby
Ask her GP to prescribe varenicline to support her quit attempt
Make an opt-out referral to the tobacco dependence adviser
Give her a stop smoking leaflet and ask her to self-refer when ready
3.w: Saving Babies' Lives v3 element 1 and NICE NG209: CO testing is offered at booking, and women with CO of 4 ppm or above, or who self-report smoking, receive an opt-out referral to an in-house tobacco dependence adviser. NRT can be offered as part of that support.

n.0: Cutting down is not the recommended goal; specialist support aims for complete cessation.
n.1: Varenicline is not recommended in pregnancy (NG209); NRT is the pharmacological option.
n.3: Self-referral leaflets have lower uptake; SBL v3 requires an opt-out referral at 4 ppm or above.

3.q: During newborn resuscitation, the midwife gives inflation breaths to Baby Lily, born at 39 weeks, using a bag-valve-mask with a pressure-limiting device. How long should each inflation breath last?
o: 2 to 3 seconds
Under 1 second
10 seconds
5 to 6 seconds
3.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: give 5 inflation breaths, each sustained for 2 to 3 seconds, to help clear lung fluid and aerate the lungs; then reassess the heart rate and chest movement.

n.1: Short breaths do not adequately aerate fluid-filled lungs at birth.
n.2: 10 seconds is longer than the recommended 2 to 3 seconds.
n.3: 5 to 6 seconds is longer than the recommended 2 to 3 seconds.

3.q: Priya and her partner have just had a stillborn daughter at 37 weeks. They seem unsure about seeing or holding her. Which approach by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Take the baby to the mortuary while they rest and ask them again tomorrow
Advise them not to see her because it may make their grief harder
Offer them the choice, with time and gentle explanation, and respect what they decide
Encourage them to hold her now because they will regret it later if they do not
3.w: Compassionate bereavement care (SPM 4.11; National Bereavement Care Pathway stillbirth pathway) offers parents personalised choices about seeing, holding and making memories with their baby, without pressure either way, and respects their decision. They can change their mind later.

n.0: Removing the baby without agreement takes away the choice; parents may want time with her now.
n.1: Advising against seeing the baby removes a choice many parents value; the decision is theirs.
n.3: Pressuring parents to hold the baby is not person-centred; they should be offered the choice without coercion.

3.q: Aisha, 30, is 33 weeks pregnant on the low-risk pathway. Her symphysis fundal height today plots below the 10th centile on her growth chart; two weeks ago it was on the 40th centile. She reports normal fetal movements. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remeasure the fundal height at her next routine appointment
Refer her for an ultrasound assessment of fetal growth
Reassure her because the fetal movements are normal
Ask a colleague to remeasure and record the higher of the two values
3.w: A fundal height plotting below the 10th centile, or a drop across centiles, is an indication for an ultrasound growth assessment. SBL v3 2.11 requires staff measuring SFH to interpret and refer when indicated, and 2.14 sets the assessment of wellbeing once FGR is suspected.

n.0: Waiting for the next routine visit delays detection of possible FGR, a major risk factor for stillbirth.
n.2: Normal movements do not exclude growth restriction; the measurement still needs investigating.
n.3: Choosing the higher of two readings is unsafe and does not address the fall across centiles.

3.q: Bella, 31, has prelabour rupture of membranes at 40 weeks and chooses expectant management at home. Which advice is most appropriate while she waits for labour?
o: Attend daily for a vaginal swab and a C-reactive protein blood test
Take her temperature 4-hourly while awake and report changes in loss
Insert a fresh tampon every 4 hours to monitor the colour of the liquor
Avoid baths and showers, as bathing increases the risk of infection
3.w: NICE NG235 1.7.8: advise her to record her temperature every 4 hours during waking hours and to report immediately any change in the colour or smell of her vaginal loss; bathing or showering is not associated with increased infection, but sexual intercourse may be. Fetal movements and heart rate are assessed every 24 hours (1.7.9).

n.0: NICE advises against lower vaginal swabs and CRP during expectant management.
n.2: Tampons should not be used after rupture of membranes; a pad allows liquor to be observed.
n.3: Bathing and showering are not associated with an increase in infection.

3.q: Nicola, 29, is 39+2 weeks pregnant. Her membranes ruptured 2 hours ago with clear liquor. She is not contracting, she feels well, her temperature is 36.8 C, the fetal heart is normal and she has no GBS history. Which options should be offered?
o: Immediate induction of labour, as expectant management is unsafe
Expectant management with intravenous antibiotics until labour starts
Expectant management for up to 24 hours or induction as soon as possible
Expectant management for up to 72 hours before induction is discussed
3.w: NICE NG235 1.7.6 and 1.7.7: offer women with PROM at or after 37+0 weeks a choice of expectant management for up to 24 hours or induction as soon as possible, discussing benefits and risks; offer induction if labour has not started after about 24 hours. About 60% go into labour within 24 hours (1.7.5).

n.0: Immediate induction is one choice; expectant management for up to 24 hours is also safe to offer without risk factors.
n.1: Antibiotics are not given without signs of infection or another indication such as GBS.
n.3: NICE offers induction at about 24 hours, not 72 hours, although she may choose to wait longer.

3.q: A community midwife is discussing place of birth with four women. Which woman should be advised to plan birth in an obstetric unit because of her antenatal risk of postpartum haemorrhage?
o: Amina, 29, para 2, BMI 32 kg/m2
Becky, 24, who had a second-degree tear last time
Dana, 33, who had a PPH needing transfusion last time
Cara, 35, with a low-risk pregnancy and a fundal placenta
3.w: NICE NG235 1.10.29 lists antenatal PPH risk factors that warrant advice to give birth in an obstetric unit, including previous PPH over 1000 mL or requiring transfusion, BMI over 35, grand multiparity (4 or more), pre-eclampsia, Hb under 85 g/L at onset of labour and placenta accreta spectrum.

n.0: BMI over 35 and parity 4 or more are the thresholds; 32 and para 2 do not meet them.
n.1: A previous second-degree tear is not an antenatal PPH risk factor in NG235.
n.3: A fundal placenta in a low-risk pregnancy is not a PPH risk factor.

3.q: Leanne is the midwife in charge of a maternity unit. Three midwifery red flag events have been reported in the past hour. What is her responsibility under NICE NG4?
o: Decide whether staffing is the cause and what action is needed
Record the events and review them at the monthly governance meeting
Close the unit to all admissions until the next shift starts
Ask the staff who reported them to resolve the issues themselves
3.w: NG4 box 3: when a red flag event occurs, the midwife in charge should be notified and should determine whether midwifery staffing is the cause and the action needed, such as redeploying staff or escalating per the staffing policy.

n.1: Monthly review is part of monitoring, but immediate assessment and action are needed now.
n.2: Closure may be one option under escalation policy, but it is not automatic and other actions are considered first.
n.3: The midwife in charge holds responsibility for assessing staffing and acting on red flags.

3.q: Fadumo, 29, is 20 weeks pregnant with a girl. On examination the midwife finds she has had type 3 FGM as a child. Fadumo has a 4-year-old daughter. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the FGM, complete a safeguarding risk assessment and plan care
Record the FGM and continue her routine midwife-led antenatal care
Report the FGM to the police within one month of the examination
Refer her daughter for a medical examination for FGM
3.w: For women aged 18 or over, FGM is recorded and a safeguarding risk assessment is completed, especially for daughters and an unborn girl; police notification under s5B applies to girls under 18. NG235 1.9.20 covers planning care for infibulated women (SPM 3.7).

n.1: Type 3 FGM needs a birth plan, including possible deinfibulation, and a safeguarding assessment.
n.2: The mandatory police reporting duty applies to girls under 18, not adult women.
n.3: Examination is not automatic; risk is assessed first and referral made if there is concern.

3.q: Baby Grace, born at 40 weeks, is 60 hours old. Her transcutaneous bilirubin reading is 262 micromol/L. She is feeding well. What should the midwife do next?
o: Start phototherapy based on the transcutaneous reading
Measure serum bilirubin to confirm the level
Reassure the parents, as the reading is below 300
Repeat the transcutaneous reading in 6 hours
3.w: NICE CG98 1.2.16: use serum bilirubin measurement if a transcutaneous bilirubinometer gives a reading above 250 micromol/L; the serum value is then plotted on the treatment threshold graph.

n.0: Treatment decisions use serum bilirubin when the transcutaneous reading exceeds 250.
n.2: There is no 300 reassurance threshold; readings over 250 need serum confirmation.
n.3: A reading above 250 needs a serum measurement, not a repeat transcutaneous reading.

3.q: Eilidh, a midwife in Scotland, sees a 15-year-old girl at an antenatal appointment and observes signs that FGM has been carried out. Which action is correct?
o: Refer under local child protection procedures without delay
Notify the police within one month under FGM Act 2003 s5B
Wait for the girl to disclose before taking any action
Record the finding and review at the next appointment
3.w: The s5B mandatory notification duty in the FGM Act 2003 extends to England and Wales. In Scotland, FGM is an offence under the Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation (Scotland) Act 2005, and a girl with FGM is a child protection concern referred without delay under local procedures (SPM 1.2: differentiate between devolved legislatures).

n.1: Section 5B does not extend to Scotland; Scottish child protection procedures apply.
n.2: Observed signs of FGM in a child are a child protection concern whether or not she discloses.
n.3: Delaying to a later appointment leaves a child protection concern without action.

3.q: Leila, 26, is exclusively breastfeeding her 2-week-old baby in June. She is taking a vitamin D supplement herself and asks whether her baby needs one too. What should the midwife advise?
o: Give the baby a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms
Start the baby's vitamin D at 6 months, when solid foods begin
Give the baby vitamin D from October to March each year
No supplement is needed while she takes vitamin D herself
3.w: NICE NG247 (table 1): breastfed babies should be given a daily supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms of vitamin D from birth, all year round. Formula-fed babies taking 500 mL or more of formula a day do not need one because formula is fortified.

n.1: Breastfed babies need vitamin D from birth, not from 6 months.
n.2: The October to March advice applies to adults; breastfed babies need vitamin D all year.
n.3: The mother's supplement does not provide enough vitamin D for the baby through breast milk.

3.q: During play, 2-week-old Kai looks at his father's face, then turns his head away, yawns and arches his back. His father keeps trying to make eye contact. How should the midwife explain Kai's behaviour?
o: He is showing signs of colic that need review by the GP
He is showing hunger and should be offered a feed straight away
He wants more eye contact and play to keep him engaged
He is showing he needs a pause from interaction to calm down
3.w: Turning away, yawning and arching are disengagement cues: the baby needs a break. NICE NG194 1.3.17: encourage parents to respond appropriately to the baby's cues to promote emotional attachment (SPM 3.16.2 understanding the newborn's needs).

n.0: These cues are normal communication, not signs of colic.
n.1: Feeding cues include rooting and hand to mouth, not turning away and yawning.
n.2: Continuing to seek eye contact when the baby is disengaging can overstimulate him.

3.q: Under Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015], when recommending a treatment, what must the clinician take reasonable care to make sure the woman knows about, in addition to its material risks?
o: The clinician's personal preference
The trust's policy on the treatment
Any reasonable alternative treatments
The national rate of complaints for it
3.w: Montgomery para 87: the clinician must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of any material risks involved in recommended treatment and of any reasonable alternative or variant treatments.

n.0: The clinician's personal preference is not part of the Montgomery duty of disclosure.
n.1: Trust policy is not what Montgomery requires to be disclosed.
n.3: Complaint rates are not part of the Montgomery duty of disclosure.

3.q: Following the stillbirth of Baby Aria at 39 weeks, the community midwife visits the parents at home. They ask whether anyone will look into what happened. Which statement about the Perinatal Mortality Review Tool (PMRT) is most accurate?
o: The coroner investigates stillbirths, so the hospital does not hold a review
The hospital reviews the care once the parents request a review in writing
The review is confidential to staff and the findings are not shared with parents
The hospital reviews the care, and they are told about the review and can contribute
3.w: The PMRT supports systematic multidisciplinary review of care for stillbirths and neonatal deaths from 22 weeks. Parents are told a review will take place and how they can contribute, and a plain-language explanation of the findings is discussed with them (NPEU PMRT).

n.0: Coroners in England and Wales do not currently have jurisdiction over stillbirths; the hospital reviews the care using the PMRT.
n.1: The PMRT review happens for every eligible death; parents do not have to request it.
n.2: Parent involvement and sharing the findings with parents are core aims of the PMRT.

3.q: Chloe, a midwife, managed a postpartum haemorrhage at 14:10 and could not write her notes during the emergency. She is now able to document at 16:30. How should she record the events?
o: Write it on a separate sheet to be added to the notes later
Write the entry at the times of the events, as it is accurate
Ask the scribe midwife to write the account in her place
Mark it as a late entry, with the time of writing and of events
3.w: NMC Code 10.1: complete records at the time or as soon as possible after an event, recording if the notes are written some time after the event. A late entry shows when it was written and the times the events happened (Code 10.4: dated and timed).

n.0: Loose sheets risk loss and break the chronological record; the late entry goes in the notes now.
n.1: Writing as if contemporaneous hides when the entry was made, which is misleading (Code 10.3).
n.2: Each professional records their own care; entries must be attributable to the person who made them (Code 10.4).

3.q: Sam is the partner of Nia, who is breastfeeding their first baby. He tells the midwife he feels left out because he cannot feed the baby. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Suggest giving one bottle of formula a day so he can share feeds
Reassure him that fathers bond with babies once feeding is finished
Suggest Nia expresses a bottle each evening from day 3 for him to give
Explain how he can support Nia and bond through skin-to-skin contact
3.w: NG194 1.5.3: give information about how the partner can support the woman to breastfeed, including the value of their involvement and how they can comfort and bond with the baby (SPM 2.12).

n.0: Introducing formula early can reduce Nia's milk supply and is not needed for bonding.
n.1: This dismisses his concerns and misses the chance to involve him now.
n.2: Routine early bottles can interfere with establishing breastfeeding and do not address his role.

3.q: Before the birth of their first baby, Yusuf and Hana ask the midwife why vitamin K is offered to newborn babies. Which explanation is accurate?
o: To strengthen the baby's immunity against early-onset infection
To prevent newborn jaundice developing in the first week of life
To prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare but serious disorder
To prevent anaemia in babies who had delayed cord clamping
3.w: NICE NG235 1.11.12 (recommendation reintroduced 2026): offer parents vitamin K prophylaxis for their babies and explain it is to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare but serious and sometimes fatal disorder.

n.0: Vitamin K has no role in immunity against infection.
n.1: Vitamin K supports clotting; it does not prevent jaundice.
n.3: Delayed cord clamping improves iron stores; vitamin K prevents bleeding, not anaemia.
