3.q: Freya, 30, is 10 days postnatal and exclusively breastfeeding. Her GP has prescribed a medicine for migraine and Freya asks the community midwife whether it is safe for her baby. Where should the midwife seek specialist evidence-based advice?
o: Her sister's experience of the same medicine
An online parenting forum with many replies
The patient information leaflet in the box
The UK Drugs in Lactation Advisory Service
3.w: The UK Drugs in Lactation Advisory Service (Specialist Pharmacy Service) gives evidence-based advice on medicines in breastfeeding; the BNF and local medicines information services are also appropriate. Manufacturer leaflets often advise against use because medicines are not tested in breastfeeding, not because of proven harm (NG133 1.9.2; SPM 3.18).

n.0: Anecdotal experience is not evidence-based advice about this baby and this medicine.
n.1: An online forum is not a reliable, evidence-based source of medicines information.
n.2: Product leaflets often carry general disclaimers rather than evidence about breastfeeding.

3.q: After explaining the oral glucose tolerance test to Zainab, 29, the midwife wants to check that she has understood how to prepare. Which method is most effective?
o: Ask, "Do you have any questions about the test?"
Ask, "Is everything clear about the test?"
Give her a leaflet and ask her to call if she has any problems
Ask her to tell you, in her own words, how to prepare for the test
3.w: Code 7.4: check people's understanding from time to time. Asking the woman to explain in her own words (teach-back) shows what she has understood and any gaps.

n.0: A question about questions often gets 'no' even when understanding is incomplete.
n.1: A closed yes or no question does not show what she has understood.
n.2: A leaflet does not check her understanding of what has just been explained.

3.q: Sadia, 28, is 37+2 weeks pregnant and has pre-eclampsia with blood pressure controlled on labetalol. Her blood results are stable and the CTG is normal. According to NICE NG133, when should birth be planned?
o: Continue surveillance until spontaneous labour
Continue surveillance and plan birth at 40 weeks
Initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours
Arrange a category 1 caesarean birth today
3.w: NICE NG133 (table 3, timing of birth in pre-eclampsia): from 37 weeks onwards, initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours. Before 34 weeks surveillance continues unless there are indications, and from 34+0 to 36+6 birth is considered case by case.

n.0: Waiting for spontaneous labour does not follow the 24 to 48 hour recommendation.
n.1: Waiting until 40 weeks is not advised once pre-eclampsia is present at 37 weeks.
n.3: A category 1 caesarean is for an immediate threat to life; her condition is stable.

3.q: Saskia, 27, is in established labour in an alongside midwifery unit. At 14:00 her temperature is 37.6 C and at 15:00 it is 37.7 C. Her pulse is 98 and the fetal heart is normal. Which action follows NICE guidance?
o: Transfer her to obstetric-led care for review
Give paracetamol and continue midwifery-led care
Recheck her temperature in 4 hours, as it is under 38 C
Recheck in 1 hour and transfer if it reaches 38 C
3.w: NICE NG235 1.8.20: a temperature of 38 C or above on a single reading, or 37.5 C or above on 2 consecutive occasions 1 hour apart, is a trigger for transfer to obstetric-led care. Intrapartum antibiotics follow NICE neonatal infection guidance.

n.1: Antipyretics may mask infection and do not replace transfer for review.
n.2: Two consecutive readings of 37.5 C or above 1 hour apart already meet the transfer criterion.
n.3: The 38 C single-reading threshold is not needed when the 37.5 C two-reading criterion is met.

3.q: Pooja, 33, is 34 weeks pregnant. She phones saying she has 'bad heartburn' that started this morning: severe pain just below her ribs on the right, not eased by antacids, with a headache. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to attend the maternity unit now for BP, urine and blood tests
Book a GP appointment for this week to review her indigestion
Advise paracetamol for the headache and to sleep propped up on pillows
Advise a stronger alginate and to call back if it persists tomorrow
3.w: Severe pain just below the ribs with headache is a recognised symptom of pre-eclampsia (NICE NG133 1.1.1), which can be mistaken for heartburn. She needs immediate assessment of BP, proteinuria and bloods (platelets, liver and renal function).

n.1: Waiting for a GP appointment delays urgent assessment of pre-eclampsia symptoms.
n.2: Masking the headache delays diagnosis; these symptoms need assessment now.
n.3: Treating as heartburn delays assessment of possible pre-eclampsia or HELLP.

3.q: Tia, 26, is 6 days after a caesarean birth and at home. At a postnatal visit she feels very unwell, with offensive lochia. Her heart rate is 134 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min and blood pressure 108/66 mmHg. What should the community midwife do?
o: Call 999 and pre-alert the hospital
Ask her GP to see her at the surgery later today
Take a high vaginal swab and revisit her tomorrow
Advise paracetamol and phone triage if she worsens
3.w: A heart rate over 130 is a high-risk criterion (NICE NG255 table 1). Outside hospital, a person meeting any high-risk criterion is referred for emergency care, usually by 999 ambulance, and secondary care is pre-alerted (NG255 1.6.1, 1.6.2).

n.1: A GP appointment later delays emergency care for a high-risk woman.
n.2: A swab and revisit delays treatment of possible sepsis with a high-risk criterion.
n.3: Paracetamol can mask fever and delays urgent assessment.

3.q: Freya, 29, is 30 weeks pregnant. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and she feels well. A dipstick shows 1+ protein, with no leucocytes or nitrites. Under NICE hypertension in pregnancy guidance, what should happen next to assess the proteinuria?
o: Send a first morning urine sample to measure protein
Repeat the dipstick at her next routine appointment
Arrange a 24-hour urine collection to measure total protein
Quantify with a protein:creatinine or albumin:creatinine ratio
3.w: If dipstick screening is positive (1+ or more), use albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio to quantify proteinuria, interpreted alongside a full clinical review (NICE NG133 1.2.1, 1.2.3).

n.0: NICE advises not to use a first morning void to quantify proteinuria (NG133 1.2.4).
n.1: A positive dipstick needs quantification now; waiting for the next routine visit delays assessment.
n.2: NICE advises against routine 24-hour urine collection to quantify proteinuria (NG133 1.2.5).

3.q: Carol, a maternity support worker, has recorded observations for Mrs Ahmed, who is 6 hours after a caesarean birth, as delegated by the midwife, Naomi. Carol tells Naomi the observations are done. What should Naomi do next?
o: Ask another support worker to check Carol's figures before the next round
Review the recorded observations and confirm they meet the required standard
Note in the handover that the observations were completed by Carol
Countersign the chart so that the record is complete for the shift
3.w: Code 11.3: confirm that the outcome of any task you have delegated meets the required standard. Naomi remains accountable for the decision to delegate and must review the observations herself so she can act on any abnormal findings.

n.0: Passing the check to another support worker does not meet Naomi's own duty under Code 11.3.
n.2: Recording who did the task in handover does not check the result or act on it.
n.3: Countersigning without reviewing the values does not confirm the outcome of the task and could miss deterioration.

3.q: Lucy, a midwife, realises she gave a woman's prescribed antibiotic 4 hours late because she forgot it during a busy shift. The woman is well. What should Lucy do first?
o: Report the incident but not tell the woman, because no harm has occurred
Tell the woman, apologise, give the dose as advised and report the incident
Give the dose now and record it at the scheduled time to avoid confusion
Ask a colleague to give the dose so that the error is not linked to her
3.w: Code 14.1 to 14.3: act immediately to put right the situation, explain to the person what has happened and apologise, and document events. The incident should be reported so the system can learn (SPM 5.2).

n.0: Openness with the woman is required by Code 14 when an error occurs.
n.2: Recording a false time is dishonest and breaches Code 10 and 20.2.
n.3: Concealing her involvement breaches the duty of candour and honesty.

3.q: Maya, 31, is exclusively breastfeeding her 3-day-old baby. She asks whether her baby needs any supplements. What should the midwife advise?
o: Give the baby daily vitamin D drops of 8.5 to 10 micrograms
Give vitamin D drops if the baby is having under 500 mL of formula
Give vitamin D drops from 6 months, when solids start
No supplements are needed while she is breastfeeding
3.w: NG247 (table 1): breastfed babies should have a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms from birth; formula-fed babies having 500 mL or more of formula a day do not need one.

n.1: This threshold applies to formula-fed babies, but Maya's baby is breastfed and needs drops from birth.
n.2: Supplements are recommended from birth for breastfed babies.
n.3: Breastfed babies are recommended vitamin D from birth.

3.q: Gemma, 28, attends her booking appointment with her partner, who answers most of the questions for her. When should the midwife ask Gemma about domestic abuse?
o: At 28 weeks, once a relationship of trust has been built
Now, in front of her partner, so he knows it is routine
When Gemma shows physical signs of injury
When Gemma is alone, at booking or the earliest opportunity
3.w: NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse at the booking appointment or at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, with an opportunity for a private one-to-one discussion (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Enquiry should be at booking or the earliest opportunity; waiting delays help.
n.1: Asking in front of a partner may put her at risk and prevents an honest answer.
n.2: Routine enquiry is for all women; most abuse has no visible signs.

3.q: Kezia, 23, has epilepsy controlled with sodium valproate. She attends the early pregnancy unit with an unplanned pregnancy of 7 weeks, confirmed on scan. She is distressed and asks the midwife what she should do about her medication. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Stop valproate today and restart it after the first trimester
Halve the valproate dose until she sees her GP next month
Continue valproate as the main risk period has already passed
Keep taking it for now and arrange urgent specialist review today
3.w: Valproate carries a high risk of malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders (MHRA safety advice; CG192 1.4.29). In epilepsy, stopping abruptly can cause seizures that harm woman and fetus, so she should not stop or change her dose without advice and needs urgent specialist review to plan the switch (SPM 3.18).

n.0: Abruptly stopping an antiseizure medicine risks status epilepticus; changes need specialist planning.
n.1: Self-adjusting the dose risks seizures and delays the specialist review she needs now.
n.2: Organogenesis is ongoing at 7 weeks and valproate also affects neurodevelopment, so urgent review is needed.

3.q: Amy, 28, had an epidural top-up 30 minutes ago. She still feels strong pain with contractions on her left side. Her BP is 118/72 mmHg and the CTG is normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to wait another hour for the top-up to work
Remove the epidural catheter and offer Entonox
Ask the anaesthetist to review the epidural
Give a further bolus from the epidural pump yourself
3.w: NICE NG235 1.6.30: if the woman is not pain-free 30 minutes after each administration of local anaesthetic or opioid solution, ask the anaesthetist to review. An epidural may need adjusting or replacing (1.6.26).

n.0: Waiting another hour delays review; NICE sets 30 minutes as the trigger.
n.1: Removing the catheter is an anaesthetic decision; the block may be fixable by adjustment.
n.3: Extra boluses outside the prescribed regimen are not given without anaesthetic review of an inadequate block.

3.q: Isabel, 33, is 40+1 weeks pregnant and asks for a membrane sweep. Her notes show that the 20-week scan reported a low-lying placenta, and there is no record of a follow-up scan. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Perform the sweep gently, as most low-lying placentas move up by term
Ask her to sign a consent form accepting the bleeding risk, then sweep
Perform the sweep and observe her for bleeding for 1 hour afterwards
Do not sweep; clarify placental position with the obstetric team first
3.w: NICE NG207 1.7.6: check that there is no evidence of a low-lying placenta on previous scans before membrane sweeping and before induction. With no follow-up scan documented, the placental site must be clarified before any vaginal examination for sweeping.

n.0: Many placentas do move away from the cervix, but this must be confirmed by scan, not assumed.
n.1: A signed form does not make an unsafe procedure safe; the placental site must be checked first.
n.2: Observing for bleeding afterwards does not prevent haemorrhage from a placenta that may be low lying.

3.q: Yasmin, 32, is in labour at term with a previous caesarean. Continuous CTG is recommended, but she declines it. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Apply the CTG anyway as she has a uterine scar
Ask the registrar to apply the CTG while the midwife reassures her
Stop monitoring the baby until she agrees to the CTG
Explain why, offer intermittent auscultation and document it
3.w: SPM 1.21: respect the right to decline and provide appropriate care. The midwife explains why continuous monitoring is advised (NICE NG229 for women with a previous caesarean), offers an alternative such as intermittent auscultation and documents the discussion.

n.0: Applying monitoring she has declined is treatment without consent.
n.1: Applying the CTG through another clinician is still monitoring without consent.
n.2: Stopping monitoring removes all fetal assessment; she should be offered an acceptable alternative.

3.q: Kiran is coordinating a delivery suite. She must allocate staff: Midwife A (newly qualified, 3 months), Midwife B (8 years' experience), and a maternity support worker. Women needing care include one with severe pre-eclampsia on intravenous magnesium sulfate and one in early labour with no risk factors. Which allocation is most appropriate?
o: Midwife B to the woman on magnesium; Midwife A to the woman in early labour
The support worker to the woman on magnesium with Midwife A overseeing
Midwife B to the woman in early labour; the support worker to the woman on magnesium
Midwife A to the woman on magnesium; Midwife B to the woman in early labour
3.w: SPM 5.19 requires appropriate assignment of care responsibilities. Kiran first assesses acuity: a woman on IV magnesium for severe pre-eclampsia needs one-to-one care from an experienced midwife. The low-risk woman in early labour is suitable for the newly qualified midwife, who can seek support (Code 13).

n.1: Monitoring a woman on IV magnesium is outside an MSW's scope, even with oversight.
n.2: An MSW cannot provide the registered care needed for magnesium therapy, and this leaves no registrant with that woman.
n.3: Placing the least experienced midwife with the highest-risk woman mismatches skill mix to acuity.

3.q: Chloe, 26, is 9 weeks pregnant. She has nausea most mornings and vomits once or twice a week. She is drinking well, passing urine normally and working. She would prefer not to take medicines. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Advise her to stop eating until the nausea passes to rest her stomach
Suggest she tries ginger, and explain symptoms usually settle by 16 to 20 weeks
Advise her GP to prescribe an antiemetic, as ginger is unsafe in pregnancy
Refer her to hospital for intravenous fluids to prevent dehydration
3.w: NICE NG201 1.4.1 and 1.4.3: reassure women that mild to moderate nausea and vomiting are common and likely to resolve before 16 to 20 weeks, and suggest ginger for those with mild to moderate symptoms who prefer a non-pharmacological option.

n.0: Avoiding food is not recommended and risks dehydration and ketosis; small frequent meals are usually advised.
n.2: Ginger is a NICE-suggested option; an antiemetic is offered if she chooses a medicine.
n.3: She is mildly affected and well hydrated, so IV fluids are not indicated.

4.q: When should the first postnatal health visitor home visit be considered, according to NICE?
o: Within 36 hours after transfer from the place of birth
Within 72 hours with the newborn physical examination
Between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery
At 6 to 8 weeks with the GP postnatal check
4.w: NG194 1.1.15: consider arranging the first postnatal health visitor home visit between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery care, so contacts are evenly spread.

n.0: 36 hours is the standard for the first midwife visit, not the health visitor.
n.1: 72 hours is the deadline for the newborn physical examination, not the health visitor visit.
n.3: 6 to 8 weeks is the GP check for the woman and baby, not the first health visitor visit.

4.q: Baby Kofi, born at 38 weeks, is 16 days old and still visibly jaundiced. He is breastfeeding well and gaining weight. His mother says his stools have become pale and chalky. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat a transcutaneous reading at the 6 to 8 week check
Arrange measurement of conjugated bilirubin and refer for expert advice
Advise a 48-hour break from breastfeeding to see if it settles
Reassure her that breast milk jaundice can last for several weeks
4.w: Prolonged jaundice is jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby. Pale chalky stools suggest cholestasis such as biliary atresia. CG98 1.7.1 to 1.7.2: look for pale stools and dark urine and measure conjugated bilirubin; over 25 micromol/L needs expert advice.

n.0: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks could delay diagnosis of biliary atresia, where timing of surgery matters.
n.2: Stopping breastfeeding is not recommended and delays investigation.
n.3: Pale chalky stools are a warning sign of liver disease, not breast milk jaundice; reassurance is unsafe.

4.q: Mei, 30, is pregnant for the first time. When is the best time to give her information about interventions that may be offered in labour, such as episiotomy?
o: In the second stage of labour, when the need arises
Antenatally, then confirmed in labour before any procedure
After the birth, during the postnatal debrief
When she is admitted to the labour ward in early labour
4.w: Informed consent relies on information given when the woman can weigh it (Montgomery; MCA 2005 s3). Discussing interventions antenatally (NICE NG201 antenatal information on labour) and confirming consent at the time supports decision-making.

n.0: Information given for the first time during the second stage is hard to weigh under pain and time pressure.
n.2: Information after the birth cannot inform consent to a procedure that has already happened.
n.3: Early labour is better than the second stage, but antenatal discussion gives her time to consider options.

4.q: Ruth, 31, is 9 weeks pregnant. After the booking discussion she says she does not want any screening for Down's, Edwards' or Patau's syndromes or the 20-week anomaly scan, because she would continue the pregnancy whatever the result. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that the 20-week scan is required to check the position of the placenta
Respect and record her decision and offer the dating scan to confirm gestation
Refer her to an obstetrician to discuss the reasons for declining screening
Ask her to sign a disclaimer stating she accepts the risks of declining
4.w: Every screening test is a personal choice and she can accept or decline any part (NICE NG201 1.2.13; FASP). The dating scan determines gestational age and multiple pregnancy, and screening is added only if she opts for it (NG201 1.2.14). Her decision is respected and documented.

n.0: Placental location is part of the 18 to 20+6 week scan (NG201 1.2.15), but she may decline it; she should be informed of what it offers, not told it is required.
n.2: Declining screening is a valid informed choice and is not a reason for obstetric referral.
n.3: A disclaimer is not required; documenting the informed discussion and her decision is the standard.

4.q: A midwifery team wants to check whether all women with a BMI of 40 kg/m2 or over were referred for an anaesthetic review as set out in the unit guideline. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: A clinical audit measuring practice against the guideline standard
A service evaluation of women's satisfaction with the clinic
A PDSA cycle testing a new referral form on one clinic
A research study comparing two referral pathways
4.w: Clinical audit measures current practice against a defined standard (here, the referral requirement in the guideline), identifies gaps and drives improvement, with re-audit to close the loop.

n.1: Satisfaction is a different question from compliance with a referral standard.
n.2: A PDSA cycle tests a change; the question is whether an existing standard is being met.
n.3: Research generates new knowledge by comparing interventions; the standard already exists.

4.q: Kate, 32, has had antenatal depression treated with an SSRI throughout pregnancy. Her baby girl was born 12 hours ago at term and is breastfeeding. Which action by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Arrange for the baby to be admitted to the neonatal unit for observation
Carry out a full neonatal assessment, alert to possible medication effects
Advise her to stop the SSRI now that the baby has been born
Advise formula feeding to avoid exposing the baby through breast milk
4.w: CG192 1.9.2: if a woman has taken psychotropic medication during pregnancy, carry out a full neonatal assessment, bearing in mind the variation in onset of adverse effects and the need for further monitoring, and keep relevant professionals and the family informed.

n.0: A well baby does not need neonatal unit admission; assessment and monitoring can continue with the mother.
n.2: Stopping an effective antidepressant abruptly after birth risks relapse at a high-risk time; decisions belong with the prescriber.
n.3: SSRIs are not a reason to stop breastfeeding; decisions are individual and made with the woman.

4.q: Martha, 29, is in established labour with her first baby in a midwifery-led unit. Her pregnancy was low risk and she is coping well. Which observation schedule does NICE recommend during the first stage?
o: Contractions half-hourly; pulse hourly; temperature, BP and respiratory rate 4-hourly
Contractions half-hourly; pulse 4-hourly; temperature, BP and respiratory rate hourly
Contractions 4-hourly; pulse hourly; temperature, BP and respiratory rate half-hourly
Contractions hourly; pulse half-hourly; temperature, BP and respiratory rate 2-hourly
4.w: NICE NG235 1.8.19: record half-hourly frequency of contractions, hourly pulse, 4-hourly temperature, BP and respiratory rate, and offer 4-hourly vaginal examination. An hourly risk assessment is also carried out (1.8.20) and bladder care reviewed at least every 4 hours (1.8.25).

n.1: Pulse is checked hourly, and temperature, BP and respiratory rate are 4-hourly, not hourly.
n.2: This reverses the frequencies; contractions are documented half-hourly.
n.3: Contractions are recorded half-hourly and pulse hourly; vital signs are 4-hourly, not 2-hourly.

4.q: Maya, 31, is exclusively breastfeeding her 3-day-old baby. She asks whether her baby needs any supplements. What should the midwife advise?
o: Give the baby daily vitamin D drops of 8.5 to 10 micrograms
Give vitamin D drops if the baby is having under 500 mL of formula
Give vitamin D drops from 6 months, when solids start
No supplements are needed while she is breastfeeding
4.w: NG247 (table 1): breastfed babies should have a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms from birth; formula-fed babies having 500 mL or more of formula a day do not need one.

n.1: This threshold applies to formula-fed babies, but Maya's baby is breastfed and needs drops from birth.
n.2: Supplements are recommended from birth for breastfed babies.
n.3: Breastfed babies are recommended vitamin D from birth.

4.q: Laura, a midwife, is arranging the reflective discussion for her revalidation. She has written her five reflective accounts. Who may she hold the reflective discussion with?
o: A consultant obstetrician registered with the GMC
A retired midwife who has left the NMC register
Another registrant on the NMC register
Her line manager, a registered physiotherapist
4.w: NMC revalidation: the reflective discussion about the five written reflective accounts must be held with another NMC-registered nurse, midwife or nursing associate.

n.0: A GMC-registered doctor may act as confirmer in some circumstances but cannot hold the reflective discussion, which must be with an NMC registrant.
n.1: A person who has left the NMC register is not a current NMC registrant.
n.3: A physiotherapist is registered with the HCPC, not the NMC, so cannot be the reflective discussion partner.

4.q: Jess, 27, smokes 15 cigarettes a day and wants to stop. Her tobacco dependence adviser suggests nicotine patches. She is worried nicotine will harm her baby. What information should the midwife give?
o: NRT risks are much lower than smoking, and patches should be removed at bedtime
NRT is safe in pregnancy and patches should be worn for 24 hours a day
NRT carries the same risks as smoking, so cutting down is safer
NRT should be avoided until 12 weeks, when varenicline is a safer choice
4.w: NG209 1.20.6-1.20.11: consider NRT with behavioural support at the earliest opportunity; explain that risks from NRT are much lower than smoking; advise removing patches before bed; do not offer varenicline, bupropion or cytisinicline in pregnancy.

n.1: NICE advises removing patches before going to bed in pregnancy (NG209 1.20.9).
n.2: Most smoking harm comes from other components of smoke, not nicotine; NRT is much safer.
n.3: Varenicline is not offered in pregnancy, and NRT should be considered at the earliest opportunity.

4.q: Saira, 27, is RhD negative and 22 weeks pregnant. She attends the community clinic with a small amount of fresh vaginal bleeding that started an hour ago. She has no pain and her baby is moving. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure her, as painless bleeding at 22 weeks needs no treatment
Give anti-D at home and review her at the next routine appointment
Refer to secondary care for review and offer anti-D immunoglobulin
Offer anti-D at 28 weeks with her routine prophylaxis
4.w: Refer women with unexplained vaginal bleeding after 13 weeks to secondary care for review (NICE NG201 1.4.17), and offer anti-D immunoglobulin to RhD-negative women at risk of isoimmunisation who bleed after 13 weeks (NG201 1.4.16). Placental localisation is also offered if the site is unknown (1.4.19).

n.0: Painless bleeding may indicate a low-lying placenta and needs assessment; RhD-negative women also need anti-D.
n.1: Anti-D is needed, but unexplained bleeding after 13 weeks also needs secondary care assessment, for example for abruption or a low-lying placenta.
n.3: Routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks does not cover a sensitising event that has happened at 22 weeks.

4.q: At a 10-day postnatal visit the midwife asks Nadia, 30, questions to help recognise depression, as recommended by NICE CG192. Which question is one of the Whooley questions?
o: Over the last 2 weeks, have you felt nervous, anxious or on edge most days?
Do you feel your baby is harder to settle than other babies of the same age?
During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?
In the past year, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?
4.w: NICE CG192 1.5.4: at the first contact in primary care, booking and early postnatal period, ask the two depression identification (Whooley) questions about feeling down, depressed or hopeless, and having little interest or pleasure in doing things, during the past month.

n.0: This is from the GAD-2 anxiety questions, which use a 2-week timeframe.
n.1: This asks about the baby's temperament, not the woman's mood or interest.
n.3: Risk questions matter but are not one of the two Whooley questions.

4.q: Ana, 30, has had a straightforward birth and chose active management. She received IM oxytocin when the baby was born. At 3 minutes the cord is clamped and cut. The uterus is soft and the cord has not lengthened. When should controlled cord traction begin?
o: At the next contraction, whether or not separation has occurred
Immediately after the cord is cut, to speed up the third stage
After signs of separation, such as cord lengthening and a gush of blood
After 30 minutes, if the placenta has not delivered spontaneously
4.w: NICE NG235 1.10.15: perform controlled cord traction as part of active management only after oxytocin and signs of placental separation (lengthening of the cord, a small gush of blood, the uterus becoming firm and rising). Traction before separation risks cord snapping or uterine inversion.

n.0: Contractions alone do not show separation; traction waits for signs of separation.
n.1: Traction before separation risks cord avulsion or uterine inversion.
n.3: 30 minutes is when a prolonged third stage is diagnosed in active management, not the timing of traction.

4.q: Which health benefit for the baby should a midwife include when discussing breastfeeding with expectant parents?
o: A lower risk of developmental dysplasia of the hip
A lower risk of physiological jaundice
Fewer gastrointestinal and respiratory infections
A lower risk of tongue-tie
4.w: Breastfed babies have fewer gastrointestinal, respiratory and ear infections and a lower risk of sudden infant death. NG194 1.5.2: discuss nutritional and health benefits for the baby (SPM 3.6).

n.0: Hip dysplasia is not influenced by feeding method.
n.1: Breastfed babies are not at lower risk of jaundice; jaundice can be more prolonged.
n.3: Tongue-tie is congenital and not affected by feeding method.

4.q: Kayleigh, 25, is 8 weeks pregnant and attends her booking appointment. She tells the midwife for the first time that she uses cocaine most weekends and drinks heavily. She is anxious and asks whether this will be reported. Which response is most appropriate first?
o: Make a referral to the police because she has disclosed illegal drug use
Offer referral to a substance misuse service and explain how care is coordinated
Tell her the booking cannot continue until she has stopped using any drugs
Record the disclosure and plan to discuss it again at the 28-week visit
4.w: NICE CG110 1.2.7: the first time a woman who misuses substances discloses that she is pregnant, offer referral to an appropriate substance misuse programme. Care is coordinated across agencies (1.2.2, 1.2.3) with a named midwife or doctor (1.2.4), and staff attitudes should not deter her from using services (1.2.1).

n.0: Drug use disclosed in a health consultation is not a police matter; the concern is her and her baby's health and wellbeing.
n.2: Making care conditional on abstinence creates a barrier that CG110 1.2.1 asks staff to overcome.
n.3: Delaying discussion until 28 weeks wastes months of potential support and treatment.

4.q: Baby Ayo is born through thick meconium-stained liquor. She cries immediately, has good tone and a heart rate over 100 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate care?
o: Avoid suction; dry and warm her and plan close observation
Suction her mouth and nose, then dry her and keep her warm
Intubate to check the trachea for meconium below the cords
Give 5 inflation breaths to clear meconium from her lungs
4.w: NICE NG235 1.11.25: in the presence of any meconium, do not suction the upper airways before the birth of the shoulders and trunk, and do not suction or intubate if the baby has normal respiration, heart rate and tone. Significant meconium needs close observation (1.11.27).

n.1: NG235 1.11.25: do not suction the upper airways if breathing, heart rate and tone are normal.
n.2: Intubation is not indicated in a vigorous baby.
n.3: Inflation breaths are for a baby who is not breathing adequately, not a vigorous crying baby (RCUK 2025 NLS).

4.q: Toni, 19, says she will breastfeed 'for a couple of weeks' before returning to college, and asks whether it is worth it for such a short time. Which response is most accurate?
o: Benefits begin once she has breastfed without formula for 6 months
Colostrum helps, but later milk gives no advantage over formula
Breastfeeding benefits her and the baby even if done for a short time
Short spells of breastfeeding confuse the baby and are best avoided
4.w: NICE NG194 1.5.2: discussions about breastfeeding should include how it can have benefits even if only done for a short time, and how it can soothe and comfort the baby. Advice respects the parents' choices (1.5.1).

n.0: There is no 6-month threshold before benefits begin; NG194 states short-term breastfeeding still helps.
n.1: Breast milk continues to provide immune and nutritional benefits beyond the first week.
n.3: Any breastfeeding is beneficial; there is no evidence that short spells confuse the baby.

4.q: Chantelle, 27, is 35 weeks pregnant and has not had the whooping cough vaccine. She asks if it is too late. What should the midwife advise?
o: It can still be given, though it gives the baby less passive protection
It can still be given and gives the same protection as at 20 weeks
It is too late, so the baby should be vaccinated at birth instead
It is too late, as it cannot be given after 32 weeks
4.w: Green Book ch 24: the vaccine can still be given later in pregnancy, including up to birth. It may offer less passive protection to the baby but protects the mother, reducing the baby's exposure.

n.1: Vaccinating after 32 weeks may give the baby less passive protection than earlier vaccination.
n.2: Pertussis vaccination of babies starts at 8 weeks in the routine schedule, not at birth.
n.3: It can still be given after 32 weeks; it may offer less passive protection but protects the mother.

4.q: Olivia, 32, is 10 weeks pregnant. Each day she drinks two mugs of filter coffee (about 140 mg caffeine each) and one can of cola (about 40 mg). What advice should the midwife give?
o: Continue, as her intake of about 320 mg is within the daily limit for pregnancy
Reduce caffeine, as her intake of about 320 mg exceeds the 200 mg daily limit
Stop the cola but continue the coffee, as cola caffeine is more harmful
Reduce caffeine, as her intake of about 180 mg is close to the daily limit
4.w: NHS and Food Standards Agency advice: limit caffeine to 200 mg a day in pregnancy, because high intake is linked to low birthweight and miscarriage. Working: 2 x 140 mg + 40 mg = 320 mg, above the limit (SPM 3.3).

n.0: The NHS limit in pregnancy is 200 mg a day; 2 x 140 + 40 = 320 mg is above it.
n.2: Caffeine from any source counts towards the limit; two filter coffees alone give 280 mg.
n.3: This miscalculates the total: 2 x 140 + 40 = 320 mg, not 180 mg.

4.q: Under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, what is needed for a midwife raising a concern about patient safety with her employer to be protected as a whistleblower?
o: She reasonably believes the disclosure is in the public interest
She raises the concern anonymously through a hotline
She has written evidence that proves the wrongdoing occurred
She has first raised the concern with the NMC
4.w: PIDA 1998 (inserting Part IVA into the Employment Rights Act 1996) protects a worker who makes a qualifying disclosure, which requires a reasonable belief that the information tends to show wrongdoing such as danger to health and safety, and that disclosure is in the public interest.

n.1: Anonymity is not a condition of protection; named concerns are protected too.
n.2: Proof is not required; a reasonable belief is enough.
n.3: Raising a concern with the employer first is the normal route; prior NMC contact is not a condition.

4.q: Gemma, 28, attends her booking appointment with her partner, who answers most of the questions for her. When should the midwife ask Gemma about domestic abuse?
o: At 28 weeks, once a relationship of trust has been built
Now, in front of her partner, so he knows it is routine
When Gemma shows physical signs of injury
When Gemma is alone, at booking or the earliest opportunity
4.w: NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse at the booking appointment or at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, with an opportunity for a private one-to-one discussion (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Enquiry should be at booking or the earliest opportunity; waiting delays help.
n.1: Asking in front of a partner may put her at risk and prevents an honest answer.
n.2: Routine enquiry is for all women; most abuse has no visible signs.

4.q: Olivia, 27, booked late at 24 weeks. She tells the midwife her last birth was "terrifying" and that staff "didn't listen". She avoids eye contact and asks to keep appointments short. Which approach will best build a trusting relationship?
o: Acknowledge her experience and agree a plan of care together
Reassure her that this hospital is different from her last one
Keep appointments short as asked and focus on clinical checks
Refer her for counselling before continuing the care discussion
4.w: SPM 1.12 and Code 2: develop trusting, compassionate, person-centred relationships by listening, acknowledging her experience and planning care in partnership. This also supports trauma-informed care.

n.1: Quick reassurance dismisses her experience and does not build trust.
n.2: Focusing on checks only does not address her distrust, which affects engagement with care.
n.3: Counselling may help later, but making it a precondition delays care and does not build the relationship itself.

4.q: First-time parents of a 6-day-old baby are worried that they will not know if their baby becomes unwell. Which advice from the midwife best reflects NICE NG194?
o: Explain that serious infection in a baby will cause a high fever
Advise taking the baby's temperature every 4 hours, day and night
Advise waiting for the health visitor's first visit to raise worries
Give information on the Baby Check scoring system and when to call 999
4.w: NICE NG194 1.3.12-1.3.13: consider giving parents information about the Baby Check scoring system, and advise them to seek advice if they think the baby is unwell and to call 999 if they think the baby is seriously ill. 1.4.4: fever may be absent in young babies with serious infection.

n.0: Fever may not be present in young babies with serious infection (NG194 1.4.4).
n.1: Routine 4-hourly temperatures are not recommended and can miss other signs of illness.
n.2: Parents should seek advice whenever they are worried, not wait for a scheduled visit.

4.q: Erin, 35, is 14 weeks pregnant and drinks about a bottle of wine every evening. She has had shakes and sweating in the mornings. She wants to stop drinking straight away. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to attend a mutual support group before referral
Refer urgently to the specialist alcohol service for assisted withdrawal
Advise her to stop drinking tonight and contact the midwife if unwell
Advise her to cut down to 14 units a week for the rest of the pregnancy
4.w: Morning shakes and sweating suggest alcohol dependence. Abrupt cessation risks withdrawal seizures, so she needs urgent specialist referral for medically assisted withdrawal, while continuing antenatal care. NG201 1.3.10: no safe level of alcohol in pregnancy (SPM 3.1, 3.3).

n.0: Peer support helps later, but her withdrawal symptoms show dependence needing specialist care now.
n.2: Sudden withdrawal in alcohol dependence can cause seizures and needs medical management.
n.3: There is no safe level in pregnancy, and 14 units is the general adult low-risk guideline.

4.q: A maternity unit is preparing for UNICEF UK Baby Friendly assessment. A formula company offers to sponsor the infant feeding study day for staff. What should the infant feeding lead do?
o: Accept the sponsorship if the company has no speaking role on the day
Accept the sponsorship if the study day covers breastfeeding as well
Decline the sponsorship because it promotes breastmilk substitutes to staff
Accept the sponsorship and declare it in the study day programme
4.w: The WHO Code and UNICEF UK Baby Friendly Stage 1 (building a firm foundation) prohibit promotion of breastmilk substitutes in health settings, including sponsorship of staff education by manufacturers (SPM 2.10).

n.0: Sponsorship itself is a form of promotion to health workers, prohibited by the WHO Code.
n.1: Covering breastfeeding does not make company sponsorship acceptable.
n.3: Declaring sponsorship does not remove the conflict of interest the Code is designed to prevent.

4.q: Precious, 33, is giving birth on a midwife-led unit. The baby's head has been born but has retracted tightly against the perineum, and the shoulders have not delivered with the next contraction and routine axial traction. What is the midwife's first action?
o: Perform an episiotomy to make more room for the shoulders
Ask Precious to push harder with the next contraction
Call for help, stating that this is shoulder dystocia
Apply firm downward traction to the baby's head
4.w: Retraction of the head (turtle sign) and failure of routine axial traction to deliver the shoulders indicate shoulder dystocia. The first step is to call for help, clearly stating the emergency, so manoeuvres can begin with the right team present (RCOG GTG 42; SPM 4.7).

n.0: Shoulder dystocia is a bony problem; episiotomy is not the first action and is not needed in every case.
n.1: Maternal pushing alone will not release an impacted shoulder and can worsen the impaction.
n.3: Downward or excessive traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury and is avoided.

4.q: Molly, 25, is 32 weeks pregnant and attends with her first episode of reduced fetal movements. The fetal heart is heard, the computerised CTG meets criteria, SFH is on her centile line and she has no risk factors. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Arrange induction of labour at 37 weeks because of the episode
Book an ultrasound scan for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler
Admit her for daily CTG monitoring until movements return to normal
Explain the results and advise her to return if movements reduce again
4.w: SBL v3 element 3: after a first episode of RFM with a normal cCTG and no other indication, a scan is not required; results are explained and she is encouraged to reattend with further concerns. A scan for growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler is offered for recurrent RFM after 28+0 weeks or if there is another indication.

n.0: Induction for RFM alone before 39+0 weeks is not recommended (SBL v3 element 3).
n.1: A scan is offered at a first presentation only when another indication exists, such as suspected SGA.
n.2: Admission for daily CTG is not indicated when assessment is normal and there are no risk factors.

4.q: Amina, 26, and her partner are both carriers of sickle cell (HbAS), confirmed through antenatal screening. Amina is 11 weeks pregnant and asks what the chance is that this baby will have sickle cell disease. What is the correct answer?
o: 1 in 4 in each pregnancy
1 in 2 in each pregnancy
1 in 4 for the first baby and lower for later babies
No chance, because neither parent has the disease
4.w: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive. When both parents are carriers, each pregnancy independently has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected baby, a 1 in 2 chance of a carrier and a 1 in 4 chance of an unaffected non-carrier. Prenatal diagnosis should be offered (NHS SCT screening; SPM 3.11).

n.1: 1 in 2 is the chance of the baby being a carrier, not of having the disease.
n.2: The chance is the same in every pregnancy; earlier outcomes do not change it.
n.3: Two carriers can each pass on the sickle gene, so the baby can inherit two copies and have the disease.

4.q: Chantelle, 29, has severe pre-eclampsia and the consultant has decided to start magnesium sulfate. Which regimen is recommended by NICE NG133?
o: 4 g IV over 30 minutes, then 1 g/hour until birth
2 g IV over 5 minutes, then 2 g/hour for 12 hours
4 g IM into each buttock, then 2 g/hour for 24 hours
4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours
4.w: NICE NG133 1.8.4 (Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen): a 4 g IV loading dose over 5 to 15 minutes, followed by an infusion of 1 g/hour maintained for 24 hours; after a fit, continue for 24 hours after the last fit.

n.0: The loading dose is given over 5 to 15 minutes and continues for 24 hours, not until birth.
n.1: The loading dose is 4 g and maintenance 1 g/hour for 24 hours.
n.2: NG133 uses intravenous loading and 1 g/hour maintenance, not this IM regimen.

4.q: Zara, 33, has read that a treatment doubles the risk of a rare complication and is frightened. The baseline risk is 1 in 10,000. How should the midwife best present this risk?
o: Explain that her risk of the complication is doubled
Explain that the risk increases by 100% compared with no treatment
Explain that the complication is too rare to be worth discussing
Explain that the risk rises from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000
4.w: NICE NG197 (shared decision making) recommends presenting risks as absolute numbers using natural frequencies with a consistent denominator, rather than relative risk alone. SPM 3.2 and 3.3 ask midwives to interpret evidence and share it in a way that supports evidence-informed decisions.

n.0: Relative risk alone exaggerates the change and does not help her weigh the decision.
n.1: This is still a relative figure and is likely to be misunderstood.
n.2: Dismissing the risk does not respect her concern or support informed decision making.

4.q: After a difficult shift, Freya would like confidential, restorative support to reflect on her experiences. Under the A-EQUIP model in England, who provides restorative clinical supervision for midwives?
o: The NMC fitness to practise team
Her named practice assessor
A Supervisor of Midwives (SoM)
A Professional Midwifery Advocate
4.w: A-EQUIP (advocating and educating for quality improvement), published by NHS England in 2017, replaced statutory supervision of midwives. Professional Midwifery Advocates deliver restorative clinical supervision to support midwives' wellbeing and practice.

n.0: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not provide restorative supervision.
n.1: Practice assessors assess students under the SSSA; they do not supervise qualified midwives.
n.2: Statutory supervision and the Supervisor of Midwives role were removed in 2017.

4.q: Ellie, 25, is visited at home 3 days after an assisted vaginal birth. She has been shivering, her lochia smells offensive and she feels unwell. Observations: heart rate 134 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, temperature 38.3 C. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat the observations in 1 hour before deciding on transfer
Take a high vaginal swab and plan review when the result is back
Arrange emergency transfer to hospital by 999 with a pre-alert
Ask the GP to prescribe oral antibiotics and review her tomorrow
4.w: NICE NG255 (2025): a recently pregnant woman with any high-risk criterion outside hospital needs emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert (1.6.1, 1.6.2). A heart rate over 130 bpm is a high-risk criterion (Table 1); assisted birth and offensive lochia add to her risk (1.2.1).

n.0: A high-risk criterion is already present, so delaying transfer for repeat observations is unsafe.
n.1: Waiting for swab results delays treatment of suspected high-risk sepsis.
n.3: Oral antibiotics in the community delay the hospital assessment and IV antibiotics within 1 hour that NG255 requires for high risk.

4.q: Ellen, a registered midwife, has supervised a student midwife on four shifts this week but is not her practice assessor. Before the student moves to another area, what is Ellen's responsibility regarding documentation?
o: Leave documentation to the academic assessor at the next tripartite meeting
Record her observations of the student in the assessment document
Give verbal feedback, as written records are for the practice assessor
Sign off the proficiencies she has seen the student achieve this week
4.w: SSSA 4.1: practice supervisors contribute to the student's record of achievement by periodically recording relevant observations on conduct, proficiency and achievement. SPM 5.21 includes evaluating and documenting student performance. Confirming proficiency is the practice assessor's role (7.1).

n.0: The academic assessor relies on practice records; Ellen's observations need recording now.
n.2: Verbal feedback is valuable, but supervisors are also expected to record observations (4.1).
n.3: Signing off proficiencies is the practice assessor's assessment role (7.1), not the supervisor's.

4.q: Eilidh, a midwife in Scotland, sees a 15-year-old girl at an antenatal appointment and observes signs that FGM has been carried out. Which action is correct?
o: Refer under local child protection procedures without delay
Notify the police within one month under FGM Act 2003 s5B
Wait for the girl to disclose before taking any action
Record the finding and review at the next appointment
4.w: The s5B mandatory notification duty in the FGM Act 2003 extends to England and Wales. In Scotland, FGM is an offence under the Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation (Scotland) Act 2005, and a girl with FGM is a child protection concern referred without delay under local procedures (SPM 1.2: differentiate between devolved legislatures).

n.1: Section 5B does not extend to Scotland; Scottish child protection procedures apply.
n.2: Observed signs of FGM in a child are a child protection concern whether or not she discloses.
n.3: Delaying to a later appointment leaves a child protection concern without action.

4.q: Emma, 33, is 36+5 weeks pregnant. A scan has confirmed an uncomplicated singleton breech presentation. After discussion of the options she says she would prefer to have a vaginal birth with the baby head down if possible. What should be offered?
o: External cephalic version
A planned vaginal breech birth
Induction of labour at 37 weeks
A repeat scan at 40 weeks
4.w: NICE NG201 1.2.38: for an uncomplicated singleton breech confirmed after 36+0 weeks, discuss ECV, vaginal breech birth and elective caesarean, and offer ECV to women who prefer cephalic vaginal birth.

n.1: Vaginal breech birth is one option, but she wants a head-down birth, which ECV aims to achieve.
n.2: Induction is not generally recommended for a breech baby (NG207 1.2.21) and does not turn the baby.
n.3: Waiting for a repeat scan delays ECV, which is offered from 36+0 weeks when the woman wishes.

4.q: Laila, 31, is 36 weeks pregnant. A scan confirms an intrauterine fetal death. She is physically well, her membranes are intact and there are no signs of infection or bleeding. She says she cannot face labour today. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Send her home and ask her to return to the unit when labour starts naturally
Advise immediate induction of labour today to reduce the risk of infection
Discuss expectant management, induction and caesarean, and respect her choice
Arrange a caesarean birth today as the quickest way to end the pregnancy
4.w: NICE NG207 1.2.28: after intrauterine fetal death, if the woman is physically well with intact membranes and no infection or bleeding, discuss the options for birth (expectant management, induction or caesarean) and respect her decision. Support for her and her family is offered (1.2.27).

n.0: Expectant management is a valid option but is a decision to be discussed and agreed, with support and follow-up, not a default discharge.
n.1: Immediate induction is offered when there are ruptured membranes, infection or bleeding (NG207 1.2.29), which Laila does not have.
n.3: Caesarean carries surgical morbidity; it is one option to discuss, not the default recommendation.

4.q: Yasmin, a band 7 midwife, overhears a colleague telling a woman in early labour, in front of others, that she is 'making a fuss' about her contractions. As a leader on the unit, what is the most appropriate response?
o: Support the woman, then speak privately with the colleague
Report the colleague directly to the NMC for unprofessional conduct
Take over the woman's care and avoid working with the colleague in future
Raise the issue with the whole team at next month's meeting
4.w: SPM 5.20 requires positive leadership and role modelling; Code 1.1 requires kindness and respect, and Code 9.1 requires honest, constructive feedback to colleagues. Yasmin first ensures the woman is supported, then addresses the behaviour privately and promptly.

n.1: A single lapse is first addressed locally through feedback and support; an immediate NMC referral is disproportionate on these facts.
n.2: Avoiding the colleague does not address the behaviour or help the colleague improve.
n.3: Waiting a month for a team meeting leaves the woman unsupported now and denies the colleague timely, private feedback.

4.q: Fatima, 34, has a BMI of 37 at booking and is otherwise well. At 36 weeks she says she still wants a home birth after a full discussion of the risks with her midwife and an obstetrician. What should the midwife do next?
o: Transfer her care to the GP until she agrees to give birth in the obstetric unit
Support her choice and agree a documented individual plan with senior input
Refuse to attend a home birth because the plan is outside guidance
Tell her she must give birth in the obstetric unit because of her BMI
4.w: NG235 advises obstetric unit birth when BMI is over 35 (1.10.29), but women may decline. SPM 1.21-1.22 require respecting her right to decline and advocating for her when her choice is outside guidance, with an individualised plan involving senior midwives (for example a consultant midwife).

n.0: Transferring care to pressure her abandons her and does not reduce risk.
n.2: A competent woman may choose her place of birth; the midwife has a duty to support and attend, and to plan for safety.
n.3: Midwives can advise but cannot compel; this disregards her autonomy and informed choice.

4.q: Zara, 26, is RhD positive and at her 28-week appointment. Her booking antibody screen was negative. The student midwife suggests that, as she is RhD positive, only a full blood count is needed. Which blood tests should be offered?
o: Full blood count and a glucose tolerance test
Full blood count, plus blood group and antibody screen
Blood group and antibodies, with Hb checked at 34 weeks
Full blood count, as her antibody screen was negative at booking
4.w: NICE NG201 1.2.16: at 28 weeks offer all women a full blood count and blood group and antibody testing; anti-D prophylaxis is added for RhD-negative women who are not sensitised. Atypical red cell antibodies other than anti-D can develop in RhD-positive women.

n.0: An OGTT is offered at 24 to 28 weeks only when GDM risk factors are present, and does not replace group and antibodies.
n.2: The FBC is recommended at 28 weeks to detect anaemia in time to treat it before birth.
n.3: A negative booking screen does not exclude antibodies developing later, so testing is repeated at 28 weeks.

4.q: Dana is the labour ward coordinator. Four requests arrive at the same moment. Which should she attend to first?
o: A woman at 38 weeks with a mild headache whose blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg
A postnatal woman 2 hours after birth asking for her prescribed paracetamol
A woman in established labour whose fetal heart rate has been 85 bpm for 4 minutes
A woman booked for elective caesarean tomorrow who needs her bloods taken
4.w: SPM 5.19 requires safe prioritising. A prolonged fetal bradycardia lasting several minutes is an obstetric emergency needing immediate assessment and escalation; Code 25.1 asks leaders to identify priorities and deal with risk.

n.0: A mild headache with normal blood pressure needs review, but a prolonged fetal bradycardia is the more urgent threat.
n.1: Analgesia is important but can follow within minutes without risk to life.
n.3: Pre-operative bloods for tomorrow are routine and can be planned later in the shift.

4.q: Sana, 27, develops a temperature of 38.4 C and offensive lochia on day 3 after birth. She is being treated for suspected puerperal sepsis. Her baby is rooming in with her. What should the midwife also do?
o: Advise Sana to stop breastfeeding until her antibiotics finish
Move the baby to the nursery to prevent cross-infection
Assess the baby for signs of infection
Arrange for the baby to start prophylactic antibiotics
4.w: NG194 1.2.8: if a woman has confirmed or suspected puerperal sepsis, assess the baby for symptoms or signs of infection. This reflects SPM 2.6, planning for woman and newborn together.

n.0: Puerperal sepsis is not a reason to stop breastfeeding; compatible antibiotics can be chosen.
n.1: Separation is not recommended; the baby should be assessed and kept with the mother where possible.
n.3: Antibiotics for the baby depend on assessment; they are not given automatically.

4.q: Tara, 31, is returning to work when her baby is 7 months old and wants to continue breastfeeding. She asks what her employer must do. What is the most accurate answer?
o: Offer flexible working that suits her feeding pattern
Assess workplace risks and provide somewhere suitable to rest
Give her paid breaks to express milk during each shift
Provide a private room with a fridge for expressing her milk
4.w: Employers must assess workplace risks for an employee who is breastfeeding (Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 reg 16; HSE guidance) and provide suitable facilities for a nursing mother to rest (Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 reg 25). Helping women know their rights supports breastfeeding in all settings (SPM 2.10).

n.0: She can request flexible working, but the employer does not have to grant it.
n.2: UK law does not give a statutory right to paid breastfeeding breaks; this is good practice, not a legal duty.
n.3: HSE describes a private room and fridge as good practice; the legal duty is a risk assessment and suitable rest facilities.

4.q: Priya, a midwife newly arrived from overseas, is preparing for the third stage of labour on a midwife-led unit. Ana, 30, has chosen active management with Syntometrine (oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms). Priya asks a colleague whether the midwives exemptions cover this combined product. What is the correct answer?
o: No, a combined product needs a patient group direction
Yes, because Syntometrine is classed as a pharmacy medicine
No, ergometrine needs an individual prescription from a doctor
Yes, both oxytocin and ergometrine are on the administration list
4.w: Schedule 17 covers parenteral POMs containing the listed substances and no other prescription-only substance. Oxytocins and ergometrine maleate are both listed, so a registered midwife may administer Syntometrine (if not contraindicated, for example by pre-eclampsia) (HMR 2012 Sch 17; NG235 1.10.11).

n.0: A combined product is covered when every POM substance in it is on the list, as here.
n.1: Syntometrine is a prescription-only medicine, not a pharmacy medicine.
n.2: Ergometrine maleate is on the Schedule 17 administration list.

4.q: At her annual appraisal, Hollie, a midwife with 2 years' experience, receives feedback from colleagues that she rarely asks for help when unsure and sometimes delays escalating concerns. She feels upset by this. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reflect on the feedback, discuss it with her manager and agree a development plan
Accept the feedback politely and continue practising in the same way
Request a transfer to another ward where colleagues know her less well
Ask which colleagues gave the feedback so that she can challenge their view
4.w: Code 9.2: gather and reflect on feedback from a variety of sources, using it to improve your practice. SPM 1.27 requires midwives to seek and respond to support and feedback. A development plan addresses the safety issue (Code standard 13 recognise and work within the limits of your competence).

n.1: Accepting feedback without changing practice ignores a safety-relevant pattern.
n.2: Moving wards avoids the feedback and leaves the development need unaddressed.
n.3: Focusing on who gave the feedback is defensive and does not use it to improve practice.

4.q: Baby Dev is 10 weeks old and has just moved to England from abroad. He has not had newborn blood spot screening. What should the health professional offer?
o: No screening, as blood spot screening ends at 8 weeks of age
Blood spot screening for the conditions except cystic fibrosis
Blood spot screening for all 10 conditions in the usual way
Cystic fibrosis screening, as the other tests are now too late
4.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: babies are eligible up to 1 year of age, except for cystic fibrosis screening, which is unreliable after 8 weeks. At 10 weeks Dev should be offered screening for the other conditions.

n.0: Eligibility continues to 1 year for the other conditions.
n.2: CF screening is unreliable after 8 weeks, so it is not offered at 10 weeks.
n.3: CF is the one test that is too late; the other conditions can still be screened.

4.q: Rania, 29, has just had her first baby. She has never had a mental illness, but her mother had postpartum psychosis after Rania's birth. During which period does CG192 advise professionals to be particularly alert for symptoms of postpartum psychosis?
o: Between 3 and 6 months after birth
The third trimester of pregnancy
The first 2 weeks after birth
The first 6 weeks after birth
4.w: CG192 1.5.11: if a woman has past or present severe mental illness or a first-degree relative with severe perinatal mental illness, be alert for possible symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after childbirth.

n.0: Onset is typically within days of birth; CG192 sets the first 2 weeks as the alert period.
n.1: Postpartum psychosis arises after birth, not in the third trimester.
n.3: Six weeks is broader than the specific CG192 alert period of the first 2 weeks.

4.q: Nina, 29, is in established labour with intermittent auscultation. At the start of labour the fetal heart rate was 125 beats per minute. Three hours later the rate after contractions is consistently 148, with no decelerations heard. Her temperature is 37.2 C. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start continuous CTG immediately and transfer without further review
Auscultate more often and carry out a full review of the clinical picture
Give intravenous fluids, as a rising fetal heart rate means dehydration
Continue auscultation every 15 minutes, as 148 is within the normal range
4.w: A rise of 20 beats per minute or more from the start of labour is significant even within 110 to 160. NICE NG229 1.2.11: auscultate more frequently (for example after 3 consecutive contractions) and carry out a full review of risk factors, maternal observations, contractions and progress. If concerns are confirmed, advise continuous CTG and transfer (1.2.12).

n.0: CTG is advised if concerns are confirmed after review; NICE first asks for more frequent auscultation and a full review.
n.2: IV fluids are not given for fetal heart rate changes unless the woman is hypotensive or septic (NG229 1.5.11).
n.3: A rise of 23 beats per minute is a concern even though the rate is under 160; it may indicate infection or hypoxia.

4.q: Abi, 34, is 27 weeks pregnant and in established preterm labour, 6 cm dilated. Her midwife is preparing for birth. Which intervention for the baby should the midwife make sure has been offered now?
o: A second course of antenatal corticosteroids
Oral erythromycin for prophylaxis against infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
Intramuscular progesterone to slow cervical change
4.w: NG25 1.10.2: offer IV magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection to women between 24+0 and 29+6 weeks who are in established preterm labour or having a planned preterm birth within 24 hours. SBL v3 5.20 sets the same standard for births under 30 weeks.

n.0: Repeat courses are avoided where possible (SBL v3 5.19) and nothing suggests she had a first course long ago.
n.1: Erythromycin is prophylaxis against infection in P-PROM; it does not protect the baby's brain before an imminent preterm birth.
n.3: Progesterone is a preventive measure started at 16 to 24 weeks, not treatment for established labour.

4.q: Abi, 24, has given birth to her first baby. She tells the midwife she has decided to formula feed and asks for help with making up feeds. Which response by the midwife is best?
o: "Formula is fine; there is no real difference between breast milk and formula."
"I will show you how to make up feeds safely and how to bottle feed responsively."
"I will note your choice and ask the infant feeding team to discuss it with you."
"Most babies do much better on breast milk, so could you try for a week first?"
4.w: Code 2.4 and 4.1 require respect for the level of involvement and the decisions a woman makes; Code 6.1 requires evidence-based advice. NG194 supports safe formula preparation and responsive bottle feeding for women who formula feed, and Baby Friendly standards support informed feeding decisions.

n.0: Saying there is no difference is inaccurate; Code 6.1 requires information to be evidence-based.
n.2: Referring her to be persuaded implies her choice needs correcting and delays the practical help she has asked for.
n.3: Pressuring her to try breastfeeding after she has made an informed choice does not respect her decision (Code 2.4).

4.q: Grace, 34, is in her third labour. Her cervix is 4 cm dilated but only partly effaced. A student midwife asks whether this is unusual. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Partial effacement at 4 cm is a sign of obstructed labour
In parous women effacement and dilatation often happen together
Partial effacement at 4 cm means she is still in the latent first stage
In parous women dilatation cannot begin until effacement is complete
4.w: In a first labour the cervix usually effaces before it dilates. In parous women effacement and dilatation commonly occur together, so a partly effaced cervix at 4 cm is normal. NICE defines established first stage as regular contractions with progressive dilatation from 4 cm (NG235 1.8.1).

n.0: Partial effacement is normal in parous women and is not a sign of obstruction.
n.2: Established labour is defined by regular contractions and progressive dilatation from 4 cm, not by complete effacement.
n.3: Effacement before dilatation is the usual pattern in first labours, not in parous women.

4.q: Fatima, 35, is 5 days after a caesarean birth. At a home visit the edge of her wound is red with an offensive discharge. Her temperature is 37.9 C, heart rate 96 bpm and other observations are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Clean the wound and review it again at the next routine visit
Arrange a same-day medical review of the wound and observations
Advise her to mention the wound at the 6 to 8 week GP review
Give a course of antibiotics using the midwives exemptions
4.w: NICE NG194 1.2.3 and 1.2.4: assess wound healing and signs of infection after caesarean; infection symptoms need medical advice without delay. Signs of wound infection are a moderate to high risk criterion for sepsis in NG255, so a prompt medical assessment is needed.

n.0: Waiting for the next routine visit delays assessment of a probable wound infection.
n.2: A 6 to 8 week review is far too late for an infected wound.
n.3: Antibiotics are not among the medicines midwives may supply or administer under the HMR 2012 Schedule 17 exemptions.

4.q: Charlotte, 30, is 29 weeks pregnant. She asks whether her sleeping position matters at this stage of pregnancy. What should the midwife advise?
o: Go to sleep on her side rather than on her back
Go to sleep on her back if she has no heartburn or back pain
Go to sleep on her back with a pillow under her knees
Go to sleep in whatever position is most comfortable
4.w: NG201 1.3.25-1.3.26: advise women to avoid going to sleep on their back after 28 weeks, explaining that there may be a link between going to sleep on the back and stillbirth in late pregnancy, so they should go to sleep on their side.

n.1: The stillbirth association with going to sleep on the back applies whatever her symptoms.
n.2: Going to sleep on the back after 28 weeks is associated with stillbirth.
n.3: Position matters after 28 weeks; she should go to sleep on her side.

4.q: Ifeoma, a midwife, is a passenger on a long-haul flight when the crew ask for help: a woman is in labour at about 38 weeks. Ifeoma is off duty and has no equipment of her own. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Wait until the crew confirm no doctor is on board before helping
Offer help within her competence and support the crew's emergency plans
Offer advice but avoid physical contact as she is outside the UK
Stay seated as her employer's indemnity does not cover care on the flight
4.w: NMC Code 15: always offer help if an emergency arises in your practice setting or anywhere else, acting within the limits of your knowledge and competence (15.1) and arranging for emergency care to be accessed promptly (15.2), taking account of safety (15.3).

n.0: Delaying help while waiting for a doctor wastes time; a midwife is competent to attend a normal birth and should offer help now.
n.2: Code 15 applies anywhere, and a midwife attending a birth in an emergency may give the hands-on care that is needed.
n.3: Indemnity concerns do not remove the professional expectation in Code 15 to offer help in an emergency anywhere.

4.q: Zara, 30, is 5 cm dilated on the labour ward and has a cord prolapse. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration. The obstetrician is present and theatre is ready. What is the recommended category of caesarean birth?
o: Category 3, aiming for birth within the day
Category 1, aiming for birth within 30 minutes
Category 1, aiming for birth within 60 minutes
Category 2, aiming for birth within 75 minutes
4.w: RCOG GTG 50: caesarean is recommended when vaginal birth is not imminent; category 1, aiming for birth within 30 minutes or less, if the fetal heart rate pattern is suspicious or pathological. Category 2 can be considered if the FHR is normal.

n.0: Category 3 is for births needing early but not urgent delivery.
n.2: Category 1 aims for 30 minutes or less, not 60.
n.3: Category 2 is considered when the fetal heart rate is normal, not with a prolonged deceleration.

4.q: A trust has completed a learning response after a woman had a major postpartum haemorrhage with a delayed transfer. Following Ockenden, what should the team make sure happens with the findings?
o: Share them with the family in plain language and feed them into training
File the report and repeat the review if a similar incident happens
Send the report to the family in technical terms for accuracy
Keep the report internal to protect staff who took part in interviews
4.w: Ockenden IEA 5: investigations must be meaningful for families and staff, reports written in language families understand, and lessons fed into multidisciplinary training and changes in practice audited. SPM 5.3 requires sharing feedback and learning with families and colleagues.

n.1: Filing without action fails to implement learning; Ockenden expects timely change.
n.2: Ockenden requires language families can understand, with medical terms explained.
n.3: Families should be involved and informed; withholding findings breaches openness.

4.q: A coordinator faces a sudden surge: three women arrive in labour, one with bleeding, while a fourth needs transfer to theatre. Which approach best reflects structured problem solving in a stressful situation?
o: Assess each woman quickly, prioritise by risk, allocate staff and review often
Deal with the women in the order they arrived to be fair to everyone
Ask each midwife to manage whichever woman they meet first
Focus on the theatre transfer first and assess the new arrivals afterwards
4.w: Structured problem solving in pressured situations means assessing, prioritising by risk (the woman who is bleeding needs immediate assessment), allocating roles, communicating the plan and reviewing as things change (SPM 5.13.1, 5.13.6).

n.1: Order of arrival ignores clinical urgency and risks delaying care for the woman who is bleeding.
n.2: Uncoordinated allocation loses oversight and may leave the highest-risk woman without the right skills.
n.3: Fixing on one task risks missing deterioration in the new arrivals.

4.q: Lydia, a midwife, is writing a reflective account for revalidation about care she gave to a woman with a postpartum haemorrhage. What must she make sure of when writing it?
o: It names the colleagues involved so that the reflection is complete
It includes the woman's hospital number so the case can be checked
It is signed by the woman to confirm the account is accurate
It contains no information that could identify the woman or colleagues
4.w: NMC revalidation guidance requires reflective accounts to be anonymised, with no information that could identify any person, in line with Code 5 (respect privacy and confidentiality).

n.0: Naming colleagues identifies them and is not required.
n.1: A hospital number is identifiable and breaches confidentiality.
n.2: Reflective accounts are the midwife's own reflection; the woman does not sign them.

4.q: Jess, 27, has just given birth. The baby cried at birth, has good tone and a heart rate over 100, and is skin to skin. Jess has chosen active management. When should the cord be clamped?
o: No earlier than 1 minute after birth, and before 5 minutes for traction
After the cord stops pulsating, then give the uterotonic
Immediately after the uterotonic is given, to allow cord traction
No earlier than 10 minutes after birth, to maximise placental transfusion
4.w: NICE NG235 1.10.14: after the uterotonic, do not clamp the cord earlier than 1 minute after birth unless there is concern about cord integrity or the baby's heart rate is below 60 and not increasing; clamp before 5 minutes to perform controlled cord traction, and support a request for later clamping.

n.1: Waiting for pulsation to stop is part of physiological management; in active management the uterotonic is given before clamping.
n.2: Immediate clamping is not recommended for a well baby; wait at least 1 minute.
n.3: In active management the cord is clamped before 5 minutes for controlled cord traction unless she requests otherwise.

4.q: Baby Leo was born at 35 weeks after spontaneous preterm labour, with membranes intact until birth. At 3 hours old he has a temperature of 35.8 C despite a warm environment and is grunting with mild recession. Which action is most appropriate under NG195?
o: Monitor him for at least 12 hours using a newborn early warning chart
Use the Kaiser calculator on the postnatal ward outside any audit
Repeat his temperature in 1 hour after skin-to-skin contact
Take investigations and start antibiotics without waiting for results
4.w: Leo has a risk factor (preterm birth after spontaneous labour) and two clinical indicators (temperature under 36 C unexplained by environment; respiratory distress). Two or more non-red-flag risk factors or indicators mean investigations and antibiotics without waiting for results (NG195 1.10.3).

n.0: Monitoring alone is for babies with 1 risk factor or indicator and no red flags.
n.1: NG195 1.10.4 allows the Kaiser calculator for babies over 34+0 weeks only as part of a prospective audit.
n.2: Rewarming and rechecking delays treatment when he already meets the threshold for antibiotics.

4.q: Kim, 36, is brought to the labour ward at 34 weeks with heavy continuing vaginal bleeding. She is confused, her heart rate is 135 beats/min and her blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. The team is gathering. What is the immediate priority?
o: Resuscitate Kim using an ABC approach
Take a full history of the bleeding and any pain
Start a CTG to establish the fetal condition
Arrange an ultrasound scan to locate the placenta
4.w: RCOG GTG 63: with major or massive haemorrhage or maternal compromise, assess maternal wellbeing and start resuscitation immediately. The mother is the priority and should be stabilised before the fetal condition is established, using an ABC approach (SPM 4.7).

n.1: A full history is taken once there is no maternal compromise.
n.2: Fetal assessment comes after the mother is stabilised.
n.3: Imaging is not the priority while she is shocked and bleeding.

4.q: During a vaginal examination in labour, Abby, 23, who had agreed to the examination, says, "Please stop, it hurts too much." The midwife has nearly finished assessing the cervix. What should the midwife do?
o: Continue, as Abby gave consent before it started
Finish quickly as the examination is nearly complete
Stop the examination at once and talk with Abby
Pause briefly, then continue once Abby has had a contraction
4.w: Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Once Abby asks to stop, continuing would be without consent (Code 4.2; SPM 1.20). The midwife stops, supports her and discusses options.

n.0: Earlier consent does not continue once she has withdrawn it.
n.1: Finishing after consent has been withdrawn is examination without consent, however near completion.
n.3: Continuing after a pause without her renewed agreement still ignores the withdrawal of consent.

4.q: Rosa, 31, is 20 weeks pregnant and has been invited to join a randomised trial of an iron supplement. She tells her midwife she is worried that saying no will mean she is treated differently at the clinic. Which response by the midwife is best?
o: 'If you decline, you will be booked into the consultant clinic instead.'
'Your partner will also need to agree because the baby is involved.'
'You can decline, or withdraw later, and your care will not change.'
'You need to give your answer today so that the trial can include you.'
4.w: Valid consent to research must be voluntary and informed; participants can decline or withdraw at any time without their standard care being affected (UK Policy Framework for Health and Social Care Research; Code 4.2 make sure you get properly informed consent). A pregnant woman with capacity gives her own consent.

n.0: Linking refusal to a change in her care pathway is coercive and has no clinical basis.
n.1: A pregnant woman with capacity consents for herself; the partner's agreement is not a legal requirement for her participation.
n.3: Pressure to decide on the spot undermines voluntary consent; she should have time to consider the information.

4.q: Sian, 31, is on an oxytocin infusion for delay in the first stage. The CTG has just been categorised as pathological by the midwife and the coordinator. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Increase the oxytocin to achieve 5 contractions in 10 minutes
Reduce the oxytocin rate by half and recheck the CTG in 30 minutes
Stop the oxytocin and seek urgent obstetric review
Continue the oxytocin, as contractions are not more than 4 in 10
