4.w: NICE NG235 1.8.56: oxytocin must be discontinued immediately if the CTG is pathological, and urgent obstetrician or senior midwife review sought. It may be restarted after review if the CTG is no longer pathological and the woman agrees (1.8.57).

n.0: The aim is 3 to 4 contractions in 10; more than 4 is excessive and harmful with a pathological trace.
n.1: Reducing the dose is the response to more than 4 contractions in 10 (1.8.55); a pathological CTG needs oxytocin stopped.
n.3: A pathological CTG requires oxytocin to stop whatever the contraction frequency.

4.q: In established labour, Mel, a midwife, classifies Lara's CTG as pathological. The registrar reviews it and says to recheck in an hour. Mel still believes urgent action is needed and the registrar is now in theatre. What should Mel do?
o: Escalate directly to the consultant obstetrician using the policy
Ask a colleague to agree the CTG before taking any action
Accept the registrar's plan and recheck the CTG in one hour
Document her disagreement in the notes and continue monitoring
4.w: SPM 1.15: know when and how to escalate concerns. A pathological CTG needs urgent obstetric review (NICE NG229). If she remains concerned, she escalates to the consultant using the escalation policy, a lesson of the Ockenden (2022) and East Kent (2022) reports.

n.1: A 'fresh eyes' review is useful, but it should not delay escalation when she already believes urgent action is needed.
n.2: Waiting an hour with a pathological CTG, when she believes action is urgent, may delay life-saving care.
n.3: Documenting disagreement without escalating leaves the risk to the baby unaddressed.

4.q: At a home visit 3 weeks after the birth, Tom, the partner of a woman in the midwife's care, says he has felt low, irritable and unable to sleep for the past 3 weeks and is struggling to cope. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest he raises it at his partner's 6 to 8 week postnatal GP check
Explain that postnatal depression affects birthing mothers rather than partners
Acknowledge his feelings and advise him to contact his GP or NHS Talking Therapies
Note his comments in the woman's records and take no further action
4.w: Fathers and partners can also have depression after the birth of a baby (NHS postnatal depression guidance), and adults can self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies. SPM 3.16.1 requires midwives to recognise and respond to the needs of adults in the family.

n.0: His partner's check is about her health, and his symptoms need attention now.
n.1: Partners can develop depression after a birth; dismissing this misses a treatable condition.
n.3: Recording without acting fails to support him or signpost help.

4.q: Under Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015], when recommending a treatment, what must the clinician take reasonable care to make sure the woman knows about, in addition to its material risks?
o: The clinician's personal preference
The trust's policy on the treatment
Any reasonable alternative treatments
The national rate of complaints for it
4.w: Montgomery para 87: the clinician must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of any material risks involved in recommended treatment and of any reasonable alternative or variant treatments.

n.0: The clinician's personal preference is not part of the Montgomery duty of disclosure.
n.1: Trust policy is not what Montgomery requires to be disclosed.
n.3: Complaint rates are not part of the Montgomery duty of disclosure.

4.q: Baby Ella, born at 39 weeks with no risk factors, has a palpable clunk on the Ortolani manoeuvre of her left hip at the NIPE newborn examination. What is the expected screening pathway?
o: Hip ultrasound at 4 to 6 weeks, outcome decided by 6 weeks
Repeat the hip examination at the 6 to 8 week infant check
Referral for review by an orthopaedic surgeon by 10 weeks
Hip ultrasound between 38 and 40 weeks corrected age
4.w: NIPE hip screen positive pathway: for babies born at 34+0 weeks or more, perform hip ultrasound between 4 and 6 weeks of age, with an orthopaedic outcome decision by 6 weeks. A palpable clunk on Ortolani or Barlow is a screen positive finding.

n.1: A screen positive newborn hip needs ultrasound, not just a repeat clinical check.
n.2: Being seen by 10 weeks applies to babies found screen positive at the 6 to 8 week infant examination.
n.3: 38 to 40 weeks corrected age is the scan timing for babies born before 34 weeks.

4.q: Lily, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has no medical or social risk factors and no safeguarding concerns. She declines further antenatal care and plans to give birth at home without a midwife. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that freebirth is unlawful in the UK
Discharge her from maternity services as she has declined care
Respect her decision, keep offering contact and document discussions
Refer to children's social care because she is declining care
4.w: A woman with capacity may decline care and give birth without a professional present; it is lawful for her to do so. With no other concerns, declining care is not itself a safeguarding issue. The midwife keeps the door open, shares information and documents (SPM 1.21).

n.0: Freebirth is lawful; art 45 of the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001 restricts who may attend, not the woman's choice.
n.1: Discharging her closes the door on care she may later accept.
n.3: Declining care, with no other concerns, is not a reason for a social care referral.

4.q: Ruby, 26, is 30 weeks pregnant. At 20:00 she phones the maternity triage line saying her baby has moved less than usual since the morning. This is the first time she has noticed this. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Attend the maternity unit now for assessment
Have a cold sugary drink and lie on her left side for an hour
Attend the antenatal clinic first thing tomorrow morning
Count ten movements over the next 2 hours, then call back
4.w: Women should contact maternity services at any time of day or night if they are concerned about reduced movements and should be assessed (NICE NG201 1.2.34; SBL v3 element 3). Delays in attending with RFM have been repeatedly identified in stillbirth reviews.

n.1: Trying to stimulate movements at home delays assessment and is not a recommended approach.
n.2: Waiting until the next day delays assessment of possible fetal compromise.
n.3: Counting a set number of movements before calling back delays assessment and is not recommended.

4.q: Kathleen, a labour ward coordinator, has a conscientious objection to abortion. She is asked to allocate a midwife to care for a woman having a termination for fetal anomaly. Following the Supreme Court decision in Doogan [2014], what is the position?
o: She must allocate staff, as this is not hands-on participation
She may refuse, as any link to a termination is covered
She may refuse, as allocation is participation in the treatment
She may refuse if she records her objection in writing
4.w: Greater Glasgow Health Board v Doogan [2014] UKSC 68 held that 'participate' in s4 means taking part in a hands-on capacity; managerial and supervisory tasks such as allocating staff are not covered by the objection.

n.1: Doogan rejected a wide reading covering any task linked to termination.
n.2: Doogan held that allocation is not participation in the treatment.
n.3: Recording an objection does not bring allocation within s4, which Doogan held is not participation.

4.q: Jade, 30, is on a stable dose of methadone and has given birth to a term baby. Her urine screen shows no other drugs. Her baby is at risk of neonatal abstinence syndrome. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Advise formula feeding because methadone passes into breast milk
Keep the baby in the ward nursery overnight so that Jade can rest
Admit the baby to the neonatal unit for observation for the first 72 hours
Keep the baby with Jade, observe for withdrawal, support breastfeeding
4.w: UK drug misuse clinical guidelines encourage breastfeeding for women on stable opioid substitution therapy. Keeping mother and baby together, with observation for withdrawal, meets SPM 2.6 (needs of both considered together).

n.0: Breastfeeding is encouraged for women on stable methadone; small amounts in milk may ease withdrawal.
n.1: Night-time separation interrupts responsive feeding and attachment and does not reduce withdrawal.
n.2: Routine admission of a well baby separates them; observation can take place with the mother.

4.q: Precious, 22, has an eclamptic seizure on the antenatal ward and remains unconscious afterwards. She needs magnesium sulfate urgently. What is the legal basis for treatment?
o: Best interests treatment under the MCA 2005
A Court of Protection order
The consent of her next of kin
Her consent once she regains consciousness
4.w: She lacks capacity at the material time (MCA 2005 s2; temporary impairment counts, s2(2)). Treatment that cannot wait is given in her best interests (s4, s5), taking account of any known wishes.

n.1: A court order is not needed for urgent treatment in an emergency.
n.2: Next of kin cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney.
n.3: Waiting for consciousness would delay treatment needed to prevent further seizures.

4.q: Chloe, 30, is postnatal after a long labour. The midwife realises she has just given Chloe a dose of dihydrocodeine that was prescribed for the woman in the next bed. Chloe is sleepy but rousable and breathing normally. What is the midwife's first priority?
o: Assess Chloe and inform the doctor and coordinator now
Tell Chloe what happened at her discharge discussion
Refer herself to the NMC before the end of her shift
Complete an incident report before telling anyone else
4.w: Code 14.1 requires the midwife to act immediately to put right the situation where harm has or could have occurred: assess and monitor Chloe (including respiratory rate and sedation) and get medical review. She then explains and apologises (Code 14.2) and documents and reports the incident (Code 14.3).

n.1: Chloe must be told promptly, not at discharge (Code 14.2).
n.2: Self-referral to the NMC is not the immediate priority and is not required for every error.
n.3: Reporting matters, but Chloe's safety and medical review come first.

4.q: Tara, 32, has pre-eclampsia treated with labetalol and has just given birth vaginally. She chose active management of the third stage. Which uterotonic is most appropriate?
o: Ergometrine 500 micrograms by intravenous injection
Carbetocin by slow intravenous injection
Oxytocin 10 units by intramuscular injection
Oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM
4.w: Oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease (NICE NG235 1.10.9). Oxytocin 10 units IM given after the birth of the baby, before cord clamping, is appropriate (1.10.11).

n.0: Ergometrine raises blood pressure and is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia by any route.
n.1: NICE recommends carbetocin for women having a caesarean birth (1.10.13), not after vaginal birth.
n.3: Ergometrine-containing preparations are contraindicated in pre-eclampsia because they raise blood pressure.

4.q: Precious, 29, had an emergency caesarean birth. Her baby, born at 32 weeks, is in the neonatal unit. Precious wants to breastfeed. Which action best supports her and her baby together?
o: Arrange donor milk so that she does not need to express after surgery
Help her hand express colostrum as soon as possible after the birth
Advise her to start expressing once she can walk to the neonatal unit
Advise her to rest and plan breastfeeding when the baby is discharged
4.w: UNICEF UK Baby Friendly neonatal standards support mothers of babies in neonatal units to start expressing early after the birth and to express frequently, so the baby receives her own milk and her supply is established. Expressing can begin at the bedside after a caesarean. SPM 2.6 asks midwives to plan for mother and baby together even when they are cared for apart.

n.0: Donor milk may bridge a gap but does not replace support for her own milk, which she wants to give.
n.2: Delaying expression until she is mobile reduces milk supply; expressing can start at the bedside.
n.3: Early expression protects her supply and gives the preterm baby colostrum now.

4.q: The midwife gives 5 inflation breaths to Baby Tom, born at 41 weeks, but sees no chest rise and the heart rate is not increasing. What should she do next?
o: Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath
Give ventilation breaths at 30 per minute as planned
Reposition the head and use a two-person jaw thrust, then repeat
Increase the inflation pressure to 50 cm H2O and continue
4.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if there is no chest rise, check and correct head position, consider two-person jaw thrust or a supraglottic airway, then repeat the 5 inflation breaths. Compressions are not effective until the lungs are aerated.

n.0: Compressions are not started until the lungs have been effectively aerated.
n.1: Ventilation breaths will not work until airway obstruction is corrected and chest rise is seen.
n.3: Pressure may be increased cautiously after airway manoeuvres, not jumped to 50 cm H2O first.

4.q: Aaliyah, 34, has suspected sepsis 2 days after a caesarean birth and meets high-risk criteria. One hour after antibiotics and two fluid boluses, her systolic blood pressure remains 86 mmHg and she is more confused. The registrar has reviewed her. What should happen now?
o: Give a third fluid bolus and recheck after 1 more hour
Change the antibiotics and await the microbiology result
Continue current treatment and repeat the lactate in 2 hours
Alert the consultant to attend her in person
4.w: NICE NG255 1.7.9 and 1.9.4: if a high-risk person does not respond within 1 hour of any intervention, or there is no improvement after a second fluid bolus, alert a consultant to attend in person. Critical care referral is also needed with systolic 90 or less (1.7.4).

n.0: NG255 calls for a consultant to attend after no improvement following a second bolus, not a third bolus.
n.1: Waiting for microbiology does not address her failure to respond now.
n.2: Waiting 2 more hours delays senior input for a deteriorating woman.

4.q: During a shoulder dystocia, a junior doctor who has just arrived tells Lauren's partner to push down hard on the top of her abdomen. What should the midwife do?
o: Stop it at once, as fundal pressure is avoided
Allow it, as it adds force to the McRoberts manoeuvre
Ask the doctor to apply it instead of the partner
Allow it once suprapubic pressure has been tried
4.w: Fundal pressure is avoided in shoulder dystocia because it increases impaction of the shoulder and is associated with brachial plexus injury and uterine rupture (RCOG GTG 42). The midwife intervenes to protect the woman and baby (SPM 4.7).

n.1: Fundal pressure does not assist McRoberts and worsens impaction.
n.2: Fundal pressure is avoided whoever applies it.
n.3: Fundal pressure is not a later step after suprapubic pressure.

4.q: Twins Ella and Isla were born at 37 weeks. At 10 hours old, Ella develops signs of shock and is started on antibiotics for suspected sepsis. Isla is feeding well and her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate plan for Isla?
o: Take investigations and start antibiotics without waiting for results
Continue routine postnatal care because she has no clinical signs
Monitor her observations every 4 hours for 12 hours before deciding
Wait for Ella's blood culture result before deciding about Isla
4.w: Suspected or confirmed infection in another baby of a multiple pregnancy is a red flag risk factor (NG195 box 1). Any red flag means investigations then antibiotics without waiting for results (NG195 1.10.3), given within 1 hour of the decision to treat (1.15.2).

n.1: A red flag risk factor applies even when the baby looks well.
n.2: Observation alone is for babies without red flags and with only 1 risk factor or indicator.
n.3: Waiting for the sibling's culture delays treatment of a baby with a red flag.

4.q: Mona, 30, attends the labour ward at 39 weeks in early labour at 3 cm dilatation. A scan confirms an unexpected breech presentation with flexed legs and an average-sized baby. She is unsure what to do. In line with NICE NG121, what should the midwife and obstetrician do?
o: Discuss the risks and offer a choice of labour or caesarean
Advise caesarean, as vaginal breech birth is not offered in labour
Advise she continues labour, as caesarean is unsafe in labour
Attempt external cephalic version before any other discussion
4.w: NICE NG121 1.15.1-1.15.3: discuss the benefits and risks of vaginal birth and caesarean (more serious problems for the woman with caesarean, for the baby with vaginal birth), explain any benefit of caesarean for the baby may be greater in early labour, and offer a choice between continuing labour and caesarean.

n.1: NG121 offers a choice; vaginal breech birth is an option after discussion.
n.2: Caesarean is a valid option in labour; NG121 offers a choice.
n.3: ECV in established labour is not the NG121 approach; informed choice of mode of birth is.

4.q: Emily, 27, is booked for her 20-week scan. She asks the midwife whether a normal scan means her baby will definitely be healthy. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It screens for 11 specific physical conditions and cannot detect every problem
It is a diagnostic test, so any condition it does not find can be ruled out
It confirms or excludes Down's syndrome, which is the main condition it looks for
It checks for all physical and chromosomal conditions, so a normal scan is reassuring
4.w: The FASP 20-week scan (18+0 to 20+6 weeks) looks for 11 physical conditions, including spina bifida, anencephaly, cleft lip, congenital heart disease and Edwards' and Patau's syndromes. Some conditions are not detectable on scan, so a normal result cannot guarantee a healthy baby (FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.1: The anomaly scan is a screening test; a normal scan does not rule out every condition.
n.2: Down's syndrome is not one of the 11 conditions; it is screened for by the combined or quadruple test.
n.3: The scan looks for a defined list of conditions and many conditions cannot be seen on ultrasound.

4.q: Nadia, a midwife, has been diagnosed with depression. She is struggling to concentrate and worries this may affect her clinical decisions. What does the NMC Code require of her?
o: Self-refer to the NMC for a fitness to practise investigation
Tell someone in authority promptly and act to address the concern
Continue working and see whether her concentration improves
Keep her diagnosis private, because health information is confidential
4.w: Code 16.3: tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity if you experience problems that may prevent you working within the Code, taking prompt action to tackle the causes. SPM 5.14 covers recognising vulnerability in oneself.

n.0: A health condition managed with support does not require self-referral to the NMC.
n.2: Waiting to see risks unsafe decisions while she is struggling.
n.3: Her diagnosis is confidential, but the effect on her practice must be raised so that safe adjustments can be made.

4.q: Aisha, 31, is on day 2 and has a perineal tear. She asks that her perineal examination is carried out by a female practitioner for religious reasons. The midwife on shift is male. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that patients cannot choose the gender of NHS staff
Postpone the examination until her 6 to 8 week GP check
Arrange for a female midwife to carry out the examination
Ask her husband to consent to the examination by the male midwife
4.w: SPM 3.27: provide culturally sensitive and individualised care. The NMC Code requires listening and responding to people's preferences (standard 2) and getting properly informed consent before any action (4.2). A reasonable request for a same-gender practitioner should be accommodated where possible without delaying care.

n.0: Reasonable preferences about the gender of the examiner should be accommodated where possible.
n.1: Delaying a perineal assessment for weeks could miss infection or poor healing.
n.3: Only Aisha can consent to her own examination; her husband cannot consent on her behalf.

4.q: Chen, 30, has a scan at 26 weeks showing a serious fetal abnormality. She asks whether termination is still lawful in England. Which statement is correct?
o: Yes, if a court approves the termination first
Yes, under ground (a), as her mental health is affected
Yes, under ground (d), which has no time limit
No, termination is not lawful after 24 weeks on any ground
4.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(1)(d): substantial risk that the child would suffer physical or mental abnormalities so as to be seriously handicapped. Grounds (b), (c) and (d) have no gestational time limit.

n.0: No court approval is required; two practitioners' opinions are needed.
n.1: Ground (a) is limited to 24 weeks, so it does not apply at 26 weeks.
n.3: Grounds (b) to (d) have no time limit, so termination can be lawful after 24 weeks.

4.q: Tom, a community midwife, regularly works through his lunch break and stays late to finish notes. He feels exhausted and short-tempered at home. Which action best reflects compassionate self-care?
o: Carry on as he is, as the workload should settle in a few weeks
Take work notes home to finish them in the evenings
Discuss workload with his manager and protect regular breaks
Reduce the time spent at each postnatal visit to catch up
4.w: SPM 5.15 requires midwives to manage the personal and emotional challenges of work and workload and incorporate compassionate self-care. Raising workload concerns and taking breaks reduces burnout risk and protects safety.

n.0: Ignoring signs of exhaustion increases the risk of burnout and errors.
n.1: Taking notes home risks confidentiality breaches and extends working hours further.
n.3: Cutting visit time reduces quality of care and does not solve the workload problem.

4.q: Sian's electronic patient record login has expired during a night shift. Her colleague offers to stay logged in so Sian can document her care under the colleague's account until IT reset the password in the morning. What should Sian do?
o: Decline and use the trust's downtime process to record her care
Accept and add her initials to each entry made under the account
Accept and copy the entries into her own account in the morning
Decline and write up all her care from memory in the morning
4.w: Code 10.4: attribute every entry to yourself. Using another person's login makes entries falsely attributed and breaches information governance. Trusts have downtime or paper processes so care can be recorded contemporaneously (Code 10.1; SPM 1.23 digital literacy).

n.1: Initials inside another person's account still leave the entries attributed to the wrong person in the system.
n.2: Using the account overnight already breaches attribution, and copying later duplicates the record.
n.3: Waiting until morning means the records are not contemporaneous, when a downtime process exists now.

4.q: Precious, 30, took sertraline throughout her pregnancy for depression and has just given birth to a healthy-looking baby at 39 weeks. She wants to keep her baby with her on the postnatal ward. In line with NICE NG235, what is the most appropriate plan for the baby?
o: Advise Precious to stop sertraline so that she can breastfeed
Give a dose of naloxone to reverse any drug effects at birth
Admit the baby to the neonatal unit for 72 hours of observation
Carry out additional monitoring for signs of withdrawal or PPHN
4.w: NICE NG235 1.11.17 recommends additional monitoring of the baby when the mother has taken an SSRI or SNRI in pregnancy, because of the risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and neonatal withdrawal. This can happen with the baby alongside the mother (SPM 3.18 adverse effects across the continuum of care).

n.0: Sertraline is generally compatible with breastfeeding, and stopping abruptly risks relapse of depression.
n.1: Naloxone reverses opioids, not SSRIs, and is not indicated for a well baby.
n.2: A well baby does not need routine separation and neonatal unit admission; monitoring can be done with the mother.

4.q: Nadia, 33, has a primary postpartum haemorrhage of 1,200 mL after a vaginal birth. Uterotonics have been given and the obstetrician asks the midwife to prepare tranexamic acid as NICE recommends. How should it be given?
o: 500 mg intravenously as a rapid bolus
1 g intramuscularly as a single injection
2 g orally with a glass of water
1 g intravenously over 10 minutes
4.w: NICE NG235 1.10.35: alongside uterotonics, give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes for PPH, repeated after at least 30 minutes if bleeding continues. Tranexamic acid is not a midwives exemption medicine and needs a prescription or PGD.

n.0: The dose is 1 g, and it is given over 10 minutes rather than as a rapid bolus.
n.1: The intramuscular route is not the route recommended for PPH.
n.2: Oral tranexamic acid is not used for acute PPH.

4.q: Jasmine, 27, is 37+2 weeks pregnant. She had one episode of reduced fetal movements yesterday. Today her computerised CTG and a growth scan are normal, and movements have returned. She asks to be induced now 'to be safe'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain induction for reduced movements alone is not recommended before 39 weeks
Advise that induction is not available until 42 weeks
Agree to induction today, as any reduced movements at term justify birth
Book induction for 38 weeks, as this is the standard timing after reduced movements
4.w: SBL v3 element 3: induction before 39+0 weeks is recommended only where there is evidence of fetal compromise or other concerns in addition to RFM. Her concerns are explored, she is encouraged to reattend if movements reduce again, and her preferences are revisited as pregnancy continues.

n.1: NG207 discusses induction from 41+0 weeks for prolonged pregnancy, and 42 weeks is not a cut-off for availability.
n.2: Induction for RFM alone before 39 weeks is not recommended and carries risks of early term birth.
n.3: There is no standard 38-week induction after RFM; SBL v3 uses 38+6 weeks as the point for discussion.

4.q: Priti, 38, has a combined test result giving a 1 in 80 chance of Down's syndrome. She is upset and asks what this means and what happens next. Which response by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Explain that the baby has Down's syndrome and arrange counselling about the pregnancy
Advise a repeat combined test in 2 weeks to see whether the chance changes
Explain it is a higher-chance result and offer NIPT, a diagnostic test or no further testing
Book an amniocentesis, as this is the next step after any higher-chance result
4.w: FASP classes a chance of 1 in 2 to 1 in 150 as a higher-chance result. Screening does not diagnose; she is offered a choice of NIPT, a diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis) or no further testing, and every step is her informed choice (NHS FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.0: A screening result gives a chance, not a diagnosis; 79 in 80 babies with this result would not have Down's syndrome.
n.1: The combined test is not repeated; further information comes from NIPT or diagnostic testing.
n.3: Diagnostic testing is one option among several; it is her choice, not an automatic next step.

4.q: Imani, 31, is in the McRoberts position and the team is managing shoulder dystocia. The midwife delivering the baby is about to apply traction to the head again to check whether the shoulders have been released. What type of traction is appropriate?
o: Lateral traction while rotating the head sideways
Routine axial traction in line with the fetal spine
Strong downward traction towards the floor
Steady upward traction towards the symphysis
4.w: Only routine axial traction, in line with the fetal spine, is used to assess whether manoeuvres have worked. Downward, lateral or excessive traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury (RCOG GTG 42).

n.0: Lateral flexion of the neck stretches the brachial plexus.
n.2: Downward traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury.
n.3: Upward traction is not used to deliver the anterior shoulder.

4.q: A first-time mother asks how she will know when her 4-day-old baby is ready to feed, as she wants to feed responsively. Which is an early feeding cue?
o: Rooting and bringing hands to mouth
Sleeping deeply with regular breathing
Crying loudly with an arched back
Yawning and turning the head away
4.w: Early feeding cues include stirring, rooting, mouth opening and hand to mouth. Crying is a late cue. NICE NG194 defines responsive feeding as feeding in response to the baby's cues.

n.1: Deep sleep with regular breathing is a quiet sleep state, not a feeding cue.
n.2: Crying is a late hunger cue; feeding is easier before the baby is distressed.
n.3: Yawning and turning away are disengagement cues, not feeding cues.

4.q: Rachel, 28, has given birth and the baby is well. The midwife is about to give the uterotonic for an active third stage. Rachel received an oxytocin infusion during labour and now has an IV cannula. Which route and timing for oxytocin is appropriate?
o: 10 units added to the infusion, after the cord has stopped pulsating
5 units by IV injection over 3 to 5 minutes, after controlled cord traction
10 units by rapid IV bolus, after the placenta has delivered
5 units by slow IV injection over 3 to 5 minutes, before the cord is clamped
4.w: NICE NG235 1.10.11 and 1.10.12: give 10 units IM, or 5 units IV by slow injection over 3 to 5 minutes for women who received oxytocin in labour, immediately after the birth of the baby and before the cord is clamped and cut.

n.0: Waiting for the cord to stop pulsating is part of physiological management, and a 10-unit infusion is not the prophylactic regimen.
n.1: The uterotonic is given before cord clamping and traction, not after traction.
n.2: Oxytocin is not given as a rapid 10-unit IV bolus, and it is given after the baby's birth, not after the placenta.

4.q: Lara, 31, has a cord prolapse at a planned home birth. Paramedics arrive to transfer her to the nearest consultant unit. Which position is recommended for her during the ambulance journey?
o: Exaggerated Sims position
Sitting upright on the stretcher
Knee-chest position
Supine with a pillow under her knees
4.w: RCOG GTG 50: knee-chest is potentially unsafe in a moving vehicle, so the exaggerated Sims position (left lateral, head down, pillow under the left hip) is used during ambulance transfer, with elevation of the presenting part.

n.1: Sitting upright increases pressure of the presenting part on the cord.
n.2: Knee-chest is advised while waiting at home but is potentially unsafe in a moving ambulance.
n.3: Supine positioning does not reduce pressure on the cord and risks aortocaval compression.

4.q: Joy, 30, took sertraline throughout pregnancy for anxiety. Her baby is born at term in good condition. Which plan for the baby is in line with NICE NG235?
o: Advise Joy to stop sertraline now to protect the breastfed baby
Routine care, as sertraline is considered safe in pregnancy
Admission to the neonatal unit for 72 hours of observation
Additional monitoring for signs of PPHN or neonatal withdrawal
4.w: NICE NG235 1.11.17: undertake additional monitoring of babies whose mothers took SSRI or SNRI antidepressants in pregnancy, because of a small increased risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) or neonatal withdrawal symptoms.

n.0: Stopping her medicine abruptly risks relapse; decisions about it belong to her prescriber with her.
n.1: NG235 recognises a small increased risk, so additional monitoring is advised.
n.2: A well baby can stay with the mother; routine neonatal unit admission is not required.

4.q: Grace, a senior midwife, notices she has become cynical about women's concerns, feels emotionally drained most days and dreads coming to work. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Keep her feelings to herself so colleagues are not burdened
Wait until her annual appraisal to mention how she feels
Take on extra shifts to keep busy and distract herself
Recognise these as signs of burnout and seek support early
4.w: Emotional exhaustion, cynicism and dread are recognised signs of burnout. SPM 5.14 asks midwives to recognise vulnerability in themselves and act to minimise risks; seeking support early (manager, PMA, occupational health) protects her wellbeing and women's care.

n.0: Withholding her feelings delays support and risks her health and practice.
n.1: Waiting for appraisal delays help that is needed now.
n.2: Extra shifts increase workload and worsen exhaustion.

4.q: Daniel and Mia agree to newborn blood spot screening for their son but do not want him screened for cystic fibrosis. What should the midwife explain?
o: They can decline CF and still have the other conditions screened
They need a consultant's written agreement to decline CF screening
CF screening is a legal requirement and cannot be declined
Declining CF screening means declining the whole blood spot test
4.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: parents can decline screening for sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis and congenital hypothyroidism individually; the inherited metabolic diseases can be declined only as a group. Screening is voluntary and based on verbal consent.

n.1: Parents give or decline consent themselves after information; no consultant agreement is needed.
n.2: Newborn screening is voluntary, so parents can decline any part that is allowed to be declined separately.
n.3: CF can be declined individually without declining the other conditions.

4.q: Comfort, 30, has pre-eclampsia and is in the second stage of labour on the delivery suite. Her blood pressure is controlled on labetalol. She has chosen active management of the third stage. Which uterotonic is most appropriate after the birth of her baby?
o: Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly
Oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM
Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly
Ergometrine 500 micrograms intravenously
4.w: NICE NG235 1.10.11-1.10.12 offers oxytocin 10 units IM for active management. Oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia and severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease (NG235 1.10.9), so oxytocin alone is used here.

n.1: Oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia because ergometrine raises blood pressure.
n.2: Carboprost is a treatment for PPH, not the routine prophylactic uterotonic.
n.3: Ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia and is not a prophylactic option in NG235.

4.q: Day 5: Esi's baby is still not feeding well despite two observed feeds with help on attachment. Esi has sore nipples, the baby makes a clicking noise, and the baby's tongue looks heart-shaped and cannot lift to the roof of the mouth. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise Esi to stop breastfeeding and express for bottle feeds
Advise formula top-ups after every feed until the baby is older
Arrange a tongue-tie assessment and keep supporting breastfeeding
Reassure Esi and review feeding again at the 6 to 8 week check
4.w: NICE NG194 1.5.15: if breastfeeding concerns persist, consider observing more feeds, adjusting positioning, giving expressed milk, referring for additional support such as a lactation consultant, and assessing for tongue-tie. The signs described suggest tongue-tie.

n.0: Stopping breastfeeding is not indicated when a treatable cause is suspected and support is ongoing.
n.1: Routine formula top-ups reduce milk supply and do not address the cause.
n.3: Waiting 6 weeks risks poor weight gain, nipple damage and early cessation of breastfeeding.

5.q: Baby Ruby was breech at 37 weeks. A successful external cephalic version was performed and she was born head first at 40 weeks. Her hip examination at the NIPE newborn check is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer for hip ultrasound, as she has a NIPE hip risk factor
Rely on the 6 to 8 week hip examination to detect any problem
Refer for a hip X-ray at 6 months of age
No further action, as she was head first at birth with normal hips
5.w: NIPE handbook: breech presentation at or after 36 completed weeks, irrespective of presentation at birth or mode of delivery (including after successful ECV), is a hip risk factor. Babies with risk factors are screen positive and need hip ultrasound, usually at 4 to 6 weeks.

n.1: A risk factor means referral for ultrasound now, not reliance on later clinical examination.
n.2: Hip ultrasound, not X-ray, is the NIPE screening test in early infancy.
n.3: Presentation at birth does not remove the risk factor; breech at 36 weeks or later counts even after ECV.

5.q: Nadia, 4 days after birth, had pre-eclampsia and takes enalapril. Her blood pressure is 146/96 mmHg, she has no symptoms and her blood results are stable. She asks to go home. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Keep her in hospital until her blood pressure is below 130/80 mmHg
Transfer with no medical follow-up, as her BP is below 150/100 mmHg
Transfer home with a medical review 2 weeks after the birth
Keep her in hospital until the enalapril can be stopped completely
5.w: NICE NG133: transfer to community care is appropriate when there are no symptoms of pre-eclampsia, BP is 150/100 mmHg or less and blood results are stable or improving. Women still on antihypertensives need medical review at 2 weeks, plus the 6 to 8 week review.

n.0: 130/80 is a treatment target, not a requirement for transfer home.
n.1: Women discharged on antihypertensives need a review at 2 weeks and again at 6 to 8 weeks.
n.3: Treatment can be reduced in the community; it does not need to stop before transfer.

5.q: Baby Ellis was born at term after significant meconium-stained liquor and is being observed on the postnatal ward. At 2 hours the midwife finds a respiratory rate of 70 breaths/min with grunting. Heart rate is 140 beats/min. What should the midwife do?
o: Encourage a breastfeed and recheck after the feed
Wrap the baby and recheck in 30 minutes
Recheck the respiratory rate at the 4-hour observation
Call the neonatal team for urgent review
5.w: NICE NG235 1.11.29: after meconium, escalate to a neonatal clinician if respiratory rate is over 60, there is grunting, heart rate under 100 or over 160, capillary refill over 3 seconds, temperature 38 C or above, saturation under 95% or central cyanosis (SPM 4.6 deterioration in the newborn).

n.0: Feeding a baby with respiratory distress risks aspiration and delays review.
n.1: Warming does not treat respiratory distress and delays review.
n.2: Two red flags (RR over 60 and grunting) need review now, not at the next observation.

5.q: Baby Noor, 2 days old and born at term, needs intravenous antibiotics for suspected early-onset infection. The paediatrician asks the midwife to prepare the first-line regimen. Which regimen does NICE NG195 recommend?
o: Benzylpenicillin with gentamicin
Amoxicillin with cefotaxime
Co-amoxiclav alone
Flucloxacillin with gentamicin
5.w: NG195 1.20.1: use intravenous benzylpenicillin with gentamicin as first-choice empirical treatment for suspected early-onset infection, unless local resistance data indicate otherwise.

n.1: Cefotaxime is added if there is evidence of Gram-negative sepsis (NG195 1.20.8), not used first line with amoxicillin.
n.2: Co-amoxiclav is not the NG195 empirical regimen for early-onset neonatal infection.
n.3: Flucloxacillin is not the NG195 first-line choice for early-onset infection.

5.q: Kiran has type 1 diabetes and has just given birth at 38 weeks. Her baby is well and is with her. According to NICE NG3, when should the baby first be fed and have a blood glucose test?
o: Feed within 30 minutes of birth; test blood glucose at 2 to 4 hours
Test cord blood glucose at birth before the first feed is given
Feed within 4 hours of birth; test blood glucose at 24 hours
Feed within 1 hour of birth; test blood glucose at 30 minutes
5.w: NICE NG3 1.5.3 and 1.5.9: women with diabetes should feed their babies as soon as possible after birth (within 30 minutes) and then every 2 to 3 hours; carry out blood glucose testing routinely at 2 to 4 hours after birth.

n.1: Routine testing is at 2 to 4 hours; cord blood glucose is not the routine NG3 test.
n.2: 4 hours is too long to wait for a feed and 24 hours too late for the first test.
n.3: NG3 advises feeding within 30 minutes, and glucose at 30 minutes is too early for the routine test.

5.q: Esme, 29, is 6 cm dilated on the labour ward when her membranes rupture spontaneously. Within a minute the fetal heart rate drops to 70 beats/min. On vaginal examination the midwife feels a pulsating loop of cord in front of the fetal head. What should the midwife do first?
o: Document the findings before taking further action
Ask Esme to push to speed up the birth
Leave to fetch the CTG machine from the next room
Call for help and elevate the presenting part
5.w: In cord prolapse, call for help immediately (emergency bell, obstetric and neonatal teams) and relieve cord compression by keeping fingers in the vagina to elevate the presenting part, then position her knee-chest or left lateral head down while preparing for birth (RCOG GTG 50; SPM 4.7).

n.0: Documentation follows emergency treatment, not before it.
n.1: At 6 cm pushing will not achieve birth and worsens cord compression.
n.2: Leaving the woman removes the elevation of the presenting part when cord compression is causing bradycardia.

5.q: Claire, a midwife, receives a letter from the NMC stating that a fitness to practise referral has been made about her care of a woman in labour. Her trust is also investigating. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Add the missing details to the labour records before they are requested
Contact the woman who complained to try to resolve the matter directly
Cooperate with both investigations and seek union or defence advice
Decline to respond to the NMC until the trust investigation has ended
5.w: NMC Code 23: cooperate with all investigations and audits. Seeking advice from a union or professional indemnity body is appropriate. Altering records breaches Code 10.3, and contacting the complainant is inappropriate.

n.0: Changing records after the event is falsification under Code 10.3; late entries must be marked as late and must not alter what was written.
n.1: Contacting the complainant directly could be seen as pressure and is not part of a fair investigation.
n.3: Code 23 requires cooperation; the NMC process does not wait for permission from the employer's investigation.

5.q: After a maternal collapse on the labour ward, the woman survived but several staff are visibly shaken. Two days later the ward manager arranges a facilitated team session. What is the main aim of this session?
o: To support staff wellbeing and help the team process the event
To ask staff to write statements for the coroner
To replace the formal learning response with an informal one
To decide which staff members should be moved off the labour ward
5.w: Facilitated team sessions after traumatic events support staff wellbeing, help people make sense of what happened and reduce the risk of lasting psychological harm, while learning continues through formal processes (SPM 5.14, 5.15).

n.1: The woman survived; coroner statements are not relevant here.
n.2: Team support sessions do not replace formal learning responses.
n.3: Moving staff is not the aim and may feel punitive.

5.q: Selin, 31, is 14 days postnatal. At a home visit she answers yes to both depression identification questions. She is caring for her baby, has no thoughts of self-harm and no history of severe mental illness. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise her to stop breastfeeding so that she can start antidepressants
Consider a full assessment with the EPDS or PHQ-9, or refer to her GP
Refer her urgently to the crisis team for assessment within 4 hours
Reassure her that these are baby blues and review her in four weeks
5.w: CG192 1.5.5: if a woman responds positively to either depression identification question, consider a full assessment using the EPDS or PHQ-9 or refer her to her GP (or to a mental health professional if a severe problem is suspected).

n.0: Breastfeeding does not need to stop to treat depression, and medication decisions follow assessment.
n.2: A 4-hour emergency assessment is for suspected postpartum psychosis; Selin has no features of psychosis or high risk.
n.3: Low mood persisting at two weeks needs assessment; dismissing it as baby blues and waiting four weeks risks missing postnatal depression.

5.q: Mariam, 31, is breastfeeding on the first day after birth. She is worried because she can only express a few drops of thick yellow milk and thinks her baby is not getting enough. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Colostrum is low in antibodies, which rise once her mature milk arrives
Colostrum comes in small amounts, is rich in antibodies and suits a newborn's needs
Colostrum is too concentrated for a newborn and should be expressed and discarded
Colostrum is mainly water, so formula top-ups are needed until her milk comes in
5.w: Colostrum is produced in small volumes in the first days, is concentrated and rich in immunoglobulins (especially secretory IgA) and protective factors, and meets the needs of a healthy term newborn. NG194 1.5.12 asks midwives to explain how much milk is produced in the early stages.

n.0: Colostrum has the highest concentration of antibodies of any milk.
n.2: Colostrum should be given to the baby, not discarded.
n.3: Colostrum is nutrient-dense, not mainly water; routine formula top-ups are not clinically indicated (NG194 1.5.12).

5.q: A public health midwife is redesigning antenatal smoking cessation support across a city with large differences in deprivation between areas. Which approach best reflects proportionate universalism?
o: Offer support to women who ask for it at booking
Offer the same level of support to every woman across the city
Offer support to women in the most deprived areas and stop it elsewhere
Offer support to all women, with intensity rising with disadvantage
5.w: Proportionate universalism (Marmot review, Fair Society, Healthy Lives, 2010) means actions are universal but with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage. SPM 2.9 asks midwives to consider the impact of social determinants of health.

n.0: Waiting for requests widens inequalities; women facing most disadvantage are least likely to ask.
n.1: Equal provision does not narrow inequalities because need is greater in deprived groups.
n.2: Targeting deprived areas alone misses disadvantaged women elsewhere and is not universal.

5.q: During a vaginal examination in labour, Abby, 23, who had agreed to the examination, says, "Please stop, it hurts too much." The midwife has nearly finished assessing the cervix. What should the midwife do?
o: Continue, as Abby gave consent before it started
Finish quickly as the examination is nearly complete
Stop the examination at once and talk with Abby
Pause briefly, then continue once Abby has had a contraction
5.w: Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Once Abby asks to stop, continuing would be without consent (Code 4.2; SPM 1.20). The midwife stops, supports her and discusses options.

n.0: Earlier consent does not continue once she has withdrawn it.
n.1: Finishing after consent has been withdrawn is examination without consent, however near completion.
n.3: Continuing after a pause without her renewed agreement still ignores the withdrawal of consent.

5.q: Jade, 29, is in the obstetric unit with suspected sepsis 3 days after birth. She meets high-risk criteria, her lactate is 4.6 mmol/L and her systolic blood pressure is 88 mmHg. The doctor asks the midwife to give an intravenous fluid bolus. What does NICE NG255 recommend?
o: 1000 mL of 5% glucose given over 1 hour
500 mL of crystalloid given over 4 hours
500 mL crystalloid over under 15 minutes
250 mL of colloid given over 30 minutes
5.w: NICE NG255 1.9.2: use crystalloids containing sodium 130-154 mmol/L as a 500 mL bolus over less than 15 minutes. With lactate over 4 or systolic 90 or less, give the bolus within 1 hour and refer to critical care (1.7.4); reassess, and give a second bolus if no improvement (1.9.4).

n.0: 5% glucose does not contain sodium in the recommended range and the volume and rate are wrong.
n.1: Giving the bolus over 4 hours is far slower than recommended.
n.3: NG255 recommends crystalloid in 500 mL boluses, not colloid.

5.q: The labour ward coordinator asks Helen, a midwife, to discharge Mrs Ahmed, 1 day after birth, to free a bed. Helen has just recorded a blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg and Mrs Ahmed has a headache. What should Helen do?
o: Explain why discharge is unsafe and request urgent medical review
Discharge her with advice to see the GP if the headache continues
Recheck the blood pressure in 4 hours before deciding on discharge
Discharge her and arrange a community blood pressure check tomorrow
5.w: SPM 1.18: recognise external pressures that may unduly influence decisions. A blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg with a headache after birth may be postnatal pre-eclampsia and needs urgent medical assessment (NICE NG133). Helen explains her rationale and escalates rather than discharging.

n.1: Discharging with GP advice ignores a possible postnatal pre-eclampsia that needs urgent review now.
n.2: Waiting 4 hours before acting delays the urgent review that hypertension with headache requires.
n.3: A check tomorrow delays assessment of a woman with hypertension and headache today.

5.q: A community midwife visits baby Rosa, aged 5 days, at home. According to NICE NG194, which finding is a red flag for serious illness?
o: Sleeping for 3 hours between feeds
Axillary temperature of 35.8 C
Small possets of milk after feeds
Respiratory rate of 52 breaths/min
5.w: NICE NG194 1.4.9: red flags for serious illness in young babies include a temperature of 38 C or over or under 36 C, respiratory rate over 60, grunting, chest indrawing, pallor or mottling, a weak or high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, seizures, bilious or projectile vomiting and non-blanching rash.

n.0: Sleeping 3 hours between feeds is normal for many newborns.
n.2: Small possets are common; bilious or forceful (projectile) vomiting is the red flag.
n.3: A respiratory rate of 52 is within the normal newborn range (the red flag is over 60).

5.q: Kiera, 32, is medically fit for discharge on day 2. Her baby needs phototherapy on the postnatal ward for at least another 24 hours. Kiera is breastfeeding. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Discharge Kiera and give the baby formula top-ups overnight
Discharge Kiera and ask her to visit for feeds
Transfer the baby to the neonatal unit so that Kiera can go home
Offer Kiera the option to stay with her baby while treatment continues
5.w: SPM 2.6 requires planning care for woman and newborn as a unit. Keeping the mother with her baby supports breastfeeding during phototherapy, with breaks for feeds of up to 30 minutes (CG98).

n.0: Breastfed babies having phototherapy should not have extra fluids routinely; expressed breast milk is used if needed (CG98).
n.1: Visiting for feeds separates them and makes responsive breastfeeding difficult.
n.2: Moving a well baby to the neonatal unit for convenience separates them and uses a cot without clinical need.

5.q: Anya, 33, is 41+2 weeks in an uncomplicated first pregnancy. After a full discussion of the risks and benefits, she declines induction of labour. What is the most appropriate response by the midwife?
o: Ask her partner to talk with her about changing her decision
Respect her decision and offer extra monitoring from 42 weeks
Refer her to the safeguarding team as the baby may be at risk
Book the induction anyway in case she changes her mind
5.w: A woman with capacity may decline induction. NICE NG207 advises that if she chooses not to have induction, her decision is respected and additional monitoring is offered from 42 weeks (twice-weekly CTG and ultrasound of the maximum amniotic pool depth). SPM 1.21.

n.0: Using her partner to pressure her undermines a voluntary decision.
n.2: Declining induction is a lawful choice, not a safeguarding concern.
n.3: Booking a procedure she has declined disregards her decision.

5.q: On a day shift the maternity unit falls below its agreed minimum midwifery staffing level, and redeployment from the community has not filled the gap. Following Ockenden, what should happen next?
o: Ask midwives to skip their breaks until the shift is over
Escalate under the staffing policy to senior managers and on-call leaders
Ask student midwives to cover the shortfall under indirect supervision
Continue as normal, as staffing usually improves in the afternoon
5.w: Ockenden IEA 2 (safe staffing): trusts must maintain a clear escalation and mitigation policy when staffing falls below minimum levels, escalating to senior management, obstetric leads, the chief nurse, medical director and others. SPM 5.5 links safe staffing with safety and quality of care.

n.0: Removing breaks increases fatigue and error; it is not a mitigation strategy.
n.2: Students are supernumerary learners and cannot be counted in staffing numbers.
n.3: Hoping staffing improves leaves women at risk and ignores the escalation policy.

5.q: Kerry has been a registered midwife for 4 years and wants to prescribe medicines such as antibiotics for women with postnatal infections in her community caseload. What must happen before she can prescribe independently?
o: She must hold a patient group direction for each antibiotic she uses
She must complete an NMC-approved prescribing programme and have it recorded
She must complete 2 years of community practice and a local competency
She must be authorised in writing by her head of midwifery
5.w: Only nurses and midwives who have completed an NMC-approved prescribing qualification and had it recorded on the register can prescribe (Code 18, note to 18.5). SPM 3.19 expects the ability to progress to a prescribing qualification after registration.

n.0: A PGD allows supply or administration to a group; it is not prescribing.
n.2: Length of experience and a local competency do not confer prescribing rights.
n.3: A head of midwifery cannot authorise prescribing; it requires a recorded qualification.

5.q: Mei, 30, has a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks. Her fasting plasma glucose is 5.8 mmol/L and her 2-hour value is 7.1 mmol/L. How should these results be interpreted?
o: The test is normal because the 2-hour value is below 7.8 mmol/L
The result is borderline and the OGTT should be repeated at 32 weeks of pregnancy
She has type 2 diabetes because the fasting value is above 5.5 mmol/L at 26 weeks
She has gestational diabetes because the fasting value is 5.6 mmol/L or above
5.w: NG3 1.2.8 diagnoses gestational diabetes if the fasting plasma glucose is 5.6 mmol/L or above OR the 2-hour value is 7.8 mmol/L or above. Either threshold is enough.

n.0: Both values do not have to be raised; a fasting level of 5.8 mmol/L alone meets the diagnostic criterion.
n.1: NG3 has no borderline category requiring repeat testing; the threshold is met now.
n.2: These are the diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes, not type 2 diabetes.

5.q: Ellie, 27, is exclusively breastfeeding her 10-day-old baby. She asks when she could become pregnant again if she does not use contraception. What should the midwife tell her?
o: From 6 weeks after the birth, after her postnatal check
From 3 weeks after the birth, even while breastfeeding
Once her periods have returned
Once she stops breastfeeding completely
5.w: Women can become pregnant from 3 weeks (day 21) after giving birth, including when breastfeeding and before periods return (NHS; FSRH Contraception After Pregnancy). NG194 1.2.1 asks midwives to discuss contraception at postnatal contacts (SPM 3.4).

n.0: Ovulation can occur from about day 21, before the 6 to 8 week check.
n.2: Ovulation happens before the first period, so she can conceive before any bleeding.
n.3: Breastfeeding reduces but does not remove the chance of pregnancy unless all LAM criteria are met.

5.q: Isla and Tom have a healthy term baby and plan to bed share. Neither smokes, drinks or takes medication. Which advice about safer bed sharing is accurate?
o: Place the baby on a soft mattress topper, lying on her side to feed
Place the baby on the sofa with a parent when very tired
Use a firm, flat mattress with the baby face up, away from pillows
Place the baby between the parents with the duvet tucked in
5.w: NG194 1.3.14: discuss safer bed sharing: firm, flat mattress; baby lying face up; not sleeping on a sofa or chair with the baby; no pillows or duvets near the baby; no other children or pets in the bed.

n.0: Babies should sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface.
n.1: Sleeping with a baby on a sofa or chair is particularly dangerous.
n.3: Duvets and pillows near the baby, and lying between parents, increase risk.

5.q: Bisi, 31, is 34 weeks pregnant and has had a cardiac arrest on the antenatal ward. CPR with manual uterine displacement is under way. The obstetric registrar says a resuscitative hysterotomy is needed. Where should it be performed?
o: Where she arrested, as soon as possible
In the obstetric theatre, after transfer on the bed
In the intensive care unit, once stabilised
In the emergency department, after a CT scan
5.w: RCUK 2025: resuscitative hysterotomy is time-sensitive; preparation should begin early and it should be performed as soon as possible at the site of the cardiac arrest by a skilled team. Moving her delays it and interrupts CPR.

n.1: Transfer to theatre delays the procedure and interrupts effective CPR.
n.2: Waiting for stabilisation defeats the purpose; the hysterotomy is part of resuscitation.
n.3: Imaging is not part of the decision and would cause harmful delay.

5.q: After a discussion, Tamsin, 27, declines group B streptococcus antibiotics in labour despite known carriage. Which record entry best documents her decision?
o: "Risks and options explained; Tamsin declines and understands."
"Refused antibiotics against medical advice; plan as before."
"Advised strongly but refused. Not my responsibility."
"Declined GBS antibiotics. Aware of risks."
5.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to refuse care; Code 10.2: record risks and steps taken. The entry shows the information given, her decision and her understanding.

n.1: 'Plan as before' and 'against advice' do not record the information given or a revised plan.
n.2: Disclaiming responsibility is unprofessional and does not record the discussion.
n.3: 'Aware of risks' does not show what information was given.

5.q: Sienna, 30, is 40+5 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated first pregnancy. She asks the midwife at what point induction of labour will be discussed with her. What is the most accurate answer?
o: From 41+0 weeks, as some risks rise if the pregnancy continues beyond then
From 39+0 weeks, as part of the routine membrane sweep discussion
From 42+0 weeks, as risks do not increase until the pregnancy is post-term
From 40+0 weeks, as every pregnancy should be induced at the due date
5.w: NICE NG207 1.2.3 and 1.2.4: explain that risks such as caesarean birth, neonatal unit admission, stillbirth and neonatal death may increase beyond 41+0 weeks, and discuss that induction from 41+0 weeks may reduce these risks, alongside its impact on her birth experience.

n.1: From 39+0 weeks sweeping is discussed; induction for prolonged pregnancy is discussed from 41+0.
n.2: NG207 describes rising risks after 41+0 weeks, so waiting until 42+0 to discuss is too late.
n.3: Induction is not offered routinely at the due date in an uncomplicated pregnancy.

5.q: Hannah, 32, is having a planned home birth. Her community midwife has no prescription chart or patient group directions for this birth. Which medicine can the registered midwife lawfully administer under the midwives exemptions in Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012?
o: Intramuscular oxytocin for the third stage
Intravenous tranexamic acid for heavy bleeding
Intravenous co-amoxiclav for suspected infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for a seizure
5.w: HMR 2012 Schedule 17 lists the parenteral prescription-only medicines a registered midwife may administer in professional practice, including oxytocins (natural and synthetic), ergometrine, carboprost, anti-D, phytomenadione and others (SPM 3.19 midwives exemptions).

n.1: Tranexamic acid is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.
n.2: Antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav are not on the Schedule 17 list.
n.3: Magnesium sulfate is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.

5.q: Leanne is the midwife in charge of a maternity unit. Three midwifery red flag events have been reported in the past hour. What is her responsibility under NICE NG4?
o: Decide whether staffing is the cause and what action is needed
Record the events and review them at the monthly governance meeting
Close the unit to all admissions until the next shift starts
Ask the staff who reported them to resolve the issues themselves
5.w: NG4 box 3: when a red flag event occurs, the midwife in charge should be notified and should determine whether midwifery staffing is the cause and the action needed, such as redeploying staff or escalating per the staffing policy.

n.1: Monthly review is part of monitoring, but immediate assessment and action are needed now.
n.2: Closure may be one option under escalation policy, but it is not automatic and other actions are considered first.
n.3: The midwife in charge holds responsibility for assessing staffing and acting on red flags.

5.q: Ruby, 31, is in established labour in an obstetric unit and asks for pethidine. The midwife explains its effects and Ruby consents. Under NICE intrapartum guidance, what else should be given with the intramuscular opioid?
o: Continuous oxygen by face mask
An antiemetic
Naloxone, to prevent respiratory depression
Intravenous fluids
5.w: NICE NG235 1.6.19: if an intravenous or intramuscular opioid is used, also administer an antiemetic. She should be told opioids give limited pain relief and may cause drowsiness, nausea and vomiting, and neonatal respiratory depression that may affect breastfeeding (1.6.18).

n.0: Routine oxygen is not part of opioid administration.
n.2: Naloxone reverses opioid effects when respiratory depression occurs; it is not given routinely alongside the opioid.
n.3: IV fluids are not routinely needed with an IM opioid.

5.q: Which health benefit for the baby should a midwife include when discussing breastfeeding with expectant parents?
o: A lower risk of developmental dysplasia of the hip
A lower risk of physiological jaundice
Fewer gastrointestinal and respiratory infections
A lower risk of tongue-tie
5.w: Breastfed babies have fewer gastrointestinal, respiratory and ear infections and a lower risk of sudden infant death. NG194 1.5.2: discuss nutritional and health benefits for the baby (SPM 3.6).

n.0: Hip dysplasia is not influenced by feeding method.
n.1: Breastfed babies are not at lower risk of jaundice; jaundice can be more prolonged.
n.3: Tongue-tie is congenital and not affected by feeding method.

5.q: Ana, 30, has had a straightforward birth and chose active management. She received IM oxytocin when the baby was born. At 3 minutes the cord is clamped and cut. The uterus is soft and the cord has not lengthened. When should controlled cord traction begin?
o: At the next contraction, whether or not separation has occurred
Immediately after the cord is cut, to speed up the third stage
After signs of separation, such as cord lengthening and a gush of blood
After 30 minutes, if the placenta has not delivered spontaneously
5.w: NICE NG235 1.10.15: perform controlled cord traction as part of active management only after oxytocin and signs of placental separation (lengthening of the cord, a small gush of blood, the uterus becoming firm and rising). Traction before separation risks cord snapping or uterine inversion.

n.0: Contractions alone do not show separation; traction waits for signs of separation.
n.1: Traction before separation risks cord avulsion or uterine inversion.
n.3: 30 minutes is when a prolonged third stage is diagnosed in active management, not the timing of traction.

5.q: Lucy and Sarah are a married couple expecting their first baby; Lucy is pregnant. At a postnatal visit, the midwife is completing the newborn records. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask the couple how they each wish to be named and involved
Record Sarah as 'friend' until parental responsibility is confirmed
Record Sarah as 'partner' and ask Lucy to answer all questions
Address questions about the baby to Lucy as the birth mother
5.w: SPM 1.10 and Code 1.3: avoid assumptions, recognise diversity and involve partners and family as the woman wishes. Asking how the couple wish to be named and involved is respectful and person-centred.

n.1: Recording a spouse and co-parent as 'friend' is inaccurate and disrespectful; the couple's own description of their relationship should guide the record.
n.2: Directing everything to Lucy excludes Sarah, who is a parent, without asking the couple's wishes.
n.3: Directing questions to the birth mother alone assumes their roles without asking them.

5.q: At the NIPE newborn examination of baby Theo, born at 40 weeks, the right testis is in the scrotum. The left testis is palpable in the groin but cannot be brought into the scrotum. There is no hypospadias. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Non-urgent review by the GP at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
Reassurance with no follow-up, as one testis is in the scrotum
Review by a senior paediatrician within 24 hours of the examination
Testicular ultrasound within 2 weeks of the examination
5.w: NIPE handbook: one or both testes palpable but not in the scrotum, without hypospadias, is screen positive on the non-urgent pathway: GP review at the 6 to 8 week NIPE infant examination. Urgent 24-hour review is for impalpable testes or hypospadias with an undescended testis.

n.1: A unilateral undescended testis is screen positive and needs follow-up.
n.2: 24-hour senior review is for bilateral or unilateral impalpable testes, or a palpable undescended testis with hypospadias.
n.3: Ultrasound within 2 weeks is not part of the NIPE testes pathway.

5.q: After the placenta is delivered, Lily, 28, has a firm, well-contracted uterus at the level of the umbilicus and only a small blood loss. A student asks what mainly stops bleeding from the placental site. What is the correct answer?
o: Vasoconstriction of the uterine arteries by circulating adrenaline
Pressure from the full bladder pressing on the placental site
Rapid formation of clot over the placental site by clotting factors
Uterine muscle contraction and retraction compressing the vessels
5.w: The interlacing, oblique fibres of the myometrium contract and retract around the spiral arteries, acting as 'living ligatures'. Clotting helps, but uterine tone is the main mechanism, which is why atony is the commonest cause of PPH (SPM 3.12.3).

n.0: Adrenaline-driven vasoconstriction is not the main way placental site bleeding is controlled.
n.1: A full bladder impedes uterine contraction and increases bleeding risk; it does not compress the placental site.
n.2: Clotting contributes, but without uterine contraction bleeding continues; uterine tone is the main mechanism.

5.q: Poppy, 31, is 39+2 weeks pregnant and attends with a first episode of reduced fetal movements. The CTG is normal and her SFH is on her usual centile. Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Explain induction is not considered until 41+0 weeks of pregnancy
Discuss induction of labour with her, as she is beyond 38+6 weeks
Arrange twice-weekly CTGs until she reaches 41 weeks
Recommend an expedited caesarean birth today
5.w: SBL v3 element 3: for RFM after 38+6 weeks, discuss induction of labour with all women (risks, benefits and her wishes), and offer birth to those with recurrent RFM after 38+6 weeks. At 39 weeks and beyond induction is not associated with more caesarean births.

n.0: 41+0 is the threshold for discussing induction for prolonged pregnancy (NG207), not for RFM after 38+6 weeks.
n.2: Serial CTG monitoring is not the recommended response; a discussion about induction is.
n.3: There is no indication for caesarean birth with a normal CTG; induction is discussed as an option.

5.q: Day 5: Esi's baby is still not feeding well despite two observed feeds with help on attachment. Esi has sore nipples, the baby makes a clicking noise, and the baby's tongue looks heart-shaped and cannot lift to the roof of the mouth. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise Esi to stop breastfeeding and express for bottle feeds
Advise formula top-ups after every feed until the baby is older
Arrange a tongue-tie assessment and keep supporting breastfeeding
Reassure Esi and review feeding again at the 6 to 8 week check
5.w: NICE NG194 1.5.15: if breastfeeding concerns persist, consider observing more feeds, adjusting positioning, giving expressed milk, referring for additional support such as a lactation consultant, and assessing for tongue-tie. The signs described suggest tongue-tie.

n.0: Stopping breastfeeding is not indicated when a treatable cause is suspected and support is ongoing.
n.1: Routine formula top-ups reduce milk supply and do not address the cause.
n.3: Waiting 6 weeks risks poor weight gain, nipple damage and early cessation of breastfeeding.

5.q: Jess is caring for a woman in established labour when the coordinator asks her to also take over care of a second woman in established labour in the next room, as no other midwife is free. Which statement is most accurate?
o: This is a matter for the coordinator, so Jess has no duty to raise a concern
This is acceptable when both women are low risk and their labours are progressing normally
This is acceptable if a maternity support worker stays with one of the women
This is a red flag event; she should raise it with the coordinator for escalation
5.w: NICE NG235 recommends one-to-one care in established labour, and NG4 box 3 lists any occasion when one midwife cannot provide continuous one-to-one care in established labour as a red flag. Code 16.1 and 16.2 require raising concerns about safety and being asked to practise beyond safe limits.

n.0: Every registrant has a duty under Code 16 to raise concerns; it is not left to the coordinator alone.
n.1: Low risk does not remove the standard of one-to-one midwifery care in established labour.
n.2: A support worker cannot replace the midwife in providing one-to-one care in established labour.

5.q: Baby Ava weighed 3,600 g at birth. On day 3 she weighs 3,240 g. What percentage of her birth weight has she lost?
5.w: Loss = 3,600 - 3,240 = 360 g. Percentage = 360 / 3,600 x 100 = 10%. Calculating weight loss accurately supports feeding assessment (SPM 1.23; NICE NG194).

n.0: 9% would be a loss of 324 g, not 360 g.
n.1: 11% would be a loss of about 396 g, not 360 g.
n.2: 36% confuses the 360 g loss with a percentage.

5.q: Jess, 27, smokes 15 cigarettes a day and wants to stop. Her tobacco dependence adviser suggests nicotine patches. She is worried nicotine will harm her baby. What information should the midwife give?
o: NRT risks are much lower than smoking, and patches should be removed at bedtime
NRT is safe in pregnancy and patches should be worn for 24 hours a day
NRT carries the same risks as smoking, so cutting down is safer
NRT should be avoided until 12 weeks, when varenicline is a safer choice
5.w: NG209 1.20.6-1.20.11: consider NRT with behavioural support at the earliest opportunity; explain that risks from NRT are much lower than smoking; advise removing patches before bed; do not offer varenicline, bupropion or cytisinicline in pregnancy.

n.1: NICE advises removing patches before going to bed in pregnancy (NG209 1.20.9).
n.2: Most smoking harm comes from other components of smoke, not nicotine; NRT is much safer.
n.3: Varenicline is not offered in pregnancy, and NRT should be considered at the earliest opportunity.

5.q: Holly is writing a reflective account using Gibbs' reflective cycle about a difficult conversation with a bereaved family. She has described the event, explored her feelings and evaluated what was good and bad. Which stage comes next?
o: Action plan
Analysis
Description
Conclusion
5.w: Gibbs' cycle runs: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan. After evaluation comes analysis, making sense of the situation and drawing on theory or evidence (SPM 5.13.1).

n.0: The action plan is the final stage, after the conclusion.
n.2: Description is the first stage, which Holly has already completed.
n.3: The conclusion follows analysis.

5.q: Freya, 29, is 30 weeks pregnant. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and she feels well. A dipstick shows 1+ protein, with no leucocytes or nitrites. Under NICE hypertension in pregnancy guidance, what should happen next to assess the proteinuria?
o: Send a first morning urine sample to measure protein
Repeat the dipstick at her next routine appointment
Arrange a 24-hour urine collection to measure total protein
Quantify with a protein:creatinine or albumin:creatinine ratio
5.w: If dipstick screening is positive (1+ or more), use albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio to quantify proteinuria, interpreted alongside a full clinical review (NICE NG133 1.2.1, 1.2.3).

n.0: NICE advises not to use a first morning void to quantify proteinuria (NG133 1.2.4).
n.1: A positive dipstick needs quantification now; waiting for the next routine visit delays assessment.
n.2: NICE advises against routine 24-hour urine collection to quantify proteinuria (NG133 1.2.5).

5.q: Rosa, 31, is 20 weeks pregnant and has been invited to join a randomised trial of an iron supplement. She tells her midwife she is worried that saying no will mean she is treated differently at the clinic. Which response by the midwife is best?
o: 'If you decline, you will be booked into the consultant clinic instead.'
'Your partner will also need to agree because the baby is involved.'
'You can decline, or withdraw later, and your care will not change.'
'You need to give your answer today so that the trial can include you.'
5.w: Valid consent to research must be voluntary and informed; participants can decline or withdraw at any time without their standard care being affected (UK Policy Framework for Health and Social Care Research; Code 4.2 make sure you get properly informed consent). A pregnant woman with capacity gives her own consent.

n.0: Linking refusal to a change in her care pathway is coercive and has no clinical basis.
n.1: A pregnant woman with capacity consents for herself; the partner's agreement is not a legal requirement for her participation.
n.3: Pressure to decide on the spot undermines voluntary consent; she should have time to consider the information.

5.q: Emily, 29, is in labour and understands the information about an epidural but forgets the details within about 20 minutes. She has weighed it up and says she wants one. Which statement about her capacity is correct?
o: She lacks capacity as she cannot retain the details for long
She lacks capacity until a psychiatrist has assessed her
She has capacity once her birth partner confirms her wishes
She has capacity, as brief retention is enough to decide
5.w: MCA 2005 s3(3): being able to retain information for a short period only does not prevent a person being regarded as able to make the decision.

n.0: Short retention is enough under s3(3).
n.1: Any professional making the decision can assess capacity; a psychiatrist is not required.
n.2: A partner's confirmation is not part of the capacity test.

5.q: A midwife is about to perform a vaginal examination in labour. Which statement about the form of consent is correct?
o: Consent is implied once a woman is admitted in labour
Written consent is legally required for any intimate examination
Verbal consent is valid and should be documented
Consent can be given by her birth partner on her behalf
5.w: Consent may be verbal, written or non-verbal; what matters is that it is informed, voluntary and given by a person with capacity. Code 4.2: get properly informed consent and document it before any action.

n.0: Admission in labour does not imply consent to each examination; consent is needed for each intervention.
n.1: No law requires written consent for every intimate examination; verbal consent is valid when informed and voluntary.
n.3: A birth partner cannot consent for an adult woman with capacity.

5.q: Leah, 33, has asthma and is 35 weeks pregnant. She is admitted with a blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg and a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia. Oral labetalol has been prescribed by the junior doctor. As the midwife prepares the first dose, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Withhold it and ask the prescriber to review because of her asthma
Give the labetalol after she has used her salbutamol inhaler
Give oral methyldopa from stock instead and record the change
Give the labetalol and check her peak flow every hour afterwards
5.w: Labetalol is a beta-blocker and is unsuitable in asthma because of the risk of bronchospasm. NICE NG133 recommends labetalol first line but nifedipine for women in whom labetalol is not suitable, so the midwife withholds the dose and asks the prescriber to review (SPM 3.18 contraindications; Code 18).

n.1: Pre-treatment with salbutamol does not make a contraindicated beta-blocker safe.
n.2: A midwife cannot substitute a different antihypertensive without a prescription.
n.3: Monitoring peak flow does not remove the risk of bronchospasm from a beta-blocker in asthma.

5.q: Ola, 33, is on continuous CTG in established labour. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes, the baseline is 140 beats per minute and there are no decelerations. Variability has been 3 to 4 beats per minute for the last 40 minutes. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Suspicious
Normal
Need for urgent intervention
Pathological
5.w: Variability under 5 beats per minute for 30 to 50 minutes is an amber feature (NICE NG229 1.4.18). Contractions, baseline and decelerations are white. One amber feature makes the CTG suspicious (NG229 1.4.32), prompting a full risk assessment and conservative measures.

n.1: A normal CTG has all four features white; reduced variability for 40 minutes is amber.
n.2: NG229 uses normal, suspicious and pathological; this is not one of its categories.
n.3: Pathological needs one red feature or two or more amber features; there is one amber feature.

5.q: Baby Ana, whose mother has type 2 diabetes, is 5 hours old. The midwife finds her jittery and floppy, with a weak cry, and she is not interested in feeding. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Give a feed and recheck the blood glucose in 3 hours
Offer skin-to-skin contact and observe her for 1 hour
Wait for a laboratory glucose result before taking action
Test blood glucose and arrange IV dextrose as soon as possible
5.w: NICE NG3 1.5.11: for babies with clinical signs of hypoglycaemia, test blood glucose and provide intravenous dextrose as soon as possible. NG3 1.5.5: hypoglycaemia with abnormal clinical signs is a reason for neonatal unit admission.
