n.0: A baby with abnormal signs needs urgent treatment; waiting 3 hours is unsafe.
n.1: Skin-to-skin does not treat symptomatic hypoglycaemia.
n.2: Treatment should not be delayed for a laboratory result when signs are present.

5.q: Nicola, 26, is 40 minutes after birth with ongoing trickling blood loss. On palpation her uterus is soft and displaced to the right, above the umbilicus. She has not passed urine since before the birth. Uterine massage has been started. What is the next most appropriate action?
o: Empty her bladder, using a catheter if she cannot void
Repeat the observations in 15 minutes and review the loss
Give a second dose of oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly
Encourage her to put the baby to the breast for 30 minutes
5.w: A full bladder displaces the uterus and stops it contracting effectively. NICE NG235 1.10.33 includes emptying the bladder alongside uterine massage, uterotonics and IV fluids in the immediate treatment of PPH (SPM 4.8 first-line management).

n.1: Waiting allows ongoing bleeding; the cause should be treated now.
n.2: A repeat IM oxytocin dose is not the NG235 treatment step, and a full bladder will still stop the uterus contracting.
n.3: Breastfeeding helps but does not correct a uterus displaced by a full bladder.

5.q: Kayleigh, 25, is 8 weeks pregnant and attends her booking appointment. She tells the midwife for the first time that she uses cocaine most weekends and drinks heavily. She is anxious and asks whether this will be reported. Which response is most appropriate first?
o: Make a referral to the police because she has disclosed illegal drug use
Offer referral to a substance misuse service and explain how care is coordinated
Tell her the booking cannot continue until she has stopped using any drugs
Record the disclosure and plan to discuss it again at the 28-week visit
5.w: NICE CG110 1.2.7: the first time a woman who misuses substances discloses that she is pregnant, offer referral to an appropriate substance misuse programme. Care is coordinated across agencies (1.2.2, 1.2.3) with a named midwife or doctor (1.2.4), and staff attitudes should not deter her from using services (1.2.1).

n.0: Drug use disclosed in a health consultation is not a police matter; the concern is her and her baby's health and wellbeing.
n.2: Making care conditional on abstinence creates a barrier that CG110 1.2.1 asks staff to overcome.
n.3: Delaying discussion until 28 weeks wastes months of potential support and treatment.

5.q: During a major postpartum haemorrhage in the birth room, the team is busy treating Rachel, 29. Her partner is standing in the corner, crying and asking repeatedly what is happening. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Allocate a team member to stay with them and explain
Ask him to wait outside until the emergency is over
Tell him everything is fine so that he stays calm
Ask the most junior doctor to explain once Rachel is stable
5.w: NICE NG235 1.10.36: allocate a member of the healthcare team to stay with the woman and her birth companions, explain what is happening, answer questions and offer support throughout the emergency (SPM 4.7).

n.1: Sending him out without support or information is not in line with NG235.
n.2: False reassurance is dishonest and undermines trust (Code 20.2).
n.3: Support should be given during the emergency, not deferred until afterwards.

5.q: Sophie, 28, wants a water birth in the alongside midwifery unit but is also keen to have the option of an epidural. What information should the midwife give her?
o: An epidural would mean transfer to the obstetric unit on the same site
An epidural can be sited in the midwifery unit by the on-call anaesthetist
An epidural can be given if she leaves the pool for 2 hours first
An epidural is not available to women who planned a midwife-led birth
5.w: NG235 1.6.26: regional analgesia is available only in obstetric units. When planning place of birth women should be told which analgesia is available in each setting, and that an epidural in a midwife-led setting requires transfer.

n.1: Epidurals are available in obstetric units only (NG235 1.6.26).
n.2: The 2-hour rule applies to opioids before entering water, not to epidurals in a midwifery unit (NG235 1.6.20).
n.3: She can change her mind and request an epidural; it means transfer to the obstetric unit.

5.q: Rosa, 33, is booking at 9 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her BMI is 32 and her mother has type 2 diabetes. Her first baby weighed 3.6 kg. She has no other risk factors. Which plan for gestational diabetes is most appropriate?
o: Arrange a random blood glucose test today and repeat it at 28 weeks
Test her urine for glucose at every antenatal appointment
Check HbA1c at booking and repeat it at 28 weeks
Offer a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
5.w: Rosa has two risk factors for gestational diabetes (BMI above 30 and a first-degree relative with diabetes). NICE recommends a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks (NG201 1.2.22; NG3 1.2.2). NG3 1.2.3 states that fasting or random glucose, HbA1c, glucose challenge or urinalysis for glucose should not be used to assess GDM risk.

n.0: Random blood glucose is not a recommended test for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.2.3).
n.1: Urinalysis for glucose is not a valid test for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.2.3).
n.2: HbA1c is not recommended for assessing gestational diabetes risk in pregnancy (NG3 1.2.3).

5.q: Rosa, 31, is 34 weeks pregnant and has been prescribed nifedipine for gestational hypertension. She shows the midwife the product leaflet, which says the medicine should not be used in pregnancy, and says she will not take it. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree that she should not take it and record that she declined it
Explain leaflet warnings often reflect a lack of testing, and discuss it
Tell her the prescriber's decision overrides the leaflet's warning
Advise her to take half the prescribed dose to lower any risk
5.w: NICE NG133 notes (alongside 1.4.5) that some nifedipine brands are contraindicated in pregnancy by the manufacturer, and explains that most medicines are not tested in pregnant or breastfeeding women, so manufacturer disclaimers are not because of specific safety concerns or evidence of harm (NG133 1.9.2). The midwife explains this, answers her questions and involves the prescriber so Rosa can make an informed decision (SPM 3.18).

n.0: Simply recording a refusal misses the chance to give the information she needs to decide.
n.2: Her informed consent is required; a prescriber's decision does not override her choice.
n.3: Self-reducing the dose gives inadequate treatment and has not been prescribed.

5.q: Precious, 32, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language (BSL). Her hearing partner offers to sign for her during labour. What is the most appropriate arrangement?
o: Ask her partner to interpret, as he is fluent in BSL
Rely on lip-reading, with staff speaking slowly and facing her
Communicate by writing notes throughout labour
Book a registered BSL interpreter for labour and appointments
5.w: Code 7.2: meet people's language and communication needs. A registered BSL interpreter gives accurate, independent communication, and the partner can support Precious rather than interpret.

n.0: A partner interpreting cannot also act as her birth supporter and may not convey clinical information accurately.
n.1: Lip-reading conveys only part of speech and is unreliable, especially in labour.
n.2: Written notes are slow and impractical during labour and may not be her preferred language.

5.q: Isabel, 33, is 40+1 weeks pregnant and asks for a membrane sweep. Her notes show that the 20-week scan reported a low-lying placenta, and there is no record of a follow-up scan. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Perform the sweep gently, as most low-lying placentas move up by term
Ask her to sign a consent form accepting the bleeding risk, then sweep
Perform the sweep and observe her for bleeding for 1 hour afterwards
Do not sweep; clarify placental position with the obstetric team first
5.w: NICE NG207 1.7.6: check that there is no evidence of a low-lying placenta on previous scans before membrane sweeping and before induction. With no follow-up scan documented, the placental site must be clarified before any vaginal examination for sweeping.

n.0: Many placentas do move away from the cervix, but this must be confirmed by scan, not assumed.
n.1: A signed form does not make an unsafe procedure safe; the placental site must be checked first.
n.2: Observing for bleeding afterwards does not prevent haemorrhage from a placenta that may be low lying.

5.q: Shoulder dystocia for Bea, 34, was resolved after 2 minutes and her baby is crying. The placenta is about to be delivered. Which maternal complication should the midwife be especially alert for?
o: Urinary tract infection
Pre-eclampsia
Post-dural puncture headache
Postpartum haemorrhage
5.w: Shoulder dystocia is associated with maternal morbidity including postpartum haemorrhage (around 11%) and obstetric anal sphincter injury (around 3.8%) (RCOG GTG 42). NICE NG235 1.10.30 lists shoulder dystocia as an intrapartum risk factor for PPH.

n.0: Urinary tract infection is not the key immediate complication of shoulder dystocia.
n.1: Pre-eclampsia is not a complication of shoulder dystocia.
n.2: Post-dural puncture headache follows epidural complications, not shoulder dystocia.

5.q: Grace, 34, is RhD negative and has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth. Cord blood shows that her baby is RhD positive. She received routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks. What is the correct plan?
o: Offer anti-D within 72 hours of the birth
Offer anti-D at her 6-week postnatal check
Anti-D is not needed, as she had antenatal prophylaxis
Offer anti-D in her next pregnancy at booking
5.w: After the birth of an RhD-positive baby to an RhD-negative woman who is not sensitised, anti-D is given as soon as possible and within 72 hours, with a test to assess the size of any fetomaternal haemorrhage. Antenatal prophylaxis does not cover exposure at birth.

n.1: Six weeks is far too late; sensitisation can occur within days of exposure.
n.2: Birth is a separate sensitising event; antenatal prophylaxis does not cover it.
n.3: Waiting until the next pregnancy allows sensitisation to occur after this birth.

5.q: During the NIPE newborn examination of baby Leo, the midwife finds that the red reflex in his left eye is absent and the pupil looks white. The right eye is normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to a community optician for an eye test at 1 year
Refer urgently so he is seen by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks
Repeat the red reflex check at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
Refer for an ophthalmology appointment within 6 weeks
5.w: NIPE handbook 12.11: babies with screen positive (abnormal) red reflex results should be urgently referred and seen by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks of the newborn examination; an absent or white reflex may indicate congenital cataract or retinoblastoma.

n.0: An optician at 1 year is far too late; surgery for severe congenital cataract is time-critical.
n.2: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks delays assessment of a possible cataract or retinoblastoma.
n.3: The NIPE standard is assessment within 2 weeks, not 6.

5.q: Mia, 27, has an ultrasound at 13 weeks showing a twin pregnancy. The sonographer cannot confidently determine chorionicity, and a second opinion from a senior sonographer is also inconclusive. How should the pregnancy be managed?
o: Repeat the scan with 3D ultrasound to confirm chorionicity
As a dichorionic pregnancy until the 20-week scan
As a monochorionic pregnancy until proven otherwise
As a dichorionic pregnancy if the twins are discordant in sex later
5.w: NICE NG137 1.1.7: if it is difficult to determine chorionicity even after referral, manage the pregnancy as monochorionic until proven otherwise, because monochorionic twins carry higher risks (such as feto-fetal transfusion syndrome).

n.0: NG137 1.1.12 advises not to use 3D ultrasound to determine chorionicity.
n.1: Assuming dichorionicity would leave a possibly monochorionic pregnancy without the closer surveillance it needs.
n.3: Discordant sex later confirms dichorionicity, but until then the safer assumption is monochorionic.

5.q: Laila, 36, chose NIPT after a higher-chance combined test. The NIPT result shows a high chance of Down's syndrome. She asks whether this means the diagnosis is certain. What is the most accurate response?
o: NIPT is diagnostic for Down's but not for Edwards' or Patau's syndromes
NIPT is diagnostic, so the result is certain and no more tests are needed
A repeat NIPT will confirm the result without any miscarriage risk
NIPT is a screening test; a diagnosis needs CVS or amniocentesis
5.w: NIPT analyses cell-free DNA mostly from the placenta and is highly accurate, but it remains a screening test. A diagnosis needs an invasive diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis), which she can choose or decline (NHS FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.0: NIPT is a screening test for all three conditions; none is diagnosed by it.
n.1: NIPT is not diagnostic; false positives occur, for example from placental mosaicism.
n.2: Repeating a screening test does not provide a diagnosis; confirmation needs a diagnostic test.

5.q: Yasmin, 32, is in labour at term with a previous caesarean. Continuous CTG is recommended, but she declines it. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Apply the CTG anyway as she has a uterine scar
Ask the registrar to apply the CTG while the midwife reassures her
Stop monitoring the baby until she agrees to the CTG
Explain why, offer intermittent auscultation and document it
5.w: SPM 1.21: respect the right to decline and provide appropriate care. The midwife explains why continuous monitoring is advised (NICE NG229 for women with a previous caesarean), offers an alternative such as intermittent auscultation and documents the discussion.

n.0: Applying monitoring she has declined is treatment without consent.
n.1: Applying the CTG through another clinician is still monitoring without consent.
n.2: Stopping monitoring removes all fetal assessment; she should be offered an acceptable alternative.

5.q: At a 10-day postnatal visit the midwife asks Nadia, 30, questions to help recognise depression, as recommended by NICE CG192. Which question is one of the Whooley questions?
o: Over the last 2 weeks, have you felt nervous, anxious or on edge most days?
Do you feel your baby is harder to settle than other babies of the same age?
During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?
In the past year, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?
5.w: NICE CG192 1.5.4: at the first contact in primary care, booking and early postnatal period, ask the two depression identification (Whooley) questions about feeling down, depressed or hopeless, and having little interest or pleasure in doing things, during the past month.

n.0: This is from the GAD-2 anxiety questions, which use a 2-week timeframe.
n.1: This asks about the baby's temperament, not the woman's mood or interest.
n.3: Risk questions matter but are not one of the two Whooley questions.

5.q: Bethany, 33, had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis 4 years ago. She has just had a straightforward vaginal birth and is otherwise well. Which postnatal thromboprophylaxis plan should the midwife expect?
o: LMWH for 10 days, as she had an uncomplicated vaginal birth
No prophylaxis, as her thrombosis was more than 2 years ago
LMWH (or warfarin) for at least 6 weeks after the birth
Anti-embolism stockings for 6 weeks, without anticoagulation
5.w: RCOG GTG 37a: all women with a previous confirmed VTE should be offered thromboprophylaxis with LMWH or warfarin for at least 6 weeks postpartum, regardless of mode of delivery. Previous VTE (other than one linked to major surgery) scores 4.

n.0: Mode of birth does not reduce the duration; previous VTE needs at least 6 weeks.
n.1: There is no time limit after which previous VTE stops counting as a risk factor.
n.3: Stockings are not a substitute for anticoagulation in a woman with previous VTE.

5.q: Amaka, 30, gave birth by emergency caesarean three weeks ago. At a postnatal visit she asks the community midwife for a copy of her labour records so she can understand what happened. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her the records belong to the trust and need a solicitor's request
Explain her right to see her records and support her request
Tell her she can request the records once the postnatal period ends
Give her the original records to take home and read
5.w: Women have a legal right of access to their health records under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 (subject access request). SPM 1.24 states records should be available for review by the woman. A debrief offer may also help her understand events.

n.0: A solicitor is not needed; a woman can request her own records directly.
n.2: Her right of access is not delayed until the end of the postnatal period.
n.3: Original records stay with the trust; she is entitled to a copy, not the originals.

5.q: Which statement best describes the scope of the midwife set out in the NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives (2019)?
o: Care for women at low risk, ending when complications arise
Care from booking until 10 days after the birth for healthy women
Intrapartum care, with antenatal and postnatal care led by GPs
Universal care for all, plus additional care in partnership with others
5.w: The 2019 standards describe the midwife providing universal care for all women and newborn infants, and additional care for those with complications, working with the interdisciplinary and multiagency team (SPM 1.7, Domains 3 and 4).

n.0: Midwives continue to care for women who develop complications, coordinating with others, rather than stopping.
n.1: The standards cover all women and newborns across the continuum, not a fixed 10-day window for healthy women.
n.2: Midwives provide antenatal, intrapartum and postnatal care; GPs are not the leads for routine antenatal and postnatal care.

5.q: Layla, 31, is 41+3 weeks pregnant. After a full discussion of benefits and risks she declines induction and wishes to wait for labour to start naturally. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer her to the safeguarding team because of the risk to the baby
Discharge her to routine care with no further appointments until labour
Respect and record her decision; discuss extra monitoring from 42 weeks
Explain that induction must be booked once a pregnancy passes 41 weeks
5.w: NICE NG207 1.2.6 to 1.2.8: if she declines induction, discuss her options, record her decision, discuss additional fetal monitoring from 42 weeks (explaining it gives a snapshot and cannot predict later problems) and offer her the chance to revisit her decision at later reviews.

n.0: Declining a recommended intervention is not a safeguarding issue; an unborn baby has no separate legal rights over her decision.
n.1: She should be offered ongoing review and monitoring from 42 weeks and the chance to change her mind.
n.3: A woman with capacity can decline induction (NG207 1.2.19); it is not compulsory.

5.q: Mia, 27, discloses domestic abuse at a postnatal visit and asks the midwife not to tell anyone. Her partner has hit her in front of their 2-year-old son. What should the midwife do?
o: Keep the disclosure confidential as Mia has requested
Wait until Mia agrees before sharing any information
Advise Mia to leave her partner before any referral is made
Explain that she will share the concern to protect the children
5.w: Children who see or hear domestic abuse are victims of it (Domestic Abuse Act 2021). Information may be shared without consent to protect children, and the midwife should explain this to Mia unless doing so would increase risk, then follow local safeguarding procedures (Code 5.4, 17; SPM 3.7).

n.0: Confidentiality does not stop sharing information to protect children at risk of harm.
n.1: Consent is not required to share information to protect a child.
n.2: Leaving can increase risk, and safeguarding action does not depend on her leaving.

5.q: Lauren, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant. Using the GAD-2, she scores 4 out of 6 for feeling nervous and being unable to stop worrying. What does NICE CG192 advise the midwife to consider?
o: Referring her directly to a specialist mother and baby unit
Using the GAD-7 for further assessment or referring her to her GP
Repeating the GAD-2 at her 28-week appointment before acting
Asking the avoidance question, as her score is below the threshold
5.w: CG192 1.5.6: if a woman scores 3 or more on the GAD-2, consider using the GAD-7 for further assessment or referring her to her GP (or to a mental health professional if a severe problem is suspected).

n.0: Mother and baby units provide inpatient care within 12 months of birth for women who need admission (CG192 1.10.1), not first-line assessment of anxiety.
n.2: A score of 3 or more is the threshold for action now, not after a delay of eight weeks.
n.3: The avoidance question is for women scoring less than 3 who still cause concern (CG192 1.5.7); Lauren scored 4.

5.q: Baby Grace, born at 40 weeks, is 60 hours old. Her transcutaneous bilirubin reading is 262 micromol/L. She is feeding well. What should the midwife do next?
o: Start phototherapy based on the transcutaneous reading
Measure serum bilirubin to confirm the level
Reassure the parents, as the reading is below 300
Repeat the transcutaneous reading in 6 hours
5.w: NICE CG98 1.2.16: use serum bilirubin measurement if a transcutaneous bilirubinometer gives a reading above 250 micromol/L; the serum value is then plotted on the treatment threshold graph.

n.0: Treatment decisions use serum bilirubin when the transcutaneous reading exceeds 250.
n.2: There is no 300 reassurance threshold; readings over 250 need serum confirmation.
n.3: A reading above 250 needs a serum measurement, not a repeat transcutaneous reading.

5.q: Holly, a newly qualified midwife, is uneasy because the registrar is about to attempt a rotational instrumental birth without the consultant present, which local policy says requires consultant agreement. Which statement by Holly is most appropriate?
o: "I'm concerned our policy needs consultant agreement. Can we call them first?"
"I'll fill in an incident form afterwards if anything goes wrong for her."
"I'm not happy, but I don't want to hold things up, so carry on."
"You're the doctor, so I'll go along with whatever you decide is best here."
5.w: Speaking up clearly, naming the concern and the policy, and proposing a safe action is the core of graded assertiveness and challenging a steep hierarchy (SPM 5.6, 5.13.2; Code 16.1).

n.1: Reporting after the event does not prevent the risk; concerns should be raised at the time.
n.2: Voicing unease but then letting things proceed does not protect the woman.
n.3: Deferring to hierarchy despite a safety concern breaches the duty to raise concerns.

5.q: Fatima, 28, speaks limited English and attends her booking appointment at 9 weeks with her husband, who offers to interpret. The midwife needs to take a full history, including questions about her mental health and safety at home. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange an independent professional interpreter for the appointment
Use a translated leaflet and ask her to nod in answer to questions
Accept her husband's offer because he knows her medical history
Ask a bilingual healthcare assistant from the ward to interpret
5.w: NICE NG201 1.1.11: interpreters should be independent of the woman rather than a family member or friend. A family interpreter can filter what is said and prevents safe disclosure of domestic abuse or mental health concerns (NG201 1.2.5; SPM 3.22).

n.1: Nodding to a leaflet does not allow informed discussion or a reliable history, and screening choices need full information.
n.2: Family members should not interpret; her husband's presence also blocks private enquiry about domestic abuse.
n.3: An untrained colleague is not a reliable interpreting service and confidentiality and accuracy cannot be assured.

5.q: Kayla, 17, is pregnant with her first baby and lives with her mother. She wants to continue the pregnancy and says she does not know anything about caring for a baby. Which additional service should the midwife offer to refer her to?
o: The Family Nurse Partnership programme
The specialist perinatal mental health team
The adult safeguarding team
The pregnancy options counselling service
5.w: The Family Nurse Partnership is an evidence-based home visiting programme for young first-time parents (usually 19 or under), running from pregnancy until the child is 2. It supports young parents who may find services hard to engage with (SPM 2.8, 2.9).

n.1: There is no indication of mental illness; this team is for moderate to severe perinatal mental health problems.
n.2: Kayla is under 18 and has no identified safeguarding concern; adult safeguarding does not apply.
n.3: She has decided to continue the pregnancy, so options counselling does not meet her needs.

5.q: Mo, a band 6 midwife, has escalated a pathological CTG to the obstetric registrar, who says to continue and review in an hour. Mo remains very concerned as the fetal heart rate has had a prolonged deceleration. What should Mo do next?
o: State her concern clearly and escalate to the consultant obstetrician
Document her disagreement and review the CTG again in an hour
Ask another midwife whether she agrees before taking any action
Accept the registrar's plan because the decision is a medical one
5.w: When concerns remain after escalation, the midwife should use the escalation or conflict of clinical opinion policy to go to the consultant. Ockenden IEA 3 requires trusts to support staff in escalating clinical concerns when professionals disagree (SPM 5.6; Code 16.1).

n.1: Documenting without acting leaves the fetus at continuing risk for another hour.
n.2: Seeking a second midwifery view is reasonable but should not delay escalation when she is already concerned.
n.3: The midwife remains accountable for acting on her concerns; deferring to hierarchy despite clear risk is unsafe.

5.q: Grace, 34, is in her third labour. Her cervix is 4 cm dilated but only partly effaced. A student midwife asks whether this is unusual. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Partial effacement at 4 cm is a sign of obstructed labour
In parous women effacement and dilatation often happen together
Partial effacement at 4 cm means she is still in the latent first stage
In parous women dilatation cannot begin until effacement is complete
5.w: In a first labour the cervix usually effaces before it dilates. In parous women effacement and dilatation commonly occur together, so a partly effaced cervix at 4 cm is normal. NICE defines established first stage as regular contractions with progressive dilatation from 4 cm (NG235 1.8.1).

n.0: Partial effacement is normal in parous women and is not a sign of obstruction.
n.2: Established labour is defined by regular contractions and progressive dilatation from 4 cm, not by complete effacement.
n.3: Effacement before dilatation is the usual pattern in first labours, not in parous women.

5.q: Lucia, 27, lacks capacity because of a severe learning disability and is 38 weeks pregnant. The team believes a planned caesarean is in her best interests, but she objects and her family disagree. There is no emergency. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask Lucia's GP to make the decision
Wait until labour starts and decide then
Apply to the Court of Protection for a decision
Proceed with the caesarean as a best interests decision
5.w: Where serious medical treatment is proposed for a person lacking capacity and there is disagreement or objection, the Court of Protection can decide what is in her best interests (MCA 2005). Planning ahead avoids an emergency decision.

n.0: A GP has no legal power to decide for an adult who lacks capacity.
n.1: Waiting for labour turns a plannable decision into an emergency with less time to safeguard her rights.
n.3: Proceeding with major surgery against objection and family disagreement, without the court, is not appropriate when time allows an application.

5.q: Ruth, 31, received oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM for active management of the third stage. On the delivery suite, 20 minutes after the placenta is delivered complete, she bleeds heavily from an atonic uterus despite massage and an empty bladder. She has no history of asthma. According to NICE NG235, which uterotonic is appropriate next?
o: Misoprostol 200 micrograms orally
A second dose of oxytocin with ergometrine IM
Carboprost intramuscularly
Ergometrine 500 micrograms intravenously
5.w: NICE NG235 table 12: after prophylaxis with oxytocin plus ergometrine, first-line treatment for atony is carboprost IM or an oxytocin infusion. Carboprost can be repeated at intervals of at least 15 minutes, up to 8 doses (NG235 1.10.34).

n.0: NG235 lists misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually or rectally, not 200 micrograms orally.
n.1: NG235 keeps a repeat of oxytocin with ergometrine for settings where other drugs are unavailable, such as a home birth; on the delivery suite carboprost or an oxytocin infusion is first line.
n.3: Ergometrine has already been given and IV ergometrine is not the NG235 next step.

5.q: Ines, 28, is 29 weeks pregnant and was admitted after an antepartum haemorrhage of about 150 mL. The bleeding has now stopped, placenta praevia has been excluded on scan and the CTG is normal. She asks if she can go home tonight. What does RCOG GTG 63 recommend?
o: She can go home after one normal CTG, with a phone call tomorrow
She should remain in hospital at least until the bleeding has stopped
She can go home now, as placenta praevia has been excluded
She should remain in hospital until she gives birth
5.w: RCOG GTG 63: women with APH heavier than spotting, or with ongoing bleeding, should remain in hospital at least until the bleeding has stopped; discharge after a reassuring assessment applies to spotting that has settled with praevia excluded. Each woman is assessed individually.

n.0: A single normal CTG does not meet the GTG 63 advice for bleeding heavier than spotting.
n.2: Going home immediately applies to spotting that has settled, and this was a heavier bleed.
n.3: GTG 63 does not require admission until birth; it advises admission at least until bleeding stops.

5.q: Hamida, 24, speaks little English. Her husband offers to interpret at her day 3 postnatal check, which includes questions about her mood, bleeding and contraception. What should the midwife do?
o: Use a translation app and give her an English leaflet
Book a professional interpreter rather than her husband
Ask her teenage daughter to interpret, as she is fluent
Accept her husband's offer, as he knows her history best
5.w: NICE NG194 1.1.5: information should be translated by an appropriate interpreter. NG201 advises independent interpreters rather than family members, so that the woman can speak freely about sensitive issues such as mood and domestic abuse.

n.0: An app and an English leaflet do not ensure she understands or can ask questions.
n.2: Using a child to interpret is inappropriate, particularly for intimate health topics.
n.3: Family interpreters may filter information and prevent disclosure of sensitive issues such as abuse.

5.q: Two weeks after caring for a woman whose baby was stillborn, Kemi, a midwife, has become withdrawn, tearful at handover and is calling in sick more often. Her colleague Amy notices. What is the most appropriate action for Amy?
o: Suggest Kemi swaps to night shifts so she is under less scrutiny
Speak to Kemi privately, listen, and encourage her to access staff support
Report Kemi's sickness pattern to the ward manager for formal review
Avoid mentioning it so that Kemi does not feel singled out
5.w: SPM 5.14 requires midwives to recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risks to their health and wellbeing. A private, compassionate conversation and signposting to support (such as the Professional Midwifery Advocate, occupational health or employee assistance) is the right first step.

n.0: Changing shifts does not address her distress and may increase isolation.
n.2: A formal sickness review is not the first response to a colleague showing distress after a traumatic event.
n.3: Ignoring signs of distress leaves Kemi without support and may risk her health and practice.

5.q: At which antenatal contacts should carbon monoxide testing be offered routinely to every pregnant woman, according to Saving Babies' Lives version 3?
o: At booking and at the 28-week appointment
At booking and at the 36-week appointment
At booking, then at every appointment for all women
At the 16-week and 36-week appointments
5.w: SBL3 element 1 and NG209 1.18.1: CO testing for all pregnant women at the first antenatal (booking) appointment and at 36 weeks, and at all other appointments for those who smoke, are quitting, used to smoke or tested 4 ppm or above at booking.

n.0: Routine testing is at booking and 36 weeks; 28 weeks is not one of the routine points.
n.2: Testing at every appointment is for women who smoke, are quitting, used to smoke or had a raised reading.
n.3: The first routine test is at booking, not 16 weeks.

5.q: Mei, 29, is well and has an uncomplicated pregnancy. She asks about a birth centre in her town that is on a different site from the hospital and has no obstetricians or anaesthetists. Which setting is she describing?
o: An alongside midwifery unit
An obstetric unit
A freestanding midwifery unit
A midwife-led triage unit
5.w: NICE NG235 1.2.1 and 1.3.3 name four birth settings: home, freestanding midwifery unit (on a separate site from an obstetric unit), alongside midwifery unit (same site) and obstetric unit. A unit away from the hospital without obstetric or anaesthetic staff is freestanding (SPM 2.1).

n.0: An alongside midwifery unit is on the same site as an obstetric unit, so transfer does not need an ambulance.
n.1: An obstetric unit has obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal staff on site, which this birth centre lacks.
n.3: Triage assesses women who call or attend with concerns; it is not a place planned for giving birth.

5.q: Rachel, 26, gave birth 20 minutes ago and wants to breastfeed. Her baby is well and in skin-to-skin contact. When should breastfeeding ideally start?
o: After the baby has been weighed and dressed
Within 6 hours of birth, once she has rested
As soon as possible, ideally within the first hour
After the first 24 hours, when the milk comes in
5.w: NG235 1.11.11: encourage women to initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible after the birth, ideally within 1 hour. NG194 1.5.7: early skin-to-skin contact so breastfeeding can start when baby and mother are ready (SPM 3.6).

n.0: Weighing and dressing should wait until after the first hour so they do not delay feeding.
n.1: Waiting several hours misses the baby's alert period after birth.
n.3: Colostrum is available from birth and early feeding helps establish supply.

5.q: Paige, 24, is 18 weeks pregnant. Her two older children were removed from her care because of neglect, and she still lives with the same partner. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to the health visitor to monitor the baby after the birth
Wait until after the birth to see how she cares for the baby
Tell Paige the baby will be removed at birth
Refer to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment
5.w: Midwives safeguard unborn babies. Previous children removed for neglect with the same circumstances is a significant concern needing referral to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment, in line with Working Together to Safeguard Children and local procedures (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Health visitor involvement is not enough when there are known significant safeguarding concerns.
n.1: Waiting removes the chance to plan support and protection before the baby is born.
n.2: Removal is not decided by the midwife and is not certain; this damages trust.

5.q: A trial of a new antenatal education programme reports the risk of caesarean birth in the intervention group compared with usual care as a relative risk of 0.80 (95% confidence interval 0.65 to 0.98). Sophie, a student midwife, asks her practice supervisor how to interpret this. Which explanation is correct?
o: An 80% relative reduction that is statistically significant at the 5% level
A 20% relative reduction that is statistically significant at the 5% level
A 20% relative reduction that is not statistically significant
A 20% relative increase that is statistically significant at the 5% level
5.w: A relative risk of 0.80 means the risk is 80% of the comparison risk, a 20% relative reduction (1 minus 0.80). The 95% confidence interval (0.65 to 0.98) lies entirely below 1.0, the line of no effect, so the result is statistically significant at the 5% level.

n.0: An RR of 0.80 is a 20% reduction, not 80%; an 80% reduction would be an RR of 0.20.
n.2: The interval does not include 1.0 (its upper limit is 0.98), so the result is statistically significant.
n.3: A relative risk below 1.0 shows a reduction in risk, not an increase.

5.q: Parents of baby Harry, born today, decline vitamin K after hearing the information. What should the midwife do next?
o: Give oral vitamin K instead, as it is less invasive
Refer them to children's social care for neglect
Tell them the baby cannot be discharged without vitamin K
Document their decision and explain signs of bleeding
5.w: Parents with parental responsibility may decline vitamin K after informed discussion (SPM 1.20, 1.21). The midwife records the decision, explains signs of vitamin K deficiency bleeding to watch for and informs the paediatric and community teams.

n.0: Oral vitamin K still needs consent; the parents declined vitamin K, not just the injection (Code 4.2).
n.1: An informed decision to decline vitamin K is not by itself neglect.
n.2: Discharge is not conditional on vitamin K; that would be coercion.

5.q: Jess, 16, books at 12 weeks. She is living with her mother, is still at school and finds hospital clinics intimidating. Which care arrangement best follows NICE CG110?
o: Care deferred until her mother can attend every appointment with her
Standard consultant-led clinic care, as she is under 18
A named midwife providing most of her care, with a direct phone number
Antenatal care through her school nurse until 28 weeks
5.w: CG110 1.4.4: offer young women under 20 a named midwife who provides most of their antenatal care, with a direct-line telephone number. Services should be age-appropriate, community-based where possible and alert to safeguarding (1.4.1, 1.4.5).

n.0: Jess can attend herself; deferring care until her mother is available is a barrier to antenatal care.
n.1: Age alone is not an indication for consultant-led care; young women need accessible, age-appropriate services.
n.3: School nurses do not provide antenatal care; the midwife does.

5.q: Precious, 34, had gestational diabetes treated with metformin. She gave birth to a healthy baby two hours ago and asks what happens to her metformin now. Which advice is correct?
o: Continue metformin for six weeks and then have an HbA1c test with her GP
Continue metformin until her capillary glucose is normal for three days
Reduce metformin to half dose and stop it at the six to eight week check
Stop metformin now; a fasting glucose test is offered 6 to 13 weeks after birth
5.w: NG3 1.6.3 advises women with gestational diabetes to stop blood glucose-lowering therapy immediately after birth. A fasting plasma glucose test is offered 6 to 13 weeks after birth (NG3 1.6.11), with annual HbA1c if negative.

n.0: Glucose-lowering therapy is stopped immediately after birth, not continued for six weeks.
n.1: Waiting for three days of normal readings is not the NG3 approach; therapy stops at birth.
n.2: Tapering to half dose is not recommended; treatment stops immediately after birth.

5.q: Nisha, 27, has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth. On visual inspection there appears to be a small tear involving the skin and perineal muscle. She is comfortable and has good analgesia. What should the midwife's systematic assessment include before classifying the tear?
o: A careful visual inspection, as the tear looks second degree
A rectal examination, with consent, to check the anal sphincters
A rectal examination after the repair is completed
A speculum examination of the cervix as the first step
5.w: NICE NG235 1.12.5 and 1.12.7: offer all women systematic assessment including a rectal examination to exclude all genital tract trauma, including buttonhole tears and sphincter injury, with explanation, consent and tested analgesia, before repair.

n.0: Visual inspection alone can miss anal sphincter injury and buttonhole tears.
n.2: Assessment must happen before repair so that sphincter injury is identified and repaired correctly.
n.3: Cervical inspection is not the first step of perineal assessment and does not assess the sphincters.

5.q: Sian, 31, is on an oxytocin infusion for delay in the first stage. The CTG has just been categorised as pathological by the midwife and the coordinator. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Increase the oxytocin to achieve 5 contractions in 10 minutes
Reduce the oxytocin rate by half and recheck the CTG in 30 minutes
Stop the oxytocin and seek urgent obstetric review
Continue the oxytocin, as contractions are not more than 4 in 10
5.w: NICE NG235 1.8.56: oxytocin must be discontinued immediately if the CTG is pathological, and urgent obstetrician or senior midwife review sought. It may be restarted after review if the CTG is no longer pathological and the woman agrees (1.8.57).

n.0: The aim is 3 to 4 contractions in 10; more than 4 is excessive and harmful with a pathological trace.
n.1: Reducing the dose is the response to more than 4 contractions in 10 (1.8.55); a pathological CTG needs oxytocin stopped.
n.3: A pathological CTG requires oxytocin to stop whatever the contraction frequency.

5.q: Megan, a labour ward midwife, has repeated an audit of documentation of the third stage of labour against the trust standard. Compliance was 62% last year. Since then, a new documentation sticker and teaching sessions were introduced. In which stage of the audit cycle is Megan now working?
o: Selecting the standard against which practice is measured
Collecting baseline data on current practice
Re-audit to measure whether the changes have improved practice
Comparing baseline data with the standard for the first time
5.w: The audit cycle runs: select a standard, measure current practice, compare with the standard, implement change, then re-audit to see whether practice has improved, closing the loop. Megan has already introduced changes after a baseline audit, so this is the re-audit (SPM 5.17).

n.0: The standard was already chosen before last year's audit.
n.1: Baseline data (62%) were collected last year; this is the repeat measurement.
n.3: The first comparison with the standard produced the 62% figure that led to the changes.

5.q: Leila, a public health midwife, wants to find out what proportion of women booked in the last 6 months were offered a carbon monoxide test at booking, and to compare this with the NICE NG209 recommendation that every woman is offered one. What type of project is this?
o: Clinical audit
Health surveillance
Research
Service evaluation
5.w: The HRA defining research table describes clinical audit as answering 'Does this service reach a predetermined, recognised or pre-established standard?' and measuring against a standard. Leila is measuring current practice against the NG209 standard (CO test offered at booking).

n.1: Health surveillance detects and manages threats to population health such as outbreaks, not compliance with a care standard.
n.2: Research aims to generate or test a hypothesis and produce generalisable new knowledge; Leila is checking local practice against an existing standard.
n.3: Service evaluation measures current service without reference to a standard ('What standard does this service achieve?'), whereas Leila has a defined standard.

5.q: Ellen, a registered midwife, has supervised a student midwife on four shifts this week but is not her practice assessor. Before the student moves to another area, what is Ellen's responsibility regarding documentation?
o: Leave documentation to the academic assessor at the next tripartite meeting
Record her observations of the student in the assessment document
Give verbal feedback, as written records are for the practice assessor
Sign off the proficiencies she has seen the student achieve this week
5.w: SSSA 4.1: practice supervisors contribute to the student's record of achievement by periodically recording relevant observations on conduct, proficiency and achievement. SPM 5.21 includes evaluating and documenting student performance. Confirming proficiency is the practice assessor's role (7.1).

n.0: The academic assessor relies on practice records; Ellen's observations need recording now.
n.2: Verbal feedback is valuable, but supervisors are also expected to record observations (4.1).
n.3: Signing off proficiencies is the practice assessor's assessment role (7.1), not the supervisor's.

5.q: Sana, 27, develops a temperature of 38.4 C and offensive lochia on day 3 after birth. She is being treated for suspected puerperal sepsis. Her baby is rooming in with her. What should the midwife also do?
o: Advise Sana to stop breastfeeding until her antibiotics finish
Move the baby to the nursery to prevent cross-infection
Assess the baby for signs of infection
Arrange for the baby to start prophylactic antibiotics
5.w: NG194 1.2.8: if a woman has confirmed or suspected puerperal sepsis, assess the baby for symptoms or signs of infection. This reflects SPM 2.6, planning for woman and newborn together.

n.0: Puerperal sepsis is not a reason to stop breastfeeding; compatible antibiotics can be chosen.
n.1: Separation is not recommended; the baby should be assessed and kept with the mother where possible.
n.3: Antibiotics for the baby depend on assessment; they are not given automatically.

5.q: Lauren, 30, tells the midwife that her partner checks her phone, controls all the money and stops her seeing friends. She has never been physically hurt. How should the midwife understand this?
o: As a safeguarding concern if the partner has a criminal record
As domestic abuse if it continues after the birth
As relationship difficulties, as there has been no violence
As domestic abuse, including coercive control and economic abuse
5.w: The Domestic Abuse Act 2021 s1 defines domestic abuse to include controlling or coercive behaviour, economic abuse and psychological and emotional abuse as well as physical violence (SPM 3.7).

n.0: A criminal record is not part of the definition of domestic abuse.
n.1: It already meets the definition of domestic abuse.
n.2: Abuse does not need physical violence; controlling and economic behaviour are abuse.

5.q: Harper, 27, is 34 weeks pregnant and has gestational hypertension. She phones the maternity triage line. Which symptom she describes needs immediate assessment for pre-eclampsia?
o: Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Leg cramps that wake her at night
Flashing lights in her vision since today
Backache after standing at work
5.w: NICE NG133 1.1.1 advises women to report immediately severe headache, problems with vision such as blurring or flashing before the eyes, severe pain just below the ribs, vomiting, and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet (SPM 4.8).

n.0: Gradual ankle swelling is common in pregnancy; sudden swelling of face, hands or feet is the warning sign.
n.1: Night cramps are common in pregnancy and are not a pre-eclampsia symptom.
n.3: Backache after standing is common and not a symptom of pre-eclampsia.

5.q: Keira, 32, is fully dilated and pushing when the cord prolapses. The fetal head is at the level of the ischial spines plus 2 cm, in a direct occipito-anterior position, and the fetal heart rate is 80 beats/min. An experienced obstetrician is present. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Move to theatre for a category 2 caesarean birth
Assisted vaginal birth in the room
Knee-chest position until spontaneous birth occurs
Give tocolysis and transfer to theatre for caesarean
5.w: RCOG GTG 50: vaginal birth, usually assisted, can be attempted at full dilatation if it is anticipated that birth would be quick and safe. With a low head and a skilled operator present, this is quicker than transferring to theatre.

n.0: Category 2 is too slow with bradycardia, and birth can be achieved vaginally here.
n.2: Waiting for spontaneous birth in knee-chest delays birth of a compromised baby.
n.3: Tocolysis is for delays before caesarean; birth can be achieved now vaginally.

5.q: A newly qualified midwife joins a trust that has paused its continuity teams because of staffing. She asks how she can still promote continuity of care. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Ask women to request her by name for every future appointment
Coordinate handovers and clear plans so care is consistent across different staff
Restart an informal continuity team with two colleagues on call
Focus on continuity of carer for postnatal visits and stop antenatal handovers
5.w: SPM 2.4 requires midwives to work across settings and with other staff to promote continuity of care and carer. When a continuity team is not possible, consistent plans, communication and handover maintain continuity of care.

n.0: Asking women to book with one named midwife cannot be guaranteed in a paused model and does not address continuity across settings.
n.2: Setting up an unofficial on-call team bypasses the trust's safe staffing decision and governance.
n.3: Stopping antenatal handovers would worsen continuity of care; good handover is the core of continuity when the same carer is not possible.

5.q: Holly, 25, is 39+3 weeks pregnant with her first baby and has a low-risk pregnancy. She attends the midwifery-led unit with irregular painful contractions for 6 hours. Her observations and the fetal heart are normal. On examination her cervix is soft, central and 2 cm dilated. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Offer support and analgesia and encourage her to go home with a plan
Admit her to the unit and start a partogram to record her progress
Perform an amniotomy to help establish labour
Transfer her to the obstetric unit for assessment of slow progress
5.w: Holly is in the latent first stage (contractions with cervical change up to 4 cm; NICE NG235 1.8.1). NG235 1.8.6: recognise that latent labour can be painful, offer individualised support and analgesia, and encourage her to remain at or return home unless this risks birth without a midwife or distress.

n.1: The partogram is used once labour is established (NG235 1.8.22), not in the latent phase.
n.2: Amniotomy is not routinely performed when labour is progressing normally (NG235 1.8.39) and is not used to establish labour.
n.3: Latent labour has no time limit for delay; there is no indication for obstetric transfer.

5.q: Fatou, 22, is an asylum seeker living in temporary accommodation. She gave birth 2 days ago and is anxious because she may be moved to another area. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Give her written information in English and close her midwifery care
Reduce her visits, because she may soon be moved to another area
Ask the Home Office to confirm her status before her next visit
Continue her postnatal care and link her with local support services
5.w: NICE NG194 1.1.7: follow the NICE guideline on pregnancy and complex social factors for women who may need additional support, including recent migrants, asylum seekers and refugees. SPM 3.27: care irrespective of social situation. NG194 1.1.8 supports clear handover if she moves.

n.0: Closing care early and giving English-only information fails her additional needs.
n.1: Women with complex social factors need more support, not fewer visits.
n.2: Her immigration status is not a precondition for postnatal midwifery care.

5.q: Natalie, 27, is 32 weeks pregnant. She describes intense itching on her palms and the soles of her feet, worse at night, for a week. There is no rash apart from scratch marks. BP and urinalysis are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recommend an emollient and reassure her that itching is due to skin stretching
Arrange blood tests for bile acids and liver function
Advise cool baths and loose cotton clothing, with no further tests
Advise an antihistamine and review at her next routine appointment
5.w: Itching of the palms and soles without a rash in the third trimester suggests intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, which needs bile acid and liver function testing and obstetric review (RCOG Green-top Guideline 43). NHS advice is that itchy palms and soles, often worse at night, need urgent assessment for cholestasis.

n.0: Itching from skin stretching usually affects the abdomen; palm and sole itching without a rash needs investigation.
n.2: Comfort measures alone miss a condition associated with adverse fetal outcomes.
n.3: An antihistamine may ease symptoms but does not exclude cholestasis, which needs testing now.

6.q: Ayan, 24, is an asylum seeker who is 30 weeks pregnant. She tells the community midwife she is being moved by the Home Office to accommodation in another city next week. Which action by the midwife is most important?
o: Delay her 32-week appointment until her new address is confirmed
Advise her to rebook with a GP in the new city after she has settled in
Make sure her hand-held notes are complete and she knows to keep them with her
Ask her to come back to this unit for each appointment after she moves
6.w: CG110 1.1.5, 1.1.10 and 1.3.8: women should take a copy of their hand-held maternity notes when moving, the notes should contain a full record of care and all test results, and women should keep them with them at all times. The midwife should also share information with the receiving service.

n.0: Delaying care creates a gap at a time when antenatal checks are important.
n.1: Waiting until she has settled risks a gap in care at 30 weeks; continuity of records and referral are needed now.
n.3: Travelling back from another city is impractical and risks missed appointments.

6.q: Ines, 28, moved to a new city for work, is 30 weeks pregnant and tells her midwife she knows nobody locally and feels lonely. Her mood screening questions are negative. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange extra antenatal appointments so she sees a midwife weekly
Advise her to move closer to family before the birth
Tell her about local antenatal groups and family hub activities
Refer her to the specialist perinatal mental health team
6.w: SPM 3.1 requires understanding the woman's lived experience and enabling access to community resources. Social isolation is a risk to wellbeing; linking her to peer groups and family hubs supports her and her transition to parenthood.

n.0: Extra clinical contacts do not address social isolation and are not clinically indicated.
n.1: This ignores her circumstances and is not a realistic or person-centred response.
n.3: Her screening is negative and loneliness alone does not meet the threshold for specialist mental health care.

6.q: Pooja, 33, is 34 weeks pregnant. She phones saying she has 'bad heartburn' that started this morning: severe pain just below her ribs on the right, not eased by antacids, with a headache. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to attend the maternity unit now for BP, urine and blood tests
Book a GP appointment for this week to review her indigestion
Advise paracetamol for the headache and to sleep propped up on pillows
Advise a stronger alginate and to call back if it persists tomorrow
6.w: Severe pain just below the ribs with headache is a recognised symptom of pre-eclampsia (NICE NG133 1.1.1), which can be mistaken for heartburn. She needs immediate assessment of BP, proteinuria and bloods (platelets, liver and renal function).

n.1: Waiting for a GP appointment delays urgent assessment of pre-eclampsia symptoms.
n.2: Masking the headache delays diagnosis; these symptoms need assessment now.
n.3: Treating as heartburn delays assessment of possible pre-eclampsia or HELLP.

6.q: Dani, 28, is 34 weeks pregnant and has been receiving midwife-led care. At a routine appointment her blood pressure is 152/100 mmHg and urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. What is the most appropriate action by the midwife?
o: Transfer her to obstetric care and close her midwifery record
Ask her GP to review her blood pressure within the next few days
Arrange same-day obstetric assessment and continue her midwifery care
Continue midwife-led care and recheck her blood pressure next week
6.w: New hypertension after 20 weeks with dipstick proteinuria raises suspicion of pre-eclampsia. NICE NG201 1.2.26 says a first episode of hypertension (140/90 mmHg or higher) after 20+0 weeks is referred to secondary care to be seen within 24 hours, and NG133 1.2.3 asks for dipstick proteinuria to be quantified with PCR or ACR, so same-day obstetric assessment is the prompt, safe step. The midwife refers for shared care while continuing to provide midwifery care (SPM 1.6).

n.0: The woman still needs midwifery care when obstetric input begins; care becomes shared rather than ended.
n.1: GP review in a few days misses the 24-hour secondary care assessment in NG201 1.2.26; she needs the obstetric team, not primary care.
n.3: A week's delay is unsafe with possible pre-eclampsia; NG201 1.2.26 expects secondary care assessment within 24 hours.

6.q: Lara, 31, has a cord prolapse at a planned home birth. Paramedics arrive to transfer her to the nearest consultant unit. Which position is recommended for her during the ambulance journey?
o: Exaggerated Sims position
Sitting upright on the stretcher
Knee-chest position
Supine with a pillow under her knees
6.w: RCOG GTG 50: knee-chest is potentially unsafe in a moving vehicle, so the exaggerated Sims position (left lateral, head down, pillow under the left hip) is used during ambulance transfer, with elevation of the presenting part.

n.1: Sitting upright increases pressure of the presenting part on the cord.
n.2: Knee-chest is advised while waiting at home but is potentially unsafe in a moving ambulance.
n.3: Supine positioning does not reduce pressure on the cord and risks aortocaval compression.

6.q: Ama, 32, is having a planned home birth and is pushing involuntarily. As the midwife watches the perineum, she sees fetal buttocks and genitalia rather than a head. No one has suspected breech before. What should the midwife do first?
o: Call for help, including a 999 ambulance and a second midwife
Carry Ama to the car for an immediate hospital transfer
Ask Ama to stop pushing until an ambulance arrives
Apply gentle traction to the buttocks to speed the birth
6.w: In an unexpected breech at advanced labour, call for help (999 ambulance, second midwife) and prepare for a vaginal breech birth. RCOG GTG 20b: women near or in the active second stage should not routinely be offered caesarean, and all midwives should be familiar with breech birth techniques.

n.1: Moving her during the active second stage risks the birth happening in transit without help.
n.2: Asking her to stop pushing will not halt the birth and wastes time needed to call help.
n.3: Traction risks extension of the arms and head; GTG 20b advises a hands-off approach.

6.q: Holly, 28, is day 2 after a caesarean birth on the postnatal ward. Her chart shows a new prescription for oral cefalexin written that morning, but there is no dose written, only the drug name, route and frequency. The doctor who wrote it has gone to theatre. What should the midwife do?
o: Give the usual adult dose and ask the doctor to add it later
Withhold the dose and contact a prescriber to complete it
Give the lowest dose in the BNF until the doctor is free
Ask a midwife colleague to confirm the usual dose, then give it
6.w: A prescription without a dose is incomplete and must not be administered. The midwife withholds the dose, contacts a prescriber (another doctor if needed) to correct it and documents the delay (Code 18; SPM 3.18 prescribing errors; SPM 3.19 safe administration).

n.0: Choosing a dose is prescribing, which the midwife is not authorised to do here.
n.2: Selecting any dose, even the lowest, is prescribing without authority.
n.3: A colleague's agreement does not make an incomplete prescription valid.

6.q: Kiran has type 1 diabetes and has just given birth at 38 weeks. Her baby is well and is with her. According to NICE NG3, when should the baby first be fed and have a blood glucose test?
o: Feed within 30 minutes of birth; test blood glucose at 2 to 4 hours
Test cord blood glucose at birth before the first feed is given
Feed within 4 hours of birth; test blood glucose at 24 hours
Feed within 1 hour of birth; test blood glucose at 30 minutes
6.w: NICE NG3 1.5.3 and 1.5.9: women with diabetes should feed their babies as soon as possible after birth (within 30 minutes) and then every 2 to 3 hours; carry out blood glucose testing routinely at 2 to 4 hours after birth.

n.1: Routine testing is at 2 to 4 hours; cord blood glucose is not the routine NG3 test.
n.2: 4 hours is too long to wait for a feed and 24 hours too late for the first test.
n.3: NG3 advises feeding within 30 minutes, and glucose at 30 minutes is too early for the routine test.

6.q: Megan, 27, is 41+4 weeks pregnant and admitted for induction. On vaginal examination her Bishop score is 8 and the fetal head is well applied to the cervix. Which method should be offered?
o: Amniotomy and an intravenous oxytocin infusion
Low-dose oral misoprostol every 2 hours
Vaginal dinoprostone controlled-release pessary
A balloon catheter for 12 hours before amniotomy
6.w: NICE NG207 1.3.9: for a Bishop score of more than 6, offer induction with amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin. She can choose whether or when to start oxytocin, knowing that delaying may lengthen labour and may raise the risk of neonatal infection (1.3.10).

n.1: Oral misoprostol is offered for a Bishop score of 6 or less.
n.2: Pharmacological ripening is offered when the Bishop score is 6 or less; her cervix is already favourable.
n.3: Mechanical ripening is for an unfavourable cervix (Bishop score 6 or less).

6.q: Fatima appraises a trial of 600 women comparing two methods of fetal heart monitoring across three hospitals. The primary outcome was validated and prespecified, and follow-up was 98%. Women were allocated by date of admission: even dates to method A, odd dates to method B. What is the main weakness in this trial?
o: The sample is too small to detect any difference in outcome
The primary outcome was chosen after the data were analysed
Follow-up was too incomplete to trust the results
Staff could predict allocation, introducing selection bias
6.w: Allocating by date is quasi-randomisation: recruiting staff can know which group the next woman will enter and may consciously or unconsciously decide whom to enrol, causing selection bias. Concealed random allocation is a key question in appraisal checklists such as CASP for RCTs.

n.0: Nothing in the stem suggests the trial was underpowered; 600 women across three sites is a substantial sample, and the flaw described is in allocation.
n.1: The stem states the primary outcome was prespecified, so selective outcome reporting is not the problem.
n.2: Follow-up was 98%, which is high and not a meaningful source of attrition bias.

6.q: A newly appointed midwife in England is told that the trust is still working through the Ockenden final report (2022). How many themes of immediate and essential actions (IEAs) did the report set for all trusts?
6.w: The Ockenden final report (30 March 2022) set out 15 immediate and essential action themes for all maternity services in England, including safe staffing, escalation and accountability, multidisciplinary training, and bereavement care.

n.0: The final report set 15 IEA themes, not 10.
n.2: Four is the number of areas for action in the East Kent report.
n.3: Seven was the number of IEAs in the first (emerging findings) Ockenden report in 2020; the final report set 15.

6.q: Fiona, 29, received intramuscular diamorphine for pain in established labour 1 hour ago. She now feels alert and asks to get into the birthing pool. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Help her into the pool and keep the water at 38 C to aid relaxation
Help her into the pool now, as she feels alert
Explain the pool is unsuitable for the rest of labour after any opioid
Explain she should wait until 2 hours after the opioid before entering water
6.w: NICE NG235 1.6.20: women should not enter water within 2 hours of opioid administration or if they feel drowsy, because of sedation and the risk of drowning. Water temperature should not exceed 37.5 C (1.6.11).

n.0: The 2-hour rule still applies, and 38 C exceeds the 37.5 C limit.
n.1: Feeling alert does not override the 2-hour rule after opioids.
n.2: After 2 hours, if she is not drowsy, she can enter the water; it is not excluded for the rest of labour.

6.q: Grace, a midwife, is 11 hours into a 12.5-hour night shift with no break. She notices she has read the same CTG twice without taking it in. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a student midwife to interpret the CTG on her behalf for now
Finish her current tasks and then take her break after handover
Drink a strong coffee and carry on with her care until the end of her shift
Tell the coordinator, take a break and ask a colleague to review the CTG
6.w: Fatigue is a recognised human factor that impairs attention and decision-making. Recognising it, telling the coordinator, taking a break and getting a second review keeps care safe (SPM 5.4, 5.14; Code 16.3 tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity about problems that may prevent you working within the Code; Code 19.2 human factors).

n.0: A student cannot take responsibility for CTG interpretation; review must be by a competent registrant.
n.1: Waiting until handover leaves a fatigued midwife making decisions for another 90 minutes.
n.2: Caffeine does not reliably restore performance, and continuing leaves her impaired while interpreting a CTG.

6.q: Dee, 31, is having a spontaneous vaginal birth. The fetal heart has been normal throughout. The midwife needs to perform an episiotomy because the perineum is rigid and not stretching after a long second stage. What must happen before the incision?
o: Wait for the next contraction to reduce pain from the incision
Perform a rectal examination to check the anal sphincter
Obtain written consent signed by Dee and her partner
Confirm that tested, effective analgesia is in place
6.w: NICE NG235 1.9.23: provide tested, effective analgesia before an episiotomy, except in an emergency because of acute fetal compromise. If performed, it should be mediolateral from the fourchette, usually to the right, at 45 to 60 degrees to the vertical at the time of the cut (1.9.21).

n.0: Timing the cut with a contraction does not replace the need for tested, effective analgesia.
n.1: Rectal examination is part of the systematic assessment after birth, not a prerequisite for episiotomy.
n.2: Verbal informed consent is required, but written consent is not the standard for episiotomy.

6.q: At booking, Hana, 31, discloses a previous termination of pregnancy and asks that her husband is not told. At a later appointment her husband is present and the midwife needs to review her obstetric history. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the husband to leave for every appointment from now on
Ask Hana privately how she wants the history discussed
Skip the obstetric history to avoid the topic
Review the history aloud, as the termination is in her records
6.w: Code 5.1: respect privacy in all aspects of care. Hana controls who knows about her history. Finding time to speak privately respects her wishes while the review is completed safely.

n.0: Excluding him from every appointment may not be what she wants; she should be asked.
n.2: Skipping the history risks missing relevant clinical information.
n.3: Discussing the termination in front of her husband breaches her confidentiality and her express wish.

6.q: Mei, 30, has a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks. Her fasting plasma glucose is 5.8 mmol/L and her 2-hour value is 7.1 mmol/L. How should these results be interpreted?
o: The test is normal because the 2-hour value is below 7.8 mmol/L
The result is borderline and the OGTT should be repeated at 32 weeks of pregnancy
She has type 2 diabetes because the fasting value is above 5.5 mmol/L at 26 weeks
She has gestational diabetes because the fasting value is 5.6 mmol/L or above
6.w: NG3 1.2.8 diagnoses gestational diabetes if the fasting plasma glucose is 5.6 mmol/L or above OR the 2-hour value is 7.8 mmol/L or above. Either threshold is enough.

n.0: Both values do not have to be raised; a fasting level of 5.8 mmol/L alone meets the diagnostic criterion.
n.1: NG3 has no borderline category requiring repeat testing; the threshold is met now.
n.2: These are the diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes, not type 2 diabetes.

6.q: A newly qualified midwife on the postnatal ward is asked by a woman with a perineal haematoma whether the midwife could inject local anaesthetic to drain it on the ward, using lidocaine under the midwives exemptions. Which statement about lidocaine under Schedule 17 is accurate?
o: It may be given by a midwife while attending a woman in childbirth
It needs a separate PGD for each perineal repair after birth
It may be given for any minor procedure in the postnatal period
It may be given by a student midwife without direct supervision
6.w: Schedule 17 allows midwives to administer lidocaine hydrochloride only while attending a woman in childbirth (for example infiltration for episiotomy or perineal repair). Management of a postnatal haematoma needs medical review and a prescription (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 1.2).

n.1: Lidocaine during childbirth is covered by the exemption and needs no PGD.
n.2: The exemption is limited to attending a woman in childbirth, not any postnatal procedure.
n.3: Student midwives must be under the direct supervision of a registered midwife.

6.q: A community midwifery manager notices that women living on one housing estate frequently miss hospital antenatal appointments, which involve two bus journeys. Which change is most likely to improve attendance?
o: Hold antenatal clinics in a local family hub on the estate
Offer every appointment as a video call instead of face to face
Send a reminder letter to each woman before every appointment
Discharge women from the clinic list after two missed appointments
6.w: SPM 2.1 and 2.2 require understanding how settings and the organisation of care affect women. Moving care closer to where women live reduces access barriers while keeping face-to-face assessment (NG201 schedule).

n.1: Video calls cannot provide BP, urine testing or fundal height measurement and may exclude women without devices or data.
n.2: Reminders do not remove the travel barrier that is causing the missed appointments.
n.3: Discharging women who miss appointments increases risk; missed contacts are a warning sign that needs follow-up.

6.q: Lauren, 25, is breastfeeding on day 3. She says feeds are very painful and her nipple looks flattened, like a new lipstick, when the baby comes off. The baby is feeding frequently and seems unsettled. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Advise nipple shields for every feed until the pain settles
Observe a full feed and support her with positioning and attachment
Rest the nipples for 24 hours by giving the baby formula feeds
Recommend a nipple cream and advise her that pain is expected
6.w: NICE NG194 1.5.12 and 1.5.15: pain when breastfeeding and a misshapen nipple after feeds suggest poor attachment. The first step is to observe a feed and adjust positioning and attachment; persisting concerns may need further support or tongue-tie assessment.

n.0: Nipple shields do not correct the underlying attachment problem and can reduce milk transfer.
n.2: Replacing feeds with formula reduces milk removal and supply and does not fix attachment.
n.3: Ongoing pain is not normal; NG194 tells women to seek help for pain when breastfeeding.

6.q: Toni, 19, says she will breastfeed 'for a couple of weeks' before returning to college, and asks whether it is worth it for such a short time. Which response is most accurate?
o: Benefits begin once she has breastfed without formula for 6 months
Colostrum helps, but later milk gives no advantage over formula
Breastfeeding benefits her and the baby even if done for a short time
Short spells of breastfeeding confuse the baby and are best avoided
6.w: NICE NG194 1.5.2: discussions about breastfeeding should include how it can have benefits even if only done for a short time, and how it can soothe and comfort the baby. Advice respects the parents' choices (1.5.1).

n.0: There is no 6-month threshold before benefits begin; NG194 states short-term breastfeeding still helps.
n.1: Breast milk continues to provide immune and nutritional benefits beyond the first week.
n.3: Any breastfeeding is beneficial; there is no evidence that short spells confuse the baby.

6.q: Megan, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant and has just had her anomaly scan. She asks when she should have the whooping cough vaccine. What should the midwife advise?
o: Now, as it is given from 16 weeks and ideally before 32 weeks
At 28 weeks, as it is given with the RSV vaccine
After the birth, as it protects the baby through breastfeeding
At 36 weeks, as protection is highest closer to the birth
6.w: Green Book ch 24: pertussis vaccine can be given from 16 weeks, usually around the mid-pregnancy scan (about 20 weeks), ideally before 32 weeks for best passive protection of the baby.

n.1: Pertussis vaccine can be given from 16 weeks; there is no need to wait until 28 weeks.
n.2: Vaccination in pregnancy gives passive antibody protection to the baby before birth.
n.3: Vaccination ideally before 32 weeks gives better passive protection for the baby.

6.q: Kayla, 21, is bottle feeding with formula. Her baby often takes the whole bottle quickly and then brings back milk. Which advice best reflects responsive bottle feeding?
o: Prop the bottle on a cushion so the baby can feed at their own pace
Hold the baby close, pace the feed and let the baby decide when to stop
Share feeds among relatives so the baby bonds with many people
Encourage the baby to finish each bottle so feeds stay regular
6.w: NICE NG194 1.5.19: responsive bottle feeding involves holding the baby close, pacing feeds, recognising signs the baby has had enough (because formula-fed babies can be overfed), the dangers of prop feeding, and minimising the number of people regularly feeding the baby.

n.0: Prop feeding is dangerous (choking) and removes the close contact of feeding.
n.2: NG194 notes a potential benefit of minimising the number of people regularly feeding the baby.
n.3: Pushing the baby to finish the bottle risks overfeeding.

6.q: Hana, 32, is 30 weeks pregnant with P-PROM confirmed yesterday. She is taking oral erythromycin and asks why she needs an injection of corticosteroid. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It helps the baby's lungs mature and reduces breathing problems if born early
It relaxes the uterus and lowers the chance of labour starting this week
It protects the baby's brain and lowers the risk of cerebral palsy
It reduces her risk of developing an infection of the womb before birth
6.w: NG25 1.9.2 recommends maternal corticosteroids between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, planned preterm birth or P-PROM. They accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce neonatal respiratory complications.

n.1: Corticosteroids are not tocolytics; nifedipine is used to delay labour.
n.2: Neuroprotection against cerebral palsy is the purpose of magnesium sulfate, not corticosteroids.
n.3: Erythromycin, not a corticosteroid, is the prophylaxis against intrauterine infection.

6.q: Sky, 17, is 12 weeks pregnant. She lives with her mother, who works full time and does not receive benefits. Sky asks if she can get help with buying healthy food. What should the midwife tell her?
o: She does not qualify because her household does not receive benefits
She qualifies for Healthy Start once the baby is born
She qualifies for Healthy Start because she is pregnant and under 18
She qualifies for Healthy Start from 20 weeks of pregnancy
6.w: The NHS Healthy Start scheme helps with milk, fruit, vegetables and pulses and gives free vitamins. Pregnant women under 18 are eligible whatever their income; women 18 and over qualify through benefits. SPM 3.3 includes supporting access to resources and services.

n.0: Benefit criteria apply to women aged 18 and over; pregnant under 18s are eligible regardless.
n.1: Pregnant women under 18 are eligible during pregnancy, not after the birth.
n.3: Eligibility is from 10 weeks of pregnancy, so she can apply now.

6.q: According to the MBRRACE-UK data brief on maternal deaths in 2022 to 2024, how did the maternal death rate for Black women compare with that for White women?
o: About ten times higher
About one and a half times higher
About the same
Nearly three times higher
6.w: MBRRACE-UK maternal mortality data brief 2022-24 (September 2026 update): Black women died at nearly three times the rate of White women. SPM 1.17.1: health inequalities and their determinants.

n.0: The figure is nearly three times, not ten.
n.1: The disparity is larger: nearly three times.
n.2: The data show a large disparity, not similar rates.

6.q: Bisi, a community midwife, is completing her revalidation portfolio. Which statement about her written reflective accounts meets the NMC requirement?
o: Five accounts on the NMC form, written in academic essay style
Five accounts in any format, each linked to her job description
Five accounts on the NMC form, each linked to the Code
Three accounts on the NMC form, each linked to the Code
6.w: NMC revalidation: five written reflective accounts in the 3-year period, recorded on the NMC reflective accounts form, each explaining what was learned from CPD, feedback or an experience and how it relates to the Code. They do not need to be lengthy or academic.

n.0: The NMC states accounts do not need to be lengthy or academic-style pieces of writing.
n.1: The NMC form is required, and accounts must relate to the Code rather than a job description.
n.3: Five accounts are required, not three.

6.q: Grace, 26, is in established labour and is considering an epidural. She has heard that it causes long-term backache and makes a caesarean more likely. Which information is accurate?
o: It lengthens the first stage of labour and is less effective than opioids
It causes long-term backache but does not affect the second stage of labour
It is not linked to long-term backache but is linked to more forceps or ventouse births
It increases the chance of an unplanned caesarean birth and shortens the second stage
