6.w: NICE NG235 1.6.26: epidural gives more effective pain relief than opioids; it is not associated with long-term backache, a longer first stage or an increased chance of unplanned caesarean birth; it is associated with a longer second stage and an increased chance of forceps or ventouse birth.

n.0: Epidural is not associated with a longer first stage and is more effective than opioids.
n.1: Epidural is not associated with long-term backache, and it does lengthen the second stage.
n.3: Epidural is not associated with more unplanned caesarean births and is associated with a longer, not shorter, second stage.

6.q: Yasmin, 27, is 38+5 weeks pregnant. Group B streptococcus was found on a urine culture at 30 weeks. She phones to say her membranes ruptured 30 minutes ago with clear fluid and she has no contractions. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Wait at home for up to 24 hours, taking oral antibiotics
Attend within 12 hours for a speculum examination
Wait at home for up to 24 hours, then attend for induction
Attend now; immediate induction of labour should be offered
6.w: NICE NG235 1.7.11 (and NG207 1.2.16): if a woman has PROM at term and a positive GBS test at any time in the current pregnancy, offer immediate induction (or caesarean if planned). Intrapartum antibiotics follow NICE neonatal infection guidance. GBS carriage is also a phone triage risk factor needing urgent in-person review (1.7.1).

n.0: Oral antibiotics at home do not replace intrapartum IV prophylaxis and immediate induction.
n.1: The 12-hour review applies to women with no risk factors on phone triage; GBS carriage requires immediate attendance.
n.2: Expectant management for 24 hours is for women without risk factors; GBS positive women are offered immediate induction.

6.q: Precious, 22, has an eclamptic seizure on the antenatal ward and remains unconscious afterwards. She needs magnesium sulfate urgently. What is the legal basis for treatment?
o: Best interests treatment under the MCA 2005
A Court of Protection order
The consent of her next of kin
Her consent once she regains consciousness
6.w: She lacks capacity at the material time (MCA 2005 s2; temporary impairment counts, s2(2)). Treatment that cannot wait is given in her best interests (s4, s5), taking account of any known wishes.

n.1: A court order is not needed for urgent treatment in an emergency.
n.2: Next of kin cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney.
n.3: Waiting for consciousness would delay treatment needed to prevent further seizures.

6.q: The midwife gives 5 inflation breaths to Baby Tom, born at 41 weeks, but sees no chest rise and the heart rate is not increasing. What should she do next?
o: Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath
Give ventilation breaths at 30 per minute as planned
Reposition the head and use a two-person jaw thrust, then repeat
Increase the inflation pressure to 50 cm H2O and continue
6.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if there is no chest rise, check and correct head position, consider two-person jaw thrust or a supraglottic airway, then repeat the 5 inflation breaths. Compressions are not effective until the lungs are aerated.

n.0: Compressions are not started until the lungs have been effectively aerated.
n.1: Ventilation breaths will not work until airway obstruction is corrected and chest rise is seen.
n.3: Pressure may be increased cautiously after airway manoeuvres, not jumped to 50 cm H2O first.

6.q: Kate, 37, smokes 10 cigarettes a day. She has had a spontaneous vaginal birth at term with no complications. Her BMI is 27 and she has no other risk factors. Using the RCOG VTE score, which postnatal plan is most appropriate?
o: No LMWH, as her postnatal score is below the threshold of 3
Consider LMWH for at least 10 days after the birth
LMWH until she has stopped smoking cigarettes
LMWH for 6 weeks after the birth
6.w: RCOG GTG 37a score: age over 35 = 1, smoker = 1, total 2. A postnatal score of 2 or more means considering LMWH thromboprophylaxis for at least 10 days. A BMI of 27 does not score.

n.0: The postnatal threshold is 2, not 3 (3 is the antenatal threshold for prophylaxis from 28 weeks).
n.2: Duration is set by the risk assessment, not by ongoing smoking; smoking cessation support is offered separately.
n.3: 6 weeks is for high-risk women such as previous VTE; a score of 2 indicates at least 10 days.

6.q: Laila, 31, is 36 weeks pregnant. A scan confirms an intrauterine fetal death. She is physically well, her membranes are intact and there are no signs of infection or bleeding. She says she cannot face labour today. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Send her home and ask her to return to the unit when labour starts naturally
Advise immediate induction of labour today to reduce the risk of infection
Discuss expectant management, induction and caesarean, and respect her choice
Arrange a caesarean birth today as the quickest way to end the pregnancy
6.w: NICE NG207 1.2.28: after intrauterine fetal death, if the woman is physically well with intact membranes and no infection or bleeding, discuss the options for birth (expectant management, induction or caesarean) and respect her decision. Support for her and her family is offered (1.2.27).

n.0: Expectant management is a valid option but is a decision to be discussed and agreed, with support and follow-up, not a default discharge.
n.1: Immediate induction is offered when there are ruptured membranes, infection or bleeding (NG207 1.2.29), which Laila does not have.
n.3: Caesarean carries surgical morbidity; it is one option to discuss, not the default recommendation.

6.q: Tia, 26, is 6 days after a caesarean birth and at home. At a postnatal visit she feels very unwell, with offensive lochia. Her heart rate is 134 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min and blood pressure 108/66 mmHg. What should the community midwife do?
o: Call 999 and pre-alert the hospital
Ask her GP to see her at the surgery later today
Take a high vaginal swab and revisit her tomorrow
Advise paracetamol and phone triage if she worsens
6.w: A heart rate over 130 is a high-risk criterion (NICE NG255 table 1). Outside hospital, a person meeting any high-risk criterion is referred for emergency care, usually by 999 ambulance, and secondary care is pre-alerted (NG255 1.6.1, 1.6.2).

n.1: A GP appointment later delays emergency care for a high-risk woman.
n.2: A swab and revisit delays treatment of possible sepsis with a high-risk criterion.
n.3: Paracetamol can mask fever and delays urgent assessment.

6.q: Naomi, a midwife on a busy postnatal ward, is working with Carol, a maternity support worker who has been trained and assessed as competent in maternal observations. Which task is most appropriate for Naomi to delegate to Carol?
o: Giving the first dose of intravenous antibiotics to a woman with a fever
Assessing a perineal wound and deciding whether the woman can go home
Carrying out the newborn and infant physical examination before discharge
Recording 4-hourly observations for a well woman after a straightforward birth
6.w: Code 11.1: delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence, making sure they understand the instructions. Routine observations for a well woman are within Carol's assessed competence; assessment, clinical decision-making and IV medicines stay with registered practitioners.

n.0: Administering IV antibiotics is a registered practitioner's task and outside an MSW's scope.
n.1: Assessing a wound and making a discharge decision require a registered midwife's clinical judgement.
n.2: The newborn and infant physical examination is carried out by a trained registered practitioner, not an MSW.

6.q: Jess, 16, books at 12 weeks. She is living with her mother, is still at school and finds hospital clinics intimidating. Which care arrangement best follows NICE CG110?
o: Care deferred until her mother can attend every appointment with her
Standard consultant-led clinic care, as she is under 18
A named midwife providing most of her care, with a direct phone number
Antenatal care through her school nurse until 28 weeks
6.w: CG110 1.4.4: offer young women under 20 a named midwife who provides most of their antenatal care, with a direct-line telephone number. Services should be age-appropriate, community-based where possible and alert to safeguarding (1.4.1, 1.4.5).

n.0: Jess can attend herself; deferring care until her mother is available is a barrier to antenatal care.
n.1: Age alone is not an indication for consultant-led care; young women need accessible, age-appropriate services.
n.3: School nurses do not provide antenatal care; the midwife does.

6.q: Marta, 34, has bipolar disorder and is 24 weeks pregnant. After specialist discussion she has decided to continue lithium because she is at high risk of relapse. Which monitoring plan is in line with NICE CG192?
o: Check plasma lithium at booking, at 28 weeks and at 36 weeks
Check plasma lithium weekly from 20 weeks until the birth
Check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks
Check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then stop it at 36 weeks
6.w: NICE CG192 1.4.37: if lithium continues in pregnancy, check plasma levels every 4 weeks, then weekly from the 36th week; keep levels in range, maintain fluid balance, plan birth in hospital, stop lithium during labour and check levels 12 hours after the last dose.

n.0: Three checks in pregnancy is less frequent than the 4-weekly monitoring recommended.
n.1: Weekly checks are recommended from 36 weeks, not from 20 weeks.
n.3: Lithium is stopped during labour, not at 36 weeks, when weekly monitoring starts.

6.q: Jasmine, 27, is 16 weeks pregnant. While she is in the toilet, her partner asks the midwife for the results of her booking blood tests, including the infection screen. Jasmine has not said whether he may be told. What should the midwife do?
o: Give the results, as he is the baby's father
Explain she will discuss results with Jasmine first
Give the normal results and withhold any abnormal ones
Give the results if he can confirm her date of birth
6.w: NMC Code 5.1 and 5.2: respect privacy and confidentiality; results belong to Jasmine, who decides who is told. The midwife discusses them with her and asks her wishes (SPM 1.24).

n.0: Being the father of the baby does not give a right to the woman's health information.
n.2: Revealing that some results are normal while withholding others still discloses information without consent.
n.3: Knowing her date of birth does not give him permission to receive her results.

6.q: Freya, 27, books at 10 weeks. She has no personal history of mental illness. Her mother had postpartum psychosis after Freya's birth. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Advise her GP to start medication to prevent psychosis after birth
Refer her for immediate mental health assessment within 4 hours
Reassure her, as a family history does not affect her own risk
Record it and watch for postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks
6.w: NICE CG192 1.5.9 and 1.5.11: ask about severe perinatal mental illness in a first-degree relative, and if present be alert for possible symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after childbirth. The history should be shared in her care plan so the postnatal team is aware.

n.0: There is no indication for preventive medication in a woman with no personal history of mental illness.
n.1: The 4-hour pathway is for sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis, which she does not have.
n.2: A first-degree family history of severe perinatal mental illness does increase her risk.

6.q: Grace, 34, is in her third labour. Her cervix is 4 cm dilated but only partly effaced. A student midwife asks whether this is unusual. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Partial effacement at 4 cm is a sign of obstructed labour
In parous women effacement and dilatation often happen together
Partial effacement at 4 cm means she is still in the latent first stage
In parous women dilatation cannot begin until effacement is complete
6.w: In a first labour the cervix usually effaces before it dilates. In parous women effacement and dilatation commonly occur together, so a partly effaced cervix at 4 cm is normal. NICE defines established first stage as regular contractions with progressive dilatation from 4 cm (NG235 1.8.1).

n.0: Partial effacement is normal in parous women and is not a sign of obstruction.
n.2: Established labour is defined by regular contractions and progressive dilatation from 4 cm, not by complete effacement.
n.3: Effacement before dilatation is the usual pattern in first labours, not in parous women.

6.q: Tess, a band 6 midwife, completes an audit showing that 70% of women with a postpartum haemorrhage had a documented quantitative blood loss measurement against a trust standard of 95%. She presents the findings at the governance meeting. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Publish the result in a journal as evidence of poor national practice
Agree an action plan to improve practice and set a date for re-audit
Lower the trust standard to 70% to reflect what is achievable
Repeat the same audit next month to confirm the figure
6.w: After comparing practice with the standard, the audit cycle moves to implementing change through an agreed action plan and then re-auditing to close the loop. Audit findings are local and are not generalisable research (HRA defining research table).

n.0: A local audit measures practice in one service against a local standard; it does not produce generalisable evidence about national practice.
n.2: Lowering the standard to match performance defeats the purpose of audit, which is to raise practice to the standard.
n.3: Repeating the audit without any change will show the same gap; change must be made before re-auditing.

6.q: Grace, 24, has decided to formula feed her baby after an informed discussion. Which action by the midwife best supports her decision?
o: Advise her to feed her baby to a fixed 3-hourly schedule
Advise her to change to a follow-on formula at 3 months old
Show her how to make up feeds safely and feed responsively
Give her a list of formula brands that are best for newborns
6.w: NG194 1.5.17-1.5.19: first infant formula is the only formula needed in the first year unless there is a medical need; give information on safe preparation and responsive bottle feeding. Baby Friendly Stage 3 includes supporting parents to make informed decisions.

n.0: Responsive feeding to the baby's cues is recommended rather than fixed schedules.
n.1: Follow-on formula is not needed; first infant formula is suitable for the first year.
n.3: Recommending brands is promotion; any first infant formula meets a baby's needs.

6.q: First-time parents of a 6-day-old baby are worried that they will not know if their baby becomes unwell. Which advice from the midwife best reflects NICE NG194?
o: Explain that serious infection in a baby will cause a high fever
Advise taking the baby's temperature every 4 hours, day and night
Advise waiting for the health visitor's first visit to raise worries
Give information on the Baby Check scoring system and when to call 999
6.w: NICE NG194 1.3.12-1.3.13: consider giving parents information about the Baby Check scoring system, and advise them to seek advice if they think the baby is unwell and to call 999 if they think the baby is seriously ill. 1.4.4: fever may be absent in young babies with serious infection.

n.0: Fever may not be present in young babies with serious infection (NG194 1.4.4).
n.1: Routine 4-hourly temperatures are not recommended and can miss other signs of illness.
n.2: Parents should seek advice whenever they are worried, not wait for a scheduled visit.

6.q: Hannah, 32, is having a planned home birth. Her community midwife has no prescription chart or patient group directions for this birth. Which medicine can the registered midwife lawfully administer under the midwives exemptions in Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012?
o: Intramuscular oxytocin for the third stage
Intravenous tranexamic acid for heavy bleeding
Intravenous co-amoxiclav for suspected infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for a seizure
6.w: HMR 2012 Schedule 17 lists the parenteral prescription-only medicines a registered midwife may administer in professional practice, including oxytocins (natural and synthetic), ergometrine, carboprost, anti-D, phytomenadione and others (SPM 3.19 midwives exemptions).

n.1: Tranexamic acid is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.
n.2: Antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav are not on the Schedule 17 list.
n.3: Magnesium sulfate is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.

6.q: Lin, 33, is hepatitis B positive. Her baby has just been born at term and is well. When should the baby receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine?
o: Within 7 days of birth
Within 24 hours of birth
After the newborn blood spot test on day 5
At 8 weeks with the routine vaccines
6.w: Green Book ch 18: babies born to hepatitis B positive mothers should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, within 24 hours (with hepatitis B immunoglobulin if indicated), then further doses.

n.0: The first dose should be given as soon as possible and within 24 hours.
n.2: Waiting until day 5 delays protection and is not linked to blood spot screening.
n.3: Babies of hepatitis B positive mothers need a dose at birth; 8 weeks is too late to prevent transmission.

6.q: Hollie, 25, is in established labour in a birth room with her partner. She wants a calm, private environment. Which action by the midwife best supports this?
o: Knocking and waiting before entering, and asking others to do the same
Asking her partner to wait outside during each vaginal examination
Turning on the main lights so that her colour can be observed
Keeping the door open so staff can see her progress from the corridor
6.w: NICE NG235 1.4.11: respect the woman's personal space, privacy and dignity, and ask others to do the same, for example by knocking and waiting before entering. A calm, private environment supports oxytocin release and physiological labour (SPM 3.24).

n.1: Her birth companion of choice should be supported to stay (NG235 1.4.13) unless she asks otherwise.
n.2: Bright lighting is not needed for routine observation and can disturb a calm environment.
n.3: An open door undermines privacy and dignity.

6.q: Baby Kai is born at 40 weeks on a midwife-led unit. After drying and stimulation he is floppy, pale and not breathing, with a heart rate of about 70 beats/min. The midwife has called for help and placed him on the resuscitaire with his head in a neutral position. What is the next step?
o: Give 5 inflation breaths at 30 cm H2O in air
Suction the mouth and nose before any breaths
Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3:1
Give oxygen at 100% by face mask held over his face
6.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if not breathing adequately, open the airway and give 5 inflation breaths of 2-3 seconds each, starting at 30 cm H2O for babies 32 weeks or more, in 21% oxygen (air). NICE NG235 1.11.22 also advises starting basic resuscitation in air.

n.1: Routine suction is not recommended and delays lung inflation.
n.2: Compressions start only if the heart rate is under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.
n.3: Term babies start in air; free-flow oxygen does not inflate fluid-filled lungs.

6.q: A maternity governance meeting is discussing the East Kent report, "Reading the signals" (Kirkup, 2022). Which list matches the report's four areas for action?
o: Safe staffing, multidisciplinary training, complex antenatal care, bereavement care
Smoking, fetal growth, fetal movements, fetal monitoring, preterm birth, diabetes
Identifying poor performance, compassion and kindness, teamworking, responding with honesty
Listening to women, workforce, safety culture, standards and structures
6.w: East Kent (19 October 2022): identifying poorly performing units; giving care with compassion and kindness; teamworking with a common purpose; responding to challenge with honesty.

n.0: These are among the Ockenden immediate and essential action themes.
n.1: These are the six elements of Saving Babies' Lives v3.
n.3: These are the four themes of the NHS England three-year delivery plan (2023).

6.q: A baby born at term needs therapeutic cooling after a difficult labour in an NHS trust in England. The parents ask whether an independent body will look into the care. Which body carries out independent maternity safety investigations in England?
o: The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
Maternity and Newborn Safety Investigations (MNSI)
The Perinatal Mortality Review Tool (PMRT) team
The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC)
6.w: MNSI carries out independent investigations of certain maternity and newborn safety events reported by NHS trusts in England, working with families and staff and making safety recommendations without blaming individuals (MNSI).

n.0: The Ombudsman considers complaints after local processes are exhausted, not safety investigations.
n.2: The PMRT supports local hospital reviews of perinatal deaths; it is not an independent investigation body.
n.3: The NMC regulates individual registrants' fitness to practise; it does not investigate maternity safety events.

6.q: A midwife is assessing four babies on the postnatal ward. Using NICE CG98, which baby has the most risk factors for developing significant hyperbilirubinaemia?
o: Born at 41 weeks; mixed feeding; first child with no siblings
Born at 36 weeks; sibling had phototherapy; exclusive breastfeeding planned
Born at 38+2 weeks; formula fed; mother had gestational diabetes
Born at 39 weeks by caesarean; formula fed; no family history of jaundice
6.w: NICE CG98 1.2.1 risk factors: gestational age under 38 weeks, a previous sibling who needed phototherapy, mother's intention to breastfeed exclusively, and visible jaundice in the first 24 hours. The baby born at 36 weeks has three of these factors.

n.0: 41 weeks with mixed feeding and no sibling history gives no CG98 risk factors.
n.2: 38+2 weeks is not under 38 weeks, and formula feeding is not a risk factor.
n.3: Caesarean birth and formula feeding at 39 weeks are not CG98 risk factors.

6.q: A midwife is preparing intramuscular vitamin K (phytomenadione) for baby Rhys, born at 40 weeks weighing 3.4 kg. Which dose should she expect to give?
o: 1 mg as a single dose
2 mg as a single dose
400 micrograms as a single dose
3.4 mg, at 1 mg per kilogram
6.w: BNF for Children (phytomenadione): neonatal prophylaxis of vitamin K deficiency bleeding by intramuscular injection is 1 mg as a single dose at birth for a term neonate. The weight-based dose of 400 micrograms/kg (max 1 mg) is for preterm neonates.

n.1: 2 mg is the oral dose of Konakion MM Paediatric, not the IM dose.
n.2: 400 micrograms is the per-kilogram preterm dose, not the term dose.
n.3: IM prophylaxis is not 1 mg per kilogram; the term dose is a single 1 mg.

6.q: Mia, 31, is 37 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated pregnancy and plans to give birth in an alongside midwifery unit. She asks who is in charge of her care. Who is her lead professional?
o: Her named midwife
A consultant obstetrician
The labour ward coordinator
Her GP
6.w: For women with uncomplicated pregnancies the midwife is the accountable, autonomous lead professional across the continuum of care (NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives 1.6).

n.1: Obstetric lead care is for women with complications or additional needs, which Mia does not have.
n.2: The coordinator manages the unit's workload; she is not the lead professional for an individual woman's care.
n.3: The GP is not the lead professional for routine maternity care in an uncomplicated pregnancy.

6.q: Following a cluster of maternal deaths from venous thromboembolism reported in national data, a midwife wants to use the findings in her practice. Which action best applies national report findings to individual care?
o: Reassess VTE risk at booking and on admission, and support informed choices
Wait for the trust to update its guideline before changing her practice
Share the national report with women at booking and let them decide what to do
Advise all pregnant women to take low molecular weight heparin from their booking visit
6.w: SPM 1.5 requires midwives to use and apply lessons from data and reports to inform practice and support women's evidence-informed decisions. Applying VTE learning means individualised risk assessment at booking, repeated on any admission or new problem and around birth (NICE NG201 1.2.18; RCOG GTG 37a), and shared decision-making about prophylaxis.

n.1: Applying current national guidance on VTE risk assessment does not depend on waiting for a local update.
n.2: Handing over a report without discussion does not support informed decision-making.
n.3: Universal prophylaxis is not recommended; prophylaxis follows individual risk assessment.

6.q: Kirsty, 32, asks why she needs an anti-D injection at 28 weeks when she feels well and has had no bleeding. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It reduces her risk of bleeding heavily at the birth
It is a vaccine that protects her baby from jaundice after birth
It stops her forming antibodies that could harm a future RhD-positive baby
It treats anaemia caused by her baby's blood entering her circulation
6.w: Small, unnoticed fetomaternal haemorrhages can expose an RhD-negative woman to RhD-positive fetal cells. Anti-D prophylaxis prevents her immune system forming anti-D antibodies, which could cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in this or a future pregnancy (NICE TA156; SPM 3.20).

n.0: Anti-D has no effect on postpartum haemorrhage risk.
n.1: Anti-D is an immunoglobulin given to the mother, not a vaccine for the baby.
n.3: Anti-D does not treat maternal anaemia; it prevents sensitisation.

6.q: Grace, 34, is RhD negative and has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth. Cord blood shows that her baby is RhD positive. She received routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks. What is the correct plan?
o: Offer anti-D within 72 hours of the birth
Offer anti-D at her 6-week postnatal check
Anti-D is not needed, as she had antenatal prophylaxis
Offer anti-D in her next pregnancy at booking
6.w: After the birth of an RhD-positive baby to an RhD-negative woman who is not sensitised, anti-D is given as soon as possible and within 72 hours, with a test to assess the size of any fetomaternal haemorrhage. Antenatal prophylaxis does not cover exposure at birth.

n.1: Six weeks is far too late; sensitisation can occur within days of exposure.
n.2: Birth is a separate sensitising event; antenatal prophylaxis does not cover it.
n.3: Waiting until the next pregnancy allows sensitisation to occur after this birth.

6.q: Layla, 31, is 41+3 weeks pregnant. After a full discussion of benefits and risks she declines induction and wishes to wait for labour to start naturally. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer her to the safeguarding team because of the risk to the baby
Discharge her to routine care with no further appointments until labour
Respect and record her decision; discuss extra monitoring from 42 weeks
Explain that induction must be booked once a pregnancy passes 41 weeks
6.w: NICE NG207 1.2.6 to 1.2.8: if she declines induction, discuss her options, record her decision, discuss additional fetal monitoring from 42 weeks (explaining it gives a snapshot and cannot predict later problems) and offer her the chance to revisit her decision at later reviews.

n.0: Declining a recommended intervention is not a safeguarding issue; an unborn baby has no separate legal rights over her decision.
n.1: She should be offered ongoing review and monitoring from 42 weeks and the chance to change her mind.
n.3: A woman with capacity can decline induction (NG207 1.2.19); it is not compulsory.

6.q: Mei, 29, is well and has an uncomplicated pregnancy. She asks about a birth centre in her town that is on a different site from the hospital and has no obstetricians or anaesthetists. Which setting is she describing?
o: An alongside midwifery unit
An obstetric unit
A freestanding midwifery unit
A midwife-led triage unit
6.w: NICE NG235 1.2.1 and 1.3.3 name four birth settings: home, freestanding midwifery unit (on a separate site from an obstetric unit), alongside midwifery unit (same site) and obstetric unit. A unit away from the hospital without obstetric or anaesthetic staff is freestanding (SPM 2.1).

n.0: An alongside midwifery unit is on the same site as an obstetric unit, so transfer does not need an ambulance.
n.1: An obstetric unit has obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal staff on site, which this birth centre lacks.
n.3: Triage assesses women who call or attend with concerns; it is not a place planned for giving birth.

6.q: During a breech birth, Nadia's baby has been born to the umbilicus with the back anterior. The buttocks were born 2 minutes ago. The baby has good tone and colour and is descending with each contraction. What should the midwife do?
o: Ask Nadia to stop pushing to protect the perineum
Keep her hands off and continue to observe progress
Grasp the legs and apply traction to deliver the arms
Deliver the head at once using Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit
6.w: RCOG GTG 20b: a hands-off approach with timely intervention if progress is not made once the umbilicus has delivered, or if there is poor tone, extended arms or neck. Intervention is generally required if more than 5 minutes from buttocks to head or more than 3 minutes from umbilicus to head. Good tone and progress mean no intervention yet.

n.0: Stopping maternal effort delays the birth when cord compression is likely.
n.2: Traction is avoided because it can cause arm and head extension.
n.3: The arms and body have not yet been born, and the head is not the next step.

6.q: Mariam, 31, is breastfeeding on the first day after birth. She is worried because she can only express a few drops of thick yellow milk and thinks her baby is not getting enough. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Colostrum is low in antibodies, which rise once her mature milk arrives
Colostrum comes in small amounts, is rich in antibodies and suits a newborn's needs
Colostrum is too concentrated for a newborn and should be expressed and discarded
Colostrum is mainly water, so formula top-ups are needed until her milk comes in
6.w: Colostrum is produced in small volumes in the first days, is concentrated and rich in immunoglobulins (especially secretory IgA) and protective factors, and meets the needs of a healthy term newborn. NG194 1.5.12 asks midwives to explain how much milk is produced in the early stages.

n.0: Colostrum has the highest concentration of antibodies of any milk.
n.2: Colostrum should be given to the baby, not discarded.
n.3: Colostrum is nutrient-dense, not mainly water; routine formula top-ups are not clinically indicated (NG194 1.5.12).

6.q: Lauren, 28, is 24 weeks pregnant and has no children. She discloses that her partner is controlling and has pushed her. She does not want any referral. She has capacity and there is no immediate danger. What should the midwife do first?
o: Complete a risk assessment and offer specialist support
Close the conversation, as she has declined referral
Refer her to the police without her agreement
Tell her partner the midwife is aware of the abuse
6.w: NICE NG201 recommends asking about domestic abuse when the woman is alone. A structured risk assessment (for example DASH) guides action: high risk may justify sharing without consent (for example a MARAC referral), while lower risk means offering specialist support and respecting her decision. The unborn baby is also considered in safeguarding.

n.1: Ending the discussion misses the risk assessment and support she needs.
n.2: Sharing without consent depends on assessed risk, which has not yet been done.
n.3: Telling the partner could put Lauren in danger.

6.q: Parents choose oral vitamin K for their baby, who is being exclusively breastfed. The unit uses Konakion MM Paediatric. Which regimen should the midwife explain, following the BNFC and manufacturer's directions?
o: 2 mg at birth and 2 mg at 4 to 7 days, with no later dose
2 mg at birth, 2 mg at 4 to 7 days and 2 mg at 1 month
A single oral dose of 1 mg given at birth
2 mg each week for the first 12 weeks of life
6.w: BNF for Children (Konakion MM Paediatric by mouth): 2 mg at birth, then 2 mg at 4 to 7 days; exclusively breastfed babies need a further 2 mg at 1 month. NICE NG235 1.11.13: oral vitamin K may need multiple doses, including after discharge, per the manufacturer's instructions.

n.0: Two doses suit babies who are not exclusively breastfed; exclusively breastfed babies need a third dose at 1 month.
n.2: A single 1 mg oral dose at birth does not protect against late vitamin K deficiency bleeding with this product.
n.3: Weekly dosing for 12 weeks is not the Konakion MM Paediatric regimen.

6.q: Ama, 23, is low risk in her first pregnancy. She asks how an alongside midwifery unit compares with the obstetric unit on the same hospital site. Which statement is accurate?
o: The midwifery unit has fewer interventions with no difference in outcome for the baby
The midwifery unit has the same interventions and outcomes as the obstetric unit
The midwifery unit has more interventions with no difference in outcome for the baby
The midwifery unit has fewer interventions and a small increase in risk for the baby
6.w: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk nulliparous women, planning birth in a midwife-led unit (freestanding or alongside) is associated with a lower rate of interventions and the outcome for the baby is no different from an obstetric unit.

n.1: Outcomes for the baby are similar, but interventions are lower in midwife-led units.
n.2: Midwife-led units are associated with a lower, not higher, rate of interventions (NG235 1.3.3).
n.3: The small increase in risk for the baby applies to planned home birth for nulliparous women, not midwife-led units.

6.q: Harriet, 36, has severe pre-eclampsia. The midwife escalated her blood pressure of 168/112 mmHg and new headache to the registrar 30 minutes ago. The registrar said they would come but is still in theatre, and her blood pressure is now 172/114 mmHg. What should the midwife do?
o: Wait for the registrar, who has already been informed
Escalate to the obstetric consultant using the escalation policy
Record the new reading and recheck it in 30 minutes
Ask the anaesthetist to prescribe an antihypertensive instead
6.w: When escalation does not produce a timely response and the woman is deteriorating, the midwife escalates further up the chain, usually to the consultant, using the unit's escalation policy, and documents this (SPM 4.6; Code 16 and 8.2). Severe hypertension needs prompt treatment (NG133).

n.0: Waiting while severe hypertension worsens delays treatment.
n.2: Rechecking without escalation leaves severe hypertension untreated.
n.3: Escalation should follow the obstetric chain and escalation policy rather than going around it.

6.q: Yasmin, 32, is in labour at term with a previous caesarean. Continuous CTG is recommended, but she declines it. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Apply the CTG anyway as she has a uterine scar
Ask the registrar to apply the CTG while the midwife reassures her
Stop monitoring the baby until she agrees to the CTG
Explain why, offer intermittent auscultation and document it
6.w: SPM 1.21: respect the right to decline and provide appropriate care. The midwife explains why continuous monitoring is advised (NICE NG229 for women with a previous caesarean), offers an alternative such as intermittent auscultation and documents the discussion.

n.0: Applying monitoring she has declined is treatment without consent.
n.1: Applying the CTG through another clinician is still monitoring without consent.
n.2: Stopping monitoring removes all fetal assessment; she should be offered an acceptable alternative.

6.q: Lucy, 30, is RhD negative and 28 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. Her booking antibody screen was negative and she has had no bleeding or trauma. Which care should be offered at this appointment?
o: Weekly antibody screens from 28 weeks instead of anti-D prophylaxis
Blood group and antibody screen, FBC and routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis
FBC and antibody screen, with anti-D given if the screen is positive
Anti-D prophylaxis after the birth, when the baby's blood group is known
6.w: At 28 weeks offer FBC, blood group and antibodies, and anti-D prophylaxis to RhD-negative women who are not known to be sensitised (NICE NG201 1.2.16; NICE TA156 1.1). RAADP protects against sensitisation from silent fetomaternal haemorrhage in late pregnancy.

n.0: Repeated antibody screening detects sensitisation after it happens; it does not prevent it.
n.2: A positive anti-D antibody screen would mean she is already sensitised, when prophylaxis no longer helps; RAADP is for women who are not sensitised.
n.3: Postnatal anti-D is also given if the baby is RhD positive, but it does not replace antenatal prophylaxis.

6.q: Priya, 28, plans to breastfeed and give one bottle of formula each evening. She asks whether her baby could be overfed with either method. Which statement is accurate?
o: A breastfed baby cannot be overfed but a formula-fed baby can, so pace bottles
Either method can lead to overfeeding, so both should be limited to set volumes
A formula-fed baby cannot be overfed, as the baby stops when the bottle is finished
A breastfed baby can be overfed if feeds last longer than 20 minutes
6.w: NICE NG194 1.5.12 and 1.5.19: it is not possible to overfeed a breastfed baby, but it is possible to overfeed a formula-fed baby, so parents should pace bottle feeds and recognise signs the baby has had enough.

n.1: Breastfed babies regulate their own intake, so set volumes for breastfeeding are not appropriate.
n.2: Encouraging a baby to finish the bottle is how formula-fed babies become overfed.
n.3: Long feeds at the breast do not cause overfeeding; NG194 states a breastfed baby cannot be overfed.

6.q: For three months, Fatima has reported unsafe staffing on the labour ward to her manager. Nothing has changed, and two near misses have occurred. Her manager says nothing more can be done. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Post a description of the staffing problem on social media
Keep a private record and wait for the annual staff survey
Raise the concern with the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
Write to a national newspaper about the staffing levels
6.w: Code 16.1: raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns using the available channels. When the line manager does not act, the next step is a higher internal route such as the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian or senior leaders, then prescribed bodies such as the CQC or NMC.

n.0: Social media posts may breach confidentiality and bypass the escalation channels the Code expects.
n.1: Waiting allows the risk to continue; Code 16 requires escalation without delay.
n.3: Going to the press first bypasses internal and regulatory routes and may lose legal protection for the disclosure.

6.q: Kerry, 34, had a caesarean in her first pregnancy and plans a vaginal birth at home with her second, against obstetric advice. What is the most appropriate action by the midwife?
o: Advise her to arrange private midwifery care for the birth
Document her plan and refer her to children's social care
Arrange a personalised care planning meeting with a consultant midwife
Tell Kerry midwives cannot attend a home birth after a caesarean
6.w: SPM 1.22: advocate for the woman when her decision is outside guidance, to minimise risk and maintain the relationship. A consultant midwife care planning meeting allows an honest discussion of risks and a plan that supports her choice (Code 2.5).

n.0: Sending her to private care withdraws NHS support instead of advocating for her.
n.1: Choosing a birth outside guidance is not a safeguarding concern.
n.3: The trust still provides midwifery care; a woman's choice of place of birth does not remove midwifery support.

6.q: Sian, 29, is 3 days postnatal at home after a second-degree tear and reports perineal pain not relieved by paracetamol. She has no contraindications to NSAIDs. Which medicine can the registered midwife supply to her under the midwives exemptions?
o: Co-codamol 30/500 tablets
Diclofenac tablets
Amoxicillin capsules
Dihydrocodeine tablets
6.w: Schedule 17 Part 1 allows registered midwives to sell or supply, in the course of their professional practice, prescription-only medicines containing diclofenac, hydrocortisone acetate, miconazole, nystatin and phytomenadione (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Co-codamol 30/500 contains codeine, which is not on the midwives supply list.
n.2: Antibiotics such as amoxicillin are not on the midwives supply list and need a prescription.
n.3: Dihydrocodeine is not on the midwives supply list.

6.q: Erin, 35, is 14 weeks pregnant and drinks about a bottle of wine every evening. She has had shakes and sweating in the mornings. She wants to stop drinking straight away. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to attend a mutual support group before referral
Refer urgently to the specialist alcohol service for assisted withdrawal
Advise her to stop drinking tonight and contact the midwife if unwell
Advise her to cut down to 14 units a week for the rest of the pregnancy
6.w: Morning shakes and sweating suggest alcohol dependence. Abrupt cessation risks withdrawal seizures, so she needs urgent specialist referral for medically assisted withdrawal, while continuing antenatal care. NG201 1.3.10: no safe level of alcohol in pregnancy (SPM 3.1, 3.3).

n.0: Peer support helps later, but her withdrawal symptoms show dependence needing specialist care now.
n.2: Sudden withdrawal in alcohol dependence can cause seizures and needs medical management.
n.3: There is no safe level in pregnancy, and 14 units is the general adult low-risk guideline.

6.q: Zainab, 25, is 38 weeks pregnant and lives with her toddler in one room of temporary accommodation. She has no cot and plans to share her bed with the new baby. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to contact the housing department herself after the baby is born
Advise her to keep the baby in a pram until she is rehoused
With her consent, liaise with the housing officer and health visitor
Make a child protection referral because the accommodation is unsuitable
6.w: SPM 2.9 requires midwives to work with other professionals and agencies when social determinants affect health. With consent, liaising with housing and the health visitor (who also supports safe sleep, NG194 1.3.14-1.3.15) addresses her needs.

n.0: Leaving it until after the birth delays help; SPM 2.9 expects the midwife to work with other agencies.
n.1: A pram is not a long-term safe sleeping space and this does not address the housing need.
n.3: Poverty and poor housing alone are not abuse; the priority is multiagency support, with a referral if risk of harm is identified.

6.q: Amira, 24, is 11 weeks pregnant. She has vomited everything, including water, for 3 days. She feels dizzy on standing, her urine shows 3+ ketones and she has lost 6% of her booking weight. Oral antiemetics from her GP have not helped. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer her the same day to hospital for assessment and intravenous fluids
Ask her GP to change to a different oral antiemetic and review in 3 days
Advise ginger capsules and small frequent meals, with review in a week
Reassure her that vomiting usually resolves by 16 weeks of pregnancy
6.w: Persistent vomiting with dehydration, ketonuria and weight loss over 5% despite oral antiemetics suggests hyperemesis gravidarum. NICE NG201 1.4.6 and 1.4.7: consider intravenous fluids and consider inpatient care if vomiting is severe and not responding to primary care or outpatient management; VTE risk should also be assessed.

n.1: Changing tablets she cannot keep down delays fluid replacement and assessment.
n.2: Ginger is for mild to moderate symptoms; she has signs of dehydration needing urgent treatment.
n.3: Reassurance is for mild to moderate symptoms; her dehydration and weight loss need treatment now.

6.q: Chloe, a specialist diabetes midwife, wants to interview women with gestational diabetes about cultural beliefs around diet, aiming to develop a theory that could be transferred to other maternity services. She plans to start next month. Which governance step is most appropriate before she begins?
o: Register it as a service evaluation with the maternity governance lead
Register it with the clinical audit department and start next month
Start interviews once women give verbal consent, as there is no intervention
Treat it as research and apply for HRA and NHS ethics committee approval
6.w: Chloe aims to generate new, transferable knowledge, which meets the UK Policy Framework definition of research (para 3.1), including non-interventional qualitative research. Research normally requires NHS REC review, arranged through HRA approval; audit and service evaluation do not (HRA defining research table).

n.0: Service evaluation judges a local service without seeking transferable findings; Chloe's aim takes it into research.
n.1: It is not an audit: there is no standard being measured, and the purpose is new transferable knowledge.
n.2: Non-interventional research is still research under the policy framework; the absence of an intervention does not remove the need for ethical review and written informed consent processes.

6.q: Grace, 34, smokes and had a previous baby below the 3rd centile. She has been placed on serial ultrasound surveillance for fetal growth starting at 28 weeks. At her 30-week community appointment, what should the midwife do about fundal height measurement?
o: Measure fundal height and refer for a scan if it falls below the 50th centile
Stop measuring fundal height, as serial scans have replaced it
Measure and plot fundal height at each visit alongside the scans
Measure fundal height weekly between her scan appointments
6.w: SBL v3 2.12: women on planned serial scan surveillance should stop having SFH measured once serial surveillance begins; growth is assessed by ultrasound.

n.0: SFH has been stopped for this pathway, and the 50th centile is not a referral trigger.
n.2: SBL v3 2.12 says SFH should cease once serial scan surveillance starts.
n.3: Weekly SFH is not part of any SBL v3 pathway and adds no information to serial scans.

6.q: Mia, 27, is RhD negative with no anti-D antibodies. She received routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks. At 31 weeks she presents with a small antepartum haemorrhage that has now settled. What does RCOG GTG 63 recommend about anti-D?
o: No anti-D is needed because routine prophylaxis was given at 28 weeks
Give anti-D immunoglobulin and do a Kleihauer test
Give anti-D after the birth if her baby is RhD positive
Wait for the Kleihauer result before deciding on anti-D
6.w: RCOG GTG 63: anti-D immunoglobulin should be given to all non-sensitised RhD-negative women after any presentation with APH, independent of whether routine antenatal prophylaxis has been given. After 20 weeks, give at least 500 iu and do a test for fetomaternal haemorrhage (Kleihauer) to see whether more is needed.

n.0: Routine prophylaxis does not remove the need for anti-D after a sensitising event.
n.2: Waiting until after the birth leaves her unprotected after a potentially sensitising event now.
n.3: Anti-D is given after any APH without waiting; the Kleihauer test decides whether additional anti-D is needed.

6.q: Ola, 33, is on continuous CTG in established labour. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes, the baseline is 140 beats per minute and there are no decelerations. Variability has been 3 to 4 beats per minute for the last 40 minutes. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Suspicious
Normal
Need for urgent intervention
Pathological
6.w: Variability under 5 beats per minute for 30 to 50 minutes is an amber feature (NICE NG229 1.4.18). Contractions, baseline and decelerations are white. One amber feature makes the CTG suspicious (NG229 1.4.32), prompting a full risk assessment and conservative measures.

n.1: A normal CTG has all four features white; reduced variability for 40 minutes is amber.
n.2: NG229 uses normal, suspicious and pathological; this is not one of its categories.
n.3: Pathological needs one red feature or two or more amber features; there is one amber feature.

6.q: At the start of a night shift, the labour ward coordinator is also allocated a woman in labour because two midwives have called in sick. Following the Ockenden findings, why is this a concern?
o: The coordinator role is held by an obstetrician during the night
A coordinator with a caseload cannot readily support staff and oversee care
Coordinators are not trained to care for women who are in established labour
It breaches the rule that coordinators must work day shifts
6.w: Ockenden found the labour ward coordinator often lacked supernumerary status and had their own caseload, preventing them from being accessible to junior staff for advice, care planning and support. Trusts must recognise the coordinator as a specialist role (IEA 2).

n.0: The labour ward coordinator is a senior midwife role on all shifts.
n.2: Coordinators are experienced midwives able to provide care; the issue is loss of oversight.
n.3: No such rule exists; the issue is supernumerary status, not shift pattern.

6.q: Baby Dev is 10 weeks old and has just moved to England from abroad. He has not had newborn blood spot screening. What should the health professional offer?
o: No screening, as blood spot screening ends at 8 weeks of age
Blood spot screening for the conditions except cystic fibrosis
Blood spot screening for all 10 conditions in the usual way
Cystic fibrosis screening, as the other tests are now too late
6.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: babies are eligible up to 1 year of age, except for cystic fibrosis screening, which is unreliable after 8 weeks. At 10 weeks Dev should be offered screening for the other conditions.

n.0: Eligibility continues to 1 year for the other conditions.
n.2: CF screening is unreliable after 8 weeks, so it is not offered at 10 weeks.
n.3: CF is the one test that is too late; the other conditions can still be screened.

6.q: Ifeoma, a midwife, is a passenger on a long-haul flight when the crew ask for help: a woman is in labour at about 38 weeks. Ifeoma is off duty and has no equipment of her own. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Wait until the crew confirm no doctor is on board before helping
Offer help within her competence and support the crew's emergency plans
Offer advice but avoid physical contact as she is outside the UK
Stay seated as her employer's indemnity does not cover care on the flight
6.w: NMC Code 15: always offer help if an emergency arises in your practice setting or anywhere else, acting within the limits of your knowledge and competence (15.1) and arranging for emergency care to be accessed promptly (15.2), taking account of safety (15.3).

n.0: Delaying help while waiting for a doctor wastes time; a midwife is competent to attend a normal birth and should offer help now.
n.2: Code 15 applies anywhere, and a midwife attending a birth in an emergency may give the hands-on care that is needed.
n.3: Indemnity concerns do not remove the professional expectation in Code 15 to offer help in an emergency anywhere.

6.q: A community midwife is discussing place of birth with four women. Which woman should be advised to plan birth in an obstetric unit because of her antenatal risk of postpartum haemorrhage?
o: Amina, 29, para 2, BMI 32 kg/m2
Becky, 24, who had a second-degree tear last time
Dana, 33, who had a PPH needing transfusion last time
Cara, 35, with a low-risk pregnancy and a fundal placenta
6.w: NICE NG235 1.10.29 lists antenatal PPH risk factors that warrant advice to give birth in an obstetric unit, including previous PPH over 1000 mL or requiring transfusion, BMI over 35, grand multiparity (4 or more), pre-eclampsia, Hb under 85 g/L at onset of labour and placenta accreta spectrum.

n.0: BMI over 35 and parity 4 or more are the thresholds; 32 and para 2 do not meet them.
n.1: A previous second-degree tear is not an antenatal PPH risk factor in NG235.
n.3: A fundal placenta in a low-risk pregnancy is not a PPH risk factor.

6.q: A midwife is explaining Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle v3 to a new colleague. Which list correctly describes its six elements?
o: Smoking; fetal growth; fetal movements; fetal monitoring; stillbirth; postnatal care
Smoking; obesity; fetal growth; induction of labour; caesarean birth; neonatal care
Smoking; fetal growth; fetal movements; fetal monitoring; preterm birth; diabetes
Smoking; folic acid; vitamin D; aspirin; fetal growth; preterm birth
6.w: SBL v3 elements: 1 reducing smoking; 2 fetal growth risk assessment, surveillance and management; 3 raising awareness of reduced fetal movement; 4 effective fetal monitoring in labour; 5 reducing preterm births and optimising perinatal care; 6 management of pre-existing diabetes.

n.0: Element 5 is preterm birth and element 6 is pre-existing diabetes; there is no stillbirth or postnatal element.
n.1: Obesity, induction, caesarean and neonatal care are not SBL v3 elements.
n.3: Folic acid, vitamin D and aspirin are interventions within elements, not elements themselves.

6.q: Before transfer home on day 1, Jo, 27, says breastfeeding is going well. The midwife has not yet observed a feed. What does NICE recommend before transfer?
o: Observe at least one effective feed as part of the feeding plan
Give a formula top-up so the baby is settled for the journey
Weigh the baby to confirm feeding is effective
Accept Jo's report and arrange a feed check on day 5
6.w: NG194 1.1.10: before transfer, make sure there is a plan for feeding the baby, including observing at least 1 effective feed; NG194 1.5.14 lists what to assess (SPM 3.6).

n.1: A top-up without clinical need can undermine breastfeeding.
n.2: Weight on day 1 does not show feeding effectiveness; normal weight loss occurs early.
n.3: NICE expects an effective feed to be observed before transfer.

6.q: Lena, 29, is 36+2 weeks pregnant. Her growth scan shows an estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler. She has no other risk factors. When does Saving Babies' Lives v3 recommend birth?
o: Await spontaneous labour with weekly growth scans and Doppler
Initiate labour or birth at 37+0 weeks and no later than 37+6
Plan birth at 40+0 weeks if the Doppler stays normal
Consider birth at 39+0 weeks, achieving birth by 39+6
6.w: SBL v3 2.18: when the EFW is below the 3rd centile with no other risk factors, initiation of labour or delivery should occur at 37+0 weeks and no later than 37+6 weeks, after discussion with the mother.

n.0: An EFW below the 3rd centile carries a high stillbirth risk; expectant management to spontaneous labour is not advised.
n.2: Waiting until 40 weeks exceeds the 37+6 limit set in SBL v3.
n.3: 39+0 to 39+6 weeks applies to an EFW between the 3rd and 10th centile (SBL v3 2.19).

6.q: Emma, 26, is low risk and asks for a physiological third stage after a spontaneous birth at home. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree, and explain that there is no difference in bleeding risk
Explain that active management is required after every home birth
Agree, and give a uterotonic before clamping the cord
Discuss her level of risk, support her choice and document the decision
6.w: NICE NG235 1.10.6 to 1.10.8: advise that active management is associated with a lower risk of PPH and transfusion; if she requests physiological management, discuss her level of risk so she can make an informed decision, support her choice and document it.

n.0: Active management is associated with a lower risk of PPH and transfusion, so this would be inaccurate information.
n.1: Physiological management is a valid choice for a woman at low risk, in any setting.
n.2: Physiological management involves no routine uterotonic; giving one before clamping is active management.

6.q: Rachel, 32, has bipolar disorder and is 6 days postnatal. Her partner phones the midwife: Rachel has not slept for 2 nights, is talking rapidly and believes strangers are watching the baby through the windows. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to specialist mental health services for assessment within 4 hours
Advise rest and sleep tonight and visit again early tomorrow morning
Ask Rachel the Whooley questions at her next routine visit
Book a routine GP appointment for her within the next 2 weeks
6.w: NICE CG192 1.5.11, 1.5.12: be alert for postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks in women with a history of severe mental illness such as bipolar disorder. If psychosis is suspected, refer to a secondary mental health service (preferably a specialist perinatal service) for assessment within 4 hours of referral.

n.1: Postpartum psychosis can deteriorate rapidly; delaying overnight puts Rachel and the baby at risk.
n.2: Screening questions are for identifying depression; she needs urgent assessment now.
n.3: 2 weeks is the CG192 timeframe for assessment after routine mental health referral, not suspected psychosis.

6.q: Following a delay in escalating a pathological CTG, Baby Jacob needed therapeutic cooling for moderate encephalopathy. Under the statutory duty of candour in England, what must the trust do?
o: Inform the parents in writing after the trust's legal team has approved the letter
Tell the parents if they ask directly whether anything went wrong with their baby's care
Tell the parents in person as soon as reasonably practicable, with an account and apology
Wait until the investigation is complete before telling the parents what happened
6.w: Regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014: for a notifiable safety incident, notify the relevant person as soon as reasonably practicable, in person, giving a true account, an apology, details of further enquiries and reasonable support, followed by written notification.

n.0: The initial notification must be in person; written notification follows it.
n.1: The duty is proactive; it does not depend on the family asking.
n.3: Notification must not wait for the investigation; further findings are shared later in writing.

6.q: Leah, 30, is 10 weeks pregnant and uses heroin daily. She tells her midwife she plans to stop suddenly today for the baby's sake. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Support her plan and arrange weekly midwife visits to monitor her
Advise her to reduce her heroin use gradually by herself over 4 weeks
Refer her to the obstetrician and wait for that review before giving any advice
Advise against stopping suddenly and refer to the specialist drug service
6.w: UK drug misuse clinical guidelines advise against abrupt withdrawal from opioids in pregnancy, because of risks to the fetus and of relapse; women should be referred to specialist drug services for opioid substitution therapy with joint maternity care (SPM 3.1, 3.3).

n.0: Abrupt opioid withdrawal in pregnancy carries risks to the fetus and of relapse; it needs specialist management.
n.1: Unsupported reduction is unsafe; specialist services can offer opioid substitution therapy.
n.2: She needs advice now; delaying risks a sudden withdrawal today.

6.q: Nia, 30, has severe pre-eclampsia and is on the delivery suite awaiting induction. She has no ongoing blood loss and is not receiving hydralazine. The midwife is setting up her intravenous maintenance fluids. What rate does NICE NG133 recommend as the limit?
o: 125 mL/hour
80 mL/hour
150 mL/hour
40 mL/hour
6.w: NICE NG133 1.8.12: in severe pre-eclampsia limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL/hour unless there are other ongoing fluid losses such as haemorrhage, because of the risk of pulmonary oedema. Volume expansion is not used unless hydralazine is the antenatal antihypertensive (1.8.11).

n.0: 125 mL/hour exceeds the recommended limit and risks pulmonary oedema.
n.2: 150 mL/hour exceeds the limit and risks pulmonary oedema.
n.3: 40 mL/hour is not the NG133 limit; maintenance fluids are limited to 80 mL/hour.

6.q: Lily, 24, is 28 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. Her BP and urinalysis are normal. The midwife is giving her information about pre-eclampsia. Which advice is most accurate?
o: Seek help immediately for severe headache, blurred vision or pain below the ribs
Seek help if she has heartburn after large meals that settles with an antacid
Wait for her next appointment to mention new headaches, as BP is checked then
Seek help if her ankles swell by evening and settle overnight with feet raised
6.w: NICE NG133 1.1.1: advise pregnant women to see a healthcare professional immediately if they have symptoms of pre-eclampsia: severe headache, problems with vision such as blurring or flashing, severe pain just below the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet.

n.1: Heartburn relieved by antacids is a common symptom; severe pain just below the ribs is the warning sign.
n.2: New severe headache needs immediate assessment; waiting for a routine appointment could delay diagnosis.
n.3: Gradual dependent ankle swelling that resolves overnight is common in pregnancy; it is sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet that is a warning sign.

6.q: Hana, 27, recently arrived in the UK, booked late at 22 weeks and has missed two appointments. She is allocated to a continuity team. Which feature of the model is most likely to improve her engagement?
o: A single extended visit with an interpreter to explain the antenatal schedule
A trusted relationship with a known midwife who can follow up missed contacts
Hospital-based clinics where all specialists can see her together
Fewer appointments so that attendance feels less demanding
6.w: Better Births and NHS England (2022) describe continuity as giving consistent, personalised care; the known relationship builds trust, helps women who find services hard to reach and allows the midwife to follow up missed appointments (SPM 2.5, 2.8).

n.0: One explanatory visit helps understanding but does not create the ongoing relationship that improves engagement over time.
n.2: Centralised clinics may add barriers for a woman struggling to attend; continuity is about the relationship, not the building.
n.3: Reducing contacts for a woman with late booking and missed appointments increases risk; she may need more contact, not less.

6.q: Nicole, 32, is 22 weeks pregnant. Her first birth 3 years ago was an emergency caesarean under general anaesthetic. She describes nightmares and flashbacks about it, avoids driving past the hospital and feels panic when thinking about this birth. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Book an elective caesarean so she does not have to face labour again
Arrange mental health assessment, as these features suggest possible PTSD
Reassure her that fear of birth is normal and will pass after this baby
Advise her to avoid talking about the previous birth to reduce distress
6.w: Nightmares, flashbacks and avoidance suggest post-traumatic stress disorder after a traumatic birth. She needs assessment through her GP or perinatal mental health service so that treatment such as trauma-focused psychological therapy can be offered (NICE CG192; NG201 1.2.10 on discussing previous traumatic birth).

n.0: Mode of birth is discussed with an obstetrician as part of her plan, but it does not treat the underlying trauma symptoms.
n.2: These symptoms go beyond normal fear of birth and need assessment rather than reassurance.
n.3: Avoidance is a symptom of PTSD; discouraging discussion does not help recovery.

6.q: After a baby sustains a brachial plexus injury, the midwife who was present wants to apologise to the parents but worries that saying sorry will be treated as admitting negligence. Which statement is accurate?
o: An apology is an admission of liability, so legal advice comes first
An apology may be given once the trust's investigation has ended
An apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence
An apology should come from the consultant rather than the midwife
6.w: Compensation Act 2006 s2: an apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty. Code 14.2 requires explaining fully and promptly and apologising.

n.0: An apology does not by itself admit liability (Compensation Act 2006 s2), so it should not be delayed for legal advice.
n.1: Code 14.2 requires a prompt apology; it should not wait for the investigation's outcome.
n.3: Every professional has the duty of candour under Code 14; the midwife may apologise herself.

6.q: Baby Ella, born at 39 weeks with no risk factors, has a palpable clunk on the Ortolani manoeuvre of her left hip at the NIPE newborn examination. What is the expected screening pathway?
o: Hip ultrasound at 4 to 6 weeks, outcome decided by 6 weeks
Repeat the hip examination at the 6 to 8 week infant check
Referral for review by an orthopaedic surgeon by 10 weeks
Hip ultrasound between 38 and 40 weeks corrected age
6.w: NIPE hip screen positive pathway: for babies born at 34+0 weeks or more, perform hip ultrasound between 4 and 6 weeks of age, with an orthopaedic outcome decision by 6 weeks. A palpable clunk on Ortolani or Barlow is a screen positive finding.

n.1: A screen positive newborn hip needs ultrasound, not just a repeat clinical check.
n.2: Being seen by 10 weeks applies to babies found screen positive at the 6 to 8 week infant examination.
n.3: 38 to 40 weeks corrected age is the scan timing for babies born before 34 weeks.

6.q: Jess, 27, smokes 15 cigarettes a day and wants to stop. Her tobacco dependence adviser suggests nicotine patches. She is worried nicotine will harm her baby. What information should the midwife give?
o: NRT risks are much lower than smoking, and patches should be removed at bedtime
NRT is safe in pregnancy and patches should be worn for 24 hours a day
NRT carries the same risks as smoking, so cutting down is safer
NRT should be avoided until 12 weeks, when varenicline is a safer choice
6.w: NG209 1.20.6-1.20.11: consider NRT with behavioural support at the earliest opportunity; explain that risks from NRT are much lower than smoking; advise removing patches before bed; do not offer varenicline, bupropion or cytisinicline in pregnancy.

n.1: NICE advises removing patches before going to bed in pregnancy (NG209 1.20.9).
n.2: Most smoking harm comes from other components of smoke, not nicotine; NRT is much safer.
n.3: Varenicline is not offered in pregnancy, and NRT should be considered at the earliest opportunity.

6.q: Bethany, 34, is discussing induction of labour at 41 weeks. She asks the midwife, "What would you do if you were me?" Which response best supports partnership working?
o: "I can't give an opinion on this, so it is your decision."
"Let's look at the options and what matters most to you."
"I would have the induction, so I think you should book it."
"The doctors will decide what is safest for you and your baby."
6.w: SPM 1.13 and Code 2.3: work in partnership, basing care on the woman's needs, views and preferences, and support shared decision-making with balanced, evidence-based information (NICE NG207 on discussing induction).

n.0: Refusing to engage leaves her without the information and support she needs to decide.
n.2: Telling her what to do substitutes the midwife's preferences for Bethany's own values.
n.3: Decisions about induction are hers to make, with information from the team; doctors do not decide for her.

6.q: When should the first postnatal health visitor home visit be considered, according to NICE?
o: Within 36 hours after transfer from the place of birth
Within 72 hours with the newborn physical examination
Between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery
At 6 to 8 weeks with the GP postnatal check
6.w: NG194 1.1.15: consider arranging the first postnatal health visitor home visit between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery care, so contacts are evenly spread.

n.0: 36 hours is the standard for the first midwife visit, not the health visitor.
n.1: 72 hours is the deadline for the newborn physical examination, not the health visitor visit.
n.3: 6 to 8 weeks is the GP check for the woman and baby, not the first health visitor visit.

6.q: Zara, 30, is in labour at term. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration, and an emergency caesarean is recommended. Zara has capacity, understands the risk to her baby and declines. What should the midwife do?
o: Proceed with the caesarean in the baby's best interests
Seek an urgent court order to allow the caesarean
Ask Zara's partner to consent to the caesarean
Respect her refusal, continue care and escalate
6.w: A competent woman may refuse treatment even if this risks the fetus; the fetus has no separate legal personality in England and Wales. The midwife continues to provide care, explains alternatives, documents and involves senior staff (SPM 1.21; Code 2.5).

n.0: The fetus has no separate legal interests that can override a competent woman's refusal.
n.1: A court cannot authorise surgery on a woman who has capacity and refuses it.
n.2: A partner cannot consent for an adult woman with capacity.

6.q: Adaeze, 26, has dark skin and usually covers most of her skin when outdoors. She is 20 weeks pregnant in June. What vitamin D advice should she receive?
o: Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily if a blood test shows deficiency
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily from 28 weeks until the birth
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily from October to March
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily all year round
6.w: NG247 1.1.12: vitamin D 10 micrograms daily October to March for all pregnant or breastfeeding women, and all year for those at increased risk (for example darker skin, or skin rarely exposed to the sun).

n.0: Supplementation is recommended without testing for women at increased risk.
n.1: There is no gestation restriction; it is recommended throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding.
n.2: Women at increased risk of deficiency, such as those with darker skin or little sun exposure, should take it all year.

6.q: Under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, what is needed for a midwife raising a concern about patient safety with her employer to be protected as a whistleblower?
o: She reasonably believes the disclosure is in the public interest
She raises the concern anonymously through a hotline
She has written evidence that proves the wrongdoing occurred
She has first raised the concern with the NMC
6.w: PIDA 1998 (inserting Part IVA into the Employment Rights Act 1996) protects a worker who makes a qualifying disclosure, which requires a reasonable belief that the information tends to show wrongdoing such as danger to health and safety, and that disclosure is in the public interest.

n.1: Anonymity is not a condition of protection; named concerns are protected too.
n.2: Proof is not required; a reasonable belief is enough.
n.3: Raising a concern with the employer first is the normal route; prior NMC contact is not a condition.

6.q: Jade, 34, is being cared for after a stillbirth at 35 weeks. She is distressed that her breasts are becoming full and leaking on day 3. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Acknowledge how distressing this is and discuss options to manage lactation
Advise her to express fully every 3 hours to prevent mastitis
Explain that this does not happen after a stillbirth and arrange a GP review
Tell her to bind her breasts tightly and restrict her fluid intake
6.w: Lactation commonly begins after a stillbirth and can be very distressing. Bereavement care includes preparing parents for this and discussing options, such as suppression measures or donating breast milk, in a sensitive, personalised way (National Bereavement Care Pathway; SPM 4.11).

n.1: Frequent full expression stimulates supply and is not the advice for a woman who wishes to suppress lactation.
n.2: Milk does come in after a stillbirth because lactation is triggered by birth of the placenta.
n.3: Tight binding and fluid restriction are not recommended and can cause discomfort and harm.

7.q: Nicola, 26, is 40 minutes after birth with ongoing trickling blood loss. On palpation her uterus is soft and displaced to the right, above the umbilicus. She has not passed urine since before the birth. Uterine massage has been started. What is the next most appropriate action?
o: Empty her bladder, using a catheter if she cannot void
Repeat the observations in 15 minutes and review the loss
Give a second dose of oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly
Encourage her to put the baby to the breast for 30 minutes
7.w: A full bladder displaces the uterus and stops it contracting effectively. NICE NG235 1.10.33 includes emptying the bladder alongside uterine massage, uterotonics and IV fluids in the immediate treatment of PPH (SPM 4.8 first-line management).

n.1: Waiting allows ongoing bleeding; the cause should be treated now.
n.2: A repeat IM oxytocin dose is not the NG235 treatment step, and a full bladder will still stop the uterus contracting.
n.3: Breastfeeding helps but does not correct a uterus displaced by a full bladder.

7.q: Ruth, 35, was discharged home on day 2 and is breastfeeding. On day 5 she tells her community midwife she has sore nipples and is thinking of stopping. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Advise her to give formula for 24 hours to let the nipples heal
Advise her to feed for 10 minutes on each breast to rest the nipples
Observe a feed, help with attachment and refer to peer support
Recommend nipple shields for each feed until the soreness settles
7.w: Sore nipples usually reflect poor attachment. NG194 1.5.14 lists assessing a feed and breast and nipple condition; professionals should support common problems (1.5.6) and work with other agencies such as peer support services to sustain breastfeeding (SPM 2.10).

n.0: Missed feeds reduce supply and may end breastfeeding, which she has not chosen.
n.1: Limiting feed length does not fix attachment and can reduce intake and supply.
n.3: Shields do not correct the usual cause, poor attachment, and can reduce milk transfer.

7.q: Sian, 29, is 3 days postnatal at home after a second-degree tear and reports perineal pain not relieved by paracetamol. She has no contraindications to NSAIDs. Which medicine can the registered midwife supply to her under the midwives exemptions?
o: Co-codamol 30/500 tablets
Diclofenac tablets
Amoxicillin capsules
Dihydrocodeine tablets
7.w: Schedule 17 Part 1 allows registered midwives to sell or supply, in the course of their professional practice, prescription-only medicines containing diclofenac, hydrocortisone acetate, miconazole, nystatin and phytomenadione (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Co-codamol 30/500 contains codeine, which is not on the midwives supply list.
n.2: Antibiotics such as amoxicillin are not on the midwives supply list and need a prescription.
n.3: Dihydrocodeine is not on the midwives supply list.

7.q: Two women with the surname Begum are on the same postnatal bay. Before giving prescribed oral iron to Jahanara Begum, 26, what is the most reliable way for the midwife to confirm she has the right woman?
o: Ask, 'Are you Mrs Begum?' and wait for her to agree
Check that the bed number matches the one on the chart
Check name, birth date and hospital number with the chart
Ask her partner to confirm her full name and the medicine
7.w: Positive identification uses at least two identifiers (name, date of birth, hospital number) on the wristband checked against the prescription, and asking the woman to state her name and date of birth where she can. Closed questions and bed numbers are unreliable (SPM 3.19 safe administration).

n.0: A closed question invites agreement and both women share the surname.
n.1: Women can move beds, so a bed number does not identify a person.
n.3: A partner's confirmation is not a substitute for checking identifiers against the chart.

7.q: Keira, 32, is fully dilated and pushing when the cord prolapses. The fetal head is at the level of the ischial spines plus 2 cm, in a direct occipito-anterior position, and the fetal heart rate is 80 beats/min. An experienced obstetrician is present. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Move to theatre for a category 2 caesarean birth
Assisted vaginal birth in the room
Knee-chest position until spontaneous birth occurs
Give tocolysis and transfer to theatre for caesarean
7.w: RCOG GTG 50: vaginal birth, usually assisted, can be attempted at full dilatation if it is anticipated that birth would be quick and safe. With a low head and a skilled operator present, this is quicker than transferring to theatre.

n.0: Category 2 is too slow with bradycardia, and birth can be achieved vaginally here.
n.2: Waiting for spontaneous birth in knee-chest delays birth of a compromised baby.
n.3: Tocolysis is for delays before caesarean; birth can be achieved now vaginally.

7.q: Adaeze, 26, has dark skin and usually covers most of her skin when outdoors. She is 20 weeks pregnant in June. What vitamin D advice should she receive?
o: Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily if a blood test shows deficiency
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily from 28 weeks until the birth
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily from October to March
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily all year round
7.w: NG247 1.1.12: vitamin D 10 micrograms daily October to March for all pregnant or breastfeeding women, and all year for those at increased risk (for example darker skin, or skin rarely exposed to the sun).

n.0: Supplementation is recommended without testing for women at increased risk.
n.1: There is no gestation restriction; it is recommended throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding.
n.2: Women at increased risk of deficiency, such as those with darker skin or little sun exposure, should take it all year.

7.q: Imogen, 29, is 35 weeks pregnant and has pre-eclampsia. She presents with constant severe abdominal pain and a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. Her uterus feels hard and is tender all over, and she looks pale and clammy. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Placenta praevia
Onset of normal labour
Placental abruption
Cervical ectropion
7.w: RCOG GTG 63: abruption should be considered when pain is continuous; a tense, 'woody' uterus indicates a significant abruption. Visible loss may underestimate concealed bleeding, so maternal signs of shock can be out of proportion. Pre-eclampsia is a risk factor (SPM 4.3).

n.0: Placenta praevia typically causes painless bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus.
n.1: Labour pain is intermittent with relaxation between contractions, not a constantly hard uterus.
n.3: A cervical ectropion causes painless spotting with a soft uterus and no shock.

7.q: Which organisation regulates midwives in all four nations of the United Kingdom?
o: The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The General Medical Council
The Health and Care Professions Council
7.w: The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) regulates nurses and midwives across the UK, and nursing associates in England, under the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001.

n.0: The CQC regulates health and care providers in England, not individual midwives.
n.2: The GMC regulates doctors.
n.3: The HCPC regulates allied health professions such as paramedics and physiotherapists.
