Her observations and the fetal heart are normal. On examination her cervix is soft, central and 2 cm dilated. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Offer support and analgesia and encourage her to go home with a plan
Admit her to the unit and start a partogram to record her progress
Perform an amniotomy to help establish labour
Transfer her to the obstetric unit for assessment of slow progress
7.w: Holly is in the latent first stage (contractions with cervical change up to 4 cm; NICE NG235 1.8.1). NG235 1.8.6: recognise that latent labour can be painful, offer individualised support and analgesia, and encourage her to remain at or return home unless this risks birth without a midwife or distress.

n.1: The partogram is used once labour is established (NG235 1.8.22), not in the latent phase.
n.2: Amniotomy is not routinely performed when labour is progressing normally (NG235 1.8.39) and is not used to establish labour.
n.3: Latent labour has no time limit for delay; there is no indication for obstetric transfer.

7.q: Megan, 23, is 10 weeks pregnant after an unplanned conception. She tells the midwife she feels 'all over the place': sometimes excited, sometimes unsure she wants a baby, and occasionally tearful. She is sleeping and eating well and answers no to both depression identification questions. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Complete an EPDS at every appointment until 20 weeks
Refer her to the perinatal mental health service for assessment of ambivalence
Ask her GP to start an antidepressant to stabilise her mood
Explain mixed feelings are common and revisit her wellbeing at each visit
7.w: Emotional lability and ambivalence are common normal psychological responses in early pregnancy, especially when unplanned (SPM 3.17.1). With negative screening questions and normal function, she needs information and support, with mental health discussed at every contact (NICE CG192 1.5.8; NG201 1.2.10).

n.0: Routine repeated EPDS without a positive response or concern is not the recommended approach; ongoing discussion at each contact is.
n.1: Normal ambivalence without signs of a mental health problem does not need specialist referral.
n.2: There is no evidence of depression, so medication is not indicated.

7.q: Isla, 31, had active management of the third stage in a freestanding midwifery unit. Forty minutes after the birth the placenta has not delivered. Her blood loss is 300 mL and she is stable. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Attempt manual removal with Entonox as analgesia
Inject oxytocin into the umbilical vein to release the placenta
Secure IV access, explain why and arrange transfer to obstetric care
Start an intravenous oxytocin infusion and wait a further hour
7.w: A third stage over 30 minutes with active management is prolonged (NICE NG235 1.10.20). For a retained placenta: secure IV access and explain why (1.10.21), do not use umbilical vein agents (1.10.22), do not use IV oxytocics routinely unless bleeding excessively (1.10.23, 1.10.24), and arrange transfer if not in an obstetric unit (1.10.27).

n.0: Manual removal must not be attempted without an anaesthetic (NG235 1.10.28).
n.1: NICE advises not to use umbilical vein agents for a retained placenta.
n.3: IV oxytocics are not used routinely for a retained placenta unless she is bleeding excessively.

7.q: Kemi, 34, transferred her care from abroad and books at 15+3 weeks. Her dating scan has confirmed the gestation. After discussion she would like screening for Down's syndrome. Which test should be offered?
o: Amniocentesis to give a definite result
The combined test with a nuchal translucency measurement
The quadruple blood test, which screens for Down's syndrome
Non-invasive prenatal testing as the first screening test
7.w: The combined test is available from 10+0 to 14+1 weeks. After that, the quadruple test (second trimester, up to 20+0 weeks) is offered and screens for Down's syndrome only (NHS FASP). NIPT is offered after a higher-chance screening result, and diagnostic tests follow a higher-chance result if chosen.

n.0: Amniocentesis is a diagnostic test with a miscarriage risk, offered after a higher-chance result if she chooses it, not as first-line screening.
n.1: The combined test window ends at 14+1 weeks, so at 15+3 it is no longer available.
n.3: In the NHS programme NIPT is offered as a further test after a higher-chance result, not as the first-line screen.

7.q: Mei, 34, is 10 days after the birth of her third baby and phones the community midwife about heavier vaginal bleeding. Her records show a booking weight of 47 kg, a postnatal haemoglobin of 92 g/L, and that she is exclusively breastfeeding. Which features in her history may worsen the consequences of a secondary postpartum haemorrhage?
o: Her age over 30 years and exclusive breastfeeding
Exclusive breastfeeding and her parity of three
Her booking weight under 50 kg and her anaemia
Her parity of three and her age over 30 years
7.w: NICE NG194 1.2.14: when a woman seeks advice about bleeding after birth, assess severity and be aware that anaemia and a weight of less than 50 kg at booking may worsen the consequences of secondary postpartum haemorrhage.

n.0: Neither age nor breastfeeding is listed in NG194 as worsening the consequences of secondary PPH.
n.1: Breastfeeding does not worsen the consequences of secondary PPH and parity is not a listed factor.
n.3: Parity and age are not the factors NG194 lists as worsening the consequences of secondary PPH.

7.q: A baby born at term needs therapeutic cooling after a difficult labour in an NHS trust in England. The parents ask whether an independent body will look into the care. Which body carries out independent maternity safety investigations in England?
o: The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
Maternity and Newborn Safety Investigations (MNSI)
The Perinatal Mortality Review Tool (PMRT) team
The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC)
7.w: MNSI carries out independent investigations of certain maternity and newborn safety events reported by NHS trusts in England, working with families and staff and making safety recommendations without blaming individuals (MNSI).

n.0: The Ombudsman considers complaints after local processes are exhausted, not safety investigations.
n.2: The PMRT supports local hospital reviews of perinatal deaths; it is not an independent investigation body.
n.3: The NMC regulates individual registrants' fitness to practise; it does not investigate maternity safety events.

7.q: Rosa, 31, is cared for by a continuity team. At 34 weeks she develops gestational hypertension and is referred to the antenatal clinic for obstetric review. Her named midwife is concerned about losing the relationship. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Continue as her named midwife while coordinating care with the obstetric team
Keep her care midwife-led and defer the obstetric referral to 36 weeks
Discharge her from the continuity team and book a new consultant midwife
Transfer her midwifery care to the hospital antenatal clinic midwives
7.w: SPM 2.5 requires continuity of midwifery carer for women with and without complications and additional care needs. The named midwife remains her midwife and works with the obstetric team (SPM 2.4: work across settings and with other staff to promote continuity of care and carer).

n.1: Gestational hypertension needs obstetric involvement now (NG133); delaying referral to protect continuity would be unsafe.
n.2: Discharging her ends continuity at the point she most benefits from a known carer, and a consultant midwife does not replace obstetric review.
n.3: Handing her to clinic midwives fragments care; SPM 2.5 expects continuity for women with complications as well as without.

7.q: Chantelle, 22, is 24 weeks pregnant. Her two older children were removed into care last year because of neglect linked to her partner's alcohol use. She still lives with the same partner. What is the most appropriate action by the midwife?
o: Wait until the baby is born and then decide whether a referral to social care is needed
Refer to children's social care but avoid telling Chantelle to protect the relationship
Make no referral, as the previous removal has already been dealt with by the court
Explain her concerns and refer to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment
7.w: Previous removal of children with the same risk factor present is a clear safeguarding concern for the unborn baby. Multi-agency assessment and a coordinated plan are needed before birth (CG110 1.1.7), and the woman should be told why and when information may be shared (CG110 1.1.9) unless that would increase the risk.

n.0: Pre-birth assessment allows support and safety planning; waiting until after birth wastes this time.
n.1: Openness is the default; CG110 1.1.9 says tell her why and when information is shared, and nothing here suggests telling her would increase the risk.
n.2: The previous proceedings concerned the older children; the unborn baby faces the same unresolved risk.

7.q: Joy, 28, attends her booking appointment at 9 weeks. She has no known mental health history. As part of a general discussion about her wellbeing, which approach does NICE CG192 recommend the midwife considers?
o: Ask her to complete the full Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at booking
Ask about mood if she shows visible signs of distress during the appointment
Ask the two depression identification questions and consider the GAD-2 for anxiety
Refer her to her GP for a mental health review before her dating scan
7.w: CG192 1.5.4: at booking and in the early postnatal period, consider asking the two depression identification questions (feeling down, depressed or hopeless; little interest or pleasure in the past month) and consider the GAD-2 for anxiety, as part of a general discussion.

n.0: The EPDS or PHQ-9 is used as part of a full assessment after a positive response or clinical concern (CG192 1.5.5), not as the first step for everyone.
n.1: Waiting for visible distress misses women who are unwilling to disclose, which CG192 1.5.1 warns is common.
n.3: Routine GP referral without any identified concern is not recommended; the midwife asks the questions herself.

7.q: During a woman's induction of labour, the obstetric registrar instructs Sam, a midwife, to increase the oxytocin infusion. The woman is having six contractions in 10 minutes and the CTG has become suspicious. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase the rate, as the instruction transfers accountability to the registrar
Ask another midwife to increase the rate so that she can monitor the CTG
Increase the rate and record the registrar's name with the time of the instruction
Withhold the increase, explain her concerns and escalate to the consultant
7.w: Midwives are accountable for their own actions (SPM 1.6, Code 13 and 16.2). Six contractions in 10 minutes is uterine hyperstimulation: NICE NG235 1.8.55 says reduce or stop oxytocin if contractions are more frequent than 4 in 10 minutes, and NG229 lists reducing or stopping oxytocin among the conservative measures for a concerning CTG. She explains her rationale and escalates.

n.0: Accountability does not transfer by instruction; a midwife who gives an unsafe dose is answerable for it.
n.1: Delegating the increase to a colleague still exposes the woman to the same unsafe action.
n.2: Documenting the instruction does not make an unsafe increase acceptable or protect the woman and baby.

8.q: Chantelle, 22, is 24 weeks pregnant. Her two older children were removed into care last year because of neglect linked to her partner's alcohol use. She still lives with the same partner. What is the most appropriate action by the midwife?
o: Wait until the baby is born and then decide whether a referral to social care is needed
Refer to children's social care but avoid telling Chantelle to protect the relationship
Make no referral, as the previous removal has already been dealt with by the court
Explain her concerns and refer to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment
8.w: Previous removal of children with the same risk factor present is a clear safeguarding concern for the unborn baby. Multi-agency assessment and a coordinated plan are needed before birth (CG110 1.1.7), and the woman should be told why and when information may be shared (CG110 1.1.9) unless that would increase the risk.

n.0: Pre-birth assessment allows support and safety planning; waiting until after birth wastes this time.
n.1: Openness is the default; CG110 1.1.9 says tell her why and when information is shared, and nothing here suggests telling her would increase the risk.
n.2: The previous proceedings concerned the older children; the unborn baby faces the same unresolved risk.

8.q: A maternity governance meeting is discussing the East Kent report, "Reading the signals" (Kirkup, 2022). Which list matches the report's four areas for action?
o: Safe staffing, multidisciplinary training, complex antenatal care, bereavement care
Smoking, fetal growth, fetal movements, fetal monitoring, preterm birth, diabetes
Identifying poor performance, compassion and kindness, teamworking, responding with honesty
Listening to women, workforce, safety culture, standards and structures
8.w: East Kent (19 October 2022): identifying poorly performing units; giving care with compassion and kindness; teamworking with a common purpose; responding to challenge with honesty.

n.0: These are among the Ockenden immediate and essential action themes.
n.1: These are the six elements of Saving Babies' Lives v3.
n.3: These are the four themes of the NHS England three-year delivery plan (2023).

8.q: Megan, 32, has moved to the area and refers herself to the maternity service when she is 11+1 weeks pregnant. She has not yet seen a midwife in this pregnancy. According to NICE antenatal care guidance, when should her booking appointment take place?
o: Within 2 weeks of her contacting the service, if possible
At the routine 16-week appointment to avoid duplicating checks
At her dating scan, which must be done before 14+1 weeks
Within 4 weeks, as the 10-week target no longer applies to her
8.w: Booking should ideally be by 10+0 weeks; when a woman contacts or is referred to maternity services later than 9+0 weeks, offer a booking appointment within 2 weeks if possible (NICE NG201 1.1.4, 1.1.5). This keeps screening windows such as the combined test (up to 14+1) open.

n.1: Waiting until 16 weeks would miss the window for first-trimester combined screening and delay risk assessment.
n.2: The dating scan is a separate contact; booking includes history, bloods and risk assessment that should not wait for or be merged into the scan.
n.3: NICE sets a 2-week target for late referrals; a 4-week wait is too long.

8.q: Kim, 36, is brought to the labour ward at 34 weeks with heavy continuing vaginal bleeding. She is confused, her heart rate is 135 beats/min and her blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. The team is gathering. What is the immediate priority?
o: Resuscitate Kim using an ABC approach
Take a full history of the bleeding and any pain
Start a CTG to establish the fetal condition
Arrange an ultrasound scan to locate the placenta
8.w: RCOG GTG 63: with major or massive haemorrhage or maternal compromise, assess maternal wellbeing and start resuscitation immediately. The mother is the priority and should be stabilised before the fetal condition is established, using an ABC approach (SPM 4.7).

n.1: A full history is taken once there is no maternal compromise.
n.2: Fetal assessment comes after the mother is stabilised.
n.3: Imaging is not the priority while she is shocked and bleeding.

8.q: Freya, 30, is 10 days postnatal and exclusively breastfeeding. Her GP has prescribed a medicine for migraine and Freya asks the community midwife whether it is safe for her baby. Where should the midwife seek specialist evidence-based advice?
o: Her sister's experience of the same medicine
An online parenting forum with many replies
The patient information leaflet in the box
The UK Drugs in Lactation Advisory Service
8.w: The UK Drugs in Lactation Advisory Service (Specialist Pharmacy Service) gives evidence-based advice on medicines in breastfeeding; the BNF and local medicines information services are also appropriate. Manufacturer leaflets often advise against use because medicines are not tested in breastfeeding, not because of proven harm (NG133 1.9.2; SPM 3.18).

n.0: Anecdotal experience is not evidence-based advice about this baby and this medicine.
n.1: An online forum is not a reliable, evidence-based source of medicines information.
n.2: Product leaflets often carry general disclaimers rather than evidence about breastfeeding.

8.q: Esme, 29, is 6 cm dilated on the labour ward when her membranes rupture spontaneously. Within a minute the fetal heart rate drops to 70 beats/min. On vaginal examination the midwife feels a pulsating loop of cord in front of the fetal head. What should the midwife do first?
o: Document the findings before taking further action
Ask Esme to push to speed up the birth
Leave to fetch the CTG machine from the next room
Call for help and elevate the presenting part
8.w: In cord prolapse, call for help immediately (emergency bell, obstetric and neonatal teams) and relieve cord compression by keeping fingers in the vagina to elevate the presenting part, then position her knee-chest or left lateral head down while preparing for birth (RCOG GTG 50; SPM 4.7).

n.0: Documentation follows emergency treatment, not before it.
n.1: At 6 cm pushing will not achieve birth and worsens cord compression.
n.2: Leaving the woman removes the elevation of the presenting part when cord compression is causing bradycardia.

8.q: At handover, a midwife suggests sending details of a woman's care plan to the community team through a personal messaging app on her own phone, because it is quicker. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree, and leave the woman's name out of the message
Agree, as the messaging app is encrypted end to end
Disagree, and send the plan through the trust's approved secure system
Disagree, and phone the details to the community midwife's mobile instead
8.w: Code 10.5: take all steps to keep records secure. Information about women must be shared through approved, secure, auditable systems so the record is complete and confidential (SPM 1.23 and 1.24).

n.0: Leaving out the name does not make a personal app an approved route; other details can still identify her.
n.1: Encryption does not make a personal device an approved, auditable route, and the information sits outside the record.
n.3: A phone call leaves no written, auditable copy of the plan in the record.

8.q: Jess, 16, books at 12 weeks. She is living with her mother, is still at school and finds hospital clinics intimidating. Which care arrangement best follows NICE CG110?
o: Care deferred until her mother can attend every appointment with her
Standard consultant-led clinic care, as she is under 18
A named midwife providing most of her care, with a direct phone number
Antenatal care through her school nurse until 28 weeks
8.w: CG110 1.4.4: offer young women under 20 a named midwife who provides most of their antenatal care, with a direct-line telephone number. Services should be age-appropriate, community-based where possible and alert to safeguarding (1.4.1, 1.4.5).

n.0: Jess can attend herself; deferring care until her mother is available is a barrier to antenatal care.
n.1: Age alone is not an indication for consultant-led care; young women need accessible, age-appropriate services.
n.3: School nurses do not provide antenatal care; the midwife does.

8.q: Mei, 30, is pregnant for the first time. When is the best time to give her information about interventions that may be offered in labour, such as episiotomy?
o: In the second stage of labour, when the need arises
Antenatally, then confirmed in labour before any procedure
After the birth, during the postnatal debrief
When she is admitted to the labour ward in early labour
8.w: Informed consent relies on information given when the woman can weigh it (Montgomery; MCA 2005 s3). Discussing interventions antenatally (NICE NG201 antenatal information on labour) and confirming consent at the time supports decision-making.

n.0: Information given for the first time during the second stage is hard to weigh under pain and time pressure.
n.2: Information after the birth cannot inform consent to a procedure that has already happened.
n.3: Early labour is better than the second stage, but antenatal discussion gives her time to consider options.

8.q: Zara, a third-year student midwife, is completing her final practice placement. Several registered midwives have supervised her. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment, who conducts the assessment that confirms Zara has achieved her practice proficiencies?
o: The practice supervisor who has worked the most shifts with her
Her nominated practice assessor, using feedback from supervisors
Her academic assessor, based on her university assignments
The ward manager, as the person accountable for the placement area
8.w: SSSA 7.1: practice assessors conduct assessments to confirm student achievement of proficiencies and programme outcomes for practice learning; 7.2: decisions are informed by feedback from practice supervisors. The academic assessor confirms achievement in the academic environment (9.1) and works with the practice assessor on progression (7.5).

n.0: Practice supervisors contribute observations to assessment (4.1, 4.2) but do not confirm proficiency.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement in the academic environment, not the practice assessment itself.
n.3: The ward manager's role is not the practice assessor's unless formally nominated as such.

8.q: Sophie, 26, had a miscarriage at 19 weeks. On discharge she asks whether she must register her baby's birth and death. Which response is accurate for England and Wales?
o: The baby must be registered as a neonatal death within 5 days
The loss must be registered as a stillbirth within 42 days
Registration is required because the loss was after 16 weeks
There is no legal requirement to register a loss before 24 weeks
8.w: A stillbirth in law is a baby born after the 24th week of pregnancy who did not breathe or show any other signs of life (Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953 s41); stillbirths must be registered. A pregnancy loss before 24 weeks is not legally registrable, although parents in England may apply for a voluntary baby loss certificate.

n.0: Neonatal death applies to a baby born alive who dies; this was a loss before 24 weeks without signs of life.
n.1: Stillbirth registration applies to babies born after 24 weeks with no signs of life.
n.2: 16 weeks is not a legal threshold for registration in England and Wales.

8.q: Tasha, 28, is 33 weeks pregnant. She phones triage for the third time this week reporting reduced fetal movements. Staff have noted she is 'anxious' and her two previous checks were normal. What should the triage midwife do?
o: Advise her to lie on her left side and count kicks for 2 hours
Invite her in for assessment, including fetal heart and CTG
Book a routine appointment with her community midwife this week
Reassure her by phone as both previous checks were normal
8.w: Each episode of reduced fetal movements needs assessment; recurrent reduced movements after 28 weeks carry higher risk and need an ultrasound scan (Saving Babies' Lives v3 element 3; NICE NG201). SPM 1.18: a label such as 'anxious' must not bias the decision.

n.0: Kick counting at home is not recommended as a replacement for assessment when movements are reduced.
n.2: A routine appointment later in the week delays assessment of reduced movements that needs to happen now.
n.3: Previous normal checks do not exclude a new problem; each episode needs assessment.

8.q: Grace, a midwife, is 11 hours into a 12.5-hour night shift with no break. She notices she has read the same CTG twice without taking it in. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a student midwife to interpret the CTG on her behalf for now
Finish her current tasks and then take her break after handover
Drink a strong coffee and carry on with her care until the end of her shift
Tell the coordinator, take a break and ask a colleague to review the CTG
8.w: Fatigue is a recognised human factor that impairs attention and decision-making. Recognising it, telling the coordinator, taking a break and getting a second review keeps care safe (SPM 5.4, 5.14; Code 16.3 tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity about problems that may prevent you working within the Code; Code 19.2 human factors).

n.0: A student cannot take responsibility for CTG interpretation; review must be by a competent registrant.
n.1: Waiting until handover leaves a fatigued midwife making decisions for another 90 minutes.
n.2: Caffeine does not reliably restore performance, and continuing leaves her impaired while interpreting a CTG.

8.q: According to the MBRRACE-UK data brief on maternal deaths in 2022 to 2024, how did the maternal death rate for Black women compare with that for White women?
o: About ten times higher
About one and a half times higher
About the same
Nearly three times higher
8.w: MBRRACE-UK maternal mortality data brief 2022-24 (September 2026 update): Black women died at nearly three times the rate of White women. SPM 1.17.1: health inequalities and their determinants.

n.0: The figure is nearly three times, not ten.
n.1: The disparity is larger: nearly three times.
n.2: The data show a large disparity, not similar rates.

8.q: A woman at 22 weeks has a severe haemorrhage and the obstetric consultant believes immediate termination is needed to save her life. There is no time to obtain a second opinion. Under the Abortion Act 1967, is this lawful?
o: Yes, under the emergency provision in s1(4)
No, two practitioners must agree before any termination
No, termination must take place in an approved clinic
Yes, if a senior midwife also signs the certificate
8.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(4): the requirement for two opinions, and the place requirement, do not apply where a registered medical practitioner believes in good faith that termination is immediately necessary to save the life, or prevent grave permanent injury to the physical or mental health, of the pregnant woman.

n.1: Section 1(4) removes the two-opinion requirement in an emergency.
n.2: Section 1(4) also removes the requirement for an NHS hospital or approved place.
n.3: A midwife's signature is not part of the Act's requirements.

8.q: Tara, a community midwife, has a recurrence of depression. She is finding it hard to concentrate on long home visits and recently forgot to complete a newborn check entry. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell her manager and seek support from occupational health
Ask a colleague to double-check her notes until she feels better
Continue working as normal and keep the condition private
Wait to declare the condition at her next revalidation
8.w: NMC Code 20.9: maintain the level of health needed to carry out the professional role; Code 16.3: tell someone in authority if problems may prevent you working within the Code. Occupational health can advise on adjustments and support (SPM 1.26).

n.1: An informal check by a colleague does not address the health problem or allow formal support and adjustments.
n.2: Keeping the condition private while errors are already occurring risks women's and babies' safety (Code 16.3).
n.3: Revalidation may be years away; the effect on practice needs addressing now.

8.q: A midwife is about to take a blood spot sample from baby Ivy on day 5. Her mother asks whether she needs to sign anything. Which approach to consent is correct?
o: Obtain written consent from the parent with parental responsibility
Treat consent as implied and take the sample
Obtain written consent signed by both parents
Give information, obtain verbal consent and record it
8.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening is offered with verbal consent after parents have been given information about the screening, and the decision is recorded. Written consent is not required.

n.0: Verbal consent is the standard; a signed form is not required.
n.1: Consent must be actively obtained after information; it cannot be assumed.
n.2: Written consent from both parents is not required for blood spot screening.

8.q: The labour ward coordinator asks Helen, a midwife, to discharge Mrs Ahmed, 1 day after birth, to free a bed. Helen has just recorded a blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg and Mrs Ahmed has a headache. What should Helen do?
o: Explain why discharge is unsafe and request urgent medical review
Discharge her with advice to see the GP if the headache continues
Recheck the blood pressure in 4 hours before deciding on discharge
Discharge her and arrange a community blood pressure check tomorrow
8.w: SPM 1.18: recognise external pressures that may unduly influence decisions. A blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg with a headache after birth may be postnatal pre-eclampsia and needs urgent medical assessment (NICE NG133). Helen explains her rationale and escalates rather than discharging.

n.1: Discharging with GP advice ignores a possible postnatal pre-eclampsia that needs urgent review now.
n.2: Waiting 4 hours before acting delays the urgent review that hypertension with headache requires.
n.3: A check tomorrow delays assessment of a woman with hypertension and headache today.

8.q: Isla, a midwife, has worked 300 practice hours in the 3 years since her registration was last renewed, after a long career break. Her revalidation date is in 2 months. She has met all the other requirements. What is the correct position?
o: She needs a return to practice programme or the test of competence
She can revalidate if her confirmer verifies her competence
She can revalidate by completing 150 extra CPD hours instead
She can revalidate because she has met all the other requirements
8.w: NMC revalidation requires 450 practice hours for a midwife in the 3 years since last renewal. Isla has 300, which is 150 short; a registrant who cannot meet the practice hours requirement must complete an approved return to practice programme or the test of competence.

n.1: A confirmer confirms the requirements have been met; they cannot waive the practice hours requirement.
n.2: CPD hours cannot be substituted for practice hours.
n.3: Practice hours are a mandatory requirement; meeting the others does not offset the 150-hour shortfall.

8.q: Jade, 25, gives birth at 22+5 weeks. The baby shows signs of life, including a heartbeat, and dies 30 minutes later. What are the registration requirements?
o: No registration is needed because the birth was before 24 weeks
Issue a certificate of pregnancy loss instead of registering
Register both the birth and the death
Register the baby as a stillbirth because the birth was before 24 weeks
8.w: A baby born alive at any gestation is a live birth. Its birth and death must both be registered. The stillbirth category applies to babies born after 24 completed weeks with no signs of life (Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953).

n.0: The 24-week threshold applies to stillbirth; a baby born alive at any gestation must be registered.
n.1: Voluntary pre-24-week loss certificates are for babies born without signs of life; a live-born baby's birth and death must be registered.
n.3: A stillbirth is a baby born after 24 weeks with no signs of life; this baby was born alive.

8.q: A midwifery team wants to check whether all women with a BMI of 40 kg/m2 or over were referred for an anaesthetic review as set out in the unit guideline. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: A clinical audit measuring practice against the guideline standard
A service evaluation of women's satisfaction with the clinic
A PDSA cycle testing a new referral form on one clinic
A research study comparing two referral pathways
8.w: Clinical audit measures current practice against a defined standard (here, the referral requirement in the guideline), identifies gaps and drives improvement, with re-audit to close the loop.

n.1: Satisfaction is a different question from compliance with a referral standard.
n.2: A PDSA cycle tests a change; the question is whether an existing standard is being met.
n.3: Research generates new knowledge by comparing interventions; the standard already exists.

8.q: Mia, 31, is 37 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated pregnancy and plans to give birth in an alongside midwifery unit. She asks who is in charge of her care. Who is her lead professional?
o: Her named midwife
A consultant obstetrician
The labour ward coordinator
Her GP
8.w: For women with uncomplicated pregnancies the midwife is the accountable, autonomous lead professional across the continuum of care (NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives 1.6).

n.1: Obstetric lead care is for women with complications or additional needs, which Mia does not have.
n.2: The coordinator manages the unit's workload; she is not the lead professional for an individual woman's care.
n.3: The GP is not the lead professional for routine maternity care in an uncomplicated pregnancy.

8.q: Olu, 33, is in established labour with severe hypertension; her last blood pressure was 164/112 mmHg and treatment has been given. How often does NICE NG133 recommend measuring her blood pressure?
o: Every 15 to 30 minutes until under 160/110
Every 4 hours, as for all women in labour
Every 2 hours until the birth of the baby
Every hour until it is below 140/90 mmHg
8.w: NICE NG133 1.7.3: during labour, measure blood pressure hourly in women with hypertension, and every 15 to 30 minutes until it is less than 160/110 mmHg in women with severe hypertension.

n.1: 4-hourly blood pressure is for women without hypertension (NG235).
n.2: 2-hourly measurement is too infrequent for severe hypertension.
n.3: Hourly measurement is for hypertension that is not severe.

8.q: Zoe, 26, tells her community midwife that a café owner asked her to stop breastfeeding her 10-week-old baby or leave. Under the Equality Act 2010, how is this treatment best described?
o: Lawful, as the baby is over 6 weeks old
Pregnancy and maternity discrimination
Lawful, as the owner may set rules for a private business
Discrimination under the Human Rights Act 1998
8.w: Equality Act 2010 s17: in services, treating a woman unfavourably because she is breastfeeding within 26 weeks of the birth is pregnancy and maternity discrimination. After 26 weeks it is treated as sex discrimination (s13).

n.0: Protection in s17 lasts for 26 weeks after the birth; 10 weeks is well within it.
n.2: Service providers, including private businesses, must not discriminate under the Equality Act 2010.
n.3: The Human Rights Act binds public authorities; a private café's conduct falls under the Equality Act.

8.q: Isla, 26, is in established labour. Her mother has told her to drink at least a litre of water every hour to keep her strength up. Which advice about drinking in labour is most accurate?
o: Avoid all fluids, as drinking increases the risk of aspiration
Drink plain water, as isotonic drinks raise the risk of hyponatraemia
Drink at least a litre an hour to prevent dehydration and ketosis
Drink when thirsty, as excess fluid can cause harm
8.w: NICE NG235 1.8.17 and 1.8.26 (updated 2025): drink when thirsty; isotonic drinks may be more beneficial than water; there is no benefit to drinking more than normal, and excessive oral or IV fluid can cause hyponatraemia (sodium under 130 mmol/L), with maternal and neonatal seizures or death.

n.0: Women should drink in labour when thirsty; fluid restriction is not advised.
n.1: Isotonic drinks may be more beneficial than water; excess water is the hyponatraemia risk.
n.2: Drinking a litre an hour risks fluid overload and hyponatraemia.

8.q: Kemi, 34, transferred her care from abroad and books at 15+3 weeks. Her dating scan has confirmed the gestation. After discussion she would like screening for Down's syndrome. Which test should be offered?
o: Amniocentesis to give a definite result
The combined test with a nuchal translucency measurement
The quadruple blood test, which screens for Down's syndrome
Non-invasive prenatal testing as the first screening test
8.w: The combined test is available from 10+0 to 14+1 weeks. After that, the quadruple test (second trimester, up to 20+0 weeks) is offered and screens for Down's syndrome only (NHS FASP). NIPT is offered after a higher-chance screening result, and diagnostic tests follow a higher-chance result if chosen.

n.0: Amniocentesis is a diagnostic test with a miscarriage risk, offered after a higher-chance result if she chooses it, not as first-line screening.
n.1: The combined test window ends at 14+1 weeks, so at 15+3 it is no longer available.
n.3: In the NHS programme NIPT is offered as a further test after a higher-chance result, not as the first-line screen.

8.q: Jodie, a registered midwife, is preparing for revalidation. Over the past 3 years she has logged 35 hours of continuing professional development, of which 12 hours were participatory learning such as workshops and simulation. What does she need to do to meet the CPD requirement?
o: Record her 35 hours as complete, since the total is met
Complete at least 8 more hours of any type of CPD
Complete at least 20 more hours of participatory CPD
Complete at least 8 more hours of participatory CPD
8.w: NMC revalidation: 35 hours of CPD in the 3 years since last renewal, of which at least 20 must be participatory. Jodie has 12 participatory hours, so she needs 20 minus 12 = 8 more participatory hours.

n.0: The 35-hour total is met, but fewer than 20 hours are participatory, so the requirement is not yet satisfied.
n.1: Extra individual (non-participatory) learning would not close the participatory shortfall.
n.2: 20 is the total participatory requirement; she already has 12, so the shortfall is 8.

8.q: Chantelle, 27, is 35 weeks pregnant and has not had the whooping cough vaccine. She asks if it is too late. What should the midwife advise?
o: It can still be given, though it gives the baby less passive protection
It can still be given and gives the same protection as at 20 weeks
It is too late, so the baby should be vaccinated at birth instead
It is too late, as it cannot be given after 32 weeks
8.w: Green Book ch 24: the vaccine can still be given later in pregnancy, including up to birth. It may offer less passive protection to the baby but protects the mother, reducing the baby's exposure.

n.1: Vaccinating after 32 weeks may give the baby less passive protection than earlier vaccination.
n.2: Pertussis vaccination of babies starts at 8 weeks in the routine schedule, not at birth.
n.3: It can still be given after 32 weeks; it may offer less passive protection but protects the mother.

8.q: A community midwife is preparing to complete midwifery care for Laila, 29, and her baby on day 14. Which action best ensures a seamless transfer of care?
o: Leave a copy of the notes in Laila's home for the health visitor
Communicate the transfer to the health visitor and inform Laila
Tell Laila that her GP will contact the health visitor at 6 weeks
Ask Laila to phone the health visitor to arrange a visit
8.w: NG194 1.1.9: midwifery services should ensure the transfer of care from midwife to health visitor is clearly communicated between professionals and that the woman or parents are informed about it (SPM 2.11: coordinator of care arranging seamless transfer).

n.0: Notes left at home are not a professional handover and may not be read.
n.2: This leaves weeks without a known professional and is not how transfer of care is arranged.
n.3: Relying on the woman to arrange the handover risks a gap; NICE expects professionals to communicate the transfer.

8.q: Dani, 24, is formula feeding her baby. The midwife watches her prepare a feed at home. Which step is correct?
o: Warm a made-up feed in the microwave and shake it before use
Use boiled water cooled in the fridge so the feed is ready faster
Use water boiled no more than 30 minutes ago, so it is at least 70 C
Put the powder in the bottle first, then add water up to the line
8.w: NHS formula guidance (NICE NG194 1.5.17 safe preparation): boil fresh water and leave it for no more than 30 minutes so it stays at least 70 C, which kills harmful bacteria in powdered formula. Put the water in the bottle first, then add the powder.

n.0: Microwaves heat unevenly and can scald the baby's mouth.
n.1: Water below 70 C will not kill bacteria that can be present in powdered formula.
n.3: Water goes in first so the powder-to-water ratio is correct.

8.q: Before transfer home, Leon and Priya ask how they will know if their baby is unwell. What information should the midwife give?
o: Contact the GP surgery whatever the urgency of the concern
Seek advice if their baby has a temperature over 39 C
Wait for the health visitor visit before seeking any advice
Use Baby Check to help decide, and call 999 if seriously ill
8.w: NG194 1.3.12-1.3.13: consider giving parents information about the Baby Check scoring system; advise them to seek advice if they think their baby is unwell and to call 999 if they think the baby is seriously ill (SPM 3.8).

n.0: If they think the baby is seriously ill they should call emergency services.
n.1: In a young baby, a lower temperature or other signs may indicate serious illness.
n.2: Parents should seek advice whenever they think their baby is unwell.

8.q: Naomi, 35, is booking at 10 weeks in her second pregnancy. In her first pregnancy she developed pre-eclampsia at 35 weeks. Her blood pressure today is 122/78 mmHg. What advice about aspirin is most appropriate?
o: Aspirin is not needed as her blood pressure is now normal
Take 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth
Take 75 mg daily from 20 weeks until 36 weeks
Take 300 mg daily from booking until 28 weeks
8.w: Hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy is a high-risk factor; one high-risk factor is enough. Advise aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth (NICE NG133 1.1.2). Aspirin for this use must be prescribed.

n.0: Risk is based on her history, not her current BP; previous pre-eclampsia is a high-risk factor.
n.2: Starting at 20 weeks and stopping at 36 weeks does not match the recommended timing of 12 weeks until birth.
n.3: 300 mg exceeds the recommended 75 to 150 mg dose, and stopping at 28 weeks is too early.

8.q: Which statement correctly describes how the Human Rights Act 1998 applies to an NHS trust providing maternity care?
o: It applies to doctors' decisions but not to midwives' decisions
The trust must act compatibly with Convention rights
It applies when a woman has brought a claim in court
It applies to private providers but not to NHS bodies
8.w: Human Rights Act 1998 s6: it is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way that is incompatible with a Convention right. NHS trusts are public authorities, so their staff, including midwives, must act compatibly.

n.0: The trust acts through all its staff, so midwives' decisions are covered too.
n.2: The duty applies to everyday decisions, not just when a court case is brought.
n.3: NHS bodies are core public authorities and are bound by s6.

8.q: Chloe, a midwife, managed a postpartum haemorrhage at 14:10 and could not write her notes during the emergency. She is now able to document at 16:30. How should she record the events?
o: Write it on a separate sheet to be added to the notes later
Write the entry at the times of the events, as it is accurate
Ask the scribe midwife to write the account in her place
Mark it as a late entry, with the time of writing and of events
8.w: NMC Code 10.1: complete records at the time or as soon as possible after an event, recording if the notes are written some time after the event. A late entry shows when it was written and the times the events happened (Code 10.4: dated and timed).

n.0: Loose sheets risk loss and break the chronological record; the late entry goes in the notes now.
n.1: Writing as if contemporaneous hides when the entry was made, which is misleading (Code 10.3).
n.2: Each professional records their own care; entries must be attributable to the person who made them (Code 10.4).

8.q: Mia, 27, is 31 weeks pregnant with her first baby and has an uncomplicated pregnancy. Which set of assessments is routinely offered at this appointment?
o: Blood pressure, full blood count and an oral glucose tolerance test
Blood pressure, urine dipstick and palpation to confirm presentation
Blood pressure, urine dipstick and a cardiotocograph of the fetal heart
Blood pressure, urine dipstick for protein and plotted fundal height
8.w: At every routine face-to-face contact NICE recommends BP and urine dipstick for proteinuria (NG201 1.2.24, 1.2.28), and SFH plotted on a chart after 24+0 weeks (NG201 1.2.30). Babies' movements are also discussed (1.2.34).

n.0: FBC is offered at booking and 28 weeks, and OGTT only for women with GDM risk factors at 24 to 28 weeks.
n.1: Routine palpation for presentation starts after 36+0 weeks (NG201 1.2.36).
n.2: CTG is not part of routine antenatal care for an uncomplicated pregnancy.

8.q: Paige, 24, is 18 weeks pregnant. Her two older children were removed from her care because of neglect, and she still lives with the same partner. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to the health visitor to monitor the baby after the birth
Wait until after the birth to see how she cares for the baby
Tell Paige the baby will be removed at birth
Refer to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment
8.w: Midwives safeguard unborn babies. Previous children removed for neglect with the same circumstances is a significant concern needing referral to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment, in line with Working Together to Safeguard Children and local procedures (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Health visitor involvement is not enough when there are known significant safeguarding concerns.
n.1: Waiting removes the chance to plan support and protection before the baby is born.
n.2: Removal is not decided by the midwife and is not certain; this damages trust.

8.q: On day 15 the community midwife completes postnatal care for Erin, 33, and her baby. Which information about ongoing care is most accurate to give Erin?
o: Her midwife will return at 6 weeks for a final postnatal check
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 6 to 8 weeks
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 2 weeks
Her health visitor will complete her own postnatal check at 6 to 8 weeks
8.w: NG194 1.2.7: the woman should have a GP review of her health 6 to 8 weeks after birth. On completing midwifery care the midwife transfers care to the health visitor and GP (SPM 2.11).

n.0: Midwifery care has ended at transfer; the midwife does not routinely return at 6 weeks.
n.2: 2 weeks is not the routine maternal check; the GP check is at 6 to 8 weeks (NG194 1.2.7).
n.3: The maternal 6 to 8 week check is by the GP; health visitors follow the Healthy Child Programme.

8.q: Olu, 31, is admitted to the intensive care unit after a major postpartum haemorrhage. Her baby is well and is being cared for by her partner on the postnatal ward. What is the most appropriate plan for the baby's care?
o: Start formula feeds because Olu is too unwell to breastfeed
Keep the baby on the postnatal ward until Olu is well enough to return
Discharge the baby home with the partner until Olu is transferred back
Plan regular contact between Olu and her baby and support her feeding wishes
8.w: SPM 2.6: ensure the needs of women and newborn infants are considered together as a priority in all settings, even when they have to be cared for separately. Contact, skin-to-skin when possible and support for expressing keep the dyad together.

n.0: Her feeding wishes should be explored; she may be able to express or have skin-to-skin contact when stable.
n.1: Separating them for the whole ICU stay ignores the needs of both and her feeding wishes.
n.2: Discharging the baby early increases separation and removes midwifery oversight of the baby.

8.q: At an antenatal visit at 32 weeks, Sian and her partner ask how they can help their baby feel secure after the birth. Which advice best supports attachment?
o: Keep to a fixed feeding and sleeping routine from the first day
Respond to her cues, with face-to-face time and skin-to-skin contact
Limit holding the baby so she does not become too dependent
Leave the baby to cry so she learns to settle herself
8.w: NG194 1.3.16-1.3.17: discuss bonding and attachment before and after birth, and encourage face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding appropriately to the baby's cues (SPM 3.9).

n.0: Responsive care, not fixed routines, supports attachment in the newborn period.
n.2: Holding and closeness support, rather than harm, attachment.
n.3: Newborns need responsive care; leaving them to cry does not build secure attachment.

8.q: Baby Omar was born at 38 weeks and is 40 hours old. At a home visit the midwife sees that he looks jaundiced; he is feeding well and alert. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Measure serum bilirubin within 2 hours and arrange urgent review
Measure bilirubin with a transcutaneous bilirubinometer within 6 hours
Estimate the level visually and recheck at the next routine visit
Check bilirubin at the next routine visit in 48 hours
8.w: NICE CG98 1.2.14, 1.2.16: in babies over 24 hours with suspected jaundice, measure the bilirubin within 6 hours; use a transcutaneous bilirubinometer in babies of 35 weeks or more and over 24 hours old.

n.0: Serum bilirubin within 2 hours is for jaundice in the first 24 hours of life.
n.2: Visual estimation is unreliable and CG98 requires measurement.
n.3: Waiting 48 hours exceeds the 6-hour measurement window.

8.q: Baby Finn was discharged home at 8 hours of age before his newborn hearing screen was done. His parents ask when it can still be carried out. What should the midwife tell them?
o: At the 6 to 8 week GP infant examination
Within 72 hours, at the same time as the NIPE newborn examination
At 12 months, alongside his routine vaccinations
Ideally in the first 4 weeks, but it can be done up to 3 months
8.w: NHS newborn hearing screening (Screening tests for you and your baby): the automated otoacoustic emission (AOAE) screen is ideally done in the first 4 weeks but can be done up to 3 months of age.

n.0: Hearing screening is a separate programme and is not part of the GP 6 to 8 week check.
n.1: Hearing screening is not tied to the 72-hour NIPE deadline and can be done later.
n.2: 12 months is far beyond the 3-month screening window.

8.q: A representative from a formula company offers the postnatal ward free sample packs of first infant formula to give to new mothers. What should the ward manager do?
o: Accept the samples and store them for use if a baby needs supplements
Accept the samples and give them to mothers who choose formula
Accept the samples if the packs carry no brand logos
Decline the samples because this breaches the WHO Code
8.w: The International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes (WHO, 1981) prohibits free samples to mothers and promotion of breastmilk substitutes in health facilities. UNICEF UK Baby Friendly Stage 1 requires no promotion of breastmilk substitutes, bottles, teats or dummies.

n.0: Supplies for clinical use must be purchased through normal channels, not accepted as promotional gifts.
n.1: Free samples to mothers are prohibited by the WHO Code whatever the feeding choice.
n.2: Removing logos does not change the prohibition on free samples to mothers.

8.q: Farah, 32, books at 9 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2 and her first baby weighed 3.6 kg. She has no previous gestational diabetes and no family history of diabetes. Which plan for gestational diabetes testing is most appropriate?
o: Offer a 75 g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
Test her urine for glucose at each visit and arrange testing if positive
Offer an HbA1c test at booking to assess her risk
Offer an oral glucose tolerance test as soon as possible after booking
8.w: A BMI of 30 kg/m2 or over is a risk factor for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.2.2). Women with risk factors other than previous GDM are offered a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks (NG3 1.2.5, 1.2.7).

n.1: NG3 1.2.3 says not to use urinalysis for glucose to assess risk; Farah already has a risk factor that warrants an OGTT.
n.2: NG3 1.2.3 says not to use HbA1c to assess the risk of developing gestational diabetes.
n.3: Early testing after booking is for women who had gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy (NG3 1.2.6); Farah has not.

8.q: Student midwife Priti will perform a vaginal examination on Marie, 27, under direct supervision. What must happen for Marie's consent to be valid?
o: Marie is told it is a student and agrees to her doing it
Marie signs a form agreeing to all student involvement
Marie's partner agrees to the student taking part
The supervising midwife consents on Marie's behalf
8.w: Valid consent must be informed and voluntary. The woman must know who will perform the procedure, including that the person is a student, and agree (Code 4.2; SPM 1.20).

n.1: A general form for all student involvement is not informed consent to a specific procedure.
n.2: A partner cannot consent for an adult woman with capacity.
n.3: The supervising midwife cannot consent for a woman with capacity.

8.q: Precious, 30, took sertraline throughout her pregnancy for depression and has just given birth to a healthy-looking baby at 39 weeks. She wants to keep her baby with her on the postnatal ward. In line with NICE NG235, what is the most appropriate plan for the baby?
o: Advise Precious to stop sertraline so that she can breastfeed
Give a dose of naloxone to reverse any drug effects at birth
Admit the baby to the neonatal unit for 72 hours of observation
Carry out additional monitoring for signs of withdrawal or PPHN
8.w: NICE NG235 1.11.17 recommends additional monitoring of the baby when the mother has taken an SSRI or SNRI in pregnancy, because of the risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and neonatal withdrawal. This can happen with the baby alongside the mother (SPM 3.18 adverse effects across the continuum of care).

n.0: Sertraline is generally compatible with breastfeeding, and stopping abruptly risks relapse of depression.
n.1: Naloxone reverses opioids, not SSRIs, and is not indicated for a well baby.
n.2: A well baby does not need routine separation and neonatal unit admission; monitoring can be done with the mother.

8.q: After a discussion, Tamsin, 27, declines group B streptococcus antibiotics in labour despite known carriage. Which record entry best documents her decision?
o: "Risks and options explained; Tamsin declines and understands."
"Refused antibiotics against medical advice; plan as before."
"Advised strongly but refused. Not my responsibility."
"Declined GBS antibiotics. Aware of risks."
8.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to refuse care; Code 10.2: record risks and steps taken. The entry shows the information given, her decision and her understanding.

n.1: 'Plan as before' and 'against advice' do not record the information given or a revised plan.
n.2: Disclaiming responsibility is unprofessional and does not record the discussion.
n.3: 'Aware of risks' does not show what information was given.

8.q: Lucy and Sarah are a married couple expecting their first baby; Lucy is pregnant. At a postnatal visit, the midwife is completing the newborn records. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask the couple how they each wish to be named and involved
Record Sarah as 'friend' until parental responsibility is confirmed
Record Sarah as 'partner' and ask Lucy to answer all questions
Address questions about the baby to Lucy as the birth mother
8.w: SPM 1.10 and Code 1.3: avoid assumptions, recognise diversity and involve partners and family as the woman wishes. Asking how the couple wish to be named and involved is respectful and person-centred.

n.1: Recording a spouse and co-parent as 'friend' is inaccurate and disrespectful; the couple's own description of their relationship should guide the record.
n.2: Directing everything to Lucy excludes Sarah, who is a parent, without asking the couple's wishes.
n.3: Directing questions to the birth mother alone assumes their roles without asking them.

8.q: Esme, 34, had a baby with a birthweight below the 3rd centile in her last pregnancy. She has been placed on a pathway of 3 to 4-weekly growth scans from 28 weeks. At her 30-week community appointment, what should the midwife do about fundal height?
o: Stop SFH measurement, as she is on serial scan surveillance
Measure SFH at alternate appointments to reduce duplication
Measure and plot SFH as well as reviewing each scan result
Measure SFH weekly between scans to detect any change
8.w: Saving Babies' Lives v3 intervention 2.12: women undergoing planned serial scan surveillance should stop SFH measurement once surveillance begins. Women at increased risk of FGR have 3 to 4-weekly scans until birth (2.13). The midwife still discusses movements and checks BP and urine.

n.1: Alternating SFH with scans is not part of the SBL v3 pathway; SFH stops.
n.2: SBL v3 states SFH should cease once serial scan surveillance begins.
n.3: Weekly SFH adds no useful information alongside scans and SFH should not be done more often than every 2 weeks anyway.

8.q: Jade, 19, has just given birth and is breastfeeding. She wants long-acting contraception before she goes home on day 1. Which method can be started now?
o: A diaphragm with spermicide
A progestogen-only implant
A combined vaginal ring
A combined patch
8.w: The implant, injection, progestogen-only pill, condoms and IUD or IUS (within 48 hours) can be started straight after the birth, including when breastfeeding (NHS; FSRH).

n.0: A diaphragm is usually fitted from about 6 weeks after the birth.
n.2: Combined methods are avoided for at least 6 weeks when breastfeeding.
n.3: Combined methods are avoided for at least 6 weeks when breastfeeding.

8.q: Joy, 32, is pregnant with her third baby. Both previous births were straightforward and she has no risk factors. She asks whether planning a home birth is safe for her baby. What should the midwife tell her?
o: Fewer interventions but a small increase in adverse outcomes for the baby
A higher risk for the baby because this will be her third birth
Similar interventions and no difference in outcome for the baby
Fewer interventions and no difference in outcome for the baby
8.w: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk multiparous women, planning birth at home or in a midwife-led unit (freestanding or alongside) is associated with a lower rate of interventions, and the outcome for the baby is no different from an obstetric unit.

n.0: This applies to low-risk nulliparous women; for multiparous women there is no difference for the baby (NG235 1.3.3).
n.1: Having had two previous straightforward births is not a risk factor; NG235 finds no difference for the baby for low-risk multiparous women.
n.2: Planned home birth is associated with a lower rate of interventions for low-risk multiparous women.

8.q: Mei, 34, is 10 days after the birth of her third baby and phones the community midwife about heavier vaginal bleeding. Her records show a booking weight of 47 kg, a postnatal haemoglobin of 92 g/L, and that she is exclusively breastfeeding. Which features in her history may worsen the consequences of a secondary postpartum haemorrhage?
o: Her age over 30 years and exclusive breastfeeding
Exclusive breastfeeding and her parity of three
Her booking weight under 50 kg and her anaemia
Her parity of three and her age over 30 years
8.w: NICE NG194 1.2.14: when a woman seeks advice about bleeding after birth, assess severity and be aware that anaemia and a weight of less than 50 kg at booking may worsen the consequences of secondary postpartum haemorrhage.

n.0: Neither age nor breastfeeding is listed in NG194 as worsening the consequences of secondary PPH.
n.1: Breastfeeding does not worsen the consequences of secondary PPH and parity is not a listed factor.
n.3: Parity and age are not the factors NG194 lists as worsening the consequences of secondary PPH.

8.q: Bella, 29, is RhD negative and received routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks. At 31 weeks she trips and falls onto her abdomen. She has mild tenderness and the baby is moving. What is the most appropriate plan regarding anti-D?
o: Withhold anti-D unless she develops vaginal bleeding in the next 72 hours
Give anti-D at the birth, combined with her postnatal dose
Withhold anti-D, as her 28-week prophylaxis covers her until the birth
Arrange obstetric assessment and offer anti-D for this sensitising event
8.w: Abdominal trauma is a potentially sensitising event. Anti-D given for a sensitising event is separate from routine prophylaxis, so RAADP does not replace it. She also needs obstetric assessment after abdominal trauma because of the risk of placental abruption.

n.0: Trauma can cause fetomaternal haemorrhage without visible bleeding, so anti-D is not conditional on bleeding.
n.1: Delaying until birth leaves her unprotected after a possible fetomaternal haemorrhage now.
n.2: Routine prophylaxis does not replace the anti-D needed after a sensitising event.

8.q: A community midwife visits baby Rosa, aged 5 days, at home. According to NICE NG194, which finding is a red flag for serious illness?
o: Sleeping for 3 hours between feeds
Axillary temperature of 35.8 C
Small possets of milk after feeds
Respiratory rate of 52 breaths/min
8.w: NICE NG194 1.4.9: red flags for serious illness in young babies include a temperature of 38 C or over or under 36 C, respiratory rate over 60, grunting, chest indrawing, pallor or mottling, a weak or high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, seizures, bilious or projectile vomiting and non-blanching rash.

n.0: Sleeping 3 hours between feeds is normal for many newborns.
n.2: Small possets are common; bilious or forceful (projectile) vomiting is the red flag.
n.3: A respiratory rate of 52 is within the normal newborn range (the red flag is over 60).

8.q: Cara, 25, had an emergency caesarean after a long labour. On day 4 she tells the midwife she does not feel close to her baby and keeps reliving the birth. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Discuss her feelings, assess her mental health and offer support
Refer her to the health visitor to discuss bonding at 6 weeks
Advise her to spend less time with the baby until she feels better
Reassure her that bonding will improve once she is home
8.w: NG194 1.3.18: discuss aspects of the postnatal period that may affect bonding, including traumatic birth. NG194 1.2.2 and CG192: assess psychological wellbeing at each contact and offer support or referral (SPM 3.9).

n.1: She needs assessment and support now, not in several weeks.
n.2: Reducing contact does not help bonding and may worsen her distress.
n.3: Reassurance without assessment misses possible birth trauma or depression; difficulties after a traumatic birth may persist.

8.q: Toni, 19, says she will breastfeed 'for a couple of weeks' before returning to college, and asks whether it is worth it for such a short time. Which response is most accurate?
o: Benefits begin once she has breastfed without formula for 6 months
Colostrum helps, but later milk gives no advantage over formula
Breastfeeding benefits her and the baby even if done for a short time
Short spells of breastfeeding confuse the baby and are best avoided
8.w: NICE NG194 1.5.2: discussions about breastfeeding should include how it can have benefits even if only done for a short time, and how it can soothe and comfort the baby. Advice respects the parents' choices (1.5.1).

n.0: There is no 6-month threshold before benefits begin; NG194 states short-term breastfeeding still helps.
n.1: Breast milk continues to provide immune and nutritional benefits beyond the first week.
n.3: Any breastfeeding is beneficial; there is no evidence that short spells confuse the baby.

8.q: Maya is the midwife at a freestanding birth centre when a woman has a sudden, heavy postpartum haemorrhage. One other midwife and a maternity support worker are on duty. What should Maya do first?
o: Phone the obstetric unit for advice before starting any treatment
Ask the support worker to estimate the blood loss before any other action
Call for help, request a 999 ambulance and give each colleague a clear role
Start the haemorrhage protocol herself and call for help once bleeding slows
8.w: In an unpredictable emergency, calling for help early, arranging transfer and allocating clear roles makes best use of a small team (SPM 5.13.6; NICE NG235 1.10.33: call for help, transfer to obstetric-led care).

n.0: Advice is useful but treatment and transfer must not wait for it.
n.1: Measuring blood loss matters, but it is not the first priority over summoning help.
n.3: Delaying the call for help until bleeding slows wastes time a small team cannot afford.

8.q: Mei, 30, has a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks. Her fasting plasma glucose is 5.8 mmol/L and her 2-hour value is 7.1 mmol/L. How should these results be interpreted?
o: The test is normal because the 2-hour value is below 7.8 mmol/L
The result is borderline and the OGTT should be repeated at 32 weeks of pregnancy
She has type 2 diabetes because the fasting value is above 5.5 mmol/L at 26 weeks
She has gestational diabetes because the fasting value is 5.6 mmol/L or above
8.w: NG3 1.2.8 diagnoses gestational diabetes if the fasting plasma glucose is 5.6 mmol/L or above OR the 2-hour value is 7.8 mmol/L or above. Either threshold is enough.

n.0: Both values do not have to be raised; a fasting level of 5.8 mmol/L alone meets the diagnostic criterion.
n.1: NG3 has no borderline category requiring repeat testing; the threshold is met now.
n.2: These are the diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes, not type 2 diabetes.

8.q: Kezia, 23, has epilepsy controlled with sodium valproate. She attends the early pregnancy unit with an unplanned pregnancy of 7 weeks, confirmed on scan. She is distressed and asks the midwife what she should do about her medication. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Stop valproate today and restart it after the first trimester
Halve the valproate dose until she sees her GP next month
Continue valproate as the main risk period has already passed
Keep taking it for now and arrange urgent specialist review today
8.w: Valproate carries a high risk of malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders (MHRA safety advice; CG192 1.4.29). In epilepsy, stopping abruptly can cause seizures that harm woman and fetus, so she should not stop or change her dose without advice and needs urgent specialist review to plan the switch (SPM 3.18).

n.0: Abruptly stopping an antiseizure medicine risks status epilepticus; changes need specialist planning.
n.1: Self-adjusting the dose risks seizures and delays the specialist review she needs now.
n.2: Organogenesis is ongoing at 7 weeks and valproate also affects neurodevelopment, so urgent review is needed.

8.q: Precious, 24, gave birth four days ago. Her partner calls the community midwife because she has not slept for two nights, is talking rapidly, believes the baby has been swapped and is frightened. She had no previous mental health problems. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Complete an EPDS questionnaire at the next routine postnatal visit
Advise her partner to let her sleep and call back if she is no better tomorrow
Book a GP appointment for later this week to review her mood
Arrange immediate referral for specialist mental health assessment within 4 hours
8.w: Sudden onset of insomnia, agitation and delusional beliefs in the first days after birth suggests postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency. CG192 1.5.12: refer to a secondary (preferably specialist perinatal) mental health service for immediate assessment within 4 hours of referral.

n.0: The EPDS screens for depression and is not the response to an acute psychotic presentation.
n.1: Waiting until tomorrow leaves a woman with possible psychosis and her baby at serious risk.
n.2: A GP appointment later in the week delays assessment of a condition that can deteriorate within hours.

8.q: Abi, 27, had pre-eclampsia and gave birth 2 days ago. She is not taking antihypertensive medicine. Her blood pressure is now 152/102 mmHg on two readings and she has no symptoms. According to NICE NG133, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Plan transfer home, as she has no symptoms of pre-eclampsia
Recheck in 4 hours and treat if her blood pressure reaches 160/110
Start antihypertensive treatment now, as her BP is 150/100 or higher
Reduce blood pressure checks to once daily now that the baby is born
8.w: NICE NG133 (postnatal care, pre-eclampsia): start antihypertensive treatment if blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg or higher. Inpatients with pre-eclampsia need BP measured at least 4 times a day.

n.0: Transfer criteria include BP of 150/100 or less, which she does not meet.
n.1: 160/110 is the threshold for severe hypertension; postnatal treatment starts at 150/100.
n.3: NG133 requires at least 4 BP checks a day while she is an inpatient with pre-eclampsia.

8.q: A community midwife is discussing place of birth with four women. Which woman should be advised to plan birth in an obstetric unit because of her antenatal risk of postpartum haemorrhage?
o: Amina, 29, para 2, BMI 32 kg/m2
Becky, 24, who had a second-degree tear last time
Dana, 33, who had a PPH needing transfusion last time
Cara, 35, with a low-risk pregnancy and a fundal placenta
8.w: NICE NG235 1.10.29 lists antenatal PPH risk factors that warrant advice to give birth in an obstetric unit, including previous PPH over 1000 mL or requiring transfusion, BMI over 35, grand multiparity (4 or more), pre-eclampsia, Hb under 85 g/L at onset of labour and placenta accreta spectrum.

n.0: BMI over 35 and parity 4 or more are the thresholds; 32 and para 2 do not meet them.
n.1: A previous second-degree tear is not an antenatal PPH risk factor in NG235.
n.3: A fundal placenta in a low-risk pregnancy is not a PPH risk factor.

8.q: Rana, 27, is 26 weeks pregnant. Her partner attends every appointment, answers questions for her and does not leave the room. She has missed two appointments. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Document that she is accompanied and continue care as usual at each appointment
Arrange a one-to-one consultation without her partner present to ask about her safety
Refer her straight to the police based on her partner's controlling behaviour
Ask her about domestic abuse in front of her partner so the question is clear
8.w: CG110 1.1.14: provide each woman with a one-to-one consultation, without her partner or family present, on at least one occasion to allow sensitive issues such as domestic abuse to be discussed. Controlling behaviour and missed appointments are warning signs of domestic abuse, and NICE NG201 1.2.5 advises asking about domestic abuse when the woman is alone.

n.0: Continuing as usual ignores clear warning signs and misses the chance to ask safely.
n.2: A police referral without her disclosure or consent, before any assessment, is premature and may increase her risk.
n.3: Asking in front of a possibly abusive partner may endanger her and is unlikely to lead to disclosure.

8.q: A labour ward coordinator is asked by the bleep holder to take over the care of a woman in active labour because the ward is short of one midwife. The coordinator is currently overseeing eight rooms. What should the coordinator do?
o: Take the woman's care and hand oversight of the ward to the most senior midwife
Stay supernumerary and escalate the shortfall through the escalation policy
Take the woman's care and review the other rooms between contractions
Decline the request and wait for the next shift to address the shortfall
8.w: NHS Resolution's Maternity Incentive Scheme (Year 7, safety action 5) states that the midwifery coordinator in charge of labour ward must have supernumerary status, to keep oversight of all birth activity, with an escalation plan for shortfalls. The coordinator stays supernumerary and escalates the gap (SPM 2.3: factors affecting safe provision, including staffing).

n.0: Taking a caseload removes the coordinator's supernumerary oversight of the whole ward, which the Maternity Incentive Scheme requires for safety.
n.2: Combining a one-to-one caseload with coordination means neither role is done safely.
n.3: Declining without escalation leaves the staffing gap unresolved and the woman without a midwife.

8.q: A labour ward midwife notices that the nitrous oxide and oxygen (Entonox) supply in empty rooms is often left connected and that a regulator has a faint hiss. In the context of sustainable healthcare, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the hiss in the ward diary for the next equipment check
Report the leak, and turn off supplies in rooms not in use
Leave the supply connected so it is ready for the next woman
Advise women to use pethidine instead of Entonox to reduce emissions
8.w: Nitrous oxide is a potent greenhouse gas and much is lost through leaks in piped systems. Reporting leaks and avoiding waste reduces environmental harm without restricting women's choice of analgesia (SPM 5.10, 5.13.3).

n.0: Waiting for a routine check leaves a known leak releasing gas.
n.2: Leaving supplies connected in empty rooms increases waste and does not deal with the leak.
n.3: Women's choice of pain relief should not be restricted; the aim is to cut waste, not to deny Entonox.

8.q: Jo, a midwife, was involved in a shoulder dystocia that is now the subject of a trust learning response. She is asked to attend an interview and give a written account. What is her professional responsibility?
o: Give an account after checking it with colleagues so the stories match
Decline the interview until the trust guarantees she will not be named
Cooperate fully and give an honest, factual account of her involvement
Ask her union to give an account so she does not have to take part
8.w: Code 23 requires registrants to cooperate with investigations and audits, and Code 10 and 20.2 require honest, accurate accounts. Critical reflection on the incident supports learning (SPM 5.2).

n.0: Aligning accounts with colleagues undermines the integrity of the investigation.
n.1: Making cooperation conditional on anonymity conflicts with the duty to cooperate.
n.3: A union may support her, but the account must be her own.

8.q: Before transfer home on day 1, Jo, 27, says breastfeeding is going well. The midwife has not yet observed a feed. What does NICE recommend before transfer?
o: Observe at least one effective feed as part of the feeding plan
Give a formula top-up so the baby is settled for the journey
Weigh the baby to confirm feeding is effective
Accept Jo's report and arrange a feed check on day 5
8.w: NG194 1.1.10: before transfer, make sure there is a plan for feeding the baby, including observing at least 1 effective feed; NG194 1.5.14 lists what to assess (SPM 3.6).

n.1: A top-up without clinical need can undermine breastfeeding.
n.2: Weight on day 1 does not show feeding effectiveness; normal weight loss occurs early.
n.3: NICE expects an effective feed to be observed before transfer.

8.q: Baby Isla is born at 28 weeks in the delivery suite. The room is warm and the resuscitaire heater is on. How should the midwife manage her temperature immediately after birth?
o: Place her skin-to-skin and cover both with a warm towel
Put her body into a plastic bag without drying, and add a hat
Give her a warm bath to bring her temperature up quickly
Dry her thoroughly and wrap her in a dry warm towel
8.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: for babies under 32 weeks, dry the head, put on a hat and place the body in a plastic (polyethylene) bag without drying, under a radiant heater; aim to keep temperature 36.5 to 37.5 C. Babies of 32 weeks or more are dried and wet towels removed.

n.0: A 28-week baby needs a plastic bag under a radiant heater and is likely to need stabilisation.
n.2: Bathing causes heat loss and is not part of newborn resuscitation.
n.3: Drying and wrapping is for babies of 32 weeks or more.

8.q: Oona, 34, is having a major postpartum haemorrhage on the delivery suite. Help has arrived and uterotonics have been given. Her oxygen saturation is 93% on air. In line with NICE NG235, how should oxygen be given?
o: Oxygen is unnecessary until saturation falls below 90%
4 L/minute by simple face mask aiming for 92%
15 L/minute by non-rebreathe mask aiming for 94 to 98%
2 L/minute by nasal cannula aiming for 88 to 92%
8.w: NICE NG235 1.10.33: consider supplementary oxygen starting at 15 L/minute using a non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag, to obtain a target saturation of 94% to 98% (SPM 4.7).

n.0: Her saturation is already below the 94 to 98% target, so oxygen is indicated now.
n.1: Low-flow oxygen by simple mask is not what NG235 advises in PPH.
n.3: 88 to 92% is the target for people at risk of hypercapnia, not for PPH.

8.q: Baby Noah was born through meconium-stained liquor 2 hours ago. His observations: respiratory rate 66 breaths/min, heart rate 150 bpm, temperature 37.3 C, oxygen saturation 97%. Which finding means a neonatologist should assess him?
o: Heart rate of 150 beats per minute
Oxygen saturation of 97%
Respiratory rate of 66 breaths/min
Temperature of 37.3 C on one reading
8.w: NICE NG235 1.11.29: after any meconium, ask a neonatologist to assess the baby if respiratory rate is above 60, there is grunting, heart rate is below 100 or above 160, capillary refill is over 3 seconds, temperature is 38 C or more (or 37.5 C twice 15 to 30 minutes apart), saturation is below 95% or there is central cyanosis.

n.0: A heart rate of 150 is within the 100 to 160 range.
n.1: 97% is above the 95% threshold.
n.3: 37.3 C is below the 37.5 C and 38 C triggers.

8.q: Kemi, 33, is 2 days postnatal on the ward and meets a high-risk criterion for sepsis. The senior doctor has assessed her and taken blood cultures. Within what time should she receive a broad-spectrum antimicrobial?
o: Within 6 hours
Within 3 hours
After the culture results are known
Within 1 hour
8.w: NICE NG255 1.7.2: for suspected sepsis with 1 or more high-risk criteria, give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial at the maximum recommended dose without delay, within 1 hour of meeting the high-risk criterion, after taking blood cultures if this does not delay treatment.

n.0: 6 hours is too long for a woman meeting a high-risk criterion.
n.1: 3 hours is the senior review window for 2 or more moderate-to-high criteria with normal lactate.
n.2: Waiting for culture results would delay treatment by a day or more.

8.q: Yasmin, 27, is 38+5 weeks pregnant. Group B streptococcus was found on a urine culture at 30 weeks. She phones to say her membranes ruptured 30 minutes ago with clear fluid and she has no contractions. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Wait at home for up to 24 hours, taking oral antibiotics
Attend within 12 hours for a speculum examination
Wait at home for up to 24 hours, then attend for induction
Attend now; immediate induction of labour should be offered
8.w: NICE NG235 1.7.11 (and NG207 1.2.16): if a woman has PROM at term and a positive GBS test at any time in the current pregnancy, offer immediate induction (or caesarean if planned).
