Intrapartum antibiotics follow NICE neonatal infection guidance. GBS carriage is also a phone triage risk factor needing urgent in-person review (1.7.1).

n.0: Oral antibiotics at home do not replace intrapartum IV prophylaxis and immediate induction.
n.1: The 12-hour review applies to women with no risk factors on phone triage; GBS carriage requires immediate attendance.
n.2: Expectant management for 24 hours is for women without risk factors; GBS positive women are offered immediate induction.

8.q: Tamsin, 30, had her first baby in 2014 and remembers a blood test for rubella immunity. At her booking appointment she asks why rubella is not on the list of infectious diseases screening offered this time. What is the correct explanation?
o: Rubella screening is offered to women who have had a previous baby
Rubella immunity is checked at the 28-week appointment instead
Antenatal rubella susceptibility screening stopped in 2016
Rubella is tested for as part of the hepatitis B screening sample
8.w: The NHS infectious diseases in pregnancy screening programme offers screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis in every pregnancy. Rubella susceptibility screening in pregnancy stopped on 1 April 2016 (IDPS programme overview).

n.0: Rubella screening stopped for all pregnant women, not according to parity.
n.1: 28-week bloods are FBC, blood group and antibodies; rubella is not tested then.
n.3: IDPS screens for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis; rubella is no longer part of it.

8.q: Chantelle, 17, lives with her mother and plans to breastfeed her first baby. According to NICE NG194, which approach to her feeding support is most appropriate?
o: Hand all feeding support to her mother from the first day
Offer extra face-to-face support and continuity from a known team
Give her a leaflet and helpline number in place of visits
Suggest formula feeding, as young mothers seldom keep breastfeeding
8.w: NICE NG194 1.5.11: younger women and women from a low income or disadvantaged background may need more support and encouragement to start and continue breastfeeding, and continuity of carer is particularly important for them.

n.0: Family support helps, but professional breastfeeding support remains part of postnatal care.
n.2: Written and phone support supplement, but do not replace, face-to-face support (NG194 1.5.9).
n.3: Steering her away from her choice is not respectful (NG194 1.5.1) and assumes failure.

8.q: During a breech birth, Nadia's baby has been born to the umbilicus with the back anterior. The buttocks were born 2 minutes ago. The baby has good tone and colour and is descending with each contraction. What should the midwife do?
o: Ask Nadia to stop pushing to protect the perineum
Keep her hands off and continue to observe progress
Grasp the legs and apply traction to deliver the arms
Deliver the head at once using Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit
8.w: RCOG GTG 20b: a hands-off approach with timely intervention if progress is not made once the umbilicus has delivered, or if there is poor tone, extended arms or neck. Intervention is generally required if more than 5 minutes from buttocks to head or more than 3 minutes from umbilicus to head. Good tone and progress mean no intervention yet.

n.0: Stopping maternal effort delays the birth when cord compression is likely.
n.2: Traction is avoided because it can cause arm and head extension.
n.3: The arms and body have not yet been born, and the head is not the next step.

8.q: Sian, 31, is on an oxytocin infusion for delay in the first stage. The CTG has just been categorised as pathological by the midwife and the coordinator. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Increase the oxytocin to achieve 5 contractions in 10 minutes
Reduce the oxytocin rate by half and recheck the CTG in 30 minutes
Stop the oxytocin and seek urgent obstetric review
Continue the oxytocin, as contractions are not more than 4 in 10
8.w: NICE NG235 1.8.56: oxytocin must be discontinued immediately if the CTG is pathological, and urgent obstetrician or senior midwife review sought. It may be restarted after review if the CTG is no longer pathological and the woman agrees (1.8.57).

n.0: The aim is 3 to 4 contractions in 10; more than 4 is excessive and harmful with a pathological trace.
n.1: Reducing the dose is the response to more than 4 contractions in 10 (1.8.55); a pathological CTG needs oxytocin stopped.
n.3: A pathological CTG requires oxytocin to stop whatever the contraction frequency.

8.q: After the placenta is delivered, Lily, 28, has a firm, well-contracted uterus at the level of the umbilicus and only a small blood loss. A student asks what mainly stops bleeding from the placental site. What is the correct answer?
o: Vasoconstriction of the uterine arteries by circulating adrenaline
Pressure from the full bladder pressing on the placental site
Rapid formation of clot over the placental site by clotting factors
Uterine muscle contraction and retraction compressing the vessels
8.w: The interlacing, oblique fibres of the myometrium contract and retract around the spiral arteries, acting as 'living ligatures'. Clotting helps, but uterine tone is the main mechanism, which is why atony is the commonest cause of PPH (SPM 3.12.3).

n.0: Adrenaline-driven vasoconstriction is not the main way placental site bleeding is controlled.
n.1: A full bladder impedes uterine contraction and increases bleeding risk; it does not compress the placental site.
n.2: Clotting contributes, but without uterine contraction bleeding continues; uterine tone is the main mechanism.

8.q: Hannah, 33, is RhD negative and booking at 9 weeks in her third pregnancy. Her antibody screen shows immune anti-D antibodies, which were first detected after her second baby's birth. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Give routine anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks as usual
Repeat the antibody screen at 28 weeks before making any referral
Give anti-D now to remove the existing antibodies
Refer for obstetric monitoring, as prophylaxis cannot help now
8.w: RAADP is for RhD-negative women who are not known to be sensitised (NICE TA156 1.1). Once immune anti-D is present, prophylaxis cannot reverse sensitisation; the pregnancy needs obstetric or fetal medicine monitoring of antibody levels and the fetus for anaemia.

n.0: Prophylaxis is not given to women already sensitised to RhD.
n.1: Her sensitisation is known now, so referral for monitoring should not wait until 28 weeks.
n.2: Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitisation; it cannot remove antibodies already formed.

8.q: Lin, 33, is hepatitis B positive. Her baby has just been born at term and is well. When should the baby receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine?
o: Within 7 days of birth
Within 24 hours of birth
After the newborn blood spot test on day 5
At 8 weeks with the routine vaccines
8.w: Green Book ch 18: babies born to hepatitis B positive mothers should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, within 24 hours (with hepatitis B immunoglobulin if indicated), then further doses.

n.0: The first dose should be given as soon as possible and within 24 hours.
n.2: Waiting until day 5 delays protection and is not linked to blood spot screening.
n.3: Babies of hepatitis B positive mothers need a dose at birth; 8 weeks is too late to prevent transmission.

8.q: Hannah, 32, is having a planned home birth. Her community midwife has no prescription chart or patient group directions for this birth. Which medicine can the registered midwife lawfully administer under the midwives exemptions in Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012?
o: Intramuscular oxytocin for the third stage
Intravenous tranexamic acid for heavy bleeding
Intravenous co-amoxiclav for suspected infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for a seizure
8.w: HMR 2012 Schedule 17 lists the parenteral prescription-only medicines a registered midwife may administer in professional practice, including oxytocins (natural and synthetic), ergometrine, carboprost, anti-D, phytomenadione and others (SPM 3.19 midwives exemptions).

n.1: Tranexamic acid is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.
n.2: Antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav are not on the Schedule 17 list.
n.3: Magnesium sulfate is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.

8.q: Baby Ivy, born at 40 weeks and breastfed, is 16 days old and still visibly jaundiced. Her mother says her stools have become pale and chalky and her urine is dark. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure her mother that breast milk jaundice is common at this age
Arrange conjugated bilirubin measurement and same-day medical review
Advise stopping breastfeeding for 48 hours to see if the jaundice fades
Recheck the jaundice at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
8.w: NICE CG98 1.7.1-1.7.2: jaundice lasting over 14 days in a term baby is prolonged; look for pale chalky stools and dark urine and measure conjugated bilirubin. Pale stools and dark urine suggest cholestasis such as biliary atresia, needing urgent expert advice.

n.0: Pale stools and dark urine are not features of breast milk jaundice.
n.2: Interrupting breastfeeding is not recommended and delays investigation.
n.3: Waiting weeks could delay time-critical diagnosis of biliary atresia.

8.q: Dana is the labour ward coordinator. Four requests arrive at the same moment. Which should she attend to first?
o: A woman at 38 weeks with a mild headache whose blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg
A postnatal woman 2 hours after birth asking for her prescribed paracetamol
A woman in established labour whose fetal heart rate has been 85 bpm for 4 minutes
A woman booked for elective caesarean tomorrow who needs her bloods taken
8.w: SPM 5.19 requires safe prioritising. A prolonged fetal bradycardia lasting several minutes is an obstetric emergency needing immediate assessment and escalation; Code 25.1 asks leaders to identify priorities and deal with risk.

n.0: A mild headache with normal blood pressure needs review, but a prolonged fetal bradycardia is the more urgent threat.
n.1: Analgesia is important but can follow within minutes without risk to life.
n.3: Pre-operative bloods for tomorrow are routine and can be planned later in the shift.

8.q: Hope, 19, attends the maternity unit for the first time at 24 weeks of pregnancy. She has not seen a midwife before and seems anxious when asked why. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make a child protection referral because late booking indicates neglect
Arrange a routine booking appointment with her community midwife in 4 weeks
Offer the combined screening test for Down's syndrome at this appointment
Complete her booking today and sensitively explore why she has booked late
8.w: Late booking is a recognised warning sign (for example of domestic abuse, concealed pregnancy or social difficulty). NG201 1.1.4-1.1.5 aims for booking by 10+0 weeks; a late booker should be booked promptly, with a sensitive exploration of reasons and safeguarding questions asked when she is alone (NG201 1.2.5; SPM 2.8).

n.0: Late booking is a warning sign to explore, not proof of harm; a referral is made if the assessment identifies risk.
n.1: She has already missed most of the antenatal schedule; delaying booking another month adds risk.
n.2: The combined test is offered up to 14+1 weeks, so it is no longer available at 24 weeks (FASP).

8.q: Mo, a band 6 midwife, has escalated a pathological CTG to the obstetric registrar, who says to continue and review in an hour. Mo remains very concerned as the fetal heart rate has had a prolonged deceleration. What should Mo do next?
o: State her concern clearly and escalate to the consultant obstetrician
Document her disagreement and review the CTG again in an hour
Ask another midwife whether she agrees before taking any action
Accept the registrar's plan because the decision is a medical one
8.w: When concerns remain after escalation, the midwife should use the escalation or conflict of clinical opinion policy to go to the consultant. Ockenden IEA 3 requires trusts to support staff in escalating clinical concerns when professionals disagree (SPM 5.6; Code 16.1).

n.1: Documenting without acting leaves the fetus at continuing risk for another hour.
n.2: Seeking a second midwifery view is reasonable but should not delay escalation when she is already concerned.
n.3: The midwife remains accountable for acting on her concerns; deferring to hierarchy despite clear risk is unsafe.

8.q: Mia, 27, has an ultrasound at 13 weeks showing a twin pregnancy. The sonographer cannot confidently determine chorionicity, and a second opinion from a senior sonographer is also inconclusive. How should the pregnancy be managed?
o: Repeat the scan with 3D ultrasound to confirm chorionicity
As a dichorionic pregnancy until the 20-week scan
As a monochorionic pregnancy until proven otherwise
As a dichorionic pregnancy if the twins are discordant in sex later
8.w: NICE NG137 1.1.7: if it is difficult to determine chorionicity even after referral, manage the pregnancy as monochorionic until proven otherwise, because monochorionic twins carry higher risks (such as feto-fetal transfusion syndrome).

n.0: NG137 1.1.12 advises not to use 3D ultrasound to determine chorionicity.
n.1: Assuming dichorionicity would leave a possibly monochorionic pregnancy without the closer surveillance it needs.
n.3: Discordant sex later confirms dichorionicity, but until then the safer assumption is monochorionic.

8.q: Faye, 30, gave birth at term 34 hours after her membranes ruptured; labour began 28 hours after rupture. She had no signs of infection and her baby is well at birth. What care does NICE recommend for the baby?
o: Observation at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours, with no routine antibiotics
Admission to the neonatal unit for observation for 24 hours
Blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics for 48 hours
Routine postnatal care, as the baby is well at birth
8.w: NICE NG235 1.11.31 and 1.11.32: closely observe a baby born to a woman with PROM more than 24 hours before established labour at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours (temperature, heart rate, breathing, colour, perfusion, tone, feeding). If there are no signs of infection, do not give antibiotics to the woman or baby.

n.1: Observation can take place in any setting with the woman; neonatal unit admission is not needed for a well baby.
n.2: Antibiotics and cultures are not given to an asymptomatic baby when there are no signs of infection (1.11.32, 1.11.35).
n.3: Routine care alone misses the recommended observations during the first 12 hours, when infection risk is greatest.

8.q: Zainab, 30, is 36 weeks pregnant and asks her midwife whether a herbal tea her family recommends will help start labour. The midwife finds no good-quality evidence about its safety or effect in pregnancy. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Avoid the topic and advise her to ask her GP at her next visit
Tell her it is safe to try because it is a natural plant-based product
Explain there is no reliable evidence, discuss possible risks and record it
Tell her it will not work, as no published research supports its use
8.w: Acting safely without good-quality evidence means being honest about uncertainty, sharing what is known about possible risks, supporting her informed decision and documenting it (SPM 5.7; Code 6.1 and 6.2).

n.0: Deflecting to the GP leaves her without the information she asked for.
n.1: 'Natural' does not mean safe; claiming safety is not supported by evidence.
n.3: Absence of evidence is not proof of no effect; the honest answer is that it is unknown.

8.q: Mei, 36, has just had a vaginal birth after a long labour augmented with oxytocin. She had a 1,200 mL PPH in her last pregnancy. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and she has no cardiac, liver or kidney disease. She has chosen active management. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Carbetocin IV, as it is the first choice after any vaginal birth
Physiological management to avoid uterotonic side effects
Oxytocin 10 units IM, as ergometrine is reserved for treatment
Oxytocin plus ergometrine IM, with an antiemetic
8.w: NICE NG235 1.10.9 and 1.10.10: oxytocin plus ergometrine may be more effective than oxytocin alone and is advised when there are risk factors for PPH (here previous PPH and augmented, prolonged labour), unless contraindicated; offer an antiemetic such as cyclizine because of nausea and vomiting.

n.0: Carbetocin is recommended for prevention of PPH at caesarean birth, not vaginal birth.
n.1: She has chosen active management, which lowers PPH risk; physiological management would increase her risk.
n.2: Oxytocin alone is less effective; with PPH risk factors and no contraindication, oxytocin plus ergometrine is advised.

8.q: Asha, 36, is being treated for an atonic postpartum haemorrhage. She was given carboprost intramuscularly 5 minutes ago and is still bleeding. The junior doctor asks the midwife to draw up a second dose of carboprost to give straight away. What is the correct response?
o: Wait at least 60 minutes after the first dose
Wait at least 15 minutes after the first dose
Give it now because the bleeding is continuing
Give misoprostol as carboprost is a single dose
8.w: NICE NG235 1.10.34: carboprost may be repeated at intervals of at least 15 minutes, up to a maximum of 8 doses. Meanwhile other measures continue (massage, oxytocin infusion, tranexamic acid, escalation to the senior team).

n.0: The minimum interval is 15 minutes, not 60 minutes.
n.2: A second dose at 5 minutes is earlier than the minimum 15-minute interval.
n.3: Carboprost can be repeated up to 8 doses; it is not a single dose.

8.q: Hana, 27, is in the latent first stage of her first labour at home. She is finding contractions painful and asks the midwife what might help at this stage. Which advice is supported by NICE?
o: Intramuscular diamorphine so that she can rest at home
Breathing exercises, a warm shower or bath, and massage
Lidocaine spray to numb the perineum during contractions
Aromatherapy oils, yoga positions and acupressure
8.w: NICE NG235 1.6.3: advise that breathing exercises, a shower or bath, and massage may reduce pain in the latent first stage. NG235 1.6.4 advises not to offer aromatherapy, yoga or acupressure for latent-phase pain (though her choice to use them is supported).

n.0: Opioids at home in the latent phase are not the NICE-advised first step and carry maternal and neonatal side effects.
n.2: Lidocaine spray is not offered for labour pain (NG235 1.9.15 advises against it in the second stage) and does not relieve contraction pain.
n.3: NICE advises not to offer or advise aromatherapy, yoga or acupressure for latent-phase pain relief.

8.q: Rosa, 33, is booking at 9 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her BMI is 32 and her mother has type 2 diabetes. Her first baby weighed 3.6 kg. She has no other risk factors. Which plan for gestational diabetes is most appropriate?
o: Arrange a random blood glucose test today and repeat it at 28 weeks
Test her urine for glucose at every antenatal appointment
Check HbA1c at booking and repeat it at 28 weeks
Offer a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
8.w: Rosa has two risk factors for gestational diabetes (BMI above 30 and a first-degree relative with diabetes). NICE recommends a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks (NG201 1.2.22; NG3 1.2.2). NG3 1.2.3 states that fasting or random glucose, HbA1c, glucose challenge or urinalysis for glucose should not be used to assess GDM risk.

n.0: Random blood glucose is not a recommended test for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.2.3).
n.1: Urinalysis for glucose is not a valid test for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.2.3).
n.2: HbA1c is not recommended for assessing gestational diabetes risk in pregnancy (NG3 1.2.3).

8.q: Kirsty, 27, is 4 days after the birth of her first baby. She has been tearful and irritable since yesterday but is sleeping when the baby sleeps, enjoys caring for the baby and has no thoughts of harm. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain this is postnatal depression and ask the GP to start an antidepressant
Refer her urgently to the perinatal mental health team for assessment today
Reassure her that these feelings normally last for about 3 months after birth
Explain the baby blues usually settle within 2 weeks and when to seek help
8.w: Feeling down, anxious or irritable for a few days after the birth is very common (the baby blues) and usually goes away within 2 weeks; if it continues or worsens she should seek help (NHS postnatal depression guidance). NG194 1.2.2: assess emotional wellbeing at every contact and arrange further assessment if there are concerns.

n.0: Transient tearfulness on day 4 does not meet the picture of postnatal depression, and medication is not indicated.
n.1: Her symptoms fit the baby blues with no risk features, so urgent specialist referral is not indicated.
n.2: The baby blues usually resolve within 2 weeks; symptoms lasting months suggest depression and need assessment.

8.q: Baby Alfie is 10 days old and feeding well, and his mother is well. The midwife plans to transfer their care to the health visiting team today. According to NICE NG194, when should the first health visitor home visit be considered?
o: Within 36 hours after transfer from midwifery care
At the 6 to 8 week infant physical examination
Between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care
At around 3 months, with the first immunisations
8.w: NICE NG194 1.1.15: consider arranging the first postnatal health visitor home visit between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery care. 1.1.9: the transfer from midwife to health visitor must be clearly communicated to professionals and parents.

n.0: 36 hours is the standard for the first midwife visit after transfer from the place of birth.
n.1: The 6 to 8 week examination is usually done in primary care and is later than the health visitor visit.
n.3: Primary immunisations start at 8 weeks, and the health visitor visit is earlier than either.

8.q: Anya, 31, is 8 weeks pregnant. She is worried because she drank two glasses of wine at a party before she knew she was pregnant. What should the midwife tell her?
o: Limit drinking to 1 to 2 units once or twice a week for the rest of pregnancy
A scan is needed at 12 weeks to look for alcohol-related harm
Avoid alcohol from now; the risk from small amounts early is likely to be low
Drinking in the first weeks causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorder in most cases
8.w: NG201 1.3.10: there is no known safe level of alcohol in pregnancy and the safest approach is to avoid alcohol altogether. UK Chief Medical Officers (2016) advise the risk of harm is likely to be low if a woman drank small amounts before she knew she was pregnant.

n.0: This was older advice; there is no known safe level of alcohol in pregnancy.
n.1: A scan cannot exclude alcohol-related harm and is not indicated for this.
n.3: This overstates the risk of small amounts and causes unnecessary distress.

8.q: Emma, 27, meets high-risk criteria for sepsis on the delivery suite 1 day after birth. Antibiotics and a fluid bolus have been given. How often does NICE NG255 recommend monitoring her?
o: Every 2 hours until her lactate is normal
Hourly for the first 4 hours, then 4-hourly
Every 4 hours with a full set of observations
Continuously, or at least every 30 minutes
8.w: NICE NG255 1.7.7: monitor people with suspected sepsis who meet any high-risk criteria continuously, or a minimum of once every 30 minutes depending on setting, using a physiological track and trigger system, and monitor mental state (1.7.8).

n.0: 2-hourly observations are less frequent than recommended.
n.1: Hourly observations are less frequent than the 30-minute minimum.
n.2: 4-hourly observations are far too infrequent for high-risk sepsis.

8.q: Hodan, 26, is booking at 10 weeks in her first pregnancy. During the history she tells the midwife she had type 3 FGM (infibulation) as a child in Somalia. She has no daughters. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Document the FGM type, refer to the specialist FGM service and plan care with her
Report the FGM to the police under the mandatory reporting duty
Advise her that a planned caesarean birth will be needed because of the FGM
Record it in her notes and plan no further action as she is an adult
8.w: Assess and discuss FGM sensitively at booking and act in line with government safeguarding guidance (NICE NG201 1.2.6): record the type, refer for specialist assessment (including possible deinfibulation), and complete a safeguarding risk assessment for any future daughter. NG235 1.9.20 explains labour risks and possible deinfibulation, so vaginal birth remains possible.

n.1: The mandatory police reporting duty (FGM Act 2003 s5B) applies to FGM in girls under 18, not to an adult woman.
n.2: Infibulation is managed with deinfibulation antenatally or in labour; it does not of itself mean a caesarean is required.
n.3: Recording alone misses specialist referral, birth planning and the safeguarding assessment for her unborn baby if a girl.

8.q: A new midwife-led postnatal drop-in clinic opened 3 months ago. Joanne, the team leader, plans to give a short questionnaire to women attending, asking how satisfied they are and what could be better. No external standard exists for the clinic. What type of project is this?
o: Research
Service evaluation
Health surveillance
Clinical audit
8.w: Service evaluation is designed to judge current care, asking 'What standard does this service achieve?', usually by asking those receiving the service, without reference to a set standard (HRA defining research table). It does not require NHS REC review.

n.0: Joanne is not testing a hypothesis or aiming for generalisable knowledge; she is judging a local service.
n.2: Health surveillance monitors threats to population health, not satisfaction with a local clinic.
n.3: Audit measures practice against a predetermined standard, and the stem states no such standard exists for the clinic.

8.q: Saffron, 26, has a cord prolapse at a freestanding midwifery unit 40 minutes from the obstetric unit. The midwife has been elevating the presenting part manually. How can elevation be maintained during the long transfer?
o: Ask Saffron to push with each contraction to speed the birth
Give Entonox so that the contractions become weaker
Fill her bladder through a urinary catheter
Replace the cord inside the vagina above the presenting part
8.w: RCOG GTG 50: compression can be prevented by elevating the presenting part manually or by filling the urinary bladder via a catheter (community midwives should carry a Foley catheter), which is useful when transfer will take time.

n.0: Pushing before full dilatation increases cord compression.
n.1: Entonox is analgesia and does not reduce contractions or relieve cord compression.
n.3: Manual replacement of the cord is not recommended.

8.q: Amal, 25, is in early established labour with her first baby. She has type 3 FGM (infibulation) and no deinfibulation was performed antenatally. Which information should the midwife give her?
o: A caesarean birth is needed because vaginal birth is unsafe with infibulation
Reinfibulation will be offered after the birth if she requests it
Infibulation does not affect labour, so no special plan is needed
Examinations may be difficult and deinfibulation may be needed in labour
8.w: NICE NG235 1.9.20: inform women with infibulated FGM of the risks of difficulty with vaginal examination, catheterisation and fetal scalp electrode application, and of delay in the second stage and spontaneous laceration, with the possible need for deinfibulation in labour.

n.0: Infibulation is managed with deinfibulation; it is not of itself an indication for caesarean birth.
n.1: Reinfibulation after birth counts as FGM, so it is unlawful (Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland; the 2005 Act in Scotland) and must not be offered.
n.2: Infibulation affects examinations and the second stage, so a plan is needed.

8.q: Mariam, 31, is breastfeeding on the first day after birth. She is worried because she can only express a few drops of thick yellow milk and thinks her baby is not getting enough. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Colostrum is low in antibodies, which rise once her mature milk arrives
Colostrum comes in small amounts, is rich in antibodies and suits a newborn's needs
Colostrum is too concentrated for a newborn and should be expressed and discarded
Colostrum is mainly water, so formula top-ups are needed until her milk comes in
8.w: Colostrum is produced in small volumes in the first days, is concentrated and rich in immunoglobulins (especially secretory IgA) and protective factors, and meets the needs of a healthy term newborn. NG194 1.5.12 asks midwives to explain how much milk is produced in the early stages.

n.0: Colostrum has the highest concentration of antibodies of any milk.
n.2: Colostrum should be given to the baby, not discarded.
n.3: Colostrum is nutrient-dense, not mainly water; routine formula top-ups are not clinically indicated (NG194 1.5.12).

9.q: A local authority asks the maternity service how it can raise breastfeeding rates among young mothers in a deprived area. Which intervention is most likely to help?
o: Community peer support linked with skilled midwifery feeding help
Posters in GP surgeries showing the benefits of breastfeeding
Free formula vouchers for mothers who stop breastfeeding
Leaflets about breastfeeding benefits given at booking
9.w: SPM 3.6 asks midwives to protect, promote and enable breastfeeding with the woman and family. Face-to-face support, including peer support, combined with skilled professional help improves breastfeeding duration (NG194 1.5 on breastfeeding support; Baby Friendly).

n.1: Posters raise awareness but do not give the practical support young mothers need.
n.2: This would promote breastmilk substitutes and is contrary to the WHO Code.
n.3: Leaflets alone rarely change behaviour or address practical barriers.

9.q: Kirsty, 32, asks why she needs an anti-D injection at 28 weeks when she feels well and has had no bleeding. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It reduces her risk of bleeding heavily at the birth
It is a vaccine that protects her baby from jaundice after birth
It stops her forming antibodies that could harm a future RhD-positive baby
It treats anaemia caused by her baby's blood entering her circulation
9.w: Small, unnoticed fetomaternal haemorrhages can expose an RhD-negative woman to RhD-positive fetal cells. Anti-D prophylaxis prevents her immune system forming anti-D antibodies, which could cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in this or a future pregnancy (NICE TA156; SPM 3.20).

n.0: Anti-D has no effect on postpartum haemorrhage risk.
n.1: Anti-D is an immunoglobulin given to the mother, not a vaccine for the baby.
n.3: Anti-D does not treat maternal anaemia; it prevents sensitisation.

9.q: A midwife is preparing a teaching session on the NHS England three-year delivery plan for maternity and neonatal services (2023). Which theme is part of the plan?
o: Reaching a national target for continuity of carer by March 2024
Moving all births into obstetric units for safety
Reducing caesarean birth rates to a fixed national target
Developing and sustaining a culture of safety, learning and support
9.w: The three-year delivery plan (30 March 2023) has four themes: listening to and working with women and families with compassion; growing, retaining and supporting the workforce; developing and sustaining a culture of safety, learning and support; and standards and structures that underpin safer, more personalised and more equitable care.

n.0: NHS England removed the national target date for continuity of carer in September 2022.
n.1: The plan supports personalised choice of place of birth, including midwifery-led settings.
n.2: The plan does not set a fixed national caesarean rate target.

9.q: Mariam, 31, is breastfeeding on the first day after birth. She is worried because she can only express a few drops of thick yellow milk and thinks her baby is not getting enough. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Colostrum is low in antibodies, which rise once her mature milk arrives
Colostrum comes in small amounts, is rich in antibodies and suits a newborn's needs
Colostrum is too concentrated for a newborn and should be expressed and discarded
Colostrum is mainly water, so formula top-ups are needed until her milk comes in
9.w: Colostrum is produced in small volumes in the first days, is concentrated and rich in immunoglobulins (especially secretory IgA) and protective factors, and meets the needs of a healthy term newborn. NG194 1.5.12 asks midwives to explain how much milk is produced in the early stages.

n.0: Colostrum has the highest concentration of antibodies of any milk.
n.2: Colostrum should be given to the baby, not discarded.
n.3: Colostrum is nutrient-dense, not mainly water; routine formula top-ups are not clinically indicated (NG194 1.5.12).

9.q: Gabby, 26, is on day 3 after a vaginal birth. She had pre-eclampsia but did not need antihypertensive treatment. Today her blood pressure is 152/102 mmHg and she has no headache or epigastric pain. What should the midwife do?
o: Recheck the blood pressure on day 5 as planned
Advise rest and recheck the blood pressure in a week
Reassure her that blood pressure peaks and settles by itself
Seek medical review to start antihypertensive treatment
9.w: NICE NG133 1.5.14: in women with pre-eclampsia who did not take antihypertensives, start treatment if blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg or higher. Ask about severe headache and epigastric pain at each measurement (1.5.15). Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia can occur after birth (SPM 4.8).

n.0: A reading of 152/102 meets the treatment threshold now; waiting is not appropriate.
n.1: Rest without treatment ignores the 150/100 threshold.
n.2: This reading meets the threshold for treatment and needs review.

9.q: Lauren, 28, is 30 weeks pregnant. She has a burning feeling behind her breastbone after large meals and when lying down at night. BP is 112/70 mmHg, urinalysis shows no protein, and she has no headache or visual symptoms. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Refer her to the day assessment unit to exclude pre-eclampsia
Ask her GP to arrange an urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Give lifestyle and diet advice and consider an antacid or alginate
Advise her to stop eating after 4 pm until the baby is born
9.w: This is typical heartburn with normal BP and urine. NICE NG201 1.4.8 and 1.4.9: give lifestyle and dietary advice and consider a trial of an antacid or alginate.

n.0: Her BP and urine are normal and the pain is typical reflux, so urgent pre-eclampsia assessment is not needed on these facts.
n.1: Endoscopy is not indicated for typical pregnancy heartburn without red flags.
n.3: Fasting from mid-afternoon is not recommended; smaller meals and not eating close to bedtime are the usual advice.

9.q: Hope, 30, is 5 days postnatal and has been admitted to the gynaecology ward with suspected puerperal sepsis. Her baby is at home with her partner and is breastfeeding by expressed milk. What should the midwife arrange for the baby?
o: An assessment of the baby for signs of infection
Antibiotics for the baby to start at once as a precaution
Formula feeds until Hope's blood cultures are negative
A routine check at the baby's 6 to 8 week examination
9.w: NICE NG194 1.2.8: if sepsis is suspected in the woman, assess the baby for infection. Group A streptococcus and other organisms can spread between mother and baby (SPM 4.8 first-line management, including the newborn).

n.1: Antibiotics are a decision after assessment of the baby, not an automatic step.
n.2: Expressed breast milk need not be stopped; the baby needs assessment.
n.3: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks misses early infection in the baby.

9.q: Twins Ella and Isla were born at 37 weeks. At 10 hours old, Ella develops signs of shock and is started on antibiotics for suspected sepsis. Isla is feeding well and her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate plan for Isla?
o: Take investigations and start antibiotics without waiting for results
Continue routine postnatal care because she has no clinical signs
Monitor her observations every 4 hours for 12 hours before deciding
Wait for Ella's blood culture result before deciding about Isla
9.w: Suspected or confirmed infection in another baby of a multiple pregnancy is a red flag risk factor (NG195 box 1). Any red flag means investigations then antibiotics without waiting for results (NG195 1.10.3), given within 1 hour of the decision to treat (1.15.2).

n.1: A red flag risk factor applies even when the baby looks well.
n.2: Observation alone is for babies without red flags and with only 1 risk factor or indicator.
n.3: Waiting for the sibling's culture delays treatment of a baby with a red flag.

9.q: Chen, 31, has been prescribed 10 days of low molecular weight heparin after her caesarean birth. She is breastfeeding and asks the midwife whether the injections will affect her baby. Which response is accurate?
o: She should express and discard milk for 4 hours after each dose
She should give formula until the 10-day course is finished
LMWH is considered safe to use while breastfeeding
A direct oral anticoagulant tablet is preferred while breastfeeding
9.w: RCOG GTG 37a: LMWH is safe in breastfeeding (warfarin is also safe). Use of direct oral anticoagulants (NOACs) is not recommended in women who are breastfeeding.

n.0: There is no need to discard milk; LMWH is safe in breastfeeding.
n.1: Interrupting breastfeeding is unnecessary and could undermine her milk supply.
n.3: GTG 37a advises that NOACs are not recommended in breastfeeding women.

9.q: Ruth, 29, is in her first labour. A student midwife notes that the upper part of the uterus feels thicker after each contraction, while the lower part is thin. Which process explains this?
o: Polarity: the lower segment contracts more strongly than the upper
Retraction: upper segment fibres stay shorter after each contraction
Hypertonus: the uterus fails to relax between contractions
Effacement: the upper segment is taken up into the cervix
9.w: Retraction is the progressive, permanent shortening of the muscle fibres of the active upper uterine segment after each contraction. The upper segment thickens and draws up the passive lower segment and cervix, causing effacement and dilatation (SPM 3.12.2).

n.0: Polarity describes the upper segment contracting strongly while the lower segment relaxes; it is not the lower segment contracting more.
n.2: Hypertonus is a contraction lasting 2 minutes or more, an abnormal finding (NICE NG229), not the normal thickening of the upper segment.
n.3: Effacement is the cervix being taken up into the lower segment, not the upper segment entering the cervix.

9.q: Nadia, a practice supervisor, has noticed that a student midwife has arrived late on four shifts and has twice given women advice that conflicts with unit guidelines, despite feedback. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Wait to see whether things improve before the final assessment
Discuss the student's performance with the other students on placement
Document the concerns and raise them with the practice and academic assessors
Tell the student she can no longer attend the placement area
9.w: SSSA 4.4: practice supervisors are expected to raise and respond to student conduct and competence concerns, and 4.3 lets them share observations with practice and academic assessors. Concerns persisting after feedback, including unsafe advice, should be documented and raised promptly.

n.0: Waiting allows unsafe advice to continue and delays support for the student.
n.1: Discussing a student's performance with peers breaches confidentiality and is unprofessional.
n.3: Removing a student from placement is not a practice supervisor's decision; it goes through the assessors and university process.

9.q: Holly, a newly qualified midwife, is uneasy because the registrar is about to attempt a rotational instrumental birth without the consultant present, which local policy says requires consultant agreement. Which statement by Holly is most appropriate?
o: "I'm concerned our policy needs consultant agreement. Can we call them first?"
"I'll fill in an incident form afterwards if anything goes wrong for her."
"I'm not happy, but I don't want to hold things up, so carry on."
"You're the doctor, so I'll go along with whatever you decide is best here."
9.w: Speaking up clearly, naming the concern and the policy, and proposing a safe action is the core of graded assertiveness and challenging a steep hierarchy (SPM 5.6, 5.13.2; Code 16.1).

n.1: Reporting after the event does not prevent the risk; concerns should be raised at the time.
n.2: Voicing unease but then letting things proceed does not protect the woman.
n.3: Deferring to hierarchy despite a safety concern breaches the duty to raise concerns.

9.q: Freya, 31, is 35 weeks pregnant. Her scan shows an estimated fetal weight on the 6th centile with normal Doppler and steady growth velocity. She has no other risk factors. She asks when her baby should be born. Which response reflects Saving Babies' Lives v3?
o: Birth should be considered at 39+0 weeks and achieved by 39+6
Birth should be planned at 41 weeks if growth continues
Birth should be initiated at 37+0 weeks and by 37+6
Birth should be planned at 34 weeks after a course of steroids
9.w: SBL v3 2.19: for an EFW between the 3rd and under the 10th centile, delivery should be considered at 39+0 weeks and achieved by 39+6 weeks; other risk factors are needed to recommend birth before 39 weeks.

n.1: Continuing past 39+6 weeks with an SGA fetus is not advised by SBL v3.
n.2: 37+0 to 37+6 weeks applies to EFW below the 3rd centile (SBL v3 2.18).
n.3: She is already 35 weeks with normal Doppler; there is no indication for preterm birth.

9.q: Parents choose oral vitamin K for their baby, who is being exclusively breastfed. The unit uses Konakion MM Paediatric. Which regimen should the midwife explain, following the BNFC and manufacturer's directions?
o: 2 mg at birth and 2 mg at 4 to 7 days, with no later dose
2 mg at birth, 2 mg at 4 to 7 days and 2 mg at 1 month
A single oral dose of 1 mg given at birth
2 mg each week for the first 12 weeks of life
9.w: BNF for Children (Konakion MM Paediatric by mouth): 2 mg at birth, then 2 mg at 4 to 7 days; exclusively breastfed babies need a further 2 mg at 1 month. NICE NG235 1.11.13: oral vitamin K may need multiple doses, including after discharge, per the manufacturer's instructions.

n.0: Two doses suit babies who are not exclusively breastfed; exclusively breastfed babies need a third dose at 1 month.
n.2: A single 1 mg oral dose at birth does not protect against late vitamin K deficiency bleeding with this product.
n.3: Weekly dosing for 12 weeks is not the Konakion MM Paediatric regimen.

9.q: Esther, 26, is 37 weeks pregnant and has a cardiac arrest in the antenatal clinic within the hospital. The midwife makes the emergency call. Which teams should be summoned?
o: Obstetric and anaesthetic teams, with no need for neonatal staff
The cardiac arrest team, with obstetrics informed afterwards
Cardiac arrest, obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams
The midwife coordinator, who will decide which teams to call
9.w: Maternal arrest needs the cardiac arrest team plus obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams, because a resuscitative hysterotomy may be needed as soon as possible and the baby will need resuscitation (RCUK 2025 special circumstances: pregnancy).

n.0: A baby born by resuscitative hysterotomy needs the neonatal team.
n.1: Obstetric staff are needed at once to prepare for resuscitative hysterotomy.
n.3: Delegating the call to the coordinator delays the multidisciplinary response.

9.q: Lauren, 28, is 24 weeks pregnant and has no children. She discloses that her partner is controlling and has pushed her. She does not want any referral. She has capacity and there is no immediate danger. What should the midwife do first?
o: Complete a risk assessment and offer specialist support
Close the conversation, as she has declined referral
Refer her to the police without her agreement
Tell her partner the midwife is aware of the abuse
9.w: NICE NG201 recommends asking about domestic abuse when the woman is alone. A structured risk assessment (for example DASH) guides action: high risk may justify sharing without consent (for example a MARAC referral), while lower risk means offering specialist support and respecting her decision. The unborn baby is also considered in safeguarding.

n.1: Ending the discussion misses the risk assessment and support she needs.
n.2: Sharing without consent depends on assessed risk, which has not yet been done.
n.3: Telling the partner could put Lauren in danger.

9.q: A labour ward midwife notices that the nitrous oxide and oxygen (Entonox) supply in empty rooms is often left connected and that a regulator has a faint hiss. In the context of sustainable healthcare, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the hiss in the ward diary for the next equipment check
Report the leak, and turn off supplies in rooms not in use
Leave the supply connected so it is ready for the next woman
Advise women to use pethidine instead of Entonox to reduce emissions
9.w: Nitrous oxide is a potent greenhouse gas and much is lost through leaks in piped systems. Reporting leaks and avoiding waste reduces environmental harm without restricting women's choice of analgesia (SPM 5.10, 5.13.3).

n.0: Waiting for a routine check leaves a known leak releasing gas.
n.2: Leaving supplies connected in empty rooms increases waste and does not deal with the leak.
n.3: Women's choice of pain relief should not be restricted; the aim is to cut waste, not to deny Entonox.

9.q: Ifeoma, a midwife, is a passenger on a long-haul flight when the crew ask for help: a woman is in labour at about 38 weeks. Ifeoma is off duty and has no equipment of her own. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Wait until the crew confirm no doctor is on board before helping
Offer help within her competence and support the crew's emergency plans
Offer advice but avoid physical contact as she is outside the UK
Stay seated as her employer's indemnity does not cover care on the flight
9.w: NMC Code 15: always offer help if an emergency arises in your practice setting or anywhere else, acting within the limits of your knowledge and competence (15.1) and arranging for emergency care to be accessed promptly (15.2), taking account of safety (15.3).

n.0: Delaying help while waiting for a doctor wastes time; a midwife is competent to attend a normal birth and should offer help now.
n.2: Code 15 applies anywhere, and a midwife attending a birth in an emergency may give the hands-on care that is needed.
n.3: Indemnity concerns do not remove the professional expectation in Code 15 to offer help in an emergency anywhere.

9.q: Ana is a newly qualified midwife in her second week of preceptorship. The coordinator allocates her a woman with severe pre-eclampsia on a magnesium sulfate infusion and no experienced midwife is assigned to support her. What is the most appropriate response from Ana?
o: Explain her experience to the coordinator and ask for support or reallocation
Accept the allocation and ask the obstetric registrar to check on her hourly
Accept the allocation and look up the magnesium protocol as she goes
Refuse to work the shift until a different allocation is offered
9.w: Skill mix should match the acuity of the women. Code 13 (recognise and work within the limits of competence) and 16.2 (raise concerns if asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training) apply. Ockenden supports protected preceptorship for newly qualified midwives.

n.1: Medical checks do not replace experienced midwifery oversight of a high-acuity woman.
n.2: Learning a high-risk protocol while providing care without support puts the woman at risk.
n.3: Refusing to work at all abandons her duty of care; the right step is to raise the concern and seek support.

9.q: While reviewing her handwritten antenatal entry, a midwife notices she recorded the symphysis fundal height as 32 cm instead of 28 cm. What is the correct way to amend the paper record?
o: Draw one line through it, then sign, date and time it
Cover the error with correction fluid and write 28 cm over it
Score through the figure until it is unreadable and write 28 cm
Tear out the page and rewrite the entry in full
9.w: Records must be accurate without falsification (Code 10.3) and attributable, dated and timed (10.4). A single line keeps the original readable, and the signed, dated correction shows who changed it and when.

n.1: Correction fluid hides the original entry, which looks like falsification.
n.2: Making the original unreadable removes the audit trail of what was first recorded.
n.3: Removing a page destroys part of the record and is falsification.

9.q: Ellie, a third-year student midwife, is caring for Fatima, 27, in established labour. Fatima requests pethidine, which the registered midwife will give under the midwives exemptions. Ellie asks whether she can draw up and administer the injection herself under direct supervision. What is the correct response?
o: Yes, once she has been signed off as competent by a practice assessor
No, pethidine must be prescribed and given by a doctor in labour
No, students may not give pethidine under the midwives exemptions
Yes, if the registered midwife directly supervises the injection
9.w: Schedule 17 allows student midwives to administer listed parenteral medicines under the direct supervision of a registered midwife, but this expressly excludes diamorphine, morphine and pethidine (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 1.2 act within the law; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Practice assessor sign-off does not change the legal exclusion of pethidine for student midwives.
n.1: Registered midwives can administer pethidine under the exemptions without a doctor's prescription.
n.3: Direct supervision covers other listed medicines but the Schedule excludes pethidine for students.

9.q: Lucia, 27, lacks capacity because of a severe learning disability and is 38 weeks pregnant. The team believes a planned caesarean is in her best interests, but she objects and her family disagree. There is no emergency. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask Lucia's GP to make the decision
Wait until labour starts and decide then
Apply to the Court of Protection for a decision
Proceed with the caesarean as a best interests decision
9.w: Where serious medical treatment is proposed for a person lacking capacity and there is disagreement or objection, the Court of Protection can decide what is in her best interests (MCA 2005). Planning ahead avoids an emergency decision.

n.0: A GP has no legal power to decide for an adult who lacks capacity.
n.1: Waiting for labour turns a plannable decision into an emergency with less time to safeguard her rights.
n.3: Proceeding with major surgery against objection and family disagreement, without the court, is not appropriate when time allows an application.

9.q: A practice development team trials a new handover tool on one postnatal ward for a single week. At the end of the week they compare missed-observation rates with what they predicted, before deciding whether to adapt or spread the tool. In the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle, which stage is the comparison?
o: Do
Plan
Study
Act
9.w: In PDSA, Plan sets out the change and predictions, Do carries out the small test, Study analyses the data and compares them with the predictions, and Act decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change before the next cycle (NHS England quality improvement guidance).

n.0: Do is running the test on the ward for the week and collecting the data.
n.1: Plan is when the change is designed and predictions are made, before the test.
n.3: Act follows the comparison and is the decision to adopt, adapt or abandon.

9.q: Amaka, 30, gave birth by emergency caesarean three weeks ago. At a postnatal visit she asks the community midwife for a copy of her labour records so she can understand what happened. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her the records belong to the trust and need a solicitor's request
Explain her right to see her records and support her request
Tell her she can request the records once the postnatal period ends
Give her the original records to take home and read
9.w: Women have a legal right of access to their health records under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 (subject access request). SPM 1.24 states records should be available for review by the woman. A debrief offer may also help her understand events.

n.0: A solicitor is not needed; a woman can request her own records directly.
n.2: Her right of access is not delayed until the end of the postnatal period.
n.3: Original records stay with the trust; she is entitled to a copy, not the originals.

9.q: Mei, 29, is well and has an uncomplicated pregnancy. She asks about a birth centre in her town that is on a different site from the hospital and has no obstetricians or anaesthetists. Which setting is she describing?
o: An alongside midwifery unit
An obstetric unit
A freestanding midwifery unit
A midwife-led triage unit
9.w: NICE NG235 1.2.1 and 1.3.3 name four birth settings: home, freestanding midwifery unit (on a separate site from an obstetric unit), alongside midwifery unit (same site) and obstetric unit. A unit away from the hospital without obstetric or anaesthetic staff is freestanding (SPM 2.1).

n.0: An alongside midwifery unit is on the same site as an obstetric unit, so transfer does not need an ambulance.
n.1: An obstetric unit has obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal staff on site, which this birth centre lacks.
n.3: Triage assesses women who call or attend with concerns; it is not a place planned for giving birth.

9.q: Baby Sam was born at 38 weeks to a mother with type 1 diabetes. He is well, pink and feeding, and his 3-hour blood glucose is 2.4 mmol/L before a feed. The postnatal ward is busy and a staff member suggests taking him to the neonatal unit for convenience of monitoring. Which response is best?
o: Admit him to the neonatal unit for monitoring for 24 hours
Keep him with his mother, continuing feeds and glucose monitoring
Separate him from his mother overnight so that she can rest
Start intravenous dextrose to prevent a later fall in glucose
9.w: NG3 1.5.2: babies of women with diabetes should stay with their mothers unless complications or abnormal clinical signs require admission. A well baby with a pre-feed glucose of at least 2.0 mmol/L continues 2 to 3 hourly feeding and monitoring (NG3 1.5.9). Keeping mother and baby together supports feeding (SPM 4.10).

n.0: Admission is for clinical indications such as hypoglycaemia with abnormal signs (NG3 1.5.5), not ward workload.
n.2: Separation disrupts feeding and is not indicated for a well baby.
n.3: IV dextrose is not needed for a well baby with a pre-feed glucose above 2.0 mmol/L who is feeding.

9.q: Asha, 29, is 16 weeks pregnant. When asked, she says that during the past month she has often felt down and hopeless, but she still enjoys time with friends. She has no history of mental illness and no thoughts of self-harm. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Use the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a fuller assessment, or refer to her GP
Refer her to the crisis team for same-day mental health assessment
Repeat the same two questions at her 28-week appointment
Reassure her, as a positive answer needs both questions to be answered yes
9.w: NICE CG192 1.5.5: if a woman responds positively to either depression identification question, is at risk or there is clinical concern, consider using the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment or referring her to her GP (or a mental health professional if a severe problem is suspected).

n.1: There are no features of a severe or urgent problem, so crisis referral is not indicated on these facts.
n.2: Waiting 12 weeks delays assessment of possible depression that was identified today.
n.3: A positive answer to either question is enough to prompt further assessment.

9.q: Hannah, 32, is having a planned home birth. Her community midwife has no prescription chart or patient group directions for this birth. Which medicine can the registered midwife lawfully administer under the midwives exemptions in Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012?
o: Intramuscular oxytocin for the third stage
Intravenous tranexamic acid for heavy bleeding
Intravenous co-amoxiclav for suspected infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for a seizure
9.w: HMR 2012 Schedule 17 lists the parenteral prescription-only medicines a registered midwife may administer in professional practice, including oxytocins (natural and synthetic), ergometrine, carboprost, anti-D, phytomenadione and others (SPM 3.19 midwives exemptions).

n.1: Tranexamic acid is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.
n.2: Antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav are not on the Schedule 17 list.
n.3: Magnesium sulfate is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.

9.q: Baby Ava weighed 3,600 g at birth. On day 3 she weighs 3,240 g. What percentage of her birth weight has she lost?
9.w: Loss = 3,600 - 3,240 = 360 g. Percentage = 360 / 3,600 x 100 = 10%. Calculating weight loss accurately supports feeding assessment (SPM 1.23; NICE NG194).

n.0: 9% would be a loss of 324 g, not 360 g.
n.1: 11% would be a loss of about 396 g, not 360 g.
n.2: 36% confuses the 360 g loss with a percentage.

9.q: Laura, 33, is 39 weeks pregnant. She reports a small gush of fluid an hour ago followed by dampness, but no contractions. The midwife cannot see liquor draining on inspection and is unsure whether the membranes have ruptured. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Perform a digital vaginal examination to feel for intact membranes
Take a lower vaginal swab and measure C-reactive protein
Offer a speculum examination and avoid digital vaginal examination
Advise induction of labour as soon as possible
9.w: NICE NG235 1.7.4: if it is uncertain whether prelabour rupture of membranes has occurred, offer a speculum examination, and avoid digital vaginal examination in the absence of contractions because of the infection risk. If rupture is certain, a speculum is not needed (1.7.3).

n.0: Digital examination without contractions should be avoided as it increases infection risk.
n.1: NICE advises against lower vaginal swabs and CRP in women with PROM at term (NG235 1.7.8).
n.3: Management choices follow confirmation of rupture; induction is not advised before confirming it.

9.q: Lydia, a midwife, is writing a reflective account for revalidation about care she gave to a woman with a postpartum haemorrhage. What must she make sure of when writing it?
o: It names the colleagues involved so that the reflection is complete
It includes the woman's hospital number so the case can be checked
It is signed by the woman to confirm the account is accurate
It contains no information that could identify the woman or colleagues
9.w: NMC revalidation guidance requires reflective accounts to be anonymised, with no information that could identify any person, in line with Code 5 (respect privacy and confidentiality).

n.0: Naming colleagues identifies them and is not required.
n.1: A hospital number is identifiable and breaches confidentiality.
n.2: Reflective accounts are the midwife's own reflection; the woman does not sign them.

9.q: At the NIPE newborn examination of baby Theo, born at 40 weeks, the right testis is in the scrotum. The left testis is palpable in the groin but cannot be brought into the scrotum. There is no hypospadias. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Non-urgent review by the GP at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
Reassurance with no follow-up, as one testis is in the scrotum
Review by a senior paediatrician within 24 hours of the examination
Testicular ultrasound within 2 weeks of the examination
9.w: NIPE handbook: one or both testes palpable but not in the scrotum, without hypospadias, is screen positive on the non-urgent pathway: GP review at the 6 to 8 week NIPE infant examination. Urgent 24-hour review is for impalpable testes or hypospadias with an undescended testis.

n.1: A unilateral undescended testis is screen positive and needs follow-up.
n.2: 24-hour senior review is for bilateral or unilateral impalpable testes, or a palpable undescended testis with hypospadias.
n.3: Ultrasound within 2 weeks is not part of the NIPE testes pathway.

9.q: Ellie, 26, is having her first baby and has no risk factors. She is considering a home birth. Which information about her baby's safety is accurate according to NICE?
o: Planned home birth carries a lower risk than a midwife-led unit
Planned home birth carries a small increase in adverse outcomes for the baby
Planned home birth carries a large increase in risk and is advised against
Planned home birth carries no difference in outcome for the baby
9.w: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk nulliparous women, planning birth at home is associated with a small increase in the risk of an adverse outcome for the baby; the same recommendation says she may choose any setting and must be supported in her choice.

n.0: For nulliparous women the evidence shows a small increase at home, not a lower risk.
n.2: NG235 describes a small increase and supports her choice; it does not advise against home birth.
n.3: No difference applies to midwife-led units for nulliparous women and to home birth for multiparous women, not home birth for a first baby.

9.q: Megan, a labour ward midwife, has repeated an audit of documentation of the third stage of labour against the trust standard. Compliance was 62% last year. Since then, a new documentation sticker and teaching sessions were introduced. In which stage of the audit cycle is Megan now working?
o: Selecting the standard against which practice is measured
Collecting baseline data on current practice
Re-audit to measure whether the changes have improved practice
Comparing baseline data with the standard for the first time
9.w: The audit cycle runs: select a standard, measure current practice, compare with the standard, implement change, then re-audit to see whether practice has improved, closing the loop. Megan has already introduced changes after a baseline audit, so this is the re-audit (SPM 5.17).

n.0: The standard was already chosen before last year's audit.
n.1: Baseline data (62%) were collected last year; this is the repeat measurement.
n.3: The first comparison with the standard produced the 62% figure that led to the changes.

9.q: Bisi, 29, is 30 weeks pregnant. At a routine appointment her blood pressure is 144/94 mmHg on two readings, having been normal before. Dipstick urinalysis is negative and she feels well. The obstetric team suspects pre-eclampsia may be developing. Which test does NICE recommend to help rule it out?
o: Uterine artery Doppler assessment
A 24-hour urine collection for total protein
First morning urine sample for protein:creatinine ratio
Placental growth factor (PlGF)-based testing
9.w: NG133 1.4.4 recommends PlGF-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia in women presenting with suspected pre-eclampsia (for example, with gestational hypertension) between 20+0 and 36+6 weeks. Bisi is at 30 weeks.

n.0: Uterine artery Doppler is used at 18+0 to 23+6 weeks to assess risk of early fetal growth restriction (SBL v3 2.7), not to rule out pre-eclampsia at 30 weeks.
n.1: NG133 1.2.5 advises against routine 24-hour urine collection to quantify proteinuria.
n.2: NG133 1.2.4 says not to use the first morning void to quantify proteinuria; and the dipstick is negative, so quantification is not indicated.

9.q: Zoe, 32, is 38 weeks pregnant and in early labour. Her membranes rupture spontaneously and there is a sudden fresh vaginal bleed of about 100 mL. Within minutes the fetal heart rate falls to 80 beats/min. Zoe is well, with a normal pulse and blood pressure. What should the midwife suspect?
o: Minor placental abruption
Cervical ectropion
A show from cervical change
Ruptured vasa praevia
9.w: RCOG GTG 63: if APH is associated with rupture of the membranes, bleeding from a ruptured vasa praevia should be considered. The bleeding is fetal blood, so the fetus is rapidly compromised while the mother stays well; this needs immediate obstetric help and urgent birth.

n.0: An abruption would usually cause pain and maternal signs; rapid fetal compromise with a well mother at membrane rupture suggests vasa praevia.
n.1: An ectropion does not cause sudden fetal bradycardia at membrane rupture.
n.2: A show is blood-stained mucus, not a 100 mL bleed with fetal bradycardia.

9.q: Leah, 33, has asthma and is 35 weeks pregnant. She is admitted with a blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg and a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia. Oral labetalol has been prescribed by the junior doctor. As the midwife prepares the first dose, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Withhold it and ask the prescriber to review because of her asthma
Give the labetalol after she has used her salbutamol inhaler
Give oral methyldopa from stock instead and record the change
Give the labetalol and check her peak flow every hour afterwards
9.w: Labetalol is a beta-blocker and is unsuitable in asthma because of the risk of bronchospasm. NICE NG133 recommends labetalol first line but nifedipine for women in whom labetalol is not suitable, so the midwife withholds the dose and asks the prescriber to review (SPM 3.18 contraindications; Code 18).

n.1: Pre-treatment with salbutamol does not make a contraindicated beta-blocker safe.
n.2: A midwife cannot substitute a different antihypertensive without a prescription.
n.3: Monitoring peak flow does not remove the risk of bronchospasm from a beta-blocker in asthma.

9.q: Baby Finn's phototherapy was stopped at 08:00 after his serum bilirubin fell well below the treatment threshold. When should his serum bilirubin be checked for rebound?
o: At 10:00, 2 hours after stopping
At 08:00 two days later, 48 hours after stopping
Between 12:00 and 14:00, 4 to 6 hours after stopping
Between 20:00 and 02:00, 12 to 18 hours after stopping
9.w: NICE CG98 1.4.5, 1.4.6: stop phototherapy once serum bilirubin has fallen at least 50 micromol/L below the threshold, and check for rebound 12 to 18 hours after stopping (08:00 + 12 to 18 hours = 20:00 to 02:00).

n.0: 2 hours is too early to detect rebound.
n.1: 48 hours is later than the CG98 rebound check window.
n.2: 4 to 6 hours is the interval for repeat measurement after starting phototherapy (CG98 1.4.4).

9.q: Baby Kai is born at 32 weeks weighing 1.5 kg. The neonatal team prescribe intramuscular phytomenadione at 400 micrograms/kg (maximum 1 mg). What dose should be given?
o: 1 mg intramuscularly
600 micrograms intramuscularly
1.5 mg intramuscularly
400 micrograms intramuscularly
9.w: BNF for Children: preterm neonate IM prophylaxis 400 micrograms/kg (max 1 mg per dose) at birth. 400 micrograms x 1.5 kg = 600 micrograms, which is below the 1 mg maximum.

n.0: 1 mg is the term dose and the preterm maximum; Kai's weight-based dose is lower.
n.2: 1.5 mg is 1 mg/kg and also exceeds the 1 mg maximum.
n.3: 400 micrograms ignores his weight; the dose is per kilogram.

9.q: Lin, 33, is hepatitis B positive. Her baby has just been born at term and is well. When should the baby receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine?
o: Within 7 days of birth
Within 24 hours of birth
After the newborn blood spot test on day 5
At 8 weeks with the routine vaccines
9.w: Green Book ch 18: babies born to hepatitis B positive mothers should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, within 24 hours (with hepatitis B immunoglobulin if indicated), then further doses.

n.0: The first dose should be given as soon as possible and within 24 hours.
n.2: Waiting until day 5 delays protection and is not linked to blood spot screening.
n.3: Babies of hepatitis B positive mothers need a dose at birth; 8 weeks is too late to prevent transmission.

9.q: Laila, 36, chose NIPT after a higher-chance combined test. The NIPT result shows a high chance of Down's syndrome. She asks whether this means the diagnosis is certain. What is the most accurate response?
o: NIPT is diagnostic for Down's but not for Edwards' or Patau's syndromes
NIPT is diagnostic, so the result is certain and no more tests are needed
A repeat NIPT will confirm the result without any miscarriage risk
NIPT is a screening test; a diagnosis needs CVS or amniocentesis
9.w: NIPT analyses cell-free DNA mostly from the placenta and is highly accurate, but it remains a screening test. A diagnosis needs an invasive diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis), which she can choose or decline (NHS FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.0: NIPT is a screening test for all three conditions; none is diagnosed by it.
n.1: NIPT is not diagnostic; false positives occur, for example from placental mosaicism.
n.2: Repeating a screening test does not provide a diagnosis; confirmation needs a diagnostic test.

9.q: Faye, 30, gave birth at term 34 hours after her membranes ruptured; labour began 28 hours after rupture. She had no signs of infection and her baby is well at birth. What care does NICE recommend for the baby?
o: Observation at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours, with no routine antibiotics
Admission to the neonatal unit for observation for 24 hours
Blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics for 48 hours
Routine postnatal care, as the baby is well at birth
9.w: NICE NG235 1.11.31 and 1.11.32: closely observe a baby born to a woman with PROM more than 24 hours before established labour at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours (temperature, heart rate, breathing, colour, perfusion, tone, feeding). If there are no signs of infection, do not give antibiotics to the woman or baby.

n.1: Observation can take place in any setting with the woman; neonatal unit admission is not needed for a well baby.
n.2: Antibiotics and cultures are not given to an asymptomatic baby when there are no signs of infection (1.11.32, 1.11.35).
n.3: Routine care alone misses the recommended observations during the first 12 hours, when infection risk is greatest.

9.q: While suturing a perineal tear, a midwife sustains a needlestick injury from a used needle. What should she do first?
o: Suck the wound, apply a plaster and report it at the end of the shift
Finish the repair, then report it to the ward manager the next week
Scrub the wound with an alcohol rub and report it the next day
Let it bleed, wash with soap and running water, then report urgently
9.w: Sharps injury first aid: allow the area to bleed (do not squeeze), wash with soap and running water, do not suck or scrub, cover, then report immediately to occupational health or the emergency department for risk assessment and possible post-exposure prophylaxis (Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013).

n.0: Sucking is unsafe and delayed reporting may miss the window for post-exposure prophylaxis.
n.1: Reporting must be immediate so the source can be tested and treatment started if needed.
n.2: Scrubbing damages tissue, and delay may miss the time-critical window for post-exposure treatment.

9.q: Baby Zara's newborn hearing screen did not show a clear response in one ear, and she has been referred to audiology. Her mother is distressed and asks what this means. What is the most appropriate explanation?
o: It does not mean she has hearing loss; audiology within 4 weeks
The screen will be repeated at her 1-year health review
It confirms permanent hearing loss, so hearing aids will be fitted
Audiology will see her at 6 months if parents notice problems
9.w: Newborn hearing screening: no clear response can be due to fluid or debris in the ear, an unsettled baby or background noise, and does not mean the baby has hearing loss. Babies referred should have an audiology appointment within 4 weeks (Screening tests for you and your baby).

n.1: A referred baby needs audiology within 4 weeks, not a repeat screen at 1 year.
n.2: A screening result does not diagnose hearing loss; audiology assessment is needed.
n.3: Audiology follow-up is arranged now, not left to parental concern.

9.q: After a baby sustains a brachial plexus injury, the midwife who was present wants to apologise to the parents but worries that saying sorry will be treated as admitting negligence. Which statement is accurate?
o: An apology is an admission of liability, so legal advice comes first
An apology may be given once the trust's investigation has ended
An apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence
An apology should come from the consultant rather than the midwife
9.w: Compensation Act 2006 s2: an apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty. Code 14.2 requires explaining fully and promptly and apologising.

n.0: An apology does not by itself admit liability (Compensation Act 2006 s2), so it should not be delayed for legal advice.
n.1: Code 14.2 requires a prompt apology; it should not wait for the investigation's outcome.
n.3: Every professional has the duty of candour under Code 14; the midwife may apologise herself.

9.q: Sara, 31, has diabetes and a scan suggests a large baby. Her obstetrician did not mention shoulder dystocia because the risk 'is only a few per cent'. Under Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015], which test decides whether a risk is material and must be disclosed?
o: Whether a responsible body of doctors would disclose the risk
Whether a reasonable person in her position would think it significant
Whether the clinician thinks the risk is relevant to the decision
Whether the risk is above a fixed percentage such as 1%
9.w: Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11 para 87: a risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or the clinician knows or should know that this particular patient would.

n.0: A responsible body of medical opinion is the Bolam test, which Montgomery replaced for disclosure of risk.
n.2: The test looks at the patient's perspective, not what the clinician alone thinks is relevant.
n.3: Materiality does not depend on a percentage threshold; a rare but serious risk can be material.

9.q: Mariam, 28, speaks limited English and attends her booking appointment with her husband, who offers to interpret. What should the midwife do?
o: Use a translation app on the midwife's phone throughout
Accept the husband as interpreter because Mariam agrees
Arrange a professional interpreter for the appointment
Give written English leaflets and rebook with her husband
9.w: NG201 advises using independent interpreters rather than family members or friends, so the woman can share information confidentially, including about domestic abuse, and make informed choices (NG201 schedule; SPM 2.8).

n.0: Informal apps are not reliable for clinical information or consent and are not a substitute for an interpreter.
n.1: Family members should not interpret; they may filter information and Mariam cannot be asked about abuse privately.
n.3: Leaflets she cannot read do not support informed choice, and rebooking delays care.

9.q: Ellen, a registered midwife, has supervised a student midwife on four shifts this week but is not her practice assessor. Before the student moves to another area, what is Ellen's responsibility regarding documentation?
o: Leave documentation to the academic assessor at the next tripartite meeting
Record her observations of the student in the assessment document
Give verbal feedback, as written records are for the practice assessor
Sign off the proficiencies she has seen the student achieve this week
9.w: SSSA 4.1: practice supervisors contribute to the student's record of achievement by periodically recording relevant observations on conduct, proficiency and achievement. SPM 5.21 includes evaluating and documenting student performance. Confirming proficiency is the practice assessor's role (7.1).

n.0: The academic assessor relies on practice records; Ellen's observations need recording now.
n.2: Verbal feedback is valuable, but supervisors are also expected to record observations (4.1).
n.3: Signing off proficiencies is the practice assessor's assessment role (7.1), not the supervisor's.

9.q: On day 15 the community midwife completes postnatal care for Erin, 33, and her baby. Which information about ongoing care is most accurate to give Erin?
o: Her midwife will return at 6 weeks for a final postnatal check
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 6 to 8 weeks
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 2 weeks
Her health visitor will complete her own postnatal check at 6 to 8 weeks
9.w: NG194 1.2.7: the woman should have a GP review of her health 6 to 8 weeks after birth. On completing midwifery care the midwife transfers care to the health visitor and GP (SPM 2.11).

n.0: Midwifery care has ended at transfer; the midwife does not routinely return at 6 weeks.
n.2: 2 weeks is not the routine maternal check; the GP check is at 6 to 8 weeks (NG194 1.2.7).
n.3: The maternal 6 to 8 week check is by the GP; health visitors follow the Healthy Child Programme.

9.q: Ffion, a midwife, is in the 13th hour of a shift. She is reviewing a complex CTG and notices she is struggling to concentrate. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Document that she was tired and continue her own review
Make a decision now and review the CTG again later in the shift
Ask a colleague to review the CTG with fresh eyes now
Have a coffee and complete the review after a short break
9.w: Code 13.3 and 16.3: ask for help and tell someone if problems may stop you working safely. A fresh-eyes review by another clinician is part of systematic CTG review (NICE NG229 1.3.6; Saving Babies' Lives v3 element 4), and recognising fatigue is part of SPM 1.18.

n.0: Recording tiredness does not make her interpretation safe; another clinician should review it.
n.1: A decision made while struggling to concentrate risks an unsafe interpretation of a complex CTG.
n.3: Delaying the review of a complex CTG for a break could delay action the baby needs.

9.q: Grace, 34, smokes and had a previous baby below the 3rd centile. She has been placed on serial ultrasound surveillance for fetal growth starting at 28 weeks. At her 30-week community appointment, what should the midwife do about fundal height measurement?
o: Measure fundal height and refer for a scan if it falls below the 50th centile
Stop measuring fundal height, as serial scans have replaced it
Measure and plot fundal height at each visit alongside the scans
Measure fundal height weekly between her scan appointments
9.w: SBL v3 2.12: women on planned serial scan surveillance should stop having SFH measured once serial surveillance begins; growth is assessed by ultrasound.

n.0: SFH has been stopped for this pathway, and the 50th centile is not a referral trigger.
n.2: SBL v3 2.12 says SFH should cease once serial scan surveillance starts.
n.3: Weekly SFH is not part of any SBL v3 pathway and adds no information to serial scans.

9.q: Isla and Tom have a healthy term baby and plan to bed share. Neither smokes, drinks or takes medication. Which advice about safer bed sharing is accurate?
o: Place the baby on a soft mattress topper, lying on her side to feed
Place the baby on the sofa with a parent when very tired
