Use a firm, flat mattress with the baby face up, away from pillows
Place the baby between the parents with the duvet tucked in
9.w: NG194 1.3.14: discuss safer bed sharing: firm, flat mattress; baby lying face up; not sleeping on a sofa or chair with the baby; no pillows or duvets near the baby; no other children or pets in the bed.

n.0: Babies should sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface.
n.1: Sleeping with a baby on a sofa or chair is particularly dangerous.
n.3: Duvets and pillows near the baby, and lying between parents, increase risk.

9.q: Tara, 32, has pre-eclampsia treated with labetalol and has just given birth vaginally. She chose active management of the third stage. Which uterotonic is most appropriate?
o: Ergometrine 500 micrograms by intravenous injection
Carbetocin by slow intravenous injection
Oxytocin 10 units by intramuscular injection
Oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM
9.w: Oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease (NICE NG235 1.10.9). Oxytocin 10 units IM given after the birth of the baby, before cord clamping, is appropriate (1.10.11).

n.0: Ergometrine raises blood pressure and is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia by any route.
n.1: NICE recommends carbetocin for women having a caesarean birth (1.10.13), not after vaginal birth.
n.3: Ergometrine-containing preparations are contraindicated in pre-eclampsia because they raise blood pressure.

9.q: Gemma, 29, chose a physiological third stage at a birth centre. One hour after the birth the placenta has not delivered. Her blood loss is 250 mL and her observations are normal. What should the midwife advise?
o: Manual removal of the placenta in the birth centre
Controlled cord traction without a uterotonic
Continue to wait, as physiological third stage has no time limit
A change to active management
9.w: NICE NG235 1.10.17 and 1.10.20: advise a change from physiological to active management if there is haemorrhage or the placenta is not delivered within 1 hour of birth. A third stage over 60 minutes with physiological management is prolonged.

n.0: Manual removal needs anaesthesia and is not done in a birth centre (NG235 1.10.28).
n.1: Controlled cord traction is performed after a uterotonic and signs of separation, as part of active management.
n.2: Physiological third stage is prolonged after 60 minutes, so a change is advised.

9.q: Kirsty, 27, is 4 days after the birth of her first baby. She has been tearful and irritable since yesterday but is sleeping when the baby sleeps, enjoys caring for the baby and has no thoughts of harm. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain this is postnatal depression and ask the GP to start an antidepressant
Refer her urgently to the perinatal mental health team for assessment today
Reassure her that these feelings normally last for about 3 months after birth
Explain the baby blues usually settle within 2 weeks and when to seek help
9.w: Feeling down, anxious or irritable for a few days after the birth is very common (the baby blues) and usually goes away within 2 weeks; if it continues or worsens she should seek help (NHS postnatal depression guidance). NG194 1.2.2: assess emotional wellbeing at every contact and arrange further assessment if there are concerns.

n.0: Transient tearfulness on day 4 does not meet the picture of postnatal depression, and medication is not indicated.
n.1: Her symptoms fit the baby blues with no risk features, so urgent specialist referral is not indicated.
n.2: The baby blues usually resolve within 2 weeks; symptoms lasting months suggest depression and need assessment.

9.q: Bella, 29, is RhD negative and received routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks. At 31 weeks she trips and falls onto her abdomen. She has mild tenderness and the baby is moving. What is the most appropriate plan regarding anti-D?
o: Withhold anti-D unless she develops vaginal bleeding in the next 72 hours
Give anti-D at the birth, combined with her postnatal dose
Withhold anti-D, as her 28-week prophylaxis covers her until the birth
Arrange obstetric assessment and offer anti-D for this sensitising event
9.w: Abdominal trauma is a potentially sensitising event. Anti-D given for a sensitising event is separate from routine prophylaxis, so RAADP does not replace it. She also needs obstetric assessment after abdominal trauma because of the risk of placental abruption.

n.0: Trauma can cause fetomaternal haemorrhage without visible bleeding, so anti-D is not conditional on bleeding.
n.1: Delaying until birth leaves her unprotected after a possible fetomaternal haemorrhage now.
n.2: Routine prophylaxis does not replace the anti-D needed after a sensitising event.

9.q: Before a woman is transferred from the maternity unit to community care, which assessment of her own health does NICE specifically recommend?
o: Checking that her lochia has changed from red to brown
Measuring her haemoglobin before she leaves the unit
Measuring the volume of her first void after the birth
Checking that she has opened her bowels after the birth
9.w: NG194 1.1.10: before transfer to community care, or before the midwife leaves after a home birth, assess the woman's health and her bladder function by measuring the volume of the first void, assess the baby, and make a feeding plan including observing at least 1 effective feed.

n.0: Lochia remains red for several days; this is not a transfer criterion.
n.1: A routine haemoglobin is not required before transfer for every woman; it is taken if there are signs or risk of anaemia.
n.3: Bowel function is discussed at postnatal contacts, but NICE specifies the first void volume before transfer.

9.q: Jess, 27, is healthy and in labour with her first baby. She has chosen active management of the third stage and asks the midwife how oxytocin plus ergometrine (Syntometrine) compares with oxytocin alone. Which explanation is accurate?
o: It is equally effective but must be given intravenously after the birth
It is more effective at reducing blood loss but causes more nausea and vomiting
It is more effective at reducing blood loss and has similar side effects
It is less effective at reducing blood loss but causes fewer side effects
9.w: NICE NG235 1.10.9 explains that oxytocin plus ergometrine may be more effective than oxytocin alone at reducing the risk of postpartum haemorrhage but is more likely to cause nausea and vomiting, so an antiemetic is offered (1.10.10). It is given IM after the birth of the baby, before cord clamping.

n.0: It is given intramuscularly, and it is somewhat more effective than oxytocin alone.
n.2: Side effects are greater: nausea and vomiting are more common.
n.3: It is more effective, not less, and has more side effects.

9.q: Kiran has type 1 diabetes and has just given birth at 38 weeks. Her baby is well and is with her. According to NICE NG3, when should the baby first be fed and have a blood glucose test?
o: Feed within 30 minutes of birth; test blood glucose at 2 to 4 hours
Test cord blood glucose at birth before the first feed is given
Feed within 4 hours of birth; test blood glucose at 24 hours
Feed within 1 hour of birth; test blood glucose at 30 minutes
9.w: NICE NG3 1.5.3 and 1.5.9: women with diabetes should feed their babies as soon as possible after birth (within 30 minutes) and then every 2 to 3 hours; carry out blood glucose testing routinely at 2 to 4 hours after birth.

n.1: Routine testing is at 2 to 4 hours; cord blood glucose is not the routine NG3 test.
n.2: 4 hours is too long to wait for a feed and 24 hours too late for the first test.
n.3: NG3 advises feeding within 30 minutes, and glucose at 30 minutes is too early for the routine test.

9.q: After a maternal collapse on the labour ward, the woman survived but several staff are visibly shaken. Two days later the ward manager arranges a facilitated team session. What is the main aim of this session?
o: To support staff wellbeing and help the team process the event
To ask staff to write statements for the coroner
To replace the formal learning response with an informal one
To decide which staff members should be moved off the labour ward
9.w: Facilitated team sessions after traumatic events support staff wellbeing, help people make sense of what happened and reduce the risk of lasting psychological harm, while learning continues through formal processes (SPM 5.14, 5.15).

n.1: The woman survived; coroner statements are not relevant here.
n.2: Team support sessions do not replace formal learning responses.
n.3: Moving staff is not the aim and may feel punitive.

9.q: Ellie, 25, is visited at home 3 days after an assisted vaginal birth. She has been shivering, her lochia smells offensive and she feels unwell. Observations: heart rate 134 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, temperature 38.3 C. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat the observations in 1 hour before deciding on transfer
Take a high vaginal swab and plan review when the result is back
Arrange emergency transfer to hospital by 999 with a pre-alert
Ask the GP to prescribe oral antibiotics and review her tomorrow
9.w: NICE NG255 (2025): a recently pregnant woman with any high-risk criterion outside hospital needs emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert (1.6.1, 1.6.2). A heart rate over 130 bpm is a high-risk criterion (Table 1); assisted birth and offensive lochia add to her risk (1.2.1).

n.0: A high-risk criterion is already present, so delaying transfer for repeat observations is unsafe.
n.1: Waiting for swab results delays treatment of suspected high-risk sepsis.
n.3: Oral antibiotics in the community delay the hospital assessment and IV antibiotics within 1 hour that NG255 requires for high risk.

9.q: Dani, 22, is formula feeding her baby and has no risk factors for blood clots. She would like to use the combined pill. When can she start it?
o: 6 weeks after the birth
Immediately after the birth
3 weeks after the birth
After her first period
9.w: Women who are not breastfeeding and have no VTE risk factors can start the combined pill, ring or patch 3 weeks after the birth (NHS; FSRH). VTE risk is raised in the early postnatal period.

n.0: The 6-week wait applies to women who are breastfeeding.
n.1: Combined methods are avoided in the first 3 weeks because of the raised VTE risk after birth.
n.3: Waiting for a period risks pregnancy, as ovulation comes first.

9.q: Rosa, 31, is cared for by a continuity team. At 34 weeks she develops gestational hypertension and is referred to the antenatal clinic for obstetric review. Her named midwife is concerned about losing the relationship. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Continue as her named midwife while coordinating care with the obstetric team
Keep her care midwife-led and defer the obstetric referral to 36 weeks
Discharge her from the continuity team and book a new consultant midwife
Transfer her midwifery care to the hospital antenatal clinic midwives
9.w: SPM 2.5 requires continuity of midwifery carer for women with and without complications and additional care needs. The named midwife remains her midwife and works with the obstetric team (SPM 2.4: work across settings and with other staff to promote continuity of care and carer).

n.1: Gestational hypertension needs obstetric involvement now (NG133); delaying referral to protect continuity would be unsafe.
n.2: Discharging her ends continuity at the point she most benefits from a known carer, and a consultant midwife does not replace obstetric review.
n.3: Handing her to clinic midwives fragments care; SPM 2.5 expects continuity for women with complications as well as without.

9.q: Alice, 29, is 34 weeks pregnant and attends for the second time in 10 days with reduced fetal movements. Her computerised CTG today meets criteria and her SFH is on her usual centile. Her last scan was at 20 weeks. What should be offered?
o: A repeat computerised CTG in 1 week, without an ultrasound scan
Reassurance, as a normal CTG excludes placental insufficiency
Induction of labour now because the episode is recurrent
A scan for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler
9.w: SBL v3 element 3 checklist: offer an ultrasound scan for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler to women presenting with recurrent RFM after 28+0 weeks, unless a growth scan was done in the previous 2 weeks.

n.0: A repeat CTG alone does not assess growth or placental function, which is the concern in recurrent RFM.
n.1: A normal CTG reflects current wellbeing and does not exclude placental insufficiency or FGR.
n.2: Birth for recurrent RFM is offered after 38+6 weeks; at 34 weeks the next step is a scan.

9.q: Over three months, Chloe has repeatedly reported to her ward manager that night staffing falls below safe levels, with no response or action. What should she do next?
o: Post about the staffing on social media to raise public awareness
Escalate to a more senior manager or the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
Stop reporting, as her concerns have already been recorded
Resign from her post so that she is not accountable for the risk
9.w: If concerns are not addressed, the midwife should escalate further, for example to senior managers, the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian and, if needed, external bodies such as the CQC (NMC raising concerns guidance; Code 16.1 raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns; SPM 5.6).

n.0: Social media is not an appropriate route and may breach confidentiality and Code 20.10.
n.2: Recording a concern does not discharge the duty if the risk continues unaddressed.
n.3: Resigning does not address the risk to women and babies.

9.q: Sadia, 28, is 37+2 weeks pregnant and has pre-eclampsia with blood pressure controlled on labetalol. Her blood results are stable and the CTG is normal. According to NICE NG133, when should birth be planned?
o: Continue surveillance until spontaneous labour
Continue surveillance and plan birth at 40 weeks
Initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours
Arrange a category 1 caesarean birth today
9.w: NICE NG133 (table 3, timing of birth in pre-eclampsia): from 37 weeks onwards, initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours. Before 34 weeks surveillance continues unless there are indications, and from 34+0 to 36+6 birth is considered case by case.

n.0: Waiting for spontaneous labour does not follow the 24 to 48 hour recommendation.
n.1: Waiting until 40 weeks is not advised once pre-eclampsia is present at 37 weeks.
n.3: A category 1 caesarean is for an immediate threat to life; her condition is stable.

9.q: Nicola, 29, is 39+2 weeks pregnant. Her membranes ruptured 2 hours ago with clear liquor. She is not contracting, she feels well, her temperature is 36.8 C, the fetal heart is normal and she has no GBS history. Which options should be offered?
o: Immediate induction of labour, as expectant management is unsafe
Expectant management with intravenous antibiotics until labour starts
Expectant management for up to 24 hours or induction as soon as possible
Expectant management for up to 72 hours before induction is discussed
9.w: NICE NG235 1.7.6 and 1.7.7: offer women with PROM at or after 37+0 weeks a choice of expectant management for up to 24 hours or induction as soon as possible, discussing benefits and risks; offer induction if labour has not started after about 24 hours. About 60% go into labour within 24 hours (1.7.5).

n.0: Immediate induction is one choice; expectant management for up to 24 hours is also safe to offer without risk factors.
n.1: Antibiotics are not given without signs of infection or another indication such as GBS.
n.3: NICE offers induction at about 24 hours, not 72 hours, although she may choose to wait longer.

9.q: Nia, 26, is 10 days after a caesarean birth. She phones the community midwife reporting sudden breathlessness and sharp chest pain on breathing in. When the midwife arrives, her heart rate is 122 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% on air. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Book an urgent GP appointment for later today
Call 999 for emergency transfer to hospital
Advise rest and recheck her observations in 1 hour
Start her remaining LMWH injections and monitor
9.w: NICE NG194 1.2.4: shortness of breath or chest pain could indicate VTE or a cardiac problem. With tachycardia and low saturations this is a suspected pulmonary embolism, an emergency needing immediate transfer. Thrombosis and thromboembolism is the leading cause of maternal death up to 6 weeks (MBRRACE-UK 2022-24).

n.0: A GP appointment later in the day delays emergency care for suspected PE.
n.2: Waiting an hour with tachycardia and hypoxia is unsafe.
n.3: Prophylactic LMWH does not treat an established PE and delays transfer.

9.q: Chloe, 25, attends her booking appointment at 8 weeks. Her partner stays with her throughout and has said he will come to every appointment. The midwife has not been able to ask about domestic abuse. Which is the most appropriate plan?
o: Arrange time alone with Chloe, such as during a urine test, and ask then
Ask about domestic abuse in front of her partner so the question is covered
Leave the question until the 36-week appointment when trust is established
Record that routine enquiry was declined because her partner was present
9.w: NICE NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse at booking, or at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, and ensure there is an opportunity for a private one-to-one discussion. Midwives create that opportunity, for example by seeing the woman alone for part of the appointment.

n.1: Asking in front of a partner is unsafe and unlikely to lead to disclosure; it could increase risk if he is abusive.
n.2: Enquiry should happen at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, not deferred to late pregnancy.
n.3: Chloe has not declined; the question was never asked. Recording a refusal would be inaccurate.

9.q: Ella, 31, is 24 weeks pregnant. On the GAD-2 she says she has felt nervous and on edge 'more than half the days' and has been unable to stop worrying 'several days' over the last 2 weeks. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Consider the GAD-7 for further assessment or refer her to her GP
Reassure her, as her GAD-2 score is below the threshold for action
Ask her to keep a worry diary and review it at her next appointment
Refer her for urgent assessment by the perinatal mental health team today
9.w: GAD-2 scoring: 'more than half the days' scores 2 and 'several days' scores 1, giving 3. NICE CG192 1.5.6: if a woman scores 3 or more, consider using the GAD-7 for further assessment or referring her to her GP (or a mental health professional if a severe problem is suspected).

n.1: Her score is 3, which meets the threshold for further assessment.
n.2: A diary delays recommended assessment after a positive GAD-2 score.
n.3: Nothing suggests a severe or urgent problem, so same-day specialist assessment is not indicated.

9.q: Kemi, 31, is 29 weeks pregnant and has just been diagnosed with gestational diabetes. Her fasting plasma glucose at diagnosis was 6.3 mmol/L, and the scan shows no macrosomia or polyhydramnios. Which first-line management is most appropriate?
o: Start insulin straight away because her fasting glucose is above 6.0 mmol/L at diagnosis
Start metformin and insulin together because she was diagnosed after 28 weeks
Diet and exercise changes, adding metformin if targets are not met in 1 to 2 weeks
Start glibenclamide straight away and review her capillary glucose results in 4 weeks
9.w: With a fasting plasma glucose below 7.0 mmol/L at diagnosis, NG3 1.2.18 and 1.2.19 recommend a trial of diet and exercise first, offering metformin if targets are not met within 1 to 2 weeks. Immediate insulin is considered for 6.0 to 6.9 mmol/L when there is macrosomia or polyhydramnios, which Kemi does not have.

n.0: Immediate insulin is offered when the fasting level is 7.0 mmol/L or above, or considered at 6.0 to 6.9 mmol/L with macrosomia or polyhydramnios; neither applies.
n.1: Gestation at diagnosis does not dictate combined therapy in NG3.
n.3: Glibenclamide is not first line, and a 4-week review is too slow if targets are not being met.

9.q: A community midwife visits baby Rosa, aged 5 days, at home. According to NICE NG194, which finding is a red flag for serious illness?
o: Sleeping for 3 hours between feeds
Axillary temperature of 35.8 C
Small possets of milk after feeds
Respiratory rate of 52 breaths/min
9.w: NICE NG194 1.4.9: red flags for serious illness in young babies include a temperature of 38 C or over or under 36 C, respiratory rate over 60, grunting, chest indrawing, pallor or mottling, a weak or high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, seizures, bilious or projectile vomiting and non-blanching rash.

n.0: Sleeping 3 hours between feeds is normal for many newborns.
n.2: Small possets are common; bilious or forceful (projectile) vomiting is the red flag.
n.3: A respiratory rate of 52 is within the normal newborn range (the red flag is over 60).

9.q: Baby Noah was born after a shoulder dystocia that took 3 minutes to resolve. At the first examination, his right arm lies limp, extended and internally rotated, and he does not move it, while the left arm moves normally. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure the parents that this is normal bruising after a fast birth
Recheck the arm movements at the 6 to 8 week examination
Ask the parents to exercise the arm at each nappy change
Refer to the neonatal team for assessment of a brachial plexus injury
9.w: A limp, internally rotated arm after shoulder dystocia suggests brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy), a recognised complication (RCOG GTG 42 reports 2.3-16%). The baby needs neonatal assessment and referral (SPM 4.7 and 4.8 first-line management and referral).

n.0: This is not explained by bruising and needs assessment, not reassurance.
n.1: Delaying assessment to 6 to 8 weeks could delay specialist care.
n.2: Exercises should only follow specialist assessment and advice.

9.q: Fatima, 29, is 16 weeks pregnant and speaks little English. She attends with her husband, who offers to interpret because he speaks English well. The midwife needs to discuss screening results and ask routine questions about domestic abuse. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange a professional interpreter, not a family member, for the appointment
Use a translation app on the midwife's phone to save waiting time
Give her written leaflets in English to take home for her husband to explain
Accept her husband's offer, as he knows her history and preferences well
9.w: CG110 1.3.10: provide an interpreter who can communicate in the woman's preferred language and who should not be a family member, legal guardian or partner. CG110 1.1.14 also requires at least one one-to-one consultation without the partner present to allow sensitive issues to be raised.

n.1: An unverified app is not a safe substitute for a professional interpreter when discussing screening results and abuse.
n.2: Leaflets in English do not meet her communication needs and still rely on her husband.
n.3: Using her husband prevents safe enquiry about domestic abuse and may filter what she says or hears.

9.q: A woman died on the labour ward last month. A journalist contacts a midwife who was present, asking for details of what happened. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Give general details, as confidentiality ends at death
Give details if the woman's family agree
Give details anonymously, without naming the woman
Decline and refer the journalist to the trust
9.w: Code 5.3: the right to privacy and confidentiality continues after death. Code 21.6: cooperate with the media only when appropriate, protecting confidentiality and dignity. Media enquiries go through the trust.

n.0: Confidentiality continues after death (Code 5.3).
n.1: Even with family agreement, an individual midwife should not brief journalists; the trust manages media contact.
n.2: Details of a recent death can identify the woman even without her name.

9.q: Emily, 27, is booked for her 20-week scan. She asks the midwife whether a normal scan means her baby will definitely be healthy. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It screens for 11 specific physical conditions and cannot detect every problem
It is a diagnostic test, so any condition it does not find can be ruled out
It confirms or excludes Down's syndrome, which is the main condition it looks for
It checks for all physical and chromosomal conditions, so a normal scan is reassuring
9.w: The FASP 20-week scan (18+0 to 20+6 weeks) looks for 11 physical conditions, including spina bifida, anencephaly, cleft lip, congenital heart disease and Edwards' and Patau's syndromes. Some conditions are not detectable on scan, so a normal result cannot guarantee a healthy baby (FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.1: The anomaly scan is a screening test; a normal scan does not rule out every condition.
n.2: Down's syndrome is not one of the 11 conditions; it is screened for by the combined or quadruple test.
n.3: The scan looks for a defined list of conditions and many conditions cannot be seen on ultrasound.

9.q: Theo's mother, Ruby, 27, has a cord prolapse on the labour ward at 8 cm dilatation. A midwife is elevating the presenting part while theatre is prepared. Which position should Ruby be helped into?
o: Semi-recumbent, sitting up on the bed
Knee-chest, on her knees with her chest down
Squatting, with support from her partner
Upright, standing beside the bed
9.w: RCOG GTG 50: knee-chest position, or left lateral with head down and a pillow under the left hip, uses gravity to reduce pressure of the presenting part on the cord while birth is arranged.

n.0: Sitting up increases pressure on the cord.
n.2: Squatting brings the presenting part down onto the cord.
n.3: Standing increases pressure of the presenting part on the cord.

9.q: Danielle, 25, is in strong labour and declines an epidural, shouting that she wants to cope without one. The registrar says she cannot be making a proper decision while in so much pain. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, what is the starting point?
o: She lacks capacity as she is refusing pain relief
She lacks capacity until her pain has been controlled
She is assumed to have capacity unless shown otherwise
Her birth partner decides while she is in pain
9.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack capacity. Pain and distress do not by themselves establish incapacity; any doubt needs a decision-specific assessment.

n.0: Refusing a recommended treatment does not show a lack of capacity (s1(4)).
n.1: Pain does not remove capacity automatically; incapacity must be established, not assumed.
n.3: Nobody can decide for an adult who has capacity, including a birth partner.

9.q: The MBRRACE-UK 2022-24 maternal mortality data brief compares women living in the most and least deprived areas. What did it report?
o: Women in the most deprived areas had about twice the rate
Rates were similar across deprivation levels
Women in the most deprived areas had about five times the rate
Women in the least deprived areas had a higher rate
9.w: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: maternal mortality in the most deprived areas was about twice that in the least deprived. Midwives must understand health inequalities and their determinants (SPM 1.17.1).

n.1: The data show a clear gradient by deprivation.
n.2: The difference was about twice, not five times.
n.3: The gradient runs the other way: higher in the most deprived areas.

9.q: A midwife attends Ruth, 30, at a planned home birth. Three hours after the birth Ruth is well and has had a cup of tea, but has not yet passed urine. The baby has had one effective breastfeed and has not passed meconium. Before the midwife leaves the home, which action is the priority?
o: Wait to measure the volume of Ruth's first void after the birth
Observe a second effective feed before leaving the family
Stay until the baby has passed meconium for the first time
Complete the full newborn physical examination before leaving
9.w: NICE NG194 1.1.10 applies before the midwife leaves after a home birth: measure the volume of the first void, assess the baby, make a feeding plan including at least 1 effective feed observed, and if meconium has not been passed, advise parents to seek advice if it is not passed within 24 hours. The feed requirement is already met, so the outstanding item is the first void.

n.1: NG194 requires at least 1 effective feed to be observed, which has already happened.
n.2: The midwife advises the parents to seek help if meconium is not passed within 24 hours of birth; she does not wait for it.
n.3: The NIPE newborn examination should be completed within 72 hours, so it is not a precondition for leaving after the birth.

9.q: Ellen, a midwife, has a conscientious objection to abortion. She is the only midwife available when a woman bleeds heavily after a medical termination and needs urgent care to prevent grave injury. What must Ellen do?
o: Provide the care, as her objection does not cover this situation
Provide care once the woman confirms the termination is complete
Wait for a midwife without an objection to arrive
Refuse, as her objection covers all care related to termination
9.w: Abortion Act 1967 s4(2): conscientious objection does not affect any duty to take part in treatment necessary to save the life or prevent grave permanent injury to the pregnant woman. Code 4.4 and 15 also apply.

n.1: Making care depend on confirmation delays emergency treatment that s4(2) requires.
n.2: Waiting risks the woman's life; the s4(2) exception requires Ellen to act.
n.3: Section 4(2) keeps the duty to take part in treatment needed to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.

9.q: After a spontaneous birth, the midwife assesses Kemi's perineum with good lighting and analgesia. The tear involves the perineal muscles and about 60% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter. The internal anal sphincter and anal mucosa are intact. How is this tear classified?
o: Third degree, 3b
Fourth degree
Third degree, 3c
Third degree, 3a
9.w: NICE NG235 1.12.3: 3a is less than 50% of external anal sphincter thickness torn; 3b is more than 50% of EAS thickness torn; 3c involves the internal anal sphincter; fourth degree involves both sphincters and the anal epithelium.

n.1: A fourth-degree tear involves the anal epithelium, which is intact.
n.2: 3c requires a tear of the internal anal sphincter, which is intact.
n.3: 3a is less than 50% of the external sphincter thickness; this tear is 60%.

9.q: During an assisted breech birth, Lena's baby needs help after the umbilicus is born. When the midwife needs to hold the baby to guide the birth, how should she hold it?
o: By the neck and shoulders, extending the head backwards
By the ankles, lifting the baby high over the abdomen
By the abdomen, with thumbs on the baby's soft tissues
Around the bony pelvic girdle, avoiding soft tissues
9.w: RCOG GTG 20b: care must be taken to avoid fetal trauma; the fetus should be grasped around the pelvic girdle, not the soft tissues, and the neck should not be hyperextended.

n.0: Hyperextending the neck can cause spinal and other injury.
n.1: Lifting the baby by the ankles risks hyperextension of the neck.
n.2: Pressure on the abdomen can injure internal organs.

9.q: Baby Isla is born at 28 weeks in the delivery suite. The room is warm and the resuscitaire heater is on. How should the midwife manage her temperature immediately after birth?
o: Place her skin-to-skin and cover both with a warm towel
Put her body into a plastic bag without drying, and add a hat
Give her a warm bath to bring her temperature up quickly
Dry her thoroughly and wrap her in a dry warm towel
9.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: for babies under 32 weeks, dry the head, put on a hat and place the body in a plastic (polyethylene) bag without drying, under a radiant heater; aim to keep temperature 36.5 to 37.5 C. Babies of 32 weeks or more are dried and wet towels removed.

n.0: A 28-week baby needs a plastic bag under a radiant heater and is likely to need stabilisation.
n.2: Bathing causes heat loss and is not part of newborn resuscitation.
n.3: Drying and wrapping is for babies of 32 weeks or more.

9.q: Lily, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has no medical or social risk factors and no safeguarding concerns. She declines further antenatal care and plans to give birth at home without a midwife. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that freebirth is unlawful in the UK
Discharge her from maternity services as she has declined care
Respect her decision, keep offering contact and document discussions
Refer to children's social care because she is declining care
9.w: A woman with capacity may decline care and give birth without a professional present; it is lawful for her to do so. With no other concerns, declining care is not itself a safeguarding issue. The midwife keeps the door open, shares information and documents (SPM 1.21).

n.0: Freebirth is lawful; art 45 of the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001 restricts who may attend, not the woman's choice.
n.1: Discharging her closes the door on care she may later accept.
n.3: Declining care, with no other concerns, is not a reason for a social care referral.

9.q: Emma, 33, is 36+5 weeks pregnant. A scan has confirmed an uncomplicated singleton breech presentation. After discussion of the options she says she would prefer to have a vaginal birth with the baby head down if possible. What should be offered?
o: External cephalic version
A planned vaginal breech birth
Induction of labour at 37 weeks
A repeat scan at 40 weeks
9.w: NICE NG201 1.2.38: for an uncomplicated singleton breech confirmed after 36+0 weeks, discuss ECV, vaginal breech birth and elective caesarean, and offer ECV to women who prefer cephalic vaginal birth.

n.1: Vaginal breech birth is one option, but she wants a head-down birth, which ECV aims to achieve.
n.2: Induction is not generally recommended for a breech baby (NG207 1.2.21) and does not turn the baby.
n.3: Waiting for a repeat scan delays ECV, which is offered from 36+0 weeks when the woman wishes.

9.q: The midwife gives 5 inflation breaths to Baby Tom, born at 41 weeks, but sees no chest rise and the heart rate is not increasing. What should she do next?
o: Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath
Give ventilation breaths at 30 per minute as planned
Reposition the head and use a two-person jaw thrust, then repeat
Increase the inflation pressure to 50 cm H2O and continue
9.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if there is no chest rise, check and correct head position, consider two-person jaw thrust or a supraglottic airway, then repeat the 5 inflation breaths. Compressions are not effective until the lungs are aerated.

n.0: Compressions are not started until the lungs have been effectively aerated.
n.1: Ventilation breaths will not work until airway obstruction is corrected and chest rise is seen.
n.3: Pressure may be increased cautiously after airway manoeuvres, not jumped to 50 cm H2O first.

9.q: Ruth, 35, was discharged home on day 2 and is breastfeeding. On day 5 she tells her community midwife she has sore nipples and is thinking of stopping. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Advise her to give formula for 24 hours to let the nipples heal
Advise her to feed for 10 minutes on each breast to rest the nipples
Observe a feed, help with attachment and refer to peer support
Recommend nipple shields for each feed until the soreness settles
9.w: Sore nipples usually reflect poor attachment. NG194 1.5.14 lists assessing a feed and breast and nipple condition; professionals should support common problems (1.5.6) and work with other agencies such as peer support services to sustain breastfeeding (SPM 2.10).

n.0: Missed feeds reduce supply and may end breastfeeding, which she has not chosen.
n.1: Limiting feed length does not fix attachment and can reduce intake and supply.
n.3: Shields do not correct the usual cause, poor attachment, and can reduce milk transfer.

9.q: Priya, 28, plans to breastfeed and give one bottle of formula each evening. She asks whether her baby could be overfed with either method. Which statement is accurate?
o: A breastfed baby cannot be overfed but a formula-fed baby can, so pace bottles
Either method can lead to overfeeding, so both should be limited to set volumes
A formula-fed baby cannot be overfed, as the baby stops when the bottle is finished
A breastfed baby can be overfed if feeds last longer than 20 minutes
9.w: NICE NG194 1.5.12 and 1.5.19: it is not possible to overfeed a breastfed baby, but it is possible to overfeed a formula-fed baby, so parents should pace bottle feeds and recognise signs the baby has had enough.

n.1: Breastfed babies regulate their own intake, so set volumes for breastfeeding are not appropriate.
n.2: Encouraging a baby to finish the bottle is how formula-fed babies become overfed.
n.3: Long feeds at the breast do not cause overfeeding; NG194 states a breastfed baby cannot be overfed.

9.q: Jess, 27, smokes 15 cigarettes a day and wants to stop. Her tobacco dependence adviser suggests nicotine patches. She is worried nicotine will harm her baby. What information should the midwife give?
o: NRT risks are much lower than smoking, and patches should be removed at bedtime
NRT is safe in pregnancy and patches should be worn for 24 hours a day
NRT carries the same risks as smoking, so cutting down is safer
NRT should be avoided until 12 weeks, when varenicline is a safer choice
9.w: NG209 1.20.6-1.20.11: consider NRT with behavioural support at the earliest opportunity; explain that risks from NRT are much lower than smoking; advise removing patches before bed; do not offer varenicline, bupropion or cytisinicline in pregnancy.

n.1: NICE advises removing patches before going to bed in pregnancy (NG209 1.20.9).
n.2: Most smoking harm comes from other components of smoke, not nicotine; NRT is much safer.
n.3: Varenicline is not offered in pregnancy, and NRT should be considered at the earliest opportunity.

9.q: Martha, a midwife, holds religious views against contraception. Postnatally, Leanne, 22, asks Martha about contraception options before discharge. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Give balanced information on options or arrange a colleague to do so
Explain her views and suggest Leanne waits until her GP check
Tell Leanne that breastfeeding is reliable contraception for now
Give leaflets and avoid discussing her personal views
9.w: Code 20.7: do not express personal beliefs inappropriately; Code 4.4 on conscientious objection does not cover contraception advice. Leanne must get evidence-based information (Code 6.1), from Martha or a colleague arranged without delay.

n.1: Sharing personal beliefs and delaying advice breaches Code 20.7 and leaves Leanne without information when she wants it.
n.2: Breastfeeding protects reliably only if strict criteria (lactational amenorrhoea) are met; presenting it as reliable is inaccurate.
n.3: Handing out leaflets without discussion does not meet her request for information about options.

9.q: Amira, 30, has received intravenous antibiotics for 48 hours for suspected endometritis. She is now apyrexial and well, and her blood cultures are negative. Which action best reflects antimicrobial stewardship?
o: Stop the antibiotics herself, as the cultures are negative
Add a second antibiotic to prevent resistance developing
Ask the prescriber to review whether to stop or switch to oral
Continue intravenous antibiotics for a full 7-day course
9.w: UKHSA Start Smart then Focus: review antibiotics at 48 to 72 hours with a clear decision to stop, switch IV to oral, change, continue or move to outpatient therapy. SPM 3.10 covers antimicrobial resistance and stewardship.

n.0: Stopping is a prescribing decision; the midwife should prompt a review, not stop treatment unilaterally.
n.1: Adding antibiotics without indication increases, rather than prevents, resistance.
n.3: Continuing IV therapy without review ignores her response and culture results.

9.q: Leila, a public health midwife, wants to find out what proportion of women booked in the last 6 months were offered a carbon monoxide test at booking, and to compare this with the NICE NG209 recommendation that every woman is offered one. What type of project is this?
o: Clinical audit
Health surveillance
Research
Service evaluation
9.w: The HRA defining research table describes clinical audit as answering 'Does this service reach a predetermined, recognised or pre-established standard?' and measuring against a standard. Leila is measuring current practice against the NG209 standard (CO test offered at booking).

n.1: Health surveillance detects and manages threats to population health such as outbreaks, not compliance with a care standard.
n.2: Research aims to generate or test a hypothesis and produce generalisable new knowledge; Leila is checking local practice against an existing standard.
n.3: Service evaluation measures current service without reference to a standard ('What standard does this service achieve?'), whereas Leila has a defined standard.

9.q: Abi is caring for a woman in labour on continuous CTG monitoring. According to Saving Babies' Lives v3, how often should a separate 'fresh eyes' review of the CTG and overall wellbeing take place?
o: At least every 2 hours
When the CTG is classified as pathological
At least hourly
At least every 4 hours
9.w: SBL v3 4.3 and 4.4: a regular (at least hourly) systematic review of maternal and fetal wellbeing, with a separate fresh eyes review at least hourly when CTG is used, or at least 4-hourly with intermittent auscultation, unless triggered earlier.

n.0: Two-hourly is less often than the SBL v3 minimum for CTG.
n.1: Fresh eyes is a scheduled safeguard; waiting for a pathological trace defeats its purpose of earlier detection.
n.3: Four-hourly fresh eyes applies to intermittent auscultation, not CTG monitoring.

9.q: Bisi, 33, started a new antibiotic yesterday for mastitis. At a home visit she shows the community midwife a raised itchy rash on her arms that began this morning. The midwife arranges same-day medical review. How should the suspected adverse drug reaction be reported?
o: To the NMC as a fitness to practise concern
To the manufacturer by letter after discharge
Through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme
Once a doctor confirms the drug caused it
9.w: Suspected adverse drug reactions are reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme. Certainty is not required: a suspicion is enough, and healthcare professionals and patients can report (SPM 3.18 adverse reactions).

n.0: The NMC regulates professionals; an adverse drug reaction is not a fitness to practise matter.
n.1: The national route is the Yellow Card scheme, and reporting should not wait until discharge.
n.3: Yellow Card reports are based on suspicion; proof of causation is not needed first.

9.q: Lily, 29, is in a midwifery-led unit. Delay in the first stage was diagnosed and an amniotomy was performed 2 hours ago. On re-examination her cervix has not changed. She is well and the fetal heart is normal. What should happen next?
o: Start an oxytocin infusion in the midwifery unit
Encourage mobilisation and re-examine in 4 hours
Diagnose delay and transfer her to obstetric-led care
Perform a further vaginal examination in another 2 hours
9.w: NICE NG235 1.8.49: if there is no progress 2 hours after amniotomy, diagnose delay and transfer to obstetric-led care, where an obstetrician offers a full assessment including consideration of oxytocin (1.8.50).

n.0: Oxytocin is considered by an obstetrician after full assessment of confirmed delay (NG235 1.8.50); it is not started in a midwifery-led unit.
n.1: Waiting a further 4 hours delays obstetric assessment of confirmed delay.
n.3: No progress 2 hours after amniotomy is the point at which delay is diagnosed and transfer is made.

9.q: Aisha, 30, is 33 weeks pregnant on the low-risk pathway. Her symphysis fundal height today plots below the 10th centile on her growth chart; two weeks ago it was on the 40th centile. She reports normal fetal movements. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remeasure the fundal height at her next routine appointment
Refer her for an ultrasound assessment of fetal growth
Reassure her because the fetal movements are normal
Ask a colleague to remeasure and record the higher of the two values
9.w: A fundal height plotting below the 10th centile, or a drop across centiles, is an indication for an ultrasound growth assessment. SBL v3 2.11 requires staff measuring SFH to interpret and refer when indicated, and 2.14 sets the assessment of wellbeing once FGR is suspected.

n.0: Waiting for the next routine visit delays detection of possible FGR, a major risk factor for stillbirth.
n.2: Normal movements do not exclude growth restriction; the measurement still needs investigating.
n.3: Choosing the higher of two readings is unsafe and does not address the fall across centiles.

9.q: Becca, 31, is 39 weeks pregnant. A vaginal swab at 35 weeks found group B streptococcus. She phones to say her waters broke an hour ago and she has no contractions. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Offer expectant management for up to 24 hours at home
Offer immediate induction of labour with intrapartum antibiotics
Offer expectant management with 4-hourly temperature checks
Offer a speculum examination and review again in 12 hours
9.w: NG235 1.7.11 and NG207 1.2.16: offer immediate induction of labour (or caesarean if planned) to women with PROM at term who are known GBS positive in this pregnancy; intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is offered for known carriage.

n.0: Expectant management is for low-risk PROM; GBS carriage in this pregnancy means immediate induction is offered.
n.2: Temperature checks are part of expectant management, which is not recommended when she carries GBS.
n.3: Delaying 12 hours increases the time for ascending infection in a known GBS carrier.

9.q: Erin, 35, is 14 weeks pregnant and drinks about a bottle of wine every evening. She has had shakes and sweating in the mornings. She wants to stop drinking straight away. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to attend a mutual support group before referral
Refer urgently to the specialist alcohol service for assisted withdrawal
Advise her to stop drinking tonight and contact the midwife if unwell
Advise her to cut down to 14 units a week for the rest of the pregnancy
9.w: Morning shakes and sweating suggest alcohol dependence. Abrupt cessation risks withdrawal seizures, so she needs urgent specialist referral for medically assisted withdrawal, while continuing antenatal care. NG201 1.3.10: no safe level of alcohol in pregnancy (SPM 3.1, 3.3).

n.0: Peer support helps later, but her withdrawal symptoms show dependence needing specialist care now.
n.2: Sudden withdrawal in alcohol dependence can cause seizures and needs medical management.
n.3: There is no safe level in pregnancy, and 14 units is the general adult low-risk guideline.

10.q: A student midwife asks whether a registered midwife needs a prescription to give intramuscular phytomenadione (vitamin K) to a healthy term newborn. Which answer is correct?
o: Yes: it needs a written prescription signed by a doctor before each dose
No: midwives may give it under the HMR 2012 midwives exemptions
No: any registered nurse or midwife may give it without a prescription
Yes: midwives may give oral vitamin K but need a prescription for the injection
10.w: Human Medicines Regulations 2012 Schedule 17 Part 3: registered midwives may administer parenteral phytomenadione in the course of their professional practice without a prescription. Student midwives may administer it under the direct supervision of a registered midwife (the exclusions for students are diamorphine, morphine and pethidine).

n.0: Phytomenadione is on the midwives exemptions list, so a prescription is not needed.
n.2: The Schedule 17 exemption covers registered midwives (and student midwives under direct supervision), not registered nurses.
n.3: The injection is the form listed in Part 3 (parenteral administration).

10.q: Marta, 34, has bipolar disorder and is 24 weeks pregnant. After specialist discussion she has decided to continue lithium because she is at high risk of relapse. Which monitoring plan is in line with NICE CG192?
o: Check plasma lithium at booking, at 28 weeks and at 36 weeks
Check plasma lithium weekly from 20 weeks until the birth
Check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks
Check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then stop it at 36 weeks
10.w: NICE CG192 1.4.37: if lithium continues in pregnancy, check plasma levels every 4 weeks, then weekly from the 36th week; keep levels in range, maintain fluid balance, plan birth in hospital, stop lithium during labour and check levels 12 hours after the last dose.

n.0: Three checks in pregnancy is less frequent than the 4-weekly monitoring recommended.
n.1: Weekly checks are recommended from 36 weeks, not from 20 weeks.
n.3: Lithium is stopped during labour, not at 36 weeks, when weekly monitoring starts.

10.q: Kathleen, a labour ward coordinator, has a conscientious objection to abortion. She is asked to allocate a midwife to care for a woman having a termination for fetal anomaly. Following the Supreme Court decision in Doogan [2014], what is the position?
o: She must allocate staff, as this is not hands-on participation
She may refuse, as any link to a termination is covered
She may refuse, as allocation is participation in the treatment
She may refuse if she records her objection in writing
10.w: Greater Glasgow Health Board v Doogan [2014] UKSC 68 held that 'participate' in s4 means taking part in a hands-on capacity; managerial and supervisory tasks such as allocating staff are not covered by the objection.

n.1: Doogan rejected a wide reading covering any task linked to termination.
n.2: Doogan held that allocation is not participation in the treatment.
n.3: Recording an objection does not bring allocation within s4, which Doogan held is not participation.

10.q: Harriet, 30, is 32 weeks pregnant and at low risk of fetal growth restriction. Her previous SFH measurements followed the 50th centile. Today's measurement, plotted on her customised chart, falls below the 10th centile. Movements are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a colleague to remeasure today and document if the result is the same
Reassure her, as SFH varies with the baby's position at this gestation
Remeasure SFH at her next routine appointment in 2 weeks
Refer for an ultrasound scan of fetal growth and wellbeing
10.w: If SFH suggests a small-for-gestational-age baby, offer an ultrasound scan for fetal growth and wellbeing; urgency depends on additional findings such as reduced movements or raised BP (NICE NG201 1.2.32; SBL v3 element 2). A drop in centile is a referral trigger.

n.0: A second measurement may be reasonable, but the plotted finding needs a scan referral rather than documentation alone.
n.1: A fall across centiles is a recognised referral criterion and should not be explained away.
n.2: Waiting 2 weeks delays assessment of possible FGR, a major risk factor for stillbirth.

10.q: A community midwife visits baby Rosa, aged 5 days, at home. According to NICE NG194, which finding is a red flag for serious illness?
o: Sleeping for 3 hours between feeds
Axillary temperature of 35.8 C
Small possets of milk after feeds
Respiratory rate of 52 breaths/min
10.w: NICE NG194 1.4.9: red flags for serious illness in young babies include a temperature of 38 C or over or under 36 C, respiratory rate over 60, grunting, chest indrawing, pallor or mottling, a weak or high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, seizures, bilious or projectile vomiting and non-blanching rash.

n.0: Sleeping 3 hours between feeds is normal for many newborns.
n.2: Small possets are common; bilious or forceful (projectile) vomiting is the red flag.
n.3: A respiratory rate of 52 is within the normal newborn range (the red flag is over 60).

10.q: Jo, a midwife in England, was involved in a stillbirth last week and feels distressed. Her manager suggests restorative clinical supervision under the A-EQUIP model. Who provides this?
o: A Professional Midwifery Advocate
The Local Supervising Authority Midwifery Officer
A Supervisor of Midwives
The NMC Midwifery Committee
10.w: Statutory supervision of midwives, including Supervisors of Midwives and Local Supervising Authorities, was removed in 2017. In England the A-EQUIP model replaced it, delivered by Professional Midwifery Advocates who offer restorative clinical supervision.

n.1: The Local Supervising Authority role ended with statutory supervision in 2017.
n.2: Supervisors of Midwives were part of statutory supervision, which ended in 2017.
n.3: The NMC is the regulator; no NMC committee provides individual restorative supervision, which under A-EQUIP comes from a Professional Midwifery Advocate.

10.q: Jess, 30, is breastfeeding her 10-day-old baby. She noticed a red, tender, wedge-shaped area on her left breast this morning. Her temperature is 37.6 C and she feels otherwise well. Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Express as much milk as possible after every feed to empty the left breast
Continue feeding on both sides and seek advice if it persists beyond 24 hours
Stop feeding from the left breast until the redness and tenderness settle
Contact the GP today for antibiotics to treat infective mastitis early
10.w: NICE NG194 1.2.4: worsening redness and swelling of the breast persisting for more than 24 hours despite self-management could indicate mastitis and needs medical advice. Self-management includes continuing to breastfeed, good positioning and attachment, rest and simple analgesia (NHS mastitis advice).

n.0: Over-expressing beyond the baby's needs increases supply and can perpetuate engorgement.
n.2: Stopping feeds on the affected side causes stasis and makes mastitis worse.
n.3: Most early mastitis settles with self-management; antibiotics are for symptoms that persist or worsen.

10.q: Lucy, 29, is planning her first pregnancy and has no medical conditions. She asks about folic acid. What should the midwife advise?
o: Take 400 micrograms daily before conception until 12 weeks
Take 5 mg daily before conception until 12 weeks
Take 400 micrograms daily throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
Take 400 micrograms daily from the positive test until 20 weeks
10.w: NG247 1.1.3-1.1.4: take 400 micrograms folic acid daily when planning pregnancy (ideally from 3 months before) and for the first 12 weeks.

n.1: 5 mg is for women at increased risk of neural tube defects, which Lucy is not (NG247 1.1.5).
n.2: Routine folic acid is recommended until 12 weeks; vitamin D is the supplement recommended beyond that.
n.3: Folic acid should start before conception, ideally 3 months before, and continue to 12 weeks.

10.q: Amira, 24, is 11 weeks pregnant. She has vomited everything, including water, for 3 days. She feels dizzy on standing, her urine shows 3+ ketones and she has lost 6% of her booking weight. Oral antiemetics from her GP have not helped. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer her the same day to hospital for assessment and intravenous fluids
Ask her GP to change to a different oral antiemetic and review in 3 days
Advise ginger capsules and small frequent meals, with review in a week
Reassure her that vomiting usually resolves by 16 weeks of pregnancy
10.w: Persistent vomiting with dehydration, ketonuria and weight loss over 5% despite oral antiemetics suggests hyperemesis gravidarum. NICE NG201 1.4.6 and 1.4.7: consider intravenous fluids and consider inpatient care if vomiting is severe and not responding to primary care or outpatient management; VTE risk should also be assessed.

n.1: Changing tablets she cannot keep down delays fluid replacement and assessment.
n.2: Ginger is for mild to moderate symptoms; she has signs of dehydration needing urgent treatment.
n.3: Reassurance is for mild to moderate symptoms; her dehydration and weight loss need treatment now.

10.q: Rosie, 26, has a mild learning disability and lives with her partner. She is going home with her baby tomorrow and the midwife needs to give her information about postnatal recovery and warning signs. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Keep information brief and leave out the warning signs
Give information in Easy Read format and check her understanding
Give the standard leaflet and ask her to sign that she has read it
Give the information to her mother, who can explain it later
10.w: NICE NG194 1.1.5 and 1.1.6: tailor the content and format of information to the woman's needs (for example Easy Read), and check that she understands it and how it relates to her. Reasonable adjustments are required under the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Warning signs are essential safety information that every woman needs (NG194 1.2.4).
n.2: A signature does not show she has understood the information.
n.3: Information should be given to Rosie herself in an accessible way; others are involved as she wishes.

10.q: A labour ward coordinator is asked by the bleep holder to take over the care of a woman in active labour because the ward is short of one midwife. The coordinator is currently overseeing eight rooms. What should the coordinator do?
o: Take the woman's care and hand oversight of the ward to the most senior midwife
Stay supernumerary and escalate the shortfall through the escalation policy
Take the woman's care and review the other rooms between contractions
Decline the request and wait for the next shift to address the shortfall
10.w: NHS Resolution's Maternity Incentive Scheme (Year 7, safety action 5) states that the midwifery coordinator in charge of labour ward must have supernumerary status, to keep oversight of all birth activity, with an escalation plan for shortfalls. The coordinator stays supernumerary and escalates the gap (SPM 2.3: factors affecting safe provision, including staffing).

n.0: Taking a caseload removes the coordinator's supernumerary oversight of the whole ward, which the Maternity Incentive Scheme requires for safety.
n.2: Combining a one-to-one caseload with coordination means neither role is done safely.
n.3: Declining without escalation leaves the staffing gap unresolved and the woman without a midwife.

10.q: Priya and her partner have just had a stillborn daughter at 37 weeks. They seem unsure about seeing or holding her. Which approach by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Take the baby to the mortuary while they rest and ask them again tomorrow
Advise them not to see her because it may make their grief harder
Offer them the choice, with time and gentle explanation, and respect what they decide
Encourage them to hold her now because they will regret it later if they do not
10.w: Compassionate bereavement care (SPM 4.11; National Bereavement Care Pathway stillbirth pathway) offers parents personalised choices about seeing, holding and making memories with their baby, without pressure either way, and respects their decision. They can change their mind later.

n.0: Removing the baby without agreement takes away the choice; parents may want time with her now.
n.1: Advising against seeing the baby removes a choice many parents value; the decision is theirs.
n.3: Pressuring parents to hold the baby is not person-centred; they should be offered the choice without coercion.

10.q: Ruth, 31, is 9 weeks pregnant. After the booking discussion she says she does not want any screening for Down's, Edwards' or Patau's syndromes or the 20-week anomaly scan, because she would continue the pregnancy whatever the result. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that the 20-week scan is required to check the position of the placenta
Respect and record her decision and offer the dating scan to confirm gestation
Refer her to an obstetrician to discuss the reasons for declining screening
Ask her to sign a disclaimer stating she accepts the risks of declining
10.w: Every screening test is a personal choice and she can accept or decline any part (NICE NG201 1.2.13; FASP). The dating scan determines gestational age and multiple pregnancy, and screening is added only if she opts for it (NG201 1.2.14). Her decision is respected and documented.

n.0: Placental location is part of the 18 to 20+6 week scan (NG201 1.2.15), but she may decline it; she should be informed of what it offers, not told it is required.
n.2: Declining screening is a valid informed choice and is not a reason for obstetric referral.
n.3: A disclaimer is not required; documenting the informed discussion and her decision is the standard.

10.q: A midwife has completed a vaginal examination wearing sterile gloves. She removes her gloves before recording the findings. What should she do next?
o: Record the findings and then decontaminate her hands
Put on a new pair of gloves to write the notes
Wipe her hands with the paper towel from the trolley
Decontaminate her hands
10.w: The WHO 5 moments for hand hygiene include after body fluid exposure risk, which includes after removing gloves. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene (SPM 3.10: principles of infection prevention and control).

n.0: Hand hygiene is needed immediately after glove removal and body fluid exposure risk, before touching notes.
n.1: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene and are not needed for writing.
n.2: Wiping with a paper towel does not decontaminate hands.

10.q: Kiera, 32, is medically fit for discharge on day 2. Her baby needs phototherapy on the postnatal ward for at least another 24 hours. Kiera is breastfeeding. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Discharge Kiera and give the baby formula top-ups overnight
Discharge Kiera and ask her to visit for feeds
Transfer the baby to the neonatal unit so that Kiera can go home
Offer Kiera the option to stay with her baby while treatment continues
10.w: SPM 2.6 requires planning care for woman and newborn as a unit. Keeping the mother with her baby supports breastfeeding during phototherapy, with breaks for feeds of up to 30 minutes (CG98).

n.0: Breastfed babies having phototherapy should not have extra fluids routinely; expressed breast milk is used if needed (CG98).
n.1: Visiting for feeds separates them and makes responsive breastfeeding difficult.
n.2: Moving a well baby to the neonatal unit for convenience separates them and uses a cot without clinical need.

10.q: Zara, a third-year student midwife, is completing her final practice placement. Several registered midwives have supervised her. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment, who conducts the assessment that confirms Zara has achieved her practice proficiencies?
o: The practice supervisor who has worked the most shifts with her
Her nominated practice assessor, using feedback from supervisors
Her academic assessor, based on her university assignments
The ward manager, as the person accountable for the placement area
10.w: SSSA 7.1: practice assessors conduct assessments to confirm student achievement of proficiencies and programme outcomes for practice learning; 7.2: decisions are informed by feedback from practice supervisors. The academic assessor confirms achievement in the academic environment (9.1) and works with the practice assessor on progression (7.5).

n.0: Practice supervisors contribute observations to assessment (4.1, 4.2) but do not confirm proficiency.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement in the academic environment, not the practice assessment itself.
n.3: The ward manager's role is not the practice assessor's unless formally nominated as such.

10.q: First-time parents of a 6-day-old baby are worried that they will not know if their baby becomes unwell. Which advice from the midwife best reflects NICE NG194?
o: Explain that serious infection in a baby will cause a high fever
Advise taking the baby's temperature every 4 hours, day and night
Advise waiting for the health visitor's first visit to raise worries
Give information on the Baby Check scoring system and when to call 999
10.w: NICE NG194 1.3.12-1.3.13: consider giving parents information about the Baby Check scoring system, and advise them to seek advice if they think the baby is unwell and to call 999 if they think the baby is seriously ill. 1.4.4: fever may be absent in young babies with serious infection.

n.0: Fever may not be present in young babies with serious infection (NG194 1.4.4).
n.1: Routine 4-hourly temperatures are not recommended and can miss other signs of illness.
n.2: Parents should seek advice whenever they are worried, not wait for a scheduled visit.

10.q: Kate, 32, has had antenatal depression treated with an SSRI throughout pregnancy. Her baby girl was born 12 hours ago at term and is breastfeeding. Which action by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Arrange for the baby to be admitted to the neonatal unit for observation
Carry out a full neonatal assessment, alert to possible medication effects
Advise her to stop the SSRI now that the baby has been born
Advise formula feeding to avoid exposing the baby through breast milk
10.w: CG192 1.9.2: if a woman has taken psychotropic medication during pregnancy, carry out a full neonatal assessment, bearing in mind the variation in onset of adverse effects and the need for further monitoring, and keep relevant professionals and the family informed.

n.0: A well baby does not need neonatal unit admission; assessment and monitoring can continue with the mother.
n.2: Stopping an effective antidepressant abruptly after birth risks relapse at a high-risk time; decisions belong with the prescriber.
n.3: SSRIs are not a reason to stop breastfeeding; decisions are individual and made with the woman.

10.q: Jess, 16, books at 12 weeks. She is living with her mother, is still at school and finds hospital clinics intimidating. Which care arrangement best follows NICE CG110?
o: Care deferred until her mother can attend every appointment with her
Standard consultant-led clinic care, as she is under 18
A named midwife providing most of her care, with a direct phone number
Antenatal care through her school nurse until 28 weeks
10.w: CG110 1.4.4: offer young women under 20 a named midwife who provides most of their antenatal care, with a direct-line telephone number. Services should be age-appropriate, community-based where possible and alert to safeguarding (1.4.1, 1.4.5).

n.0: Jess can attend herself; deferring care until her mother is available is a barrier to antenatal care.
n.1: Age alone is not an indication for consultant-led care; young women need accessible, age-appropriate services.
n.3: School nurses do not provide antenatal care; the midwife does.

10.q: Lucy, 30, is RhD negative and 28 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. Her booking antibody screen was negative and she has had no bleeding or trauma. Which care should be offered at this appointment?
o: Weekly antibody screens from 28 weeks instead of anti-D prophylaxis
Blood group and antibody screen, FBC and routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis
FBC and antibody screen, with anti-D given if the screen is positive
Anti-D prophylaxis after the birth, when the baby's blood group is known
10.w: At 28 weeks offer FBC, blood group and antibodies, and anti-D prophylaxis to RhD-negative women who are not known to be sensitised (NICE NG201 1.2.16; NICE TA156 1.1). RAADP protects against sensitisation from silent fetomaternal haemorrhage in late pregnancy.

n.0: Repeated antibody screening detects sensitisation after it happens; it does not prevent it.
n.2: A positive anti-D antibody screen would mean she is already sensitised, when prophylaxis no longer helps; RAADP is for women who are not sensitised.
n.3: Postnatal anti-D is also given if the baby is RhD positive, but it does not replace antenatal prophylaxis.

10.q: Baby Ava weighed 3,600 g at birth. On day 3 she weighs 3,240 g. What percentage of her birth weight has she lost?
10.w: Loss = 3,600 - 3,240 = 360 g. Percentage = 360 / 3,600 x 100 = 10%. Calculating weight loss accurately supports feeding assessment (SPM 1.23; NICE NG194).

n.0: 9% would be a loss of 324 g, not 360 g.
n.1: 11% would be a loss of about 396 g, not 360 g.
n.2: 36% confuses the 360 g loss with a percentage.

10.q: A public health midwife is redesigning antenatal smoking cessation support across a city with large differences in deprivation between areas. Which approach best reflects proportionate universalism?
o: Offer support to women who ask for it at booking
Offer the same level of support to every woman across the city
Offer support to women in the most deprived areas and stop it elsewhere
Offer support to all women, with intensity rising with disadvantage
10.w: Proportionate universalism (Marmot review, Fair Society, Healthy Lives, 2010) means actions are universal but with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage. SPM 2.9 asks midwives to consider the impact of social determinants of health.

n.0: Waiting for requests widens inequalities; women facing most disadvantage are least likely to ask.
n.1: Equal provision does not narrow inequalities because need is greater in deprived groups.
n.2: Targeting deprived areas alone misses disadvantaged women elsewhere and is not universal.

10.q: Fiona, 29, received intramuscular diamorphine for pain in established labour 1 hour ago. She now feels alert and asks to get into the birthing pool. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Help her into the pool and keep the water at 38 C to aid relaxation
Help her into the pool now, as she feels alert
Explain the pool is unsuitable for the rest of labour after any opioid
Explain she should wait until 2 hours after the opioid before entering water
10.w: NICE NG235 1.6.20: women should not enter water within 2 hours of opioid administration or if they feel drowsy, because of sedation and the risk of drowning. Water temperature should not exceed 37.5 C (1.6.11).

n.0: The 2-hour rule still applies, and 38 C exceeds the 37.5 C limit.
n.1: Feeling alert does not override the 2-hour rule after opioids.
n.2: After 2 hours, if she is not drowsy, she can enter the water; it is not excluded for the rest of labour.

10.q: Daniel and Mia agree to newborn blood spot screening for their son but do not want him screened for cystic fibrosis. What should the midwife explain?
o: They can decline CF and still have the other conditions screened
They need a consultant's written agreement to decline CF screening
CF screening is a legal requirement and cannot be declined
Declining CF screening means declining the whole blood spot test
10.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: parents can decline screening for sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis and congenital hypothyroidism individually; the inherited metabolic diseases can be declined only as a group. Screening is voluntary and based on verbal consent.

n.1: Parents give or decline consent themselves after information; no consultant agreement is needed.
n.2: Newborn screening is voluntary, so parents can decline any part that is allowed to be declined separately.
n.3: CF can be declined individually without declining the other conditions.

10.q: During the NIPE newborn examination of baby Leo, the midwife finds that the red reflex in his left eye is absent and the pupil looks white. The right eye is normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to a community optician for an eye test at 1 year
Refer urgently so he is seen by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks
Repeat the red reflex check at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
Refer for an ophthalmology appointment within 6 weeks
10.w: NIPE handbook 12.11: babies with screen positive (abnormal) red reflex results should be urgently referred and seen by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks of the newborn examination; an absent or white reflex may indicate congenital cataract or retinoblastoma.

n.0: An optician at 1 year is far too late; surgery for severe congenital cataract is time-critical.
n.2: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks delays assessment of a possible cataract or retinoblastoma.
n.3: The NIPE standard is assessment within 2 weeks, not 6.

10.q: Priti, 38, has a combined test result giving a 1 in 80 chance of Down's syndrome. She is upset and asks what this means and what happens next. Which response by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Explain that the baby has Down's syndrome and arrange counselling about the pregnancy
Advise a repeat combined test in 2 weeks to see whether the chance changes
Explain it is a higher-chance result and offer NIPT, a diagnostic test or no further testing
Book an amniocentesis, as this is the next step after any higher-chance result
10.w: FASP classes a chance of 1 in 2 to 1 in 150 as a higher-chance result. Screening does not diagnose; she is offered a choice of NIPT, a diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis) or no further testing, and every step is her informed choice (NHS FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.0: A screening result gives a chance, not a diagnosis; 79 in 80 babies with this result would not have Down's syndrome.
n.1: The combined test is not repeated; further information comes from NIPT or diagnostic testing.
n.3: Diagnostic testing is one option among several; it is her choice, not an automatic next step.

10.q: Jo, a midwife, was involved in a shoulder dystocia that is now the subject of a trust learning response. She is asked to attend an interview and give a written account. What is her professional responsibility?
o: Give an account after checking it with colleagues so the stories match
Decline the interview until the trust guarantees she will not be named
Cooperate fully and give an honest, factual account of her involvement
Ask her union to give an account so she does not have to take part
10.w: Code 23 requires registrants to cooperate with investigations and audits, and Code 10 and 20.2 require honest, accurate accounts. Critical reflection on the incident supports learning (SPM 5.2).

n.0: Aligning accounts with colleagues undermines the integrity of the investigation.
n.1: Making cooperation conditional on anonymity conflicts with the duty to cooperate.
n.3: A union may support her, but the account must be her own.

10.q: After a one-week trial of a new triage call script, Ola collects data on call times and compares it with the previous month. Which stage of the PDSA cycle is she completing?
o: The Do stage
The Plan stage
The Study stage
The Act stage
10.w: In the Study stage the team analyses the data, compares results with predictions and reflects on what was learned. Act then decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change (SPM 5.1).

n.0: Do was the one-week trial itself.
n.1: Planning set out the change and predictions before the trial.
n.3: Act follows Study and decides what to do next with the change.

10.q: A midwife enters a side room on the antenatal ward and finds Olga, 30, who is 33 weeks pregnant, slumped in a chair. She does not respond to voice or a firm shake and is not breathing normally. What should the midwife do?
o: Check a capillary blood glucose before calling anyone
Put out an obstetric arrest call and start CPR
Lay her flat and listen for the fetal heart
Put her in the recovery position and observe her
10.w: An unresponsive woman who is not breathing normally is in cardiac arrest: call for help (cardiac arrest call stating maternal or obstetric arrest so obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams attend) and start CPR, relieving aortocaval compression as she is over 20 weeks (RCUK 2025 special circumstances: pregnancy).

n.0: Glucose is checked as part of finding reversible causes, after help is called and CPR started.
n.2: The fetal heart is not assessed during maternal arrest; maternal resuscitation is the priority.
n.3: The recovery position is for an unresponsive person who is breathing normally.

10.q: Lan, 29, tells the midwife that in her culture new mothers rest at home for a month, are cared for by their mothers, and avoid showering in the early weeks. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Record that she has declined postnatal care because of her cultural beliefs
Explore her wishes and adapt care, offering hygiene advice for her to weigh up
Ask her mother to decide which postnatal care is acceptable
Tell her the tradition is unsafe and that she must shower every day from now
10.w: SPM 3.22 and 3.27: midwives support the needs and preferences that women identify and provide culturally sensitive care. NG194 1.1.1 and 1.1.5: listen and respond to her preferences and give individualised information so she can make informed decisions, including perineal hygiene advice (1.2.16).

n.0: She has not declined care; her cultural practices can be accommodated within postnatal care.
n.2: Decisions about her care are hers; her mother is involved only as she wishes.
n.3: A directive, dismissive response undermines trust and her right to make informed choices.

10.q: Fadumo, 29, is 20 weeks pregnant with a girl. On examination the midwife finds she has had type 3 FGM as a child. Fadumo has a 4-year-old daughter. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the FGM, complete a safeguarding risk assessment and plan care
Record the FGM and continue her routine midwife-led antenatal care
Report the FGM to the police within one month of the examination
Refer her daughter for a medical examination for FGM
10.w: For women aged 18 or over, FGM is recorded and a safeguarding risk assessment is completed, especially for daughters and an unborn girl; police notification under s5B applies to girls under 18. NG235 1.9.20 covers planning care for infibulated women (SPM 3.7).

n.1: Type 3 FGM needs a birth plan, including possible deinfibulation, and a safeguarding assessment.
n.2: The mandatory police reporting duty applies to girls under 18, not adult women.
n.3: Examination is not automatic; risk is assessed first and referral made if there is concern.

10.q: Lucy is coordinating the birth centre on a night shift. Two midwives have called in sick, leaving three women in established labour with two midwives. No bank staff are available. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the women's birth partners to call a midwife when contractions change
Escalate to the manager on call under the staffing escalation policy
Continue to manage the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Ask the two student midwives on shift to care for the third woman
10.w: Code 25.1 requires leaders to identify priorities, manage staff and resources effectively and deal with risk; Code 16.1 requires raising and escalating concerns about safety, and standard 16 to act without delay. Escalating through the staffing policy allows the manager on call to redeploy staff or divert admissions.

n.0: Relying on birth partners to monitor labour transfers a professional responsibility to people without training.
n.2: Waiting until morning delays action while women in labour are receiving unsafe staffing levels.
n.3: Students are supernumerary and must be supervised; they cannot replace a registered midwife to make up numbers.

10.q: Tamsin, 26, has severe pre-eclampsia and is receiving magnesium sulfate 1 g/hour after a 4 g loading dose. On her hourly check the midwife finds she is drowsy, her respiratory rate is 10 breaths/min and her patellar reflexes are absent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase the infusion because absent reflexes signal seizure risk
Stop the infusion, call for help and prepare calcium gluconate
