Arrange a personalised care planning meeting with a consultant midwife
Tell Kerry midwives cannot attend a home birth after a caesarean
11.w: SPM 1.22: advocate for the woman when her decision is outside guidance, to minimise risk and maintain the relationship. A consultant midwife care planning meeting allows an honest discussion of risks and a plan that supports her choice (Code 2.5).

n.0: Sending her to private care withdraws NHS support instead of advocating for her.
n.1: Choosing a birth outside guidance is not a safeguarding concern.
n.3: The trust still provides midwifery care; a woman's choice of place of birth does not remove midwifery support.

11.q: Freya, 31, is 35 weeks pregnant. Her scan shows an estimated fetal weight on the 6th centile with normal Doppler and steady growth velocity. She has no other risk factors. She asks when her baby should be born. Which response reflects Saving Babies' Lives v3?
o: Birth should be considered at 39+0 weeks and achieved by 39+6
Birth should be planned at 41 weeks if growth continues
Birth should be initiated at 37+0 weeks and by 37+6
Birth should be planned at 34 weeks after a course of steroids
11.w: SBL v3 2.19: for an EFW between the 3rd and under the 10th centile, delivery should be considered at 39+0 weeks and achieved by 39+6 weeks; other risk factors are needed to recommend birth before 39 weeks.

n.1: Continuing past 39+6 weeks with an SGA fetus is not advised by SBL v3.
n.2: 37+0 to 37+6 weeks applies to EFW below the 3rd centile (SBL v3 2.18).
n.3: She is already 35 weeks with normal Doppler; there is no indication for preterm birth.

11.q: Olivia, 27, booked late at 24 weeks. She tells the midwife her last birth was "terrifying" and that staff "didn't listen". She avoids eye contact and asks to keep appointments short. Which approach will best build a trusting relationship?
o: Acknowledge her experience and agree a plan of care together
Reassure her that this hospital is different from her last one
Keep appointments short as asked and focus on clinical checks
Refer her for counselling before continuing the care discussion
11.w: SPM 1.12 and Code 2: develop trusting, compassionate, person-centred relationships by listening, acknowledging her experience and planning care in partnership. This also supports trauma-informed care.

n.1: Quick reassurance dismisses her experience and does not build trust.
n.2: Focusing on checks only does not address her distrust, which affects engagement with care.
n.3: Counselling may help later, but making it a precondition delays care and does not build the relationship itself.

11.q: Amira, 24, is 11 weeks pregnant. She has vomited everything, including water, for 3 days. She feels dizzy on standing, her urine shows 3+ ketones and she has lost 6% of her booking weight. Oral antiemetics from her GP have not helped. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer her the same day to hospital for assessment and intravenous fluids
Ask her GP to change to a different oral antiemetic and review in 3 days
Advise ginger capsules and small frequent meals, with review in a week
Reassure her that vomiting usually resolves by 16 weeks of pregnancy
11.w: Persistent vomiting with dehydration, ketonuria and weight loss over 5% despite oral antiemetics suggests hyperemesis gravidarum. NICE NG201 1.4.6 and 1.4.7: consider intravenous fluids and consider inpatient care if vomiting is severe and not responding to primary care or outpatient management; VTE risk should also be assessed.

n.1: Changing tablets she cannot keep down delays fluid replacement and assessment.
n.2: Ginger is for mild to moderate symptoms; she has signs of dehydration needing urgent treatment.
n.3: Reassurance is for mild to moderate symptoms; her dehydration and weight loss need treatment now.

11.q: When should the first postnatal health visitor home visit be considered, according to NICE?
o: Within 36 hours after transfer from the place of birth
Within 72 hours with the newborn physical examination
Between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery
At 6 to 8 weeks with the GP postnatal check
11.w: NG194 1.1.15: consider arranging the first postnatal health visitor home visit between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery care, so contacts are evenly spread.

n.0: 36 hours is the standard for the first midwife visit, not the health visitor.
n.1: 72 hours is the deadline for the newborn physical examination, not the health visitor visit.
n.3: 6 to 8 weeks is the GP check for the woman and baby, not the first health visitor visit.

11.q: Ruth, 30, is in her first labour in a midwifery-led unit. Delay was suspected 2 hours ago and she has now progressed from 5 cm to 5.5 cm. Her membranes are intact, she and the baby are well, and she has no other risk factors. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start an oxytocin infusion in the midwifery unit and re-examine in 4 hours
Wait another 2 hours before diagnosing delay, as she has made progress
Transfer her to the obstetric unit so that an amniotomy can be performed
Diagnose delay, offer amniotomy in the unit and re-examine 2 hours later
11.w: Progress of under 1 cm in 2 hours confirms delay (NICE NG235 1.8.45). Consider amniotomy after explaining it shortens labour by about an hour and may make contractions stronger (1.8.46). Do not transfer for amniotomy alone (1.8.47); re-examine 2 hours later (1.8.48).

n.0: Oxytocin needs obstetric assessment and is not started in a midwifery-led unit.
n.1: Progress under 1 cm in 2 hours already meets the definition of delay.
n.2: NICE advises not to transfer to obstetric-led care for amniotomy alone.

11.q: Rebecca, 31, is 26 weeks pregnant. She has a thick white vaginal discharge with itching and soreness. She has no abdominal pain, fever or urinary symptoms. Which treatment is recommended by NICE?
o: Oral fluconazole as a single 150 mg dose
Oral metronidazole tablets for 7 days
A vaginal imidazole such as clotrimazole
Douching with diluted vinegar daily
11.w: Thick white discharge with itching and soreness suggests vaginal candidiasis. NICE NG201 1.4.13: offer a vaginal imidazole (such as clotrimazole or econazole) to treat vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy.

n.0: Oral antifungals such as fluconazole are avoided in pregnancy; NICE recommends a vaginal imidazole.
n.1: Metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis, which typically causes thin grey discharge with a fishy odour, not itching.
n.3: Douching is not a recommended treatment and can disturb normal vaginal flora.

11.q: Charlotte, 31, is RhD negative. A non-invasive test of cell-free fetal DNA in her blood shows that her baby is predicted to be RhD negative. At 28 weeks she asks whether she still needs anti-D prophylaxis. What is the most accurate response?
o: Anti-D prophylaxis is not needed, as the baby is predicted to be RhD negative
Anti-D prophylaxis is not needed, as her own RhD status is now irrelevant
Anti-D prophylaxis is still needed, as fetal genotyping does not change care
Anti-D prophylaxis is needed at 28 and 34 weeks, as the result may be wrong
11.w: High-throughput non-invasive prenatal testing for fetal RHD genotype (NICE DG25, referenced in NG201 1.2.16) identifies women carrying an RhD-negative baby, who do not need antenatal anti-D. Where the baby is predicted RhD positive or the result is inconclusive, prophylaxis is offered.

n.1: Her RhD-negative status remains relevant; it is the baby's predicted group that removes the need for prophylaxis in this pregnancy.
n.2: The purpose of fetal RHD genotyping is to target anti-D, avoiding unnecessary doses when the baby is RhD negative.
n.3: The test is highly accurate; a predicted RhD-negative result means prophylaxis is not offered.

11.q: Nadia, 33, has a primary postpartum haemorrhage of 1,200 mL after a vaginal birth. Uterotonics have been given and the obstetrician asks the midwife to prepare tranexamic acid as NICE recommends. How should it be given?
o: 500 mg intravenously as a rapid bolus
1 g intramuscularly as a single injection
2 g orally with a glass of water
1 g intravenously over 10 minutes
11.w: NICE NG235 1.10.35: alongside uterotonics, give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes for PPH, repeated after at least 30 minutes if bleeding continues. Tranexamic acid is not a midwives exemption medicine and needs a prescription or PGD.

n.0: The dose is 1 g, and it is given over 10 minutes rather than as a rapid bolus.
n.1: The intramuscular route is not the route recommended for PPH.
n.2: Oral tranexamic acid is not used for acute PPH.

11.q: Twins Ella and Isla were born at 37 weeks. At 10 hours old, Ella develops signs of shock and is started on antibiotics for suspected sepsis. Isla is feeding well and her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate plan for Isla?
o: Take investigations and start antibiotics without waiting for results
Continue routine postnatal care because she has no clinical signs
Monitor her observations every 4 hours for 12 hours before deciding
Wait for Ella's blood culture result before deciding about Isla
11.w: Suspected or confirmed infection in another baby of a multiple pregnancy is a red flag risk factor (NG195 box 1). Any red flag means investigations then antibiotics without waiting for results (NG195 1.10.3), given within 1 hour of the decision to treat (1.15.2).

n.1: A red flag risk factor applies even when the baby looks well.
n.2: Observation alone is for babies without red flags and with only 1 risk factor or indicator.
n.3: Waiting for the sibling's culture delays treatment of a baby with a red flag.

11.q: During a breech birth, Nadia's baby has been born to the umbilicus with the back anterior. The buttocks were born 2 minutes ago. The baby has good tone and colour and is descending with each contraction. What should the midwife do?
o: Ask Nadia to stop pushing to protect the perineum
Keep her hands off and continue to observe progress
Grasp the legs and apply traction to deliver the arms
Deliver the head at once using Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit
11.w: RCOG GTG 20b: a hands-off approach with timely intervention if progress is not made once the umbilicus has delivered, or if there is poor tone, extended arms or neck. Intervention is generally required if more than 5 minutes from buttocks to head or more than 3 minutes from umbilicus to head. Good tone and progress mean no intervention yet.

n.0: Stopping maternal effort delays the birth when cord compression is likely.
n.2: Traction is avoided because it can cause arm and head extension.
n.3: The arms and body have not yet been born, and the head is not the next step.

11.q: Precious, 24, gave birth four days ago. Her partner calls the community midwife because she has not slept for two nights, is talking rapidly, believes the baby has been swapped and is frightened. She had no previous mental health problems. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Complete an EPDS questionnaire at the next routine postnatal visit
Advise her partner to let her sleep and call back if she is no better tomorrow
Book a GP appointment for later this week to review her mood
Arrange immediate referral for specialist mental health assessment within 4 hours
11.w: Sudden onset of insomnia, agitation and delusional beliefs in the first days after birth suggests postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency. CG192 1.5.12: refer to a secondary (preferably specialist perinatal) mental health service for immediate assessment within 4 hours of referral.

n.0: The EPDS screens for depression and is not the response to an acute psychotic presentation.
n.1: Waiting until tomorrow leaves a woman with possible psychosis and her baby at serious risk.
n.2: A GP appointment later in the week delays assessment of a condition that can deteriorate within hours.

11.q: Dani, 22, is formula feeding her baby and has no risk factors for blood clots. She would like to use the combined pill. When can she start it?
o: 6 weeks after the birth
Immediately after the birth
3 weeks after the birth
After her first period
11.w: Women who are not breastfeeding and have no VTE risk factors can start the combined pill, ring or patch 3 weeks after the birth (NHS; FSRH). VTE risk is raised in the early postnatal period.

n.0: The 6-week wait applies to women who are breastfeeding.
n.1: Combined methods are avoided in the first 3 weeks because of the raised VTE risk after birth.
n.3: Waiting for a period risks pregnancy, as ovulation comes first.

11.q: Baby Ruby was breech at 37 weeks. A successful external cephalic version was performed and she was born head first at 40 weeks. Her hip examination at the NIPE newborn check is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer for hip ultrasound, as she has a NIPE hip risk factor
Rely on the 6 to 8 week hip examination to detect any problem
Refer for a hip X-ray at 6 months of age
No further action, as she was head first at birth with normal hips
11.w: NIPE handbook: breech presentation at or after 36 completed weeks, irrespective of presentation at birth or mode of delivery (including after successful ECV), is a hip risk factor. Babies with risk factors are screen positive and need hip ultrasound, usually at 4 to 6 weeks.

n.1: A risk factor means referral for ultrasound now, not reliance on later clinical examination.
n.2: Hip ultrasound, not X-ray, is the NIPE screening test in early infancy.
n.3: Presentation at birth does not remove the risk factor; breech at 36 weeks or later counts even after ECV.

11.q: Danielle, 25, is in strong labour and declines an epidural, shouting that she wants to cope without one. The registrar says she cannot be making a proper decision while in so much pain. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, what is the starting point?
o: She lacks capacity as she is refusing pain relief
She lacks capacity until her pain has been controlled
She is assumed to have capacity unless shown otherwise
Her birth partner decides while she is in pain
11.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack capacity. Pain and distress do not by themselves establish incapacity; any doubt needs a decision-specific assessment.

n.0: Refusing a recommended treatment does not show a lack of capacity (s1(4)).
n.1: Pain does not remove capacity automatically; incapacity must be established, not assumed.
n.3: Nobody can decide for an adult who has capacity, including a birth partner.

11.q: Chloe, 26, is 9 weeks pregnant. She has nausea most mornings and vomits once or twice a week. She is drinking well, passing urine normally and working. She would prefer not to take medicines. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Advise her to stop eating until the nausea passes to rest her stomach
Suggest she tries ginger, and explain symptoms usually settle by 16 to 20 weeks
Advise her GP to prescribe an antiemetic, as ginger is unsafe in pregnancy
Refer her to hospital for intravenous fluids to prevent dehydration
11.w: NICE NG201 1.4.1 and 1.4.3: reassure women that mild to moderate nausea and vomiting are common and likely to resolve before 16 to 20 weeks, and suggest ginger for those with mild to moderate symptoms who prefer a non-pharmacological option.

n.0: Avoiding food is not recommended and risks dehydration and ketosis; small frequent meals are usually advised.
n.2: Ginger is a NICE-suggested option; an antiemetic is offered if she chooses a medicine.
n.3: She is mildly affected and well hydrated, so IV fluids are not indicated.

11.q: Jasmine, 31, had the whooping cough vaccine in her last pregnancy 18 months ago. She is now 18 weeks pregnant again. What should the midwife advise?
o: No vaccine is needed, as she is protected for 5 years
Have the vaccine again in this pregnancy
Have the vaccine if her baby is born before 32 weeks
Have a blood test to check her antibody level first
11.w: Green Book ch 24: pertussis vaccine is recommended in every pregnancy, because antibodies wane and the aim is to maximise passive protection for each new baby.

n.0: Maternal antibody levels fall, so vaccination is needed every pregnancy to protect each baby.
n.2: The vaccine is offered every pregnancy, not according to the baby's gestation at birth.
n.3: No antibody test is needed; vaccination is recommended in every pregnancy.

11.q: Becky, 22, has a child protection plan for her unborn baby. She is ready for discharge from the postnatal ward on a Saturday evening. What should the midwife do before Becky and her baby leave?
o: Confirm the plan agreed with children's social care is in place
Keep the baby on the ward until the social worker visits on Monday
Discharge them and ask the health visitor to visit within 7 days
Discharge them and email the social worker on Monday morning
11.w: Multiagency working (Working Together to Safeguard Children) requires discharge of a baby subject to a child protection plan to follow the plan agreed with children's social care, using out-of-hours services if needed (SPM 2.4, 2.11).

n.1: There is no legal basis to keep the baby without a plan or order; this action is not the midwife's to take alone.
n.2: The health visitor visit is part of routine care; it does not replace the agreed safeguarding discharge plan.
n.3: Discharging without confirming the agreed plan may leave the baby at risk over the weekend.

11.q: Lucy, a midwife, realises she gave a woman's prescribed antibiotic 4 hours late because she forgot it during a busy shift. The woman is well. What should Lucy do first?
o: Report the incident but not tell the woman, because no harm has occurred
Tell the woman, apologise, give the dose as advised and report the incident
Give the dose now and record it at the scheduled time to avoid confusion
Ask a colleague to give the dose so that the error is not linked to her
11.w: Code 14.1 to 14.3: act immediately to put right the situation, explain to the person what has happened and apologise, and document events. The incident should be reported so the system can learn (SPM 5.2).

n.0: Openness with the woman is required by Code 14 when an error occurs.
n.2: Recording a false time is dishonest and breaches Code 10 and 20.2.
n.3: Concealing her involvement breaches the duty of candour and honesty.

11.q: Sienna, 30, is 40+5 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated first pregnancy. She asks the midwife at what point induction of labour will be discussed with her. What is the most accurate answer?
o: From 41+0 weeks, as some risks rise if the pregnancy continues beyond then
From 39+0 weeks, as part of the routine membrane sweep discussion
From 42+0 weeks, as risks do not increase until the pregnancy is post-term
From 40+0 weeks, as every pregnancy should be induced at the due date
11.w: NICE NG207 1.2.3 and 1.2.4: explain that risks such as caesarean birth, neonatal unit admission, stillbirth and neonatal death may increase beyond 41+0 weeks, and discuss that induction from 41+0 weeks may reduce these risks, alongside its impact on her birth experience.

n.1: From 39+0 weeks sweeping is discussed; induction for prolonged pregnancy is discussed from 41+0.
n.2: NG207 describes rising risks after 41+0 weeks, so waiting until 42+0 to discuss is too late.
n.3: Induction is not offered routinely at the due date in an uncomplicated pregnancy.

11.q: Nadia, 4 days after birth, had pre-eclampsia and takes enalapril. Her blood pressure is 146/96 mmHg, she has no symptoms and her blood results are stable. She asks to go home. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Keep her in hospital until her blood pressure is below 130/80 mmHg
Transfer with no medical follow-up, as her BP is below 150/100 mmHg
Transfer home with a medical review 2 weeks after the birth
Keep her in hospital until the enalapril can be stopped completely
11.w: NICE NG133: transfer to community care is appropriate when there are no symptoms of pre-eclampsia, BP is 150/100 mmHg or less and blood results are stable or improving. Women still on antihypertensives need medical review at 2 weeks, plus the 6 to 8 week review.

n.0: 130/80 is a treatment target, not a requirement for transfer home.
n.1: Women discharged on antihypertensives need a review at 2 weeks and again at 6 to 8 weeks.
n.3: Treatment can be reduced in the community; it does not need to stop before transfer.

11.q: Esther, 26, is 37 weeks pregnant and has a cardiac arrest in the antenatal clinic within the hospital. The midwife makes the emergency call. Which teams should be summoned?
o: Obstetric and anaesthetic teams, with no need for neonatal staff
The cardiac arrest team, with obstetrics informed afterwards
Cardiac arrest, obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams
The midwife coordinator, who will decide which teams to call
11.w: Maternal arrest needs the cardiac arrest team plus obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams, because a resuscitative hysterotomy may be needed as soon as possible and the baby will need resuscitation (RCUK 2025 special circumstances: pregnancy).

n.0: A baby born by resuscitative hysterotomy needs the neonatal team.
n.1: Obstetric staff are needed at once to prepare for resuscitative hysterotomy.
n.3: Delegating the call to the coordinator delays the multidisciplinary response.

11.q: Baby Grace, born at 40 weeks, is 60 hours old. Her transcutaneous bilirubin reading is 262 micromol/L. She is feeding well. What should the midwife do next?
o: Start phototherapy based on the transcutaneous reading
Measure serum bilirubin to confirm the level
Reassure the parents, as the reading is below 300
Repeat the transcutaneous reading in 6 hours
11.w: NICE CG98 1.2.16: use serum bilirubin measurement if a transcutaneous bilirubinometer gives a reading above 250 micromol/L; the serum value is then plotted on the treatment threshold graph.

n.0: Treatment decisions use serum bilirubin when the transcutaneous reading exceeds 250.
n.2: There is no 300 reassurance threshold; readings over 250 need serum confirmation.
n.3: A reading above 250 needs a serum measurement, not a repeat transcutaneous reading.

11.q: Baby Ruby, born at term and breastfed, is having phototherapy for jaundice. Her mother asks about feeding during treatment. Which advice is in line with NICE CG98?
o: Keep phototherapy continuous and give feeds by nasogastric tube
Take breaks of up to 30 minutes to breastfeed, without extra fluids
Give extra water or dextrose between feeds to flush out the bilirubin
Stop breastfeeding and give formula until the levels fall
11.w: NICE CG98 1.4.15: during phototherapy, use short breaks of up to 30 minutes for breastfeeding, nappy changing and cuddles; continue lactation and do not give additional fluids or feeds routinely to breastfed babies (expressed breast milk if extra is needed).

n.0: Short feeding breaks are encouraged during single phototherapy; tube feeding is not routine.
n.2: CG98 advises against giving additional water or dextrose routinely.
n.3: Breastfeeding should continue; stopping is not recommended.

11.q: A community midwife is discussing place of birth with four women. Which woman should be advised to plan birth in an obstetric unit because of her antenatal risk of postpartum haemorrhage?
o: Amina, 29, para 2, BMI 32 kg/m2
Becky, 24, who had a second-degree tear last time
Dana, 33, who had a PPH needing transfusion last time
Cara, 35, with a low-risk pregnancy and a fundal placenta
11.w: NICE NG235 1.10.29 lists antenatal PPH risk factors that warrant advice to give birth in an obstetric unit, including previous PPH over 1000 mL or requiring transfusion, BMI over 35, grand multiparity (4 or more), pre-eclampsia, Hb under 85 g/L at onset of labour and placenta accreta spectrum.

n.0: BMI over 35 and parity 4 or more are the thresholds; 32 and para 2 do not meet them.
n.1: A previous second-degree tear is not an antenatal PPH risk factor in NG235.
n.3: A fundal placenta in a low-risk pregnancy is not a PPH risk factor.

11.q: Leah asks how she can play with her 1-week-old daughter to support her development. Which advice about newborn vision is most accurate?
o: Hold her face about 20 to 30 cm away and talk, as newborns prefer faces
Hang a mobile about 1 metre above the cot, as newborns focus at a distance
Wait until 6 weeks before face-to-face play, as newborns cannot see faces
Show bright cartoons on a tablet held close to her face to train vision
11.w: Newborns focus best at about 20 to 30 cm and show a preference for faces. NICE NG194 1.3.17: face-to-face interaction promotes emotional attachment and supports very early development (SPM 3.13.4).

n.1: Newborns focus best close up, not at a metre or more.
n.2: Newborns can see and prefer faces from birth; face-to-face play should start straight away.
n.3: Screens are not recommended for babies and do not replace face-to-face interaction.

11.q: During a major postpartum haemorrhage in the birth room, the team is busy treating Rachel, 29. Her partner is standing in the corner, crying and asking repeatedly what is happening. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Allocate a team member to stay with them and explain
Ask him to wait outside until the emergency is over
Tell him everything is fine so that he stays calm
Ask the most junior doctor to explain once Rachel is stable
11.w: NICE NG235 1.10.36: allocate a member of the healthcare team to stay with the woman and her birth companions, explain what is happening, answer questions and offer support throughout the emergency (SPM 4.7).

n.1: Sending him out without support or information is not in line with NG235.
n.2: False reassurance is dishonest and undermines trust (Code 20.2).
n.3: Support should be given during the emergency, not deferred until afterwards.

11.q: A student midwife is preparing a presentation on the NHS England three year delivery plan for maternity and neonatal services (2023). Which is one of the plan's four themes?
o: Achieving national continuity of carer targets
Growing, retaining and supporting the workforce
Reducing caesarean birth to a set national rate
Centralising births into larger obstetric units
11.w: The three year delivery plan (30 Mar 2023) has four themes: listening to and working with women and families with compassion; growing, retaining and supporting the workforce; developing and sustaining a culture of safety, learning and support; and standards and structures that underpin safer, more personalised and more equitable care (3YP).

n.0: National continuity targets were removed in September 2022; the plan does not set them.
n.2: The plan does not set a caesarean rate target; national reviews warned against using such rates as performance measures.
n.3: Centralisation is not a theme; the plan focuses on listening, workforce, safety culture and standards.

11.q: Holly is writing a reflective account using Gibbs' reflective cycle about a difficult conversation with a bereaved family. She has described the event, explored her feelings and evaluated what was good and bad. Which stage comes next?
o: Action plan
Analysis
Description
Conclusion
11.w: Gibbs' cycle runs: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan. After evaluation comes analysis, making sense of the situation and drawing on theory or evidence (SPM 5.13.1).

n.0: The action plan is the final stage, after the conclusion.
n.2: Description is the first stage, which Holly has already completed.
n.3: The conclusion follows analysis.

11.q: A midwife has completed a vaginal examination wearing sterile gloves. She removes her gloves before recording the findings. What should she do next?
o: Record the findings and then decontaminate her hands
Put on a new pair of gloves to write the notes
Wipe her hands with the paper towel from the trolley
Decontaminate her hands
11.w: The WHO 5 moments for hand hygiene include after body fluid exposure risk, which includes after removing gloves. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene (SPM 3.10: principles of infection prevention and control).

n.0: Hand hygiene is needed immediately after glove removal and body fluid exposure risk, before touching notes.
n.1: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene and are not needed for writing.
n.2: Wiping with a paper towel does not decontaminate hands.

11.q: Kayla, 15, gave birth 4 weeks ago. At a postnatal visit she asks the midwife for contraception and does not want her parents told. She understands the information and is likely to have sex again. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Tell her she needs a parent's signature before contraception can be supplied
Refuse the request until she is 16
Arrange contraception if she is Gillick competent and the Fraser guidelines are met
Tell her parents, as she is under 16
11.w: Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985): a young person under 16 may consent if competent, and the Fraser guidelines apply to contraception advice. Confidentiality is respected unless there is a risk of serious harm. Safeguarding considerations still apply to sex under 16.

n.0: A competent young person can consent without a parent's signature.
n.1: Refusing contraception to a competent young person who is likely to have sex increases her risk of pregnancy.
n.3: Being under 16 does not by itself require parents to be told if she is competent and there is no serious risk.

11.q: A midwife is preparing intramuscular vitamin K (phytomenadione) for baby Rhys, born at 40 weeks weighing 3.4 kg. Which dose should she expect to give?
o: 1 mg as a single dose
2 mg as a single dose
400 micrograms as a single dose
3.4 mg, at 1 mg per kilogram
11.w: BNF for Children (phytomenadione): neonatal prophylaxis of vitamin K deficiency bleeding by intramuscular injection is 1 mg as a single dose at birth for a term neonate. The weight-based dose of 400 micrograms/kg (max 1 mg) is for preterm neonates.

n.1: 2 mg is the oral dose of Konakion MM Paediatric, not the IM dose.
n.2: 400 micrograms is the per-kilogram preterm dose, not the term dose.
n.3: IM prophylaxis is not 1 mg per kilogram; the term dose is a single 1 mg.

11.q: Daisy, 25, is at her booking appointment at 9 weeks. As part of a general conversation about her wellbeing, the midwife plans to ask about her mental health. Which approach follows NICE antenatal and postnatal mental health guidance?
o: Ask about mental health at the 28-week appointment once rapport is built
Ask whether she has ever been prescribed antidepressants by her GP
Ask her to complete the full EPDS questionnaire before any discussion
Ask the two depression identification questions and the GAD-2 questions
11.w: NICE CG192 1.5.4: at the booking visit and in the early postnatal period, consider asking the two depression identification (Whooley) questions and the 2-item GAD scale as part of a general discussion about mental health and wellbeing. Fuller tools such as the EPDS or PHQ-9 follow a positive response or concern (1.5.5).

n.0: Enquiry is recommended at booking; delaying until 28 weeks may miss early illness.
n.1: Medication history is useful, but it does not identify current depression or anxiety.
n.2: The EPDS or PHQ-9 is used as part of a full assessment after a positive response or concern, not as the first step.

11.q: Poppy, 31, is 39+2 weeks pregnant and attends with a first episode of reduced fetal movements. The CTG is normal and her SFH is on her usual centile. Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Explain induction is not considered until 41+0 weeks of pregnancy
Discuss induction of labour with her, as she is beyond 38+6 weeks
Arrange twice-weekly CTGs until she reaches 41 weeks
Recommend an expedited caesarean birth today
11.w: SBL v3 element 3: for RFM after 38+6 weeks, discuss induction of labour with all women (risks, benefits and her wishes), and offer birth to those with recurrent RFM after 38+6 weeks. At 39 weeks and beyond induction is not associated with more caesarean births.

n.0: 41+0 is the threshold for discussing induction for prolonged pregnancy (NG207), not for RFM after 38+6 weeks.
n.2: Serial CTG monitoring is not the recommended response; a discussion about induction is.
n.3: There is no indication for caesarean birth with a normal CTG; induction is discussed as an option.

11.q: Isla, 31, had active management of the third stage in a freestanding midwifery unit. Forty minutes after the birth the placenta has not delivered. Her blood loss is 300 mL and she is stable. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Attempt manual removal with Entonox as analgesia
Inject oxytocin into the umbilical vein to release the placenta
Secure IV access, explain why and arrange transfer to obstetric care
Start an intravenous oxytocin infusion and wait a further hour
11.w: A third stage over 30 minutes with active management is prolonged (NICE NG235 1.10.20). For a retained placenta: secure IV access and explain why (1.10.21), do not use umbilical vein agents (1.10.22), do not use IV oxytocics routinely unless bleeding excessively (1.10.23, 1.10.24), and arrange transfer if not in an obstetric unit (1.10.27).

n.0: Manual removal must not be attempted without an anaesthetic (NG235 1.10.28).
n.1: NICE advises not to use umbilical vein agents for a retained placenta.
n.3: IV oxytocics are not used routinely for a retained placenta unless she is bleeding excessively.

11.q: On a busy postnatal ward, Ellie, a midwife, asks a maternity support worker who has been trained and assessed in the task to complete four-hourly observations on a well woman. Which statement about accountability is correct?
o: Accountability for the task passes to the support worker once she accepts it
The support worker's manager becomes accountable for the delegated task
The ward coordinator is accountable as she allocates the staffing
Ellie is accountable for delegating and for checking the outcome is safe
11.w: NMC Code 11: be accountable for decisions to delegate; delegate within the other person's competence (11.1), make sure they are supervised and supported (11.2) and confirm the outcome meets the required standard (11.3). The support worker is responsible for how she performs the task.

n.0: The support worker is responsible for her own performance, but the midwife's accountability for the delegation decision does not pass to her.
n.1: The support worker's line manager does not take over accountability for a clinical delegation decision made by the midwife.
n.2: Allocating staff does not make the coordinator accountable for an individual midwife's delegation decision.

11.q: Abi is caring for a woman in labour on continuous CTG monitoring. According to Saving Babies' Lives v3, how often should a separate 'fresh eyes' review of the CTG and overall wellbeing take place?
o: At least every 2 hours
When the CTG is classified as pathological
At least hourly
At least every 4 hours
11.w: SBL v3 4.3 and 4.4: a regular (at least hourly) systematic review of maternal and fetal wellbeing, with a separate fresh eyes review at least hourly when CTG is used, or at least 4-hourly with intermittent auscultation, unless triggered earlier.

n.0: Two-hourly is less often than the SBL v3 minimum for CTG.
n.1: Fresh eyes is a scheduled safeguard; waiting for a pathological trace defeats its purpose of earlier detection.
n.3: Four-hourly fresh eyes applies to intermittent auscultation, not CTG monitoring.

11.q: Olivia, 29, had a caesarean birth in labour for failure to progress. Her BMI is 24, she does not smoke and has no other risk factors. The midwife completes her postnatal VTE risk assessment using the RCOG score. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: LMWH thromboprophylaxis for at least 10 days after the birth
Anti-embolism stockings until mobile, with no LMWH needed
Early mobilisation and good hydration, with no LMWH needed
LMWH thromboprophylaxis for 6 weeks after the birth
11.w: RCOG GTG 37a risk assessment (amended by the RCOG position statement, Sept 2026): caesarean section in labour scores 2. A postnatal score of 2 or more means considering LMWH thromboprophylaxis for at least 10 days.

n.1: Her score of 2 meets the threshold for pharmacological prophylaxis; stockings are for women who cannot have LMWH.
n.2: Mobilisation and hydration are advised for everyone, but a score of 2 means LMWH should also be considered.
n.3: 6 weeks is for high-risk women such as those with previous VTE; a score of 2 indicates at least 10 days.

11.q: At a planned home birth, Nadia, 30, is 6 cm dilated. Her pulse is 124 bpm and, 20 minutes later, 126 bpm. Her temperature and blood pressure are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange transfer to an obstetric unit
Offer oral fluids and continue at home
Recheck her pulse in one hour
Transfer if her temperature rises
11.w: NG235 1.8.20 lists maternal pulse over 120 bpm on 2 occasions 15 to 30 minutes apart as an indication to transfer to obstetric-led care. Here the readings 20 minutes apart are both over 120, so the midwife should arrange transfer.

n.1: Hydration may help, but it does not change the need to transfer once the pulse criterion is met.
n.2: Two readings over 120 bpm taken 15 to 30 minutes apart already meet the transfer criterion (NG235 1.8.20).
n.3: Tachycardia is itself a transfer trigger; waiting for fever delays care for possible sepsis or bleeding.

11.q: Sara, 30, attends a preconception appointment and asks why she should start folic acid 400 micrograms before trying to conceive rather than waiting for a positive pregnancy test. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: The placenta cannot transfer folate until the end of the first trimester
The neural tube closes at about 12 weeks, so earlier doses build up maternal stores
Folic acid mainly protects the fetus from anaemia in the third trimester
The neural tube closes about 4 weeks after conception, often before pregnancy is confirmed
11.w: The neural tube closes around day 28 after conception (about 6 weeks of gestation), when many women do not yet know they are pregnant. Folic acid 400 micrograms daily is advised when planning pregnancy and for the first 12 weeks to reduce neural tube defects (NICE NG247 1.1.3, 1.1.4; SPM 3.13.1).

n.0: Folate crosses to the embryo from early pregnancy; the reason for early dosing is the timing of neural tube closure.
n.1: The neural tube closes in the fourth week after conception, not at 12 weeks; 12 weeks is when supplementation can stop.
n.2: The purpose of periconceptional folic acid is prevention of neural tube defects, not third-trimester fetal anaemia.

11.q: Immediately after a cord prolapse that ended in a category 1 caesarean and a healthy baby, the coordinator gathers the team for a ten-minute 'hot debrief'. What is the main purpose of this debrief?
o: To agree a single account of events to give to the investigators
To check on staff wellbeing and capture learning while it is fresh
To decide which team member should complete the incident report form
To identify which team member was responsible for the delay
11.w: A hot debrief is a short, supportive team reflection soon after an event. It checks on staff wellbeing, captures what went well and what could improve, and flags issues for follow-up (SPM 5.9, 5.13.1).

n.0: Agreeing a single account undermines honest individual reporting.
n.2: Allocating paperwork is not the purpose of a debrief.
n.3: Debriefs are supportive and system-focused, not about blaming individuals.

11.q: A woman at 22 weeks has a severe haemorrhage and the obstetric consultant believes immediate termination is needed to save her life. There is no time to obtain a second opinion. Under the Abortion Act 1967, is this lawful?
o: Yes, under the emergency provision in s1(4)
No, two practitioners must agree before any termination
No, termination must take place in an approved clinic
Yes, if a senior midwife also signs the certificate
11.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(4): the requirement for two opinions, and the place requirement, do not apply where a registered medical practitioner believes in good faith that termination is immediately necessary to save the life, or prevent grave permanent injury to the physical or mental health, of the pregnant woman.

n.1: Section 1(4) removes the two-opinion requirement in an emergency.
n.2: Section 1(4) also removes the requirement for an NHS hospital or approved place.
n.3: A midwife's signature is not part of the Act's requirements.

11.q: A student midwife is learning to check babies for jaundice on the postnatal ward. Which technique reflects NICE CG98?
o: Use visual inspection of skin colour to estimate the baby's bilirubin level
Check the clothed baby's face under the cot's artificial light at night
Examine the naked baby in bright natural light, including sclerae and gums
Check the face, as jaundice not yet reaching the trunk is safe
11.w: NICE CG98 1.2.5, 1.2.6: check for jaundice with the baby naked in bright and preferably natural light; examine sclerae, gums and blanched skin, which is especially important in babies with darker skin tones. Visual inspection should not be used to estimate the bilirubin level.

n.0: CG98 advises against relying on visual inspection to estimate bilirubin levels.
n.1: Clothing and dim artificial light make jaundice harder to see.
n.3: The spread of jaundice is not a safe guide to its level; any concern needs measurement.

11.q: Abi, 34, is 27 weeks pregnant and in established preterm labour, 6 cm dilated. Her midwife is preparing for birth. Which intervention for the baby should the midwife make sure has been offered now?
o: A second course of antenatal corticosteroids
Oral erythromycin for prophylaxis against infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
Intramuscular progesterone to slow cervical change
11.w: NG25 1.10.2: offer IV magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection to women between 24+0 and 29+6 weeks who are in established preterm labour or having a planned preterm birth within 24 hours. SBL v3 5.20 sets the same standard for births under 30 weeks.

n.0: Repeat courses are avoided where possible (SBL v3 5.19) and nothing suggests she had a first course long ago.
n.1: Erythromycin is prophylaxis against infection in P-PROM; it does not protect the baby's brain before an imminent preterm birth.
n.3: Progesterone is a preventive measure started at 16 to 24 weeks, not treatment for established labour.

11.q: At the NIPE newborn examination of baby Sami, born at 39 weeks, neither testis can be palpated in the scrotum, groin or perineum. There is no hypospadias. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to paediatric urology for review at 6 months
Arrange review by a senior paediatrician within 24 hours
Refer for GP review at the 6 to 8 week infant check
Reassure the parents that the testes will descend by 1 year
11.w: NIPE handbook 15.10: bilateral impalpable testes need urgent review by a consultant paediatrician or associate specialist within 24 hours of the newborn examination, because they may indicate a disorder of sex development.

n.0: Specialist review at 6 months is too late for bilateral impalpable testes.
n.2: GP review at 6 to 8 weeks is the non-urgent pathway, used when testes are palpable but undescended without hypospadias.
n.3: Bilateral impalpable testes need urgent assessment, not reassurance.

11.q: A midwife is caring for a woman with a rare genetic condition. There is no national guideline and the local policy does not mention it. The woman is now in early labour. What is the safest approach?
o: Transfer her care to the consultant and stop providing midwifery care
Follow the standard low-risk pathway until a relevant guideline can be found
Delay any decisions until a specialist can see her the next working day
Seek senior and multidisciplinary advice, agree a plan with her and record why
11.w: When evidence or guidance is absent, safe practice means drawing on senior and multidisciplinary expertise, involving the woman in planning, and recording the reasoning (SPM 5.7, 5.13.1; Code 13.2 make a timely referral to another practitioner and 13.3 ask for help with anything beyond your competence).

n.0: Consultant involvement is appropriate, but the midwife continues to provide midwifery care alongside.
n.1: Treating a rare condition as low risk without advice may miss specific risks.
n.2: She is in labour now; waiting until the next working day is unsafe.

11.q: Megan, 30, has chosen induction of labour after an intrauterine fetal death at 38 weeks. She has had no previous caesarean birth. Which regimen does NICE NG207 recommend?
o: Artificial rupture of membranes followed by a 24-hour wait
Vaginal dinoprostone gel alone, repeated every 6 hours
Oral mifepristone 200 mg, then dinoprostone or misoprostol
Intravenous oxytocin alone from the start of the induction
11.w: NG207 1.2.31: for women choosing induced labour after intrauterine fetal death, offer oral mifepristone 200 mg followed by vaginal dinoprostone or oral or vaginal misoprostol (or a mechanical method), based on clinical circumstances and national protocols.

n.0: Artificial rupture of membranes is not the recommended first step and increases infection risk.
n.1: NG207 combines mifepristone with a prostaglandin for fetal death; dinoprostone alone is not the recommended regimen.
n.3: NG207 lists intravenous oxytocin alone among methods the evidence does not support for induction.

11.q: Chantelle, 29, has severe pre-eclampsia and the consultant has decided to start magnesium sulfate. Which regimen is recommended by NICE NG133?
o: 4 g IV over 30 minutes, then 1 g/hour until birth
2 g IV over 5 minutes, then 2 g/hour for 12 hours
4 g IM into each buttock, then 2 g/hour for 24 hours
4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours
11.w: NICE NG133 1.8.4 (Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen): a 4 g IV loading dose over 5 to 15 minutes, followed by an infusion of 1 g/hour maintained for 24 hours; after a fit, continue for 24 hours after the last fit.

n.0: The loading dose is given over 5 to 15 minutes and continues for 24 hours, not until birth.
n.1: The loading dose is 4 g and maintenance 1 g/hour for 24 hours.
n.2: NG133 uses intravenous loading and 1 g/hour maintenance, not this IM regimen.

11.q: Saskia, 27, is in established labour in an alongside midwifery unit. At 14:00 her temperature is 37.6 C and at 15:00 it is 37.7 C. Her pulse is 98 and the fetal heart is normal. Which action follows NICE guidance?
o: Transfer her to obstetric-led care for review
Give paracetamol and continue midwifery-led care
Recheck her temperature in 4 hours, as it is under 38 C
Recheck in 1 hour and transfer if it reaches 38 C
11.w: NICE NG235 1.8.20: a temperature of 38 C or above on a single reading, or 37.5 C or above on 2 consecutive occasions 1 hour apart, is a trigger for transfer to obstetric-led care. Intrapartum antibiotics follow NICE neonatal infection guidance.

n.1: Antipyretics may mask infection and do not replace transfer for review.
n.2: Two consecutive readings of 37.5 C or above 1 hour apart already meet the transfer criterion.
n.3: The 38 C single-reading threshold is not needed when the 37.5 C two-reading criterion is met.

11.q: Naomi, a midwife on a busy postnatal ward, is working with Carol, a maternity support worker who has been trained and assessed as competent in maternal observations. Which task is most appropriate for Naomi to delegate to Carol?
o: Giving the first dose of intravenous antibiotics to a woman with a fever
Assessing a perineal wound and deciding whether the woman can go home
Carrying out the newborn and infant physical examination before discharge
Recording 4-hourly observations for a well woman after a straightforward birth
11.w: Code 11.1: delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence, making sure they understand the instructions. Routine observations for a well woman are within Carol's assessed competence; assessment, clinical decision-making and IV medicines stay with registered practitioners.

n.0: Administering IV antibiotics is a registered practitioner's task and outside an MSW's scope.
n.1: Assessing a wound and making a discharge decision require a registered midwife's clinical judgement.
n.2: The newborn and infant physical examination is carried out by a trained registered practitioner, not an MSW.

11.q: Ruth, 31, received oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM for active management of the third stage. On the delivery suite, 20 minutes after the placenta is delivered complete, she bleeds heavily from an atonic uterus despite massage and an empty bladder. She has no history of asthma. According to NICE NG235, which uterotonic is appropriate next?
o: Misoprostol 200 micrograms orally
A second dose of oxytocin with ergometrine IM
Carboprost intramuscularly
Ergometrine 500 micrograms intravenously
11.w: NICE NG235 table 12: after prophylaxis with oxytocin plus ergometrine, first-line treatment for atony is carboprost IM or an oxytocin infusion. Carboprost can be repeated at intervals of at least 15 minutes, up to 8 doses (NG235 1.10.34).

n.0: NG235 lists misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually or rectally, not 200 micrograms orally.
n.1: NG235 keeps a repeat of oxytocin with ergometrine for settings where other drugs are unavailable, such as a home birth; on the delivery suite carboprost or an oxytocin infusion is first line.
n.3: Ergometrine has already been given and IV ergometrine is not the NG235 next step.

11.q: Molly, 33, is 10 days after an emergency caesarean under general anaesthetic. She tells the midwife she keeps replaying the birth, which she found frightening, and has questions about what happened. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest she requests a copy of her notes and reads them through on her own
Advise her to ask about the birth at her 6 to 8 week GP check
Give her time to talk about the birth and offer the birth reflection service
Reassure her that she and the baby are well now, so it is best to move on
11.w: NICE NG194 1.2.5: at each postnatal contact, give the woman the opportunity to talk about her birth experience and provide information about relevant support and birth reflection services. CG192 also covers care after traumatic birth.

n.0: Reading clinical notes alone without support may increase distress and does not answer her questions.
n.1: NG194 asks midwives to offer this opportunity at each contact rather than deferring it.
n.3: Dismissing her distress misses a chance to support her and identify trauma symptoms.

11.q: Ellie, 26, is having her first baby and has no risk factors. She is considering a home birth. Which information about her baby's safety is accurate according to NICE?
o: Planned home birth carries a lower risk than a midwife-led unit
Planned home birth carries a small increase in adverse outcomes for the baby
Planned home birth carries a large increase in risk and is advised against
Planned home birth carries no difference in outcome for the baby
11.w: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk nulliparous women, planning birth at home is associated with a small increase in the risk of an adverse outcome for the baby; the same recommendation says she may choose any setting and must be supported in her choice.

n.0: For nulliparous women the evidence shows a small increase at home, not a lower risk.
n.2: NG235 describes a small increase and supports her choice; it does not advise against home birth.
n.3: No difference applies to midwife-led units for nulliparous women and to home birth for multiparous women, not home birth for a first baby.

11.q: Lucy is coordinating the birth centre on a night shift. Two midwives have called in sick, leaving three women in established labour with two midwives. No bank staff are available. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the women's birth partners to call a midwife when contractions change
Escalate to the manager on call under the staffing escalation policy
Continue to manage the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Ask the two student midwives on shift to care for the third woman
11.w: Code 25.1 requires leaders to identify priorities, manage staff and resources effectively and deal with risk; Code 16.1 requires raising and escalating concerns about safety, and standard 16 to act without delay. Escalating through the staffing policy allows the manager on call to redeploy staff or divert admissions.

n.0: Relying on birth partners to monitor labour transfers a professional responsibility to people without training.
n.2: Waiting until morning delays action while women in labour are receiving unsafe staffing levels.
n.3: Students are supernumerary and must be supervised; they cannot replace a registered midwife to make up numbers.

11.q: Ellen, a registered midwife, has supervised a student midwife on four shifts this week but is not her practice assessor. Before the student moves to another area, what is Ellen's responsibility regarding documentation?
o: Leave documentation to the academic assessor at the next tripartite meeting
Record her observations of the student in the assessment document
Give verbal feedback, as written records are for the practice assessor
Sign off the proficiencies she has seen the student achieve this week
11.w: SSSA 4.1: practice supervisors contribute to the student's record of achievement by periodically recording relevant observations on conduct, proficiency and achievement. SPM 5.21 includes evaluating and documenting student performance. Confirming proficiency is the practice assessor's role (7.1).

n.0: The academic assessor relies on practice records; Ellen's observations need recording now.
n.2: Verbal feedback is valuable, but supervisors are also expected to record observations (4.1).
n.3: Signing off proficiencies is the practice assessor's assessment role (7.1), not the supervisor's.

11.q: Fatima, 29, is 16 weeks pregnant and speaks little English. She attends with her husband, who offers to interpret because he speaks English well. The midwife needs to discuss screening results and ask routine questions about domestic abuse. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange a professional interpreter, not a family member, for the appointment
Use a translation app on the midwife's phone to save waiting time
Give her written leaflets in English to take home for her husband to explain
Accept her husband's offer, as he knows her history and preferences well
11.w: CG110 1.3.10: provide an interpreter who can communicate in the woman's preferred language and who should not be a family member, legal guardian or partner. CG110 1.1.14 also requires at least one one-to-one consultation without the partner present to allow sensitive issues to be raised.

n.1: An unverified app is not a safe substitute for a professional interpreter when discussing screening results and abuse.
n.2: Leaflets in English do not meet her communication needs and still rely on her husband.
n.3: Using her husband prevents safe enquiry about domestic abuse and may filter what she says or hears.

11.q: Rosie, 26, has a mild learning disability and lives with her partner. She is going home with her baby tomorrow and the midwife needs to give her information about postnatal recovery and warning signs. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Keep information brief and leave out the warning signs
Give information in Easy Read format and check her understanding
Give the standard leaflet and ask her to sign that she has read it
Give the information to her mother, who can explain it later
11.w: NICE NG194 1.1.5 and 1.1.6: tailor the content and format of information to the woman's needs (for example Easy Read), and check that she understands it and how it relates to her. Reasonable adjustments are required under the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Warning signs are essential safety information that every woman needs (NG194 1.2.4).
n.2: A signature does not show she has understood the information.
n.3: Information should be given to Rosie herself in an accessible way; others are involved as she wishes.

11.q: A student midwife is supporting Mia, 22, to breastfeed for the first time. The baby is struggling to latch and the student is about to guide the baby's head and Mia's breast with her hands. What should the student do first?
o: Explain the technique afterwards once the baby has latched
Ask Mia's permission before giving any hands-on help
Help the baby latch quickly before the baby becomes upset
Ask Mia's partner to leave so that Mia can concentrate
11.w: NICE NG194 1.5.8: those providing breastfeeding support should obtain consent before offering physical assistance, respect the woman's personal space, cultural influences and preferences, and build her confidence. NMC Code 4.2 requires consent before any action.

n.0: Explaining after the event does not obtain consent for physical contact.
n.2: Speed does not override consent; hands-on help must be agreed first.
n.3: The partner should be involved according to Mia's wishes (NG194 1.1.3), not sent away by staff.

11.q: Olivia, a community midwife, has been Lily's practice supervisor for the first four weeks of a placement. Lily's nominated practice assessor goes on long-term sick leave and the manager asks Olivia to become Lily's practice assessor for the same placement while still supervising her. What is the correct position?
o: Olivia can take both roles for the remaining weeks of this placement
Olivia should not hold both roles for Lily at the same time
Olivia can take both roles because she knows Lily's practice best
Olivia can take both roles if the academic assessor agrees in writing
11.w: SSSA 7.10: practice assessors are not simultaneously the practice supervisor and academic assessor for the same student. Holding both roles at the same time removes the separation between supporting learning and assessing it.

n.0: The separation applies throughout the period the roles are held, including the rest of this placement.
n.2: Knowing the student well is why supervisor feedback informs assessment (7.2), but the roles must still be held by different people.
n.3: The standards contain no written-agreement exception to the separation in 7.10.

11.q: Chloe, a specialist diabetes midwife, wants to interview women with gestational diabetes about cultural beliefs around diet, aiming to develop a theory that could be transferred to other maternity services. She plans to start next month. Which governance step is most appropriate before she begins?
o: Register it as a service evaluation with the maternity governance lead
Register it with the clinical audit department and start next month
Start interviews once women give verbal consent, as there is no intervention
Treat it as research and apply for HRA and NHS ethics committee approval
11.w: Chloe aims to generate new, transferable knowledge, which meets the UK Policy Framework definition of research (para 3.1), including non-interventional qualitative research. Research normally requires NHS REC review, arranged through HRA approval; audit and service evaluation do not (HRA defining research table).

n.0: Service evaluation judges a local service without seeking transferable findings; Chloe's aim takes it into research.
n.1: It is not an audit: there is no standard being measured, and the purpose is new transferable knowledge.
n.2: Non-interventional research is still research under the policy framework; the absence of an intervention does not remove the need for ethical review and written informed consent processes.

11.q: Ellen, a midwife, has a conscientious objection to abortion. She is the only midwife available when a woman bleeds heavily after a medical termination and needs urgent care to prevent grave injury. What must Ellen do?
o: Provide the care, as her objection does not cover this situation
Provide care once the woman confirms the termination is complete
Wait for a midwife without an objection to arrive
Refuse, as her objection covers all care related to termination
11.w: Abortion Act 1967 s4(2): conscientious objection does not affect any duty to take part in treatment necessary to save the life or prevent grave permanent injury to the pregnant woman. Code 4.4 and 15 also apply.

n.1: Making care depend on confirmation delays emergency treatment that s4(2) requires.
n.2: Waiting risks the woman's life; the s4(2) exception requires Ellen to act.
n.3: Section 4(2) keeps the duty to take part in treatment needed to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.

11.q: Mei, 35, is 12 weeks pregnant and attends her booking appointment. She lists two prescribed medicines from her GP. The midwife is completing her medicines history. Which further step is most important to make the history complete and safe?
o: Ask her to bring her tablets to the 16-week appointment
Record the prescribed medicines and recheck them at 28 weeks
Ask about over the counter, herbal and supplement products
Ask the GP practice to fax the repeat prescription list
11.w: A full medicines history includes over the counter, herbal and supplement products as well as prescribed medicines, because these can interact or be unsafe in pregnancy. Code 18.3 requires care to be compatible with other treatment, including (where possible) over the counter medicines; SPM 3.18 covers polypharmacy and over the counter use.

n.0: Delaying to 16 weeks leaves the history incomplete at booking when it is needed.
n.1: Waiting until 28 weeks leaves non-prescribed products unchecked through organogenesis.
n.3: Confirming the repeat list adds nothing about non-prescribed products, which are the gap in this history.

11.q: Sian, 29, is 3 days postnatal at home after a second-degree tear and reports perineal pain not relieved by paracetamol. She has no contraindications to NSAIDs. Which medicine can the registered midwife supply to her under the midwives exemptions?
o: Co-codamol 30/500 tablets
Diclofenac tablets
Amoxicillin capsules
Dihydrocodeine tablets
11.w: Schedule 17 Part 1 allows registered midwives to sell or supply, in the course of their professional practice, prescription-only medicines containing diclofenac, hydrocortisone acetate, miconazole, nystatin and phytomenadione (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Co-codamol 30/500 contains codeine, which is not on the midwives supply list.
n.2: Antibiotics such as amoxicillin are not on the midwives supply list and need a prescription.
n.3: Dihydrocodeine is not on the midwives supply list.

11.q: Yasmin, 32, is in labour at term with a previous caesarean. Continuous CTG is recommended, but she declines it. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Apply the CTG anyway as she has a uterine scar
Ask the registrar to apply the CTG while the midwife reassures her
Stop monitoring the baby until she agrees to the CTG
Explain why, offer intermittent auscultation and document it
11.w: SPM 1.21: respect the right to decline and provide appropriate care. The midwife explains why continuous monitoring is advised (NICE NG229 for women with a previous caesarean), offers an alternative such as intermittent auscultation and documents the discussion.

n.0: Applying monitoring she has declined is treatment without consent.
n.1: Applying the CTG through another clinician is still monitoring without consent.
n.2: Stopping monitoring removes all fetal assessment; she should be offered an acceptable alternative.

11.q: After shoulder dystocia was resolved by McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, the midwife is completing the documentation for Olivia, 36. Which detail is especially important to include alongside the times and manoeuvres?
o: The colour of the liquor when the membranes ruptured
Which of the baby's shoulders was anterior
The time of her last vaginal examination before birth
Her pain score during the second stage of labour
11.w: Documentation after shoulder dystocia should include time of birth of the head and body, the anterior shoulder, the manoeuvres used with their timing and sequence, staff present and their arrival times, the condition of the baby and cord blood gases (RCOG GTG 42). The anterior shoulder is linked to the side of any brachial plexus injury.

n.0: Liquor colour is recorded in labour but is not a key shoulder dystocia record.
n.2: The last vaginal examination time is routine labour documentation, not specific to this emergency.
n.3: Pain scores may be recorded but are not a key element of shoulder dystocia documentation.

11.q: Ayesha, 29, has chronic kidney disease and attends for booking at 10 weeks. Her blood pressure is normal. The midwife identifies that she is at high risk of pre-eclampsia. What advice about aspirin is in line with NICE NG133?
o: Take aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 20 weeks until 36 weeks
Take aspirin 300 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth
Take aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from booking until 28 weeks
Take aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth
11.w: NICE NG133 1.1.2: women at high risk of pre-eclampsia (including chronic kidney disease) are advised to take aspirin 75 mg to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth. For this indication aspirin must be prescribed rather than bought.

n.0: Aspirin starts at 12 weeks, not 20, and continues until the birth.
n.1: The recommended dose is 75 to 150 mg, not 300 mg.
n.2: Aspirin continues until the birth rather than stopping at 28 weeks.

11.q: Lucy and Sarah are a married couple expecting their first baby; Lucy is pregnant. At a postnatal visit, the midwife is completing the newborn records. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask the couple how they each wish to be named and involved
Record Sarah as 'friend' until parental responsibility is confirmed
Record Sarah as 'partner' and ask Lucy to answer all questions
Address questions about the baby to Lucy as the birth mother
11.w: SPM 1.10 and Code 1.3: avoid assumptions, recognise diversity and involve partners and family as the woman wishes. Asking how the couple wish to be named and involved is respectful and person-centred.

n.1: Recording a spouse and co-parent as 'friend' is inaccurate and disrespectful; the couple's own description of their relationship should guide the record.
n.2: Directing everything to Lucy excludes Sarah, who is a parent, without asking the couple's wishes.
n.3: Directing questions to the birth mother alone assumes their roles without asking them.

11.q: A continuity team of six midwives covers its own women in labour on call. One midwife has worked a 13-hour day and is called at 03:00 to a woman in early labour. A second team midwife is available and rested. Which action best balances continuity and safety?
o: Advise the woman to attend the labour ward and be seen by core staff
Ask the rested team midwife, known to the woman, to attend the call
Delay the visit until 07:00 when the midwife has rested for four hours
Attend the call herself because the woman expects her named midwife
11.w: Continuity models work through small teams so a known midwife is available; safety and staff wellbeing must be protected (Code 13 work within limits of competence; NHS England 2022 on safe staffing). A rested team colleague keeps continuity and safety.

n.0: Sending her to an unknown team when a known, rested team member is free loses continuity without any safety gain.
n.2: Delaying assessment of a woman in labour for staff convenience is unsafe and could miss progress or complications.
n.3: Working fatigued after a 13-hour shift risks unsafe care; Code 13 and safe staffing take priority over seeing the named midwife.

11.q: Rhian, 27, is on continuous CTG in labour. The baseline is 135, variability is 10 beats per minute and contractions are 3 in 10. For the last 15 minutes there have been late decelerations with each contraction. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Pathological, needing urgent obstetric and senior midwife review
Suspicious, needing review if they continue for 30 minutes
Normal, as baseline and variability are reassuring
Suspicious, as the decelerations have lasted under 30 minutes
11.w: Late decelerations are a red feature regardless of how long they have been present (NICE NG229 1.4.24, amended 2025). Any red feature makes the CTG pathological (1.4.32), requiring urgent review by an obstetrician and senior midwife, exclusion of acute events and conservative measures (1.5.7).

n.1: Late decelerations are red at any duration, so the trace is already pathological.
n.2: Reassuring baseline and variability do not offset a red feature.
n.3: The 30-minute timing applies to variable decelerations with concerning characteristics, not late decelerations.

11.q: Bella, 29, is 14 weeks pregnant in England and requests a termination because continuing the pregnancy is affecting her mental health. Under the Abortion Act 1967 s1, how many registered medical practitioners must form the opinion that a ground is met?
o: One doctor and one midwife
Three
One
Two
11.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(1): a pregnancy may be lawfully terminated by a registered medical practitioner when two registered medical practitioners are of the opinion, formed in good faith, that a ground in s1(1)(a) to (d) applies.

n.0: The opinions must be those of two registered medical practitioners; a midwife's opinion does not count towards them.
n.1: The Act requires two, not three, practitioners.
n.2: One practitioner is enough in an emergency under s1(4), which does not apply here.

11.q: Rebecca, a midwife, took a career break and has practised for 200 hours in the three years since she last renewed her registration. Her revalidation date is next year. What must she do to renew?
o: Make up the missing hours by extra CPD before renewal
Renew now and complete the remaining hours during the next cycle
Complete a return to practice programme or Test of Competence
Ask her confirmer to sign that her hours are sufficient
11.w: NMC practice hours requirement: a registrant who has not practised the minimum hours (450 for a midwife) must successfully complete an approved return to practice programme or a Test of Competence before applying to renew.

n.0: CPD hours are a separate requirement and cannot replace practice hours.
n.1: Hours cannot be carried forward; the requirement must be met before the date of the renewal application.
n.3: The confirmer cannot certify hours that were not worked; the shortfall needs a return to practice route.

11.q: Lauren, 28, is 30 weeks pregnant. She has a burning feeling behind her breastbone after large meals and when lying down at night. BP is 112/70 mmHg, urinalysis shows no protein, and she has no headache or visual symptoms. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Refer her to the day assessment unit to exclude pre-eclampsia
Ask her GP to arrange an urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Give lifestyle and diet advice and consider an antacid or alginate
Advise her to stop eating after 4 pm until the baby is born
11.w: This is typical heartburn with normal BP and urine. NICE NG201 1.4.8 and 1.4.9: give lifestyle and dietary advice and consider a trial of an antacid or alginate.

n.0: Her BP and urine are normal and the pain is typical reflux, so urgent pre-eclampsia assessment is not needed on these facts.
n.1: Endoscopy is not indicated for typical pregnancy heartburn without red flags.
n.3: Fasting from mid-afternoon is not recommended; smaller meals and not eating close to bedtime are the usual advice.

11.q: Precious, 33, is giving birth on a midwife-led unit. The baby's head has been born but has retracted tightly against the perineum, and the shoulders have not delivered with the next contraction and routine axial traction. What is the midwife's first action?
o: Perform an episiotomy to make more room for the shoulders
Ask Precious to push harder with the next contraction
Call for help, stating that this is shoulder dystocia
Apply firm downward traction to the baby's head
11.w: Retraction of the head (turtle sign) and failure of routine axial traction to deliver the shoulders indicate shoulder dystocia. The first step is to call for help, clearly stating the emergency, so manoeuvres can begin with the right team present (RCOG GTG 42; SPM 4.7).

n.0: Shoulder dystocia is a bony problem; episiotomy is not the first action and is not needed in every case.
n.1: Maternal pushing alone will not release an impacted shoulder and can worsen the impaction.
n.3: Downward or excessive traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury and is avoided.

11.q: Baby Ellis was born at term after significant meconium-stained liquor and is being observed on the postnatal ward. At 2 hours the midwife finds a respiratory rate of 70 breaths/min with grunting. Heart rate is 140 beats/min. What should the midwife do?
o: Encourage a breastfeed and recheck after the feed
Wrap the baby and recheck in 30 minutes
Recheck the respiratory rate at the 4-hour observation
Call the neonatal team for urgent review
11.w: NICE NG235 1.11.29: after meconium, escalate to a neonatal clinician if respiratory rate is over 60, there is grunting, heart rate under 100 or over 160, capillary refill over 3 seconds, temperature 38 C or above, saturation under 95% or central cyanosis (SPM 4.6 deterioration in the newborn).

n.0: Feeding a baby with respiratory distress risks aspiration and delays review.
n.1: Warming does not treat respiratory distress and delays review.
n.2: Two red flags (RR over 60 and grunting) need review now, not at the next observation.

11.q: Nicole, 32, is 22 weeks pregnant. Her first birth 3 years ago was an emergency caesarean under general anaesthetic. She describes nightmares and flashbacks about it, avoids driving past the hospital and feels panic when thinking about this birth. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Book an elective caesarean so she does not have to face labour again
Arrange mental health assessment, as these features suggest possible PTSD
Reassure her that fear of birth is normal and will pass after this baby
Advise her to avoid talking about the previous birth to reduce distress
11.w: Nightmares, flashbacks and avoidance suggest post-traumatic stress disorder after a traumatic birth. She needs assessment through her GP or perinatal mental health service so that treatment such as trauma-focused psychological therapy can be offered (NICE CG192; NG201 1.2.10 on discussing previous traumatic birth).

n.0: Mode of birth is discussed with an obstetrician as part of her plan, but it does not treat the underlying trauma symptoms.
n.2: These symptoms go beyond normal fear of birth and need assessment rather than reassurance.
n.3: Avoidance is a symptom of PTSD; discouraging discussion does not help recovery.

11.q: Ola, 33, is on continuous CTG in established labour. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes, the baseline is 140 beats per minute and there are no decelerations. Variability has been 3 to 4 beats per minute for the last 40 minutes. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Suspicious
Normal
Need for urgent intervention
Pathological
11.w: Variability under 5 beats per minute for 30 to 50 minutes is an amber feature (NICE NG229 1.4.18). Contractions, baseline and decelerations are white. One amber feature makes the CTG suspicious (NG229 1.4.32), prompting a full risk assessment and conservative measures.

n.1: A normal CTG has all four features white; reduced variability for 40 minutes is amber.
n.2: NG229 uses normal, suspicious and pathological; this is not one of its categories.
n.3: Pathological needs one red feature or two or more amber features; there is one amber feature.

11.q: After a baby sustains a brachial plexus injury, the midwife who was present wants to apologise to the parents but worries that saying sorry will be treated as admitting negligence. Which statement is accurate?
o: An apology is an admission of liability, so legal advice comes first
An apology may be given once the trust's investigation has ended
An apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence
An apology should come from the consultant rather than the midwife
11.w: Compensation Act 2006 s2: an apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty. Code 14.2 requires explaining fully and promptly and apologising.

n.0: An apology does not by itself admit liability (Compensation Act 2006 s2), so it should not be delayed for legal advice.
n.1: Code 14.2 requires a prompt apology; it should not wait for the investigation's outcome.
n.3: Every professional has the duty of candour under Code 14; the midwife may apologise herself.

11.q: On day 15 the community midwife completes postnatal care for Erin, 33, and her baby. Which information about ongoing care is most accurate to give Erin?
o: Her midwife will return at 6 weeks for a final postnatal check
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 6 to 8 weeks
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 2 weeks
Her health visitor will complete her own postnatal check at 6 to 8 weeks
11.w: NG194 1.2.7: the woman should have a GP review of her health 6 to 8 weeks after birth. On completing midwifery care the midwife transfers care to the health visitor and GP (SPM 2.11).

n.0: Midwifery care has ended at transfer; the midwife does not routinely return at 6 weeks.
n.2: 2 weeks is not the routine maternal check; the GP check is at 6 to 8 weeks (NG194 1.2.7).
n.3: The maternal 6 to 8 week check is by the GP; health visitors follow the Healthy Child Programme.

11.q: Bella, 31, has prelabour rupture of membranes at 40 weeks and chooses expectant management at home. Which advice is most appropriate while she waits for labour?
o: Attend daily for a vaginal swab and a C-reactive protein blood test
Take her temperature 4-hourly while awake and report changes in loss
Insert a fresh tampon every 4 hours to monitor the colour of the liquor
Avoid baths and showers, as bathing increases the risk of infection
11.w: NICE NG235 1.7.8: advise her to record her temperature every 4 hours during waking hours and to report immediately any change in the colour or smell of her vaginal loss; bathing or showering is not associated with increased infection, but sexual intercourse may be. Fetal movements and heart rate are assessed every 24 hours (1.7.9).

n.0: NICE advises against lower vaginal swabs and CRP during expectant management.
n.2: Tampons should not be used after rupture of membranes; a pad allows liquor to be observed.
n.3: Bathing and showering are not associated with an increase in infection.

11.q: Bethan, 26, is having an unexpected breech birth on a midwife-led unit. The baby was born to the umbilicus 4 minutes ago with no further progress over the last 2 contractions. The baby looks pale and has poor tone. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Assist the birth with manoeuvres, without traction
Ask Bethan to stand up and walk to aid descent
Apply firm traction to the baby's pelvis to deliver the shoulders
Wait for 2 more contractions as the mother is still pushing
11.w: RCOG GTG 20b: intervention to expedite breech birth is required if there is poor fetal condition or delay of more than 3 minutes from umbilicus to head (or 5 minutes from buttocks to head). Assistance is given without traction, using manoeuvres to release arms and deliver the head.

n.1: Changing position by walking is not the response to delay with a compromised baby.
n.2: Traction risks extension of the arms and head; manoeuvres are used without traction.
n.3: With poor tone and over 3 minutes since the umbilicus, waiting increases the risk of hypoxia.

11.q: Before transfer home on day 1, Jo, 27, says breastfeeding is going well. The midwife has not yet observed a feed. What does NICE recommend before transfer?
o: Observe at least one effective feed as part of the feeding plan
Give a formula top-up so the baby is settled for the journey
Weigh the baby to confirm feeding is effective
