Accept Jo's report and arrange a feed check on day 5
11.w: NG194 1.1.10: before transfer, make sure there is a plan for feeding the baby, including observing at least 1 effective feed; NG194 1.5.14 lists what to assess (SPM 3.6).

n.1: A top-up without clinical need can undermine breastfeeding.
n.2: Weight on day 1 does not show feeding effectiveness; normal weight loss occurs early.
n.3: NICE expects an effective feed to be observed before transfer.

11.q: Natalie, 35, is having a planned caesarean for her fourth baby and asks for sterilisation at the same time. Her husband tells the midwife he does not agree. Natalie has capacity and has received full counselling. Whose consent is legally needed?
o: Natalie's and her husband's
Natalie's alone
Natalie's, with a second consultant's approval
Her husband's, as it affects the family
11.w: An adult with capacity consents to treatment on her own body; no spouse or partner consent is required. This upholds her sexual and reproductive rights (SPM 1.3) and Article 8.

n.0: A husband has no legal right to consent or veto treatment on his wife's body.
n.2: No second consultant approval is required for sterilisation in an adult with capacity.
n.3: A spouse cannot consent for a woman who has capacity.

11.q: A labour ward midwife notices that the nitrous oxide and oxygen (Entonox) supply in empty rooms is often left connected and that a regulator has a faint hiss. In the context of sustainable healthcare, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the hiss in the ward diary for the next equipment check
Report the leak, and turn off supplies in rooms not in use
Leave the supply connected so it is ready for the next woman
Advise women to use pethidine instead of Entonox to reduce emissions
11.w: Nitrous oxide is a potent greenhouse gas and much is lost through leaks in piped systems. Reporting leaks and avoiding waste reduces environmental harm without restricting women's choice of analgesia (SPM 5.10, 5.13.3).

n.0: Waiting for a routine check leaves a known leak releasing gas.
n.2: Leaving supplies connected in empty rooms increases waste and does not deal with the leak.
n.3: Women's choice of pain relief should not be restricted; the aim is to cut waste, not to deny Entonox.

11.q: Aisha, 30, is 33 weeks pregnant on the low-risk pathway. Her symphysis fundal height today plots below the 10th centile on her growth chart; two weeks ago it was on the 40th centile. She reports normal fetal movements. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remeasure the fundal height at her next routine appointment
Refer her for an ultrasound assessment of fetal growth
Reassure her because the fetal movements are normal
Ask a colleague to remeasure and record the higher of the two values
11.w: A fundal height plotting below the 10th centile, or a drop across centiles, is an indication for an ultrasound growth assessment. SBL v3 2.11 requires staff measuring SFH to interpret and refer when indicated, and 2.14 sets the assessment of wellbeing once FGR is suspected.

n.0: Waiting for the next routine visit delays detection of possible FGR, a major risk factor for stillbirth.
n.2: Normal movements do not exclude growth restriction; the measurement still needs investigating.
n.3: Choosing the higher of two readings is unsafe and does not address the fall across centiles.

11.q: Chloe, 24, is 34 weeks pregnant with pre-eclampsia. On the antenatal ward she reports a severe frontal headache and seeing spots. Her blood pressure is 168/112 mmHg and she has three beats of ankle clonus. What is the most appropriate immediate action by the midwife?
o: Give oral paracetamol for the headache and recheck her blood pressure in one hour
Call the obstetric team urgently and prepare magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive treatment
Prepare diazepam for seizure prophylaxis and start intravenous fluids at 125 mL/hour
Increase her blood pressure checks to every four hours and repeat her bloods tomorrow
11.w: Severe hypertension with severe headache, visual disturbance and clonus are features of severe pre-eclampsia. NG133 1.8.3 advises considering IV magnesium sulfate when there are severe features, and severe hypertension needs urgent antihypertensive treatment (1.8.6) with BP every 15 to 30 minutes until below 160/110. The midwife's role is to escalate immediately and prepare.

n.0: Treating the headache symptomatically and waiting an hour delays treatment of a woman at imminent risk of eclampsia or stroke.
n.2: NG133 1.8.5 advises against diazepam as an alternative to magnesium sulfate, and maintenance fluids should be limited to 80 mL/hour (1.8.12).
n.3: Four-hourly checks are far too infrequent with severe hypertension; NG133 advises every 15 to 30 minutes until BP is under 160/110 mmHg.

12.q: Lin, 33, is hepatitis B positive. Her baby has just been born at term and is well. When should the baby receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine?
o: Within 7 days of birth
Within 24 hours of birth
After the newborn blood spot test on day 5
At 8 weeks with the routine vaccines
12.w: Green Book ch 18: babies born to hepatitis B positive mothers should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, within 24 hours (with hepatitis B immunoglobulin if indicated), then further doses.

n.0: The first dose should be given as soon as possible and within 24 hours.
n.2: Waiting until day 5 delays protection and is not linked to blood spot screening.
n.3: Babies of hepatitis B positive mothers need a dose at birth; 8 weeks is too late to prevent transmission.

12.q: Megan, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant and has just had her anomaly scan. She asks when she should have the whooping cough vaccine. What should the midwife advise?
o: Now, as it is given from 16 weeks and ideally before 32 weeks
At 28 weeks, as it is given with the RSV vaccine
After the birth, as it protects the baby through breastfeeding
At 36 weeks, as protection is highest closer to the birth
12.w: Green Book ch 24: pertussis vaccine can be given from 16 weeks, usually around the mid-pregnancy scan (about 20 weeks), ideally before 32 weeks for best passive protection of the baby.

n.1: Pertussis vaccine can be given from 16 weeks; there is no need to wait until 28 weeks.
n.2: Vaccination in pregnancy gives passive antibody protection to the baby before birth.
n.3: Vaccination ideally before 32 weeks gives better passive protection for the baby.

12.q: Baby Finn was discharged home at 8 hours of age before his newborn hearing screen was done. His parents ask when it can still be carried out. What should the midwife tell them?
o: At the 6 to 8 week GP infant examination
Within 72 hours, at the same time as the NIPE newborn examination
At 12 months, alongside his routine vaccinations
Ideally in the first 4 weeks, but it can be done up to 3 months
12.w: NHS newborn hearing screening (Screening tests for you and your baby): the automated otoacoustic emission (AOAE) screen is ideally done in the first 4 weeks but can be done up to 3 months of age.

n.0: Hearing screening is a separate programme and is not part of the GP 6 to 8 week check.
n.1: Hearing screening is not tied to the 72-hour NIPE deadline and can be done later.
n.2: 12 months is far beyond the 3-month screening window.

12.q: Mia, 31, is 37 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated pregnancy and plans to give birth in an alongside midwifery unit. She asks who is in charge of her care. Who is her lead professional?
o: Her named midwife
A consultant obstetrician
The labour ward coordinator
Her GP
12.w: For women with uncomplicated pregnancies the midwife is the accountable, autonomous lead professional across the continuum of care (NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives 1.6).

n.1: Obstetric lead care is for women with complications or additional needs, which Mia does not have.
n.2: The coordinator manages the unit's workload; she is not the lead professional for an individual woman's care.
n.3: The GP is not the lead professional for routine maternity care in an uncomplicated pregnancy.

12.q: Sophie, 28, is in established labour in a midwifery-led unit and is coping well with her partner present. The unit is busy and her midwife is asked to help another woman for 40 minutes. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Leave Sophie with the call bell and check on her every 15 minutes
Stay with Sophie and ask the coordinator to find support elsewhere
Ask a maternity support worker to stay with Sophie while she is away
Leave Sophie with her partner, as a birth companion is present
12.w: NICE NG235 1.4.5 and 1.4.6: services should support one-to-one care in labour, and a woman in established labour should not be left alone except for short periods or at her request. Escalating staffing pressure to the coordinator is the appropriate response.

n.0: Leaving her for 40 minutes with periodic checks is not one-to-one care.
n.2: A support worker cannot provide the midwifery care, assessment and monitoring needed in established labour.
n.3: A birth companion does not replace one-to-one midwifery care in established labour.

12.q: Imogen, 29, is 35 weeks pregnant and has pre-eclampsia. She presents with constant severe abdominal pain and a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. Her uterus feels hard and is tender all over, and she looks pale and clammy. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Placenta praevia
Onset of normal labour
Placental abruption
Cervical ectropion
12.w: RCOG GTG 63: abruption should be considered when pain is continuous; a tense, 'woody' uterus indicates a significant abruption. Visible loss may underestimate concealed bleeding, so maternal signs of shock can be out of proportion. Pre-eclampsia is a risk factor (SPM 4.3).

n.0: Placenta praevia typically causes painless bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus.
n.1: Labour pain is intermittent with relaxation between contractions, not a constantly hard uterus.
n.3: A cervical ectropion causes painless spotting with a soft uterus and no shock.

12.q: Baby Tom, 3.2 kg, is prescribed an intravenous antibiotic at 5 mg/kg. The vial contains 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up?
o: 3.2 mL
1.6 mL
16 mL
12.w: Dose = 5 mg/kg x 3.2 kg = 16 mg. Volume = 16 mg / 10 mg per mL = 1.6 mL. Accurate numeracy for safe practice is part of SPM 1.23.

n.0: 3.2 mL would give 32 mg, double the prescribed dose.
n.1: 0.16 mL is a tenfold underdose (16 divided by 100 instead of 10).
n.3: 16 mL confuses the dose in mg with the volume in mL, a tenfold overdose.

12.q: Kayleigh, 25, is 8 weeks pregnant and attends her booking appointment. She tells the midwife for the first time that she uses cocaine most weekends and drinks heavily. She is anxious and asks whether this will be reported. Which response is most appropriate first?
o: Make a referral to the police because she has disclosed illegal drug use
Offer referral to a substance misuse service and explain how care is coordinated
Tell her the booking cannot continue until she has stopped using any drugs
Record the disclosure and plan to discuss it again at the 28-week visit
12.w: NICE CG110 1.2.7: the first time a woman who misuses substances discloses that she is pregnant, offer referral to an appropriate substance misuse programme. Care is coordinated across agencies (1.2.2, 1.2.3) with a named midwife or doctor (1.2.4), and staff attitudes should not deter her from using services (1.2.1).

n.0: Drug use disclosed in a health consultation is not a police matter; the concern is her and her baby's health and wellbeing.
n.2: Making care conditional on abstinence creates a barrier that CG110 1.2.1 asks staff to overcome.
n.3: Delaying discussion until 28 weeks wastes months of potential support and treatment.

12.q: A team holds a multidisciplinary meeting each month where staff reflect on recent cases, including those that went well, and agree changes to practice. Which statement best describes the value of this activity?
o: Shared reflection helps the whole team learn and improve the service
It replaces the need to report incidents through the formal system
It is mainly a way to identify staff who need performance management
It satisfies mandatory training requirements for every attendee
12.w: Team reflection activities promote shared learning and improvements in practice and services (SPM 5.9). They complement, not replace, formal incident reporting.

n.1: Incidents must still be reported through the formal system.
n.2: The purpose is learning and improvement, not performance management.
n.3: Reflective meetings are not a substitute for mandatory training.

12.q: Lily, 24, is 28 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. Her BP and urinalysis are normal. The midwife is giving her information about pre-eclampsia. Which advice is most accurate?
o: Seek help immediately for severe headache, blurred vision or pain below the ribs
Seek help if she has heartburn after large meals that settles with an antacid
Wait for her next appointment to mention new headaches, as BP is checked then
Seek help if her ankles swell by evening and settle overnight with feet raised
12.w: NICE NG133 1.1.1: advise pregnant women to see a healthcare professional immediately if they have symptoms of pre-eclampsia: severe headache, problems with vision such as blurring or flashing, severe pain just below the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet.

n.1: Heartburn relieved by antacids is a common symptom; severe pain just below the ribs is the warning sign.
n.2: New severe headache needs immediate assessment; waiting for a routine appointment could delay diagnosis.
n.3: Gradual dependent ankle swelling that resolves overnight is common in pregnancy; it is sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet that is a warning sign.

12.q: Emma, 33, is 36+5 weeks pregnant. A scan has confirmed an uncomplicated singleton breech presentation. After discussion of the options she says she would prefer to have a vaginal birth with the baby head down if possible. What should be offered?
o: External cephalic version
A planned vaginal breech birth
Induction of labour at 37 weeks
A repeat scan at 40 weeks
12.w: NICE NG201 1.2.38: for an uncomplicated singleton breech confirmed after 36+0 weeks, discuss ECV, vaginal breech birth and elective caesarean, and offer ECV to women who prefer cephalic vaginal birth.

n.1: Vaginal breech birth is one option, but she wants a head-down birth, which ECV aims to achieve.
n.2: Induction is not generally recommended for a breech baby (NG207 1.2.21) and does not turn the baby.
n.3: Waiting for a repeat scan delays ECV, which is offered from 36+0 weeks when the woman wishes.

12.q: Baby Isla is born at 28 weeks in the delivery suite. The room is warm and the resuscitaire heater is on. How should the midwife manage her temperature immediately after birth?
o: Place her skin-to-skin and cover both with a warm towel
Put her body into a plastic bag without drying, and add a hat
Give her a warm bath to bring her temperature up quickly
Dry her thoroughly and wrap her in a dry warm towel
12.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: for babies under 32 weeks, dry the head, put on a hat and place the body in a plastic (polyethylene) bag without drying, under a radiant heater; aim to keep temperature 36.5 to 37.5 C. Babies of 32 weeks or more are dried and wet towels removed.

n.0: A 28-week baby needs a plastic bag under a radiant heater and is likely to need stabilisation.
n.2: Bathing causes heat loss and is not part of newborn resuscitation.
n.3: Drying and wrapping is for babies of 32 weeks or more.

12.q: Rosie, 29, has a 3-month-old baby and has used the lactational amenorrhoea method so far. She has now started giving a formula feed at night so her partner can help. What should the midwife advise?
o: Continue LAM, adding condoms when the baby reaches 6 months
Continue LAM until her periods return
Start another method, as LAM is no longer reliable
Continue LAM, as her baby is under 6 months old
12.w: LAM is reliable only if the baby is under 6 months, the woman is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding and she has no periods. Giving formula, stopping night feeds or longer intervals between feeds mean another method should be used (NHS; FSRH).

n.0: She needs another method now because she is giving formula.
n.1: Return of periods is one trigger, but giving formula also ends LAM reliability.
n.3: LAM relies on exclusive or near-exclusive breastfeeding, which has stopped.

12.q: Nadia, a midwife, realises she has given Ms Cole, 6 hours after birth, a second dose of an oral analgesic 2 hours early. Ms Cole is resting comfortably. What should Nadia do first?
o: Assess Ms Cole and seek medical advice
Complete an incident report on the trust system
Explain the error to Ms Cole and apologise
Tell the ward manager about the error
12.w: NMC Code 14.1: act immediately to put right the situation if harm has occurred or could occur. Assessing the woman and getting advice comes first; then explain and apologise (14.2), document and escalate (14.3), and report the incident.

n.1: Reporting matters but comes after making the woman safe.
n.2: Candour with Ms Cole is required promptly, but after checking she is safe and getting advice on any treatment.
n.3: The manager must be told, but assessing the woman's safety is the immediate priority.

12.q: A midwife is assessing four babies on the postnatal ward. Using NICE CG98, which baby has the most risk factors for developing significant hyperbilirubinaemia?
o: Born at 41 weeks; mixed feeding; first child with no siblings
Born at 36 weeks; sibling had phototherapy; exclusive breastfeeding planned
Born at 38+2 weeks; formula fed; mother had gestational diabetes
Born at 39 weeks by caesarean; formula fed; no family history of jaundice
12.w: NICE CG98 1.2.1 risk factors: gestational age under 38 weeks, a previous sibling who needed phototherapy, mother's intention to breastfeed exclusively, and visible jaundice in the first 24 hours. The baby born at 36 weeks has three of these factors.

n.0: 41 weeks with mixed feeding and no sibling history gives no CG98 risk factors.
n.2: 38+2 weeks is not under 38 weeks, and formula feeding is not a risk factor.
n.3: Caesarean birth and formula feeding at 39 weeks are not CG98 risk factors.

12.q: Grace, 29, receives her combined screening result: a 1 in 2,400 chance of Down's syndrome and a 1 in 10,000 chance of Edwards' or Patau's syndrome. She asks whether she should have more tests. What is the most accurate explanation?
o: This is a higher-chance result, so NIPT should be offered next
This result excludes chromosomal conditions, so the 20-week scan is unnecessary
This is a lower-chance result, so no further screening for these conditions is offered
This result is borderline, so a quadruple test should be offered at 16 weeks
12.w: FASP: results of 1 in 151 or lower chance are lower-chance results and no further screening for these conditions is offered. She should still be offered the 20-week anomaly scan, which screens for a different set of physical conditions.

n.0: A higher-chance result is 1 in 2 to 1 in 150; 1 in 2,400 is well below that.
n.1: A lower-chance result does not exclude a condition, and the 20-week scan screens for 11 other physical conditions.
n.3: There is no borderline category leading to a quadruple test after a combined test result.

12.q: Sophie, 28, wants a water birth in the alongside midwifery unit but is also keen to have the option of an epidural. What information should the midwife give her?
o: An epidural would mean transfer to the obstetric unit on the same site
An epidural can be sited in the midwifery unit by the on-call anaesthetist
An epidural can be given if she leaves the pool for 2 hours first
An epidural is not available to women who planned a midwife-led birth
12.w: NG235 1.6.26: regional analgesia is available only in obstetric units. When planning place of birth women should be told which analgesia is available in each setting, and that an epidural in a midwife-led setting requires transfer.

n.1: Epidurals are available in obstetric units only (NG235 1.6.26).
n.2: The 2-hour rule applies to opioids before entering water, not to epidurals in a midwifery unit (NG235 1.6.20).
n.3: She can change her mind and request an epidural; it means transfer to the obstetric unit.

12.q: After a difficult shift, Freya would like confidential, restorative support to reflect on her experiences. Under the A-EQUIP model in England, who provides restorative clinical supervision for midwives?
o: The NMC fitness to practise team
Her named practice assessor
A Supervisor of Midwives (SoM)
A Professional Midwifery Advocate
12.w: A-EQUIP (advocating and educating for quality improvement), published by NHS England in 2017, replaced statutory supervision of midwives. Professional Midwifery Advocates deliver restorative clinical supervision to support midwives' wellbeing and practice.

n.0: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not provide restorative supervision.
n.1: Practice assessors assess students under the SSSA; they do not supervise qualified midwives.
n.2: Statutory supervision and the Supervisor of Midwives role were removed in 2017.

12.q: Baby Kai is born at 30 weeks in November. His mother was not vaccinated against RSV in pregnancy. Which protection against RSV is he eligible for?
o: No RSV protection, as his mother missed the vaccine
RSV vaccine at 8 weeks with his routine vaccines
RSV vaccine for his mother now, to protect him through breastfeeding
A long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody
12.w: Green Book ch 27a (June 2026): very or extremely preterm infants (born under 32 weeks) are offered a long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab or clesrovimab).

n.0: Very preterm infants are offered RSV protection directly.
n.1: The RSV vaccine is given to pregnant women, not to babies in the routine schedule.
n.2: Maternal vaccination protects the baby through placental antibody transfer in pregnancy, not breast milk after birth.

12.q: A midwife is reviewing data on inequalities to plan an outreach project. According to MBRRACE-UK 2022-24, how did the maternal mortality rate for Black women compare with that for White women?
o: Nearly three times higher
About five times higher
About the same
About twice as high
12.w: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: there was a nearly three-fold difference in maternal mortality rates for Black women compared with White women; women in the most deprived areas had twice the rate of those in the least deprived.

n.1: The 2022-24 data show a nearly three-fold, not five-fold, difference.
n.2: A large and persistent inequality was reported; the rates were not similar.
n.3: A twofold difference is the gap between the most and least deprived areas, not between Black and White women.

12.q: Toni, 32, is in established labour at a freestanding midwifery unit. Her pulse was 124 beats per minute, and 126 on repeat 20 minutes later. She is drinking and passing urine, her temperature is 37.1 C and the fetal heart is normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start intravenous fluids and continue care in the midwifery unit
Arrange transfer to obstetric-led care, explaining the reason to Toni
Continue midwifery-led care, as her temperature is normal
Encourage oral fluids and recheck her pulse in 1 hour
12.w: NICE NG235 1.8.20: a maternal pulse over 120 beats per minute on 2 occasions 15 to 30 minutes apart is a trigger for transfer to obstetric-led care, following the principles in section 1.5 (discuss reasons, obtain consent, arrange transfer as soon as possible).

n.0: Treating the pulse in the midwifery unit does not address the need for obstetric assessment.
n.2: A persistent tachycardia over 120 is a trigger on its own, whatever her temperature.
n.3: Waiting an hour delays action on a recognised transfer criterion that may indicate sepsis or haemorrhage.

12.q: Isla, 28, has epilepsy controlled on lamotrigine and is 20 weeks pregnant. She tells the midwife she has had two brief seizures this month after being seizure-free for 2 years. She has been taking every dose. What is the best explanation and action?
o: Lamotrigine absorption is blocked by her folic acid, so stop folic acid
Pregnancy slows lamotrigine metabolism, so she should miss a dose
Seizures are expected in pregnancy, so review at the next routine visit
Lamotrigine clearance rises in pregnancy, so refer for urgent review
12.w: Lamotrigine clearance increases markedly in pregnancy, so blood levels can fall and seizures return despite full adherence. Increased seizures need prompt referral to the obstetric and epilepsy team for dose review (SPM 3.18 pharmacology in pregnancy; SPM 4.3 complications). Folic acid should continue.

n.0: Folic acid does not block lamotrigine absorption and should be continued in women taking antiseizure medicines.
n.1: Clearance increases rather than slows, and missing doses would increase seizure risk further.
n.2: Increased seizures are not an expected finding to leave until a routine visit; they risk harm to woman and fetus.

12.q: Megan, 23, is 10 weeks pregnant after an unplanned conception. She tells the midwife she feels 'all over the place': sometimes excited, sometimes unsure she wants a baby, and occasionally tearful. She is sleeping and eating well and answers no to both depression identification questions. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Complete an EPDS at every appointment until 20 weeks
Refer her to the perinatal mental health service for assessment of ambivalence
Ask her GP to start an antidepressant to stabilise her mood
Explain mixed feelings are common and revisit her wellbeing at each visit
12.w: Emotional lability and ambivalence are common normal psychological responses in early pregnancy, especially when unplanned (SPM 3.17.1). With negative screening questions and normal function, she needs information and support, with mental health discussed at every contact (NICE CG192 1.5.8; NG201 1.2.10).

n.0: Routine repeated EPDS without a positive response or concern is not the recommended approach; ongoing discussion at each contact is.
n.1: Normal ambivalence without signs of a mental health problem does not need specialist referral.
n.2: There is no evidence of depression, so medication is not indicated.

12.q: Sadie, 32, is in established labour with no oxytocin. The CTG suddenly shows the fetal heart rate fall to 80 beats per minute, and it has stayed there for 3 minutes. There is no cord visible and no bleeding. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start intravenous fluids to correct presumed dehydration and recheck in 15 minutes
Give facial oxygen by mask and continue to observe the CTG for 10 minutes
Seek urgent obstetric review, start conservative measures and prepare for urgent birth
Call for obstetric review if the bradycardia is still present at 9 minutes
12.w: NICE NG229 1.5.9: for an acute bradycardia or a prolonged deceleration of 3 minutes or more, urgently seek obstetric review, expedite birth if there is an acute event, start conservative measures (such as position change), prepare for urgent birth with neonatal support, and expedite birth if the bradycardia persists for 9 minutes (or sooner with risk factors).

n.0: IV fluids are not given for fetal heart rate abnormalities unless the woman is hypotensive or septic (NG229 1.5.11).
n.1: Maternal facial oxygen is not offered as a conservative measure because it may harm the baby (NG229 1.5.12).
n.3: 9 minutes is when birth should be expedited; obstetric review is sought immediately.

12.q: Which statement best describes the scope of the midwife set out in the NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives (2019)?
o: Care for women at low risk, ending when complications arise
Care from booking until 10 days after the birth for healthy women
Intrapartum care, with antenatal and postnatal care led by GPs
Universal care for all, plus additional care in partnership with others
12.w: The 2019 standards describe the midwife providing universal care for all women and newborn infants, and additional care for those with complications, working with the interdisciplinary and multiagency team (SPM 1.7, Domains 3 and 4).

n.0: Midwives continue to care for women who develop complications, coordinating with others, rather than stopping.
n.1: The standards cover all women and newborns across the continuum, not a fixed 10-day window for healthy women.
n.2: Midwives provide antenatal, intrapartum and postnatal care; GPs are not the leads for routine antenatal and postnatal care.

12.q: Harriet, 30, is 32 weeks pregnant and at low risk of fetal growth restriction. Her previous SFH measurements followed the 50th centile. Today's measurement, plotted on her customised chart, falls below the 10th centile. Movements are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a colleague to remeasure today and document if the result is the same
Reassure her, as SFH varies with the baby's position at this gestation
Remeasure SFH at her next routine appointment in 2 weeks
Refer for an ultrasound scan of fetal growth and wellbeing
12.w: If SFH suggests a small-for-gestational-age baby, offer an ultrasound scan for fetal growth and wellbeing; urgency depends on additional findings such as reduced movements or raised BP (NICE NG201 1.2.32; SBL v3 element 2). A drop in centile is a referral trigger.

n.0: A second measurement may be reasonable, but the plotted finding needs a scan referral rather than documentation alone.
n.1: A fall across centiles is a recognised referral criterion and should not be explained away.
n.2: Waiting 2 weeks delays assessment of possible FGR, a major risk factor for stillbirth.

12.q: Dani, 24, is formula feeding her baby. The midwife watches her prepare a feed at home. Which step is correct?
o: Warm a made-up feed in the microwave and shake it before use
Use boiled water cooled in the fridge so the feed is ready faster
Use water boiled no more than 30 minutes ago, so it is at least 70 C
Put the powder in the bottle first, then add water up to the line
12.w: NHS formula guidance (NICE NG194 1.5.17 safe preparation): boil fresh water and leave it for no more than 30 minutes so it stays at least 70 C, which kills harmful bacteria in powdered formula. Put the water in the bottle first, then add the powder.

n.0: Microwaves heat unevenly and can scald the baby's mouth.
n.1: Water below 70 C will not kill bacteria that can be present in powdered formula.
n.3: Water goes in first so the powder-to-water ratio is correct.

12.q: Lucy is coordinating the birth centre on a night shift. Two midwives have called in sick, leaving three women in established labour with two midwives. No bank staff are available. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the women's birth partners to call a midwife when contractions change
Escalate to the manager on call under the staffing escalation policy
Continue to manage the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Ask the two student midwives on shift to care for the third woman
12.w: Code 25.1 requires leaders to identify priorities, manage staff and resources effectively and deal with risk; Code 16.1 requires raising and escalating concerns about safety, and standard 16 to act without delay. Escalating through the staffing policy allows the manager on call to redeploy staff or divert admissions.

n.0: Relying on birth partners to monitor labour transfers a professional responsibility to people without training.
n.2: Waiting until morning delays action while women in labour are receiving unsafe staffing levels.
n.3: Students are supernumerary and must be supervised; they cannot replace a registered midwife to make up numbers.

12.q: A local audit finds that stillbirth occurred in 8 per 1,000 births to women who smoked and 4 per 1,000 births to women who did not smoke. A woman asks how much smoking raises the risk. Which figure is the relative risk?
12.w: Relative risk = risk in exposed group / risk in unexposed group = (8/1,000) / (4/1,000) = 2. The absolute risk difference is 4 per 1,000. SPM 3.2 requires midwives to interpret data and use it in conversations with women.

n.0: 4 per 1,000 is the absolute risk difference, not the relative risk.
n.1: 0.5 is the ratio the wrong way round (non-smokers compared with smokers).
n.3: 8 per 1,000 is the absolute risk among smokers, not a ratio.

12.q: Paige, 24, is 18 weeks pregnant. Her two older children were removed from her care because of neglect, and she still lives with the same partner. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to the health visitor to monitor the baby after the birth
Wait until after the birth to see how she cares for the baby
Tell Paige the baby will be removed at birth
Refer to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment
12.w: Midwives safeguard unborn babies. Previous children removed for neglect with the same circumstances is a significant concern needing referral to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment, in line with Working Together to Safeguard Children and local procedures (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Health visitor involvement is not enough when there are known significant safeguarding concerns.
n.1: Waiting removes the chance to plan support and protection before the baby is born.
n.2: Removal is not decided by the midwife and is not certain; this damages trust.

12.q: After shoulder dystocia was resolved by McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, the midwife is completing the documentation for Olivia, 36. Which detail is especially important to include alongside the times and manoeuvres?
o: The colour of the liquor when the membranes ruptured
Which of the baby's shoulders was anterior
The time of her last vaginal examination before birth
Her pain score during the second stage of labour
12.w: Documentation after shoulder dystocia should include time of birth of the head and body, the anterior shoulder, the manoeuvres used with their timing and sequence, staff present and their arrival times, the condition of the baby and cord blood gases (RCOG GTG 42). The anterior shoulder is linked to the side of any brachial plexus injury.

n.0: Liquor colour is recorded in labour but is not a key shoulder dystocia record.
n.2: The last vaginal examination time is routine labour documentation, not specific to this emergency.
n.3: Pain scores may be recorded but are not a key element of shoulder dystocia documentation.

12.q: Kayla, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant. She becomes tearful when asked about her mood and says she has not told anyone how low she feels because she is afraid her baby will be taken into care. Which response by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Acknowledge her fear and explain help aims to support her to care for her baby
Advise her to wait until after the birth to seek help, when it will be easier
Tell her social care becomes involved when a mother declines treatment
Reassure her that the information will stay between the two of them
12.w: NICE CG192 1.5.1 recognises that women may not disclose mental health problems for fear of stigma or that their baby will be taken into care. Responding with compassion and acknowledging her role in caring for her baby (CG192 1.3.1) supports disclosure and access to help, while being honest about information sharing.

n.1: Delaying help is unsafe; untreated perinatal depression affects the woman and baby.
n.2: This is inaccurate; safeguarding involvement depends on risk to the child, not on refusing treatment.
n.3: Midwives cannot promise absolute confidentiality, as information may need to be shared with the team or for safeguarding.

12.q: Esme, 34, had a baby with a birthweight below the 3rd centile in her last pregnancy. She has been placed on a pathway of 3 to 4-weekly growth scans from 28 weeks. At her 30-week community appointment, what should the midwife do about fundal height?
o: Stop SFH measurement, as she is on serial scan surveillance
Measure SFH at alternate appointments to reduce duplication
Measure and plot SFH as well as reviewing each scan result
Measure SFH weekly between scans to detect any change
12.w: Saving Babies' Lives v3 intervention 2.12: women undergoing planned serial scan surveillance should stop SFH measurement once surveillance begins. Women at increased risk of FGR have 3 to 4-weekly scans until birth (2.13). The midwife still discusses movements and checks BP and urine.

n.1: Alternating SFH with scans is not part of the SBL v3 pathway; SFH stops.
n.2: SBL v3 states SFH should cease once serial scan surveillance begins.
n.3: Weekly SFH adds no useful information alongside scans and SFH should not be done more often than every 2 weeks anyway.

12.q: Nicola, 26, is 40 minutes after birth with ongoing trickling blood loss. On palpation her uterus is soft and displaced to the right, above the umbilicus. She has not passed urine since before the birth. Uterine massage has been started. What is the next most appropriate action?
o: Empty her bladder, using a catheter if she cannot void
Repeat the observations in 15 minutes and review the loss
Give a second dose of oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly
Encourage her to put the baby to the breast for 30 minutes
12.w: A full bladder displaces the uterus and stops it contracting effectively. NICE NG235 1.10.33 includes emptying the bladder alongside uterine massage, uterotonics and IV fluids in the immediate treatment of PPH (SPM 4.8 first-line management).

n.1: Waiting allows ongoing bleeding; the cause should be treated now.
n.2: A repeat IM oxytocin dose is not the NG235 treatment step, and a full bladder will still stop the uterus contracting.
n.3: Breastfeeding helps but does not correct a uterus displaced by a full bladder.

12.q: Lauren, 25, is breastfeeding on day 3. She says feeds are very painful and her nipple looks flattened, like a new lipstick, when the baby comes off. The baby is feeding frequently and seems unsettled. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Advise nipple shields for every feed until the pain settles
Observe a full feed and support her with positioning and attachment
Rest the nipples for 24 hours by giving the baby formula feeds
Recommend a nipple cream and advise her that pain is expected
12.w: NICE NG194 1.5.12 and 1.5.15: pain when breastfeeding and a misshapen nipple after feeds suggest poor attachment. The first step is to observe a feed and adjust positioning and attachment; persisting concerns may need further support or tongue-tie assessment.

n.0: Nipple shields do not correct the underlying attachment problem and can reduce milk transfer.
n.2: Replacing feeds with formula reduces milk removal and supply and does not fix attachment.
n.3: Ongoing pain is not normal; NG194 tells women to seek help for pain when breastfeeding.

12.q: Becky, 22, has a child protection plan for her unborn baby. She is ready for discharge from the postnatal ward on a Saturday evening. What should the midwife do before Becky and her baby leave?
o: Confirm the plan agreed with children's social care is in place
Keep the baby on the ward until the social worker visits on Monday
Discharge them and ask the health visitor to visit within 7 days
Discharge them and email the social worker on Monday morning
12.w: Multiagency working (Working Together to Safeguard Children) requires discharge of a baby subject to a child protection plan to follow the plan agreed with children's social care, using out-of-hours services if needed (SPM 2.4, 2.11).

n.1: There is no legal basis to keep the baby without a plan or order; this action is not the midwife's to take alone.
n.2: The health visitor visit is part of routine care; it does not replace the agreed safeguarding discharge plan.
n.3: Discharging without confirming the agreed plan may leave the baby at risk over the weekend.

12.q: Hannah, 32, is having a planned home birth. Her community midwife has no prescription chart or patient group directions for this birth. Which medicine can the registered midwife lawfully administer under the midwives exemptions in Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012?
o: Intramuscular oxytocin for the third stage
Intravenous tranexamic acid for heavy bleeding
Intravenous co-amoxiclav for suspected infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for a seizure
12.w: HMR 2012 Schedule 17 lists the parenteral prescription-only medicines a registered midwife may administer in professional practice, including oxytocins (natural and synthetic), ergometrine, carboprost, anti-D, phytomenadione and others (SPM 3.19 midwives exemptions).

n.1: Tranexamic acid is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.
n.2: Antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav are not on the Schedule 17 list.
n.3: Magnesium sulfate is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.

12.q: Jess, 27, has just given birth. The baby cried at birth, has good tone and a heart rate over 100, and is skin to skin. Jess has chosen active management. When should the cord be clamped?
o: No earlier than 1 minute after birth, and before 5 minutes for traction
After the cord stops pulsating, then give the uterotonic
Immediately after the uterotonic is given, to allow cord traction
No earlier than 10 minutes after birth, to maximise placental transfusion
12.w: NICE NG235 1.10.14: after the uterotonic, do not clamp the cord earlier than 1 minute after birth unless there is concern about cord integrity or the baby's heart rate is below 60 and not increasing; clamp before 5 minutes to perform controlled cord traction, and support a request for later clamping.

n.1: Waiting for pulsation to stop is part of physiological management; in active management the uterotonic is given before clamping.
n.2: Immediate clamping is not recommended for a well baby; wait at least 1 minute.
n.3: In active management the cord is clamped before 5 minutes for controlled cord traction unless she requests otherwise.

12.q: Anya, 33, is 41+2 weeks in an uncomplicated first pregnancy. After a full discussion of the risks and benefits, she declines induction of labour. What is the most appropriate response by the midwife?
o: Ask her partner to talk with her about changing her decision
Respect her decision and offer extra monitoring from 42 weeks
Refer her to the safeguarding team as the baby may be at risk
Book the induction anyway in case she changes her mind
12.w: A woman with capacity may decline induction. NICE NG207 advises that if she chooses not to have induction, her decision is respected and additional monitoring is offered from 42 weeks (twice-weekly CTG and ultrasound of the maximum amniotic pool depth). SPM 1.21.

n.0: Using her partner to pressure her undermines a voluntary decision.
n.2: Declining induction is a lawful choice, not a safeguarding concern.
n.3: Booking a procedure she has declined disregards her decision.

12.q: Megan, 25, is 25 weeks pregnant and in suspected preterm labour at a local unit with a special care baby unit but no neonatal intensive care. She has been given her first steroid dose. Which plan best reflects Saving Babies' Lives v3?
o: Plan birth locally and ask the NICU team to attend for the birth
Plan birth locally and transfer the baby to a NICU after stabilisation
Transfer her once the second steroid dose has been given in 24 hours
Arrange in utero transfer to a maternity service on the same site as a NICU
12.w: SBL v3 5.18: babies born under 27 weeks (or under 800 g, or multiples under 28 weeks) should be born in a maternity service on the same site as a designated NICU, moving them in utero whenever possible. Acute tocolysis may be used to allow in utero transfer (5.17).

n.0: Bringing a team in does not replace birth on a NICU site, which is the SBL v3 standard.
n.1: Postnatal transfer of an extremely preterm baby carries higher risk than in utero transfer, which SBL v3 prefers.
n.2: Delaying transfer for 24 hours risks birth in a unit without NICU; the second dose can follow at the receiving unit.

12.q: Before the birth of their first baby, Yusuf and Hana ask the midwife why vitamin K is offered to newborn babies. Which explanation is accurate?
o: To strengthen the baby's immunity against early-onset infection
To prevent newborn jaundice developing in the first week of life
To prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare but serious disorder
To prevent anaemia in babies who had delayed cord clamping
12.w: NICE NG235 1.11.12 (recommendation reintroduced 2026): offer parents vitamin K prophylaxis for their babies and explain it is to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare but serious and sometimes fatal disorder.

n.0: Vitamin K has no role in immunity against infection.
n.1: Vitamin K supports clotting; it does not prevent jaundice.
n.3: Delayed cord clamping improves iron stores; vitamin K prevents bleeding, not anaemia.

12.q: At a home visit, Kirsty, 24, who is 30 weeks pregnant, tells the midwife her partner hit her 2-year-old son last night, leaving a bruise. She begs the midwife not to tell anyone. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain why and refer to children's social care today
Keep it confidential, as Kirsty has asked
Share the information if Kirsty agrees after thinking about it
Advise Kirsty to contact children's social care herself
12.w: Code 17.1 and 17.2: protect people at risk and share information where someone may be at risk of harm, in line with the law. A child with an injury from an adult is at risk, so the midwife shares without waiting for consent, explaining why to Kirsty where this is safe.

n.1: Confidentiality does not prevent sharing to protect a child at risk of harm.
n.2: Waiting for her agreement delays protection for a child who has been injured.
n.3: Leaving the referral to Kirsty may mean it is not made, and the midwife holds the concern.

12.q: Harper, 27, is 34 weeks pregnant and has gestational hypertension. She phones the maternity triage line. Which symptom she describes needs immediate assessment for pre-eclampsia?
o: Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Leg cramps that wake her at night
Flashing lights in her vision since today
Backache after standing at work
12.w: NICE NG133 1.1.1 advises women to report immediately severe headache, problems with vision such as blurring or flashing before the eyes, severe pain just below the ribs, vomiting, and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet (SPM 4.8).

n.0: Gradual ankle swelling is common in pregnancy; sudden swelling of face, hands or feet is the warning sign.
n.1: Night cramps are common in pregnancy and are not a pre-eclampsia symptom.
n.3: Backache after standing is common and not a symptom of pre-eclampsia.

12.q: Following the stillbirth of Baby Aria at 39 weeks, the community midwife visits the parents at home. They ask whether anyone will look into what happened. Which statement about the Perinatal Mortality Review Tool (PMRT) is most accurate?
o: The coroner investigates stillbirths, so the hospital does not hold a review
The hospital reviews the care once the parents request a review in writing
The review is confidential to staff and the findings are not shared with parents
The hospital reviews the care, and they are told about the review and can contribute
12.w: The PMRT supports systematic multidisciplinary review of care for stillbirths and neonatal deaths from 22 weeks. Parents are told a review will take place and how they can contribute, and a plain-language explanation of the findings is discussed with them (NPEU PMRT).

n.0: Coroners in England and Wales do not currently have jurisdiction over stillbirths; the hospital reviews the care using the PMRT.
n.1: The PMRT review happens for every eligible death; parents do not have to request it.
n.2: Parent involvement and sharing the findings with parents are core aims of the PMRT.

12.q: Precious, 22, has an eclamptic seizure on the antenatal ward and remains unconscious afterwards. She needs magnesium sulfate urgently. What is the legal basis for treatment?
o: Best interests treatment under the MCA 2005
A Court of Protection order
The consent of her next of kin
Her consent once she regains consciousness
12.w: She lacks capacity at the material time (MCA 2005 s2; temporary impairment counts, s2(2)). Treatment that cannot wait is given in her best interests (s4, s5), taking account of any known wishes.

n.1: A court order is not needed for urgent treatment in an emergency.
n.2: Next of kin cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney.
n.3: Waiting for consciousness would delay treatment needed to prevent further seizures.

12.q: Grace, 35, who is Black British, is 3 days after a caesarean. She mentions feeling 'not quite right' but her observations are within normal limits. Which principle from NICE NG194 should guide the midwife's response?
o: Ethnicity is no longer relevant to risk once the birth has been uncomplicated
Higher maternal mortality in Black women is explained by older maternal age
Closer monitoring is reserved for women living in the most deprived areas
Some minority ethnic groups have higher mortality and may need closer monitoring
12.w: NICE NG194 1.1.2: MBRRACE-UK reports show that women from some minority ethnic backgrounds, and those in deprived areas, have a higher risk of death and may need closer monitoring. Her concern should be taken seriously and explored.

n.0: Increased risk continues into the postnatal period; ethnicity remains relevant after birth.
n.1: The disparity is not explained by age; MBRRACE-UK shows higher risk across groups.
n.2: NG194 identifies both minority ethnic background and deprivation as reasons for closer monitoring.

12.q: Holly is writing a reflective account using Gibbs' reflective cycle about a difficult conversation with a bereaved family. She has described the event, explored her feelings and evaluated what was good and bad. Which stage comes next?
o: Action plan
Analysis
Description
Conclusion
12.w: Gibbs' cycle runs: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan. After evaluation comes analysis, making sense of the situation and drawing on theory or evidence (SPM 5.13.1).

n.0: The action plan is the final stage, after the conclusion.
n.2: Description is the first stage, which Holly has already completed.
n.3: The conclusion follows analysis.

12.q: Jade, 25, gives birth at 22+5 weeks. The baby shows signs of life, including a heartbeat, and dies 30 minutes later. What are the registration requirements?
o: No registration is needed because the birth was before 24 weeks
Issue a certificate of pregnancy loss instead of registering
Register both the birth and the death
Register the baby as a stillbirth because the birth was before 24 weeks
12.w: A baby born alive at any gestation is a live birth. Its birth and death must both be registered. The stillbirth category applies to babies born after 24 completed weeks with no signs of life (Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953).

n.0: The 24-week threshold applies to stillbirth; a baby born alive at any gestation must be registered.
n.1: Voluntary pre-24-week loss certificates are for babies born without signs of life; a live-born baby's birth and death must be registered.
n.3: A stillbirth is a baby born after 24 weeks with no signs of life; this baby was born alive.

12.q: Chloe, 24, had a second-degree tear sutured after a vaginal birth 5 days ago. At a home visit she reports increasing perineal pain and needs more pain relief than before. On examination the wound edges have separated with a small amount of discharge. Her observations are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise warm salt baths and review the wound at the next visit in 2 days
Refer her urgently to specialist maternity services to be seen the same day
Take a wound swab and decide on referral once the result is available
Ask the GP to examine the wound at her 6 to 8 week postnatal check
12.w: NICE NG194 1.2.20: if the perineal wound breaks down or there are ongoing healing concerns, refer urgently to specialist maternity services, to be seen the same day in the case of a perineal wound breakdown. Increasing pain and need for analgesia are warning features (1.2.15).

n.0: Self-care and a delayed review do not meet the same-day standard for wound breakdown.
n.2: A swab may be useful, but referral must not wait for results when the wound has broken down.
n.3: Waiting for the 6 to 8 week GP review would leave a broken-down wound unassessed for weeks.

12.q: Baby Kofi, born at 38 weeks, is 16 days old and still visibly jaundiced. He is breastfeeding well and gaining weight. His mother says his stools have become pale and chalky. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat a transcutaneous reading at the 6 to 8 week check
Arrange measurement of conjugated bilirubin and refer for expert advice
Advise a 48-hour break from breastfeeding to see if it settles
Reassure her that breast milk jaundice can last for several weeks
12.w: Prolonged jaundice is jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby. Pale chalky stools suggest cholestasis such as biliary atresia. CG98 1.7.1 to 1.7.2: look for pale stools and dark urine and measure conjugated bilirubin; over 25 micromol/L needs expert advice.

n.0: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks could delay diagnosis of biliary atresia, where timing of surgery matters.
n.2: Stopping breastfeeding is not recommended and delays investigation.
n.3: Pale chalky stools are a warning sign of liver disease, not breast milk jaundice; reassurance is unsafe.

12.q: Isla, 30, is 38 weeks pregnant with her first baby and the pregnancy is uncomplicated. Her BP is 116/74 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein. In addition to routine checks, which discussion is specifically recommended at this appointment?
o: Whether she would like the second-trimester screening tests
Options for managing a pregnancy that goes beyond term
Arranging her first measurement of symphysis fundal height
Her first discussion about birth preferences and place of birth
12.w: NICE NG201 1.3.17: from 38 weeks discuss prolonged pregnancy and the options for managing it, in line with NG207 (membrane sweep after 39+0 and induction discussion from 41+0).

n.0: Screening windows closed long before 38 weeks; the quadruple test runs to 20+0 weeks.
n.2: SFH is measured at each appointment after 24+0 weeks, with the first by 28+6, not first at 38 weeks.
n.3: Birth preferences should be raised before 28 weeks (NG201 1.3.14), so 38 weeks is too late for a first discussion.

12.q: Ellie, a third-year student midwife, is caring for Fatima, 27, in established labour. Fatima requests pethidine, which the registered midwife will give under the midwives exemptions. Ellie asks whether she can draw up and administer the injection herself under direct supervision. What is the correct response?
o: Yes, once she has been signed off as competent by a practice assessor
No, pethidine must be prescribed and given by a doctor in labour
No, students may not give pethidine under the midwives exemptions
Yes, if the registered midwife directly supervises the injection
12.w: Schedule 17 allows student midwives to administer listed parenteral medicines under the direct supervision of a registered midwife, but this expressly excludes diamorphine, morphine and pethidine (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 1.2 act within the law; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Practice assessor sign-off does not change the legal exclusion of pethidine for student midwives.
n.1: Registered midwives can administer pethidine under the exemptions without a doctor's prescription.
n.3: Direct supervision covers other listed medicines but the Schedule excludes pethidine for students.

12.q: Comfort, 30, is undocumented and 20 weeks pregnant. She tells the midwife she has been avoiding antenatal care because she is afraid of being charged. What is the most accurate information to give her?
o: She will need to pay a deposit before her next antenatal appointment
She should register with a private clinic for the rest of her antenatal care
Antenatal care is deferred until her immigration status is confirmed
Maternity care is immediately necessary and will not be withheld or delayed
12.w: Under the NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015 guidance, maternity services are always treated as immediately necessary and must never be withheld or delayed because of charges. Midwives should help women who fear charging to access care (SPM 2.8).

n.0: Maternity care must not be withheld or delayed pending payment, even when charges apply.
n.1: Sending her to private care adds a barrier and is not needed; NHS maternity care must be provided.
n.2: Care cannot be deferred for immigration checks; maternity services are always immediately necessary.

12.q: Zara, 30, is 5 cm dilated on the labour ward and has a cord prolapse. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration. The obstetrician is present and theatre is ready. What is the recommended category of caesarean birth?
o: Category 3, aiming for birth within the day
Category 1, aiming for birth within 30 minutes
Category 1, aiming for birth within 60 minutes
Category 2, aiming for birth within 75 minutes
12.w: RCOG GTG 50: caesarean is recommended when vaginal birth is not imminent; category 1, aiming for birth within 30 minutes or less, if the fetal heart rate pattern is suspicious or pathological. Category 2 can be considered if the FHR is normal.

n.0: Category 3 is for births needing early but not urgent delivery.
n.2: Category 1 aims for 30 minutes or less, not 60.
n.3: Category 2 is considered when the fetal heart rate is normal, not with a prolonged deceleration.

12.q: Which settings should be offered as options for planned place of birth to a low-risk woman in England, according to NICE NG235?
o: Home or obstetric unit with a midwife present
Home, freestanding or alongside midwifery unit, or obstetric unit
Freestanding or alongside midwifery unit for low-risk women
Alongside midwifery unit or obstetric unit, both on the hospital site
12.w: NG235 1.3.3: women should be told they may choose any birth setting (home, freestanding midwifery unit, alongside midwifery unit or obstetric unit) and be supported in that choice; NG235 1.2.1 asks that all 4 settings are available (SPM 2.1).

n.0: This omits both kinds of midwifery unit, which NG235 recommends as options.
n.2: Low-risk women may also choose home or an obstetric unit; NG235 does not limit them to midwifery units.
n.3: Restricting options to the hospital site omits home and freestanding units, which NG235 says women may choose.

12.q: Tess, a band 6 midwife, completes an audit showing that 70% of women with a postpartum haemorrhage had a documented quantitative blood loss measurement against a trust standard of 95%. She presents the findings at the governance meeting. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Publish the result in a journal as evidence of poor national practice
Agree an action plan to improve practice and set a date for re-audit
Lower the trust standard to 70% to reflect what is achievable
Repeat the same audit next month to confirm the figure
12.w: After comparing practice with the standard, the audit cycle moves to implementing change through an agreed action plan and then re-auditing to close the loop. Audit findings are local and are not generalisable research (HRA defining research table).

n.0: A local audit measures practice in one service against a local standard; it does not produce generalisable evidence about national practice.
n.2: Lowering the standard to match performance defeats the purpose of audit, which is to raise practice to the standard.
n.3: Repeating the audit without any change will show the same gap; change must be made before re-auditing.

12.q: Jess, 16, books at 12 weeks. She is living with her mother, is still at school and finds hospital clinics intimidating. Which care arrangement best follows NICE CG110?
o: Care deferred until her mother can attend every appointment with her
Standard consultant-led clinic care, as she is under 18
A named midwife providing most of her care, with a direct phone number
Antenatal care through her school nurse until 28 weeks
12.w: CG110 1.4.4: offer young women under 20 a named midwife who provides most of their antenatal care, with a direct-line telephone number. Services should be age-appropriate, community-based where possible and alert to safeguarding (1.4.1, 1.4.5).

n.0: Jess can attend herself; deferring care until her mother is available is a barrier to antenatal care.
n.1: Age alone is not an indication for consultant-led care; young women need accessible, age-appropriate services.
n.3: School nurses do not provide antenatal care; the midwife does.

12.q: Yasmin, 27, is 38+5 weeks pregnant. Group B streptococcus was found on a urine culture at 30 weeks. She phones to say her membranes ruptured 30 minutes ago with clear fluid and she has no contractions. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Wait at home for up to 24 hours, taking oral antibiotics
Attend within 12 hours for a speculum examination
Wait at home for up to 24 hours, then attend for induction
Attend now; immediate induction of labour should be offered
12.w: NICE NG235 1.7.11 (and NG207 1.2.16): if a woman has PROM at term and a positive GBS test at any time in the current pregnancy, offer immediate induction (or caesarean if planned). Intrapartum antibiotics follow NICE neonatal infection guidance. GBS carriage is also a phone triage risk factor needing urgent in-person review (1.7.1).

n.0: Oral antibiotics at home do not replace intrapartum IV prophylaxis and immediate induction.
n.1: The 12-hour review applies to women with no risk factors on phone triage; GBS carriage requires immediate attendance.
n.2: Expectant management for 24 hours is for women without risk factors; GBS positive women are offered immediate induction.

12.q: A community midwife is reviewing her caseload of four new mothers. According to NICE NG194, which mother is most likely to need additional support with bonding and emotional attachment?
o: Ann, 34, who plans to return to work when the baby is 9 months
Josie, 19, who grew up in local authority care
Mae, 30, a second-time mother with an uncomplicated birth
Lia, 28, who has chosen to formula feed her baby
12.w: NICE NG194 1.3.19: some parents may need additional support with bonding and emotional attachment, for example those who have been through the care system, have experienced adverse childhood events or a traumatic birth, or have complex psychosocial needs.

n.0: Planning a return to work is not listed as a factor needing extra attachment support.
n.2: An uncomplicated second birth is not one of the NG194 factors for additional bonding support.
n.3: Formula feeding by choice does not by itself indicate a need for attachment support; parents can bond when bottle feeding (NG194 1.5.19).

12.q: Baby Noah was born through meconium-stained liquor 2 hours ago. His observations: respiratory rate 66 breaths/min, heart rate 150 bpm, temperature 37.3 C, oxygen saturation 97%. Which finding means a neonatologist should assess him?
o: Heart rate of 150 beats per minute
Oxygen saturation of 97%
Respiratory rate of 66 breaths/min
Temperature of 37.3 C on one reading
12.w: NICE NG235 1.11.29: after any meconium, ask a neonatologist to assess the baby if respiratory rate is above 60, there is grunting, heart rate is below 100 or above 160, capillary refill is over 3 seconds, temperature is 38 C or more (or 37.5 C twice 15 to 30 minutes apart), saturation is below 95% or there is central cyanosis.

n.0: A heart rate of 150 is within the 100 to 160 range.
n.1: 97% is above the 95% threshold.
n.3: 37.3 C is below the 37.5 C and 38 C triggers.

12.q: Kerry has been a registered midwife for 4 years and wants to prescribe medicines such as antibiotics for women with postnatal infections in her community caseload. What must happen before she can prescribe independently?
o: She must hold a patient group direction for each antibiotic she uses
She must complete an NMC-approved prescribing programme and have it recorded
She must complete 2 years of community practice and a local competency
She must be authorised in writing by her head of midwifery
12.w: Only nurses and midwives who have completed an NMC-approved prescribing qualification and had it recorded on the register can prescribe (Code 18, note to 18.5). SPM 3.19 expects the ability to progress to a prescribing qualification after registration.

n.0: A PGD allows supply or administration to a group; it is not prescribing.
n.2: Length of experience and a local competency do not confer prescribing rights.
n.3: A head of midwifery cannot authorise prescribing; it requires a recorded qualification.

12.q: At her annual appraisal, Hollie, a midwife with 2 years' experience, receives feedback from colleagues that she rarely asks for help when unsure and sometimes delays escalating concerns. She feels upset by this. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reflect on the feedback, discuss it with her manager and agree a development plan
Accept the feedback politely and continue practising in the same way
Request a transfer to another ward where colleagues know her less well
Ask which colleagues gave the feedback so that she can challenge their view
12.w: Code 9.2: gather and reflect on feedback from a variety of sources, using it to improve your practice. SPM 1.27 requires midwives to seek and respond to support and feedback. A development plan addresses the safety issue (Code standard 13 recognise and work within the limits of your competence).

n.1: Accepting feedback without changing practice ignores a safety-relevant pattern.
n.2: Moving wards avoids the feedback and leaves the development need unaddressed.
n.3: Focusing on who gave the feedback is defensive and does not use it to improve practice.

12.q: Tamsin, 28, is transferred home from the birth centre at 18:00 on Monday after an uncomplicated birth. By what time should the first postnatal visit by a midwife take place?
o: By 18:00 on Thursday
By 06:00 on Thursday
By 06:00 on Wednesday
By 18:00 on Wednesday
12.w: NG194 1.1.14: the first postnatal visit by a midwife takes place within 36 hours after transfer of care from the place of birth or after a home birth, face to face and usually at home. 18:00 Monday plus 36 hours = 06:00 Wednesday.

n.0: This is 72 hours after transfer, which is well beyond the 36-hour standard.
n.1: This is 60 hours after transfer, which is later than the 36-hour standard.
n.3: This is 48 hours after transfer, which is later than the 36-hour standard.

12.q: Isla and Tom have a healthy term baby and plan to bed share. Neither smokes, drinks or takes medication. Which advice about safer bed sharing is accurate?
o: Place the baby on a soft mattress topper, lying on her side to feed
Place the baby on the sofa with a parent when very tired
Use a firm, flat mattress with the baby face up, away from pillows
Place the baby between the parents with the duvet tucked in
12.w: NG194 1.3.14: discuss safer bed sharing: firm, flat mattress; baby lying face up; not sleeping on a sofa or chair with the baby; no pillows or duvets near the baby; no other children or pets in the bed.

n.0: Babies should sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface.
n.1: Sleeping with a baby on a sofa or chair is particularly dangerous.
n.3: Duvets and pillows near the baby, and lying between parents, increase risk.

12.q: Rosie, 34, is 32 weeks pregnant and attends maternity triage with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding that has soaked one pad. Her 20-week scan reported a low-lying placenta. Her observations are normal and the fetal heart rate is 140 beats/min. Which action should the midwife avoid?
o: A digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
Blood tests including a full blood count and group and save
An ultrasound scan to locate the placenta
A speculum examination by the obstetrician
12.w: RCOG GTG 63: if placenta praevia is possible (previous low placenta, high presenting part or painless bleeding), digital vaginal examination should not be performed until ultrasound has excluded placenta praevia, as it can provoke major haemorrhage.

n.1: Bloods are recommended for all women with APH (FBC and group and save as a minimum).
n.2: Ultrasound is needed to locate the placenta before any digital examination.
n.3: A speculum examination can safely identify cervical dilatation or a lower genital tract cause.

12.q: Zara, 28, is 32 weeks pregnant and presents with irregular tightenings and intact membranes. The obstetric team is unsure whether she is in preterm labour. Which diagnostic test does NICE suggest considering first at this gestation?
o: Transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length
A high vaginal swab for group B streptococcus
Serum C-reactive protein and white cell count
A digital vaginal examination repeated after 4 hours
12.w: NG25 1.7.4: at 30+0 weeks or more with suspected preterm labour, consider transvaginal cervical length measurement. A length over 15 mm makes preterm labour unlikely. NG25 1.7.5 lists fetal fibronectin as an alternative, but Saving Babies' Lives v3.2 (5.9) reports that fetal fibronectin cassettes have been discontinued.

n.1: A GBS swab does not diagnose preterm labour.
n.2: CRP and white cell count are used with other findings to diagnose intrauterine infection in P-PROM, not preterm labour.
n.3: Serial digital examinations are not the recommended diagnostic test and add infection risk.

12.q: Precious, 32, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language (BSL). Her hearing partner offers to sign for her during labour. What is the most appropriate arrangement?
o: Ask her partner to interpret, as he is fluent in BSL
Rely on lip-reading, with staff speaking slowly and facing her
Communicate by writing notes throughout labour
Book a registered BSL interpreter for labour and appointments
12.w: Code 7.2: meet people's language and communication needs. A registered BSL interpreter gives accurate, independent communication, and the partner can support Precious rather than interpret.

n.0: A partner interpreting cannot also act as her birth supporter and may not convey clinical information accurately.
n.1: Lip-reading conveys only part of speech and is unreliable, especially in labour.
n.2: Written notes are slow and impractical during labour and may not be her preferred language.

12.q: Several women of Black African origin tell a community midwife that they felt their concerns were dismissed during labour. What is the most effective way for the midwife to advocate for change?
o: Advise each of the women to make an individual complaint to the trust
Share the stories on social media to raise public awareness of racism
Apologise to each woman and explain that the staff on duty were very busy
Gather the feedback, raise it through governance and work with the local MNVP
12.w: Advocating for change (SPM 5.13.4) means collecting evidence and raising it through the right channels, co-producing improvements with service users such as the Maternity and Neonatal Voices Partnership (MNVP). MBRRACE-UK shows Black women have nearly three times the maternal mortality of White women, so these concerns are a safety issue.

n.0: Complaints are their right, but leaving it to women alone puts the burden on them and misses system learning.
n.1: Social media is not an appropriate route and may breach confidentiality.
n.2: Explaining it away as busyness fails to recognise a pattern that needs action.

12.q: Aisha, 30, is 33 weeks pregnant on the low-risk pathway. Her symphysis fundal height today plots below the 10th centile on her growth chart; two weeks ago it was on the 40th centile. She reports normal fetal movements. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remeasure the fundal height at her next routine appointment
Refer her for an ultrasound assessment of fetal growth
Reassure her because the fetal movements are normal
Ask a colleague to remeasure and record the higher of the two values
12.w: A fundal height plotting below the 10th centile, or a drop across centiles, is an indication for an ultrasound growth assessment. SBL v3 2.11 requires staff measuring SFH to interpret and refer when indicated, and 2.14 sets the assessment of wellbeing once FGR is suspected.

n.0: Waiting for the next routine visit delays detection of possible FGR, a major risk factor for stillbirth.
n.2: Normal movements do not exclude growth restriction; the measurement still needs investigating.
n.3: Choosing the higher of two readings is unsafe and does not address the fall across centiles.

12.q: Lauren, 33, had a third-degree tear in her first birth, repaired with a good recovery and no continence symptoms. She is now 36 weeks and asks whether she will need an episiotomy and how likely another severe tear is. Which response is accurate?
o: An episiotomy will be performed to protect the repaired sphincter
A planned caesarean birth is required after any third-degree tear
No routine episiotomy, and her risk of a repeat severe tear is not raised
Her risk of a repeat severe tear is raised, so an episiotomy is advised
12.w: NICE NG235 1.9.17 and 1.9.18: inform a woman with previous severe perineal trauma that her risk of repeat severe trauma is not increased compared with women having their first baby, and do not offer episiotomy routinely after previous third- or fourth-degree trauma. Mode of birth is discussed considering symptoms and previous repair (1.9.19).

n.0: Routine episiotomy is not recommended after previous third-degree trauma.
n.1: Caesarean is not required; mode of birth is an informed choice considering her symptoms and history.
n.3: NICE states the risk of repeat severe trauma is not increased compared with a first birth.

12.q: Baby Finn's phototherapy was stopped at 08:00 after his serum bilirubin fell well below the treatment threshold. When should his serum bilirubin be checked for rebound?
o: At 10:00, 2 hours after stopping
At 08:00 two days later, 48 hours after stopping
Between 12:00 and 14:00, 4 to 6 hours after stopping
Between 20:00 and 02:00, 12 to 18 hours after stopping
12.w: NICE CG98 1.4.5, 1.4.6: stop phototherapy once serum bilirubin has fallen at least 50 micromol/L below the threshold, and check for rebound 12 to 18 hours after stopping (08:00 + 12 to 18 hours = 20:00 to 02:00).

n.0: 2 hours is too early to detect rebound.
n.1: 48 hours is later than the CG98 rebound check window.
n.2: 4 to 6 hours is the interval for repeat measurement after starting phototherapy (CG98 1.4.4).

12.q: Chloe, 25, attends her booking appointment at 8 weeks. Her partner stays with her throughout and has said he will come to every appointment. The midwife has not been able to ask about domestic abuse. Which is the most appropriate plan?
o: Arrange time alone with Chloe, such as during a urine test, and ask then
Ask about domestic abuse in front of her partner so the question is covered
Leave the question until the 36-week appointment when trust is established
Record that routine enquiry was declined because her partner was present
12.w: NICE NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse at booking, or at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, and ensure there is an opportunity for a private one-to-one discussion. Midwives create that opportunity, for example by seeing the woman alone for part of the appointment.

n.1: Asking in front of a partner is unsafe and unlikely to lead to disclosure; it could increase risk if he is abusive.
n.2: Enquiry should happen at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, not deferred to late pregnancy.
n.3: Chloe has not declined; the question was never asked. Recording a refusal would be inaccurate.

12.q: Sophie, 36, has capacity and declines a recommended blood transfusion after a postpartum haemorrhage, saying she prefers iron infusions. Staff feel this is unwise. What does the Mental Capacity Act 2005 say?
o: Staff can override unwise decisions in an emergency
An unwise decision does not mean she lacks capacity
An unwise decision shows that she lacks capacity
Unwise decisions must be reviewed by the Court of Protection
12.w: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Her choice must be respected while care continues.

n.0: A capacitous refusal cannot be overridden, even in an emergency.
n.2: The Act states the opposite: an unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity.
n.3: The Court of Protection is not needed when a person has capacity.

12.q: Ruth, 28, is a Jehovah's Witness at 20 weeks and tells the midwife she will not accept blood transfusion under any circumstances. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell her blood will be given if her life is at risk
Note her religion and take no further action until labour
Ask the hospital chaplain to discuss her decision with her
Arrange a care plan with senior obstetric and anaesthetic staff
12.w: An adult with capacity may refuse blood. SPM 1.22: advocate when decisions are outside guidance and plan to minimise risk. An individual plan records what she will and will not accept (for example cell salvage), optimises haemoglobin and involves senior staff early.

n.0: Giving blood to a competent woman who has refused it would be unlawful.
n.1: Waiting until labour misses the chance to plan and optimise her care.
n.2: Asking a chaplain to discuss her decision suggests pressure to change it rather than respect for it.

12.q: A midwifery team wants to check whether all women with a BMI of 40 kg/m2 or over were referred for an anaesthetic review as set out in the unit guideline. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: A clinical audit measuring practice against the guideline standard
A service evaluation of women's satisfaction with the clinic
A PDSA cycle testing a new referral form on one clinic
A research study comparing two referral pathways
12.w: Clinical audit measures current practice against a defined standard (here, the referral requirement in the guideline), identifies gaps and drives improvement, with re-audit to close the loop.

n.1: Satisfaction is a different question from compliance with a referral standard.
n.2: A PDSA cycle tests a change; the question is whether an existing standard is being met.
n.3: Research generates new knowledge by comparing interventions; the standard already exists.

12.q: Two midwives in a crowded hospital lift are talking about a woman's recent stillbirth, using her first name and room number. A third midwife is also in the lift. What should she do?
o: Report both midwives to the NMC after the shift
Leave it to the midwives' own manager to address later
Join the conversation to make sure the details are accurate
Quietly remind them to stop discussing the woman
12.w: Code 5.1: respect privacy in all aspects of care; Code 16 and 20.3: act on concerns and promote professional behaviour. A prompt, quiet reminder protects the woman's confidentiality now.

n.0: An NMC referral is disproportionate as a first step and does not stop the breach now.
n.1: Leaving it for someone else lets the breach continue now; every registrant should act on poor practice (Code 16, 20.3).
n.2: Joining in adds to the breach of confidentiality.

12.q: In a trial, 10% of women given usual care developed an obstetric anal sphincter injury, compared with 6% of women given a perineal protection bundle. Zainab, a practice development midwife, wants to explain the result to colleagues in terms of how many women need the bundle to prevent one injury. What is the number needed to treat?
12.w: Absolute risk reduction = 10% minus 6% = 4% (0.04). Number needed to treat = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.04 = 25 women given the bundle to prevent one injury. Interpreting trial data in this way is part of SPM 1.4.
