n.0: 4 is the absolute risk reduction expressed as a percentage, not the number needed to treat.
n.2: 17 is 1 divided by 0.06, which uses the intervention group risk instead of the difference between groups.
n.3: 40 is the relative risk reduction as a percentage (4 divided by 10), not the NNT.

12.q: After a maternal collapse on the labour ward, the woman survived but several staff are visibly shaken. Two days later the ward manager arranges a facilitated team session. What is the main aim of this session?
o: To support staff wellbeing and help the team process the event
To ask staff to write statements for the coroner
To replace the formal learning response with an informal one
To decide which staff members should be moved off the labour ward
12.w: Facilitated team sessions after traumatic events support staff wellbeing, help people make sense of what happened and reduce the risk of lasting psychological harm, while learning continues through formal processes (SPM 5.14, 5.15).

n.1: The woman survived; coroner statements are not relevant here.
n.2: Team support sessions do not replace formal learning responses.
n.3: Moving staff is not the aim and may feel punitive.

12.q: Baby Alfie is 10 days old and feeding well, and his mother is well. The midwife plans to transfer their care to the health visiting team today. According to NICE NG194, when should the first health visitor home visit be considered?
o: Within 36 hours after transfer from midwifery care
At the 6 to 8 week infant physical examination
Between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care
At around 3 months, with the first immunisations
12.w: NICE NG194 1.1.15: consider arranging the first postnatal health visitor home visit between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery care. 1.1.9: the transfer from midwife to health visitor must be clearly communicated to professionals and parents.

n.0: 36 hours is the standard for the first midwife visit after transfer from the place of birth.
n.1: The 6 to 8 week examination is usually done in primary care and is later than the health visitor visit.
n.3: Primary immunisations start at 8 weeks, and the health visitor visit is earlier than either.

12.q: Aoife, a midwife, is moving from a post in Belfast to a new post in Cardiff. She is checking which law on termination of pregnancy will apply to her new role. Which statement about the territorial extent of the Abortion Act 1967 is correct?
o: It extends to England and Wales, but not Scotland
It extends to England, Wales and Scotland
It extends to all four nations of the United Kingdom
It extends to England, Scotland and Northern Ireland
12.w: The Abortion Act 1967 extends to England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own separate legal framework, so the Act will apply in Cardiff but did not apply in Belfast. Midwives must differentiate between UK legislatures (SPM 1.2).

n.0: The Act also extends to Scotland.
n.2: The Act does not extend to Northern Ireland, which has its own framework.
n.3: The Act extends to Wales and does not extend to Northern Ireland.

12.q: Chloe, 24, is 34 weeks pregnant with pre-eclampsia. On the antenatal ward she reports a severe frontal headache and seeing spots. Her blood pressure is 168/112 mmHg and she has three beats of ankle clonus. What is the most appropriate immediate action by the midwife?
o: Give oral paracetamol for the headache and recheck her blood pressure in one hour
Call the obstetric team urgently and prepare magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive treatment
Prepare diazepam for seizure prophylaxis and start intravenous fluids at 125 mL/hour
Increase her blood pressure checks to every four hours and repeat her bloods tomorrow
12.w: Severe hypertension with severe headache, visual disturbance and clonus are features of severe pre-eclampsia. NG133 1.8.3 advises considering IV magnesium sulfate when there are severe features, and severe hypertension needs urgent antihypertensive treatment (1.8.6) with BP every 15 to 30 minutes until below 160/110. The midwife's role is to escalate immediately and prepare.

n.0: Treating the headache symptomatically and waiting an hour delays treatment of a woman at imminent risk of eclampsia or stroke.
n.2: NG133 1.8.5 advises against diazepam as an alternative to magnesium sulfate, and maintenance fluids should be limited to 80 mL/hour (1.8.12).
n.3: Four-hourly checks are far too infrequent with severe hypertension; NG133 advises every 15 to 30 minutes until BP is under 160/110 mmHg.

12.q: Baby Kai is born at 32 weeks weighing 1.5 kg. The neonatal team prescribe intramuscular phytomenadione at 400 micrograms/kg (maximum 1 mg). What dose should be given?
o: 1 mg intramuscularly
600 micrograms intramuscularly
1.5 mg intramuscularly
400 micrograms intramuscularly
12.w: BNF for Children: preterm neonate IM prophylaxis 400 micrograms/kg (max 1 mg per dose) at birth. 400 micrograms x 1.5 kg = 600 micrograms, which is below the 1 mg maximum.

n.0: 1 mg is the term dose and the preterm maximum; Kai's weight-based dose is lower.
n.2: 1.5 mg is 1 mg/kg and also exceeds the 1 mg maximum.
n.3: 400 micrograms ignores his weight; the dose is per kilogram.

12.q: Kayla, 21, is bottle feeding with formula. Her baby often takes the whole bottle quickly and then brings back milk. Which advice best reflects responsive bottle feeding?
o: Prop the bottle on a cushion so the baby can feed at their own pace
Hold the baby close, pace the feed and let the baby decide when to stop
Share feeds among relatives so the baby bonds with many people
Encourage the baby to finish each bottle so feeds stay regular
12.w: NICE NG194 1.5.19: responsive bottle feeding involves holding the baby close, pacing feeds, recognising signs the baby has had enough (because formula-fed babies can be overfed), the dangers of prop feeding, and minimising the number of people regularly feeding the baby.

n.0: Prop feeding is dangerous (choking) and removes the close contact of feeding.
n.2: NG194 notes a potential benefit of minimising the number of people regularly feeding the baby.
n.3: Pushing the baby to finish the bottle risks overfeeding.

12.q: After the placenta is delivered, Lily, 28, has a firm, well-contracted uterus at the level of the umbilicus and only a small blood loss. A student asks what mainly stops bleeding from the placental site. What is the correct answer?
o: Vasoconstriction of the uterine arteries by circulating adrenaline
Pressure from the full bladder pressing on the placental site
Rapid formation of clot over the placental site by clotting factors
Uterine muscle contraction and retraction compressing the vessels
12.w: The interlacing, oblique fibres of the myometrium contract and retract around the spiral arteries, acting as 'living ligatures'. Clotting helps, but uterine tone is the main mechanism, which is why atony is the commonest cause of PPH (SPM 3.12.3).

n.0: Adrenaline-driven vasoconstriction is not the main way placental site bleeding is controlled.
n.1: A full bladder impedes uterine contraction and increases bleeding risk; it does not compress the placental site.
n.2: Clotting contributes, but without uterine contraction bleeding continues; uterine tone is the main mechanism.

12.q: Lucy, 35, is pregnant with her second baby. Her first birth was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of 1,400 mL requiring transfusion. She asks to give birth in the alongside midwifery unit. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree to the alongside unit because it is on the same site as the obstetric unit
Explain her bleeding risk and advise planned birth in the obstetric unit
Agree to the alongside unit with active management of the third stage
Tell her a midwifery unit cannot be offered and book a planned caesarean
12.w: NG235 1.10.29 lists previous PPH over 1,000 mL or blood transfusion as an antenatal risk factor for which women should be advised to give birth in an obstetric unit. The midwife explains the risk, records the discussion and respects her informed decision (SPM 2.2).

n.0: Being on the same site does not provide the obstetric care advised after a previous PPH over 1,000 mL.
n.2: Active management reduces PPH risk but does not replace the advice for obstetric unit care with this history.
n.3: Previous PPH is not an indication for caesarean, and she keeps the right to make an informed choice.

12.q: Sara, 28, is 32 weeks pregnant and in cardiac arrest on the labour ward. CPR is under way on a firm surface. The midwife is asked to relieve aortocaval compression. According to RCUK 2025, which method is preferred?
o: Manual displacement of the uterus to her left
Tilting the whole bed 30 degrees to the left
Turning her fully onto her left side
Placing a wedge under her right hip
12.w: RCUK 2025: above 20 weeks, relieve aortocaval compression as early as possible and maintain it throughout resuscitation. Manual left uterine displacement is preferred over lateral tilt because it allows effective chest compressions.

n.1: RCUK 2025 prefers manual displacement over lateral tilt, which reduces compression quality.
n.2: Full lateral positioning prevents effective chest compressions.
n.3: A wedge creates a lateral tilt, which RCUK 2025 ranks below manual displacement.

12.q: Saskia, 27, is in established labour in an alongside midwifery unit. At 14:00 her temperature is 37.6 C and at 15:00 it is 37.7 C. Her pulse is 98 and the fetal heart is normal. Which action follows NICE guidance?
o: Transfer her to obstetric-led care for review
Give paracetamol and continue midwifery-led care
Recheck her temperature in 4 hours, as it is under 38 C
Recheck in 1 hour and transfer if it reaches 38 C
12.w: NICE NG235 1.8.20: a temperature of 38 C or above on a single reading, or 37.5 C or above on 2 consecutive occasions 1 hour apart, is a trigger for transfer to obstetric-led care. Intrapartum antibiotics follow NICE neonatal infection guidance.

n.1: Antipyretics may mask infection and do not replace transfer for review.
n.2: Two consecutive readings of 37.5 C or above 1 hour apart already meet the transfer criterion.
n.3: The 38 C single-reading threshold is not needed when the 37.5 C two-reading criterion is met.

12.q: Chen, 31, has been prescribed 10 days of low molecular weight heparin after her caesarean birth. She is breastfeeding and asks the midwife whether the injections will affect her baby. Which response is accurate?
o: She should express and discard milk for 4 hours after each dose
She should give formula until the 10-day course is finished
LMWH is considered safe to use while breastfeeding
A direct oral anticoagulant tablet is preferred while breastfeeding
12.w: RCOG GTG 37a: LMWH is safe in breastfeeding (warfarin is also safe). Use of direct oral anticoagulants (NOACs) is not recommended in women who are breastfeeding.

n.0: There is no need to discard milk; LMWH is safe in breastfeeding.
n.1: Interrupting breastfeeding is unnecessary and could undermine her milk supply.
n.3: GTG 37a advises that NOACs are not recommended in breastfeeding women.

12.q: Marta, 34, has bipolar disorder and is 24 weeks pregnant. After specialist discussion she has decided to continue lithium because she is at high risk of relapse. Which monitoring plan is in line with NICE CG192?
o: Check plasma lithium at booking, at 28 weeks and at 36 weeks
Check plasma lithium weekly from 20 weeks until the birth
Check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks
Check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then stop it at 36 weeks
12.w: NICE CG192 1.4.37: if lithium continues in pregnancy, check plasma levels every 4 weeks, then weekly from the 36th week; keep levels in range, maintain fluid balance, plan birth in hospital, stop lithium during labour and check levels 12 hours after the last dose.

n.0: Three checks in pregnancy is less frequent than the 4-weekly monitoring recommended.
n.1: Weekly checks are recommended from 36 weeks, not from 20 weeks.
n.3: Lithium is stopped during labour, not at 36 weeks, when weekly monitoring starts.

12.q: Grace, 34, is 16 weeks pregnant in November. She asks whether she needs any vitamin supplements now. What should the midwife advise?
o: Vitamin D 25 micrograms daily
Folic acid 400 micrograms daily
Vitamin D 10 micrograms daily
Vitamin A 700 micrograms daily
12.w: NG247 1.1.12: all pregnant or breastfeeding women should take vitamin D 10 micrograms (400 IU) daily from October to March, and all year if at increased risk of deficiency.

n.0: The recommended dose in pregnancy is 10 micrograms (400 IU) daily.
n.1: Routine folic acid is recommended to 12 weeks; at 16 weeks it is no longer needed.
n.3: Vitamin A supplements are avoided in pregnancy because high intake can harm the baby.

12.q: Three weeks after discharge, the father of a baby Ruth cared for on the postnatal ward sends her a social media friend request and invites her for a drink to say thanks. Ruth had no previous relationship with the family. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the friend request but decline the invitation for a drink
Decline both, keeping a clear professional boundary with the family
Accept the drink if a colleague from the ward also attends
Accept both, as the family is no longer in her care
12.w: NMC Code 20.6: stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past, their families and carers. Ruth should politely decline both.

n.0: An online friendship with the family of a former patient still blurs the professional boundary that Code 20.6 protects.
n.2: A colleague's presence does not change the nature of a social relationship with a family recently in her care.
n.3: Code 20.6 expressly includes people who have been in your care in the past, so discharge does not end the boundary.

12.q: Molly, 25, is 32 weeks pregnant and attends with her first episode of reduced fetal movements. The fetal heart is heard, the computerised CTG meets criteria, SFH is on her centile line and she has no risk factors. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Arrange induction of labour at 37 weeks because of the episode
Book an ultrasound scan for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler
Admit her for daily CTG monitoring until movements return to normal
Explain the results and advise her to return if movements reduce again
12.w: SBL v3 element 3: after a first episode of RFM with a normal cCTG and no other indication, a scan is not required; results are explained and she is encouraged to reattend with further concerns. A scan for growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler is offered for recurrent RFM after 28+0 weeks or if there is another indication.

n.0: Induction for RFM alone before 39+0 weeks is not recommended (SBL v3 element 3).
n.1: A scan is offered at a first presentation only when another indication exists, such as suspected SGA.
n.2: Admission for daily CTG is not indicated when assessment is normal and there are no risk factors.

12.q: At a day 5 postnatal visit, the midwife notices a small bruise on the cheek of a 5-day-old baby. The parents say they do not know how it happened. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure the parents that bruising is common in newborns
Record the bruise in the notes and check it again at the next visit
Follow child protection procedures with urgent paediatric review
Ask the parents to take the baby to their GP within a week
12.w: NICE CG89 (child maltreatment): suspect maltreatment if there is bruising in a child who is not independently mobile. Follow local safeguarding procedures with urgent paediatric assessment (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Bruises in non-mobile babies are uncommon and must be investigated.
n.1: Bruising in a baby who is not mobile must not be left for review; it needs action now.
n.3: This delays assessment and leaves the baby at possible risk.

12.q: During a shift, Kezia, a first-year student midwife, gives an unclear handover about a postnatal woman, leaving out her blood loss. Her practice supervisor, Rachel, wants to give feedback that helps Kezia improve. Which approach is best?
o: Wait until the end of placement and include the issue in the final report
Correct Kezia in front of the team so that everyone learns from the error
Re-do the handover herself and model a complete one for Kezia
Give private, specific feedback that day and agree a plan
12.w: SPM 5.21: support students, promoting reflection and providing constructive feedback. Code 9.1: give honest, accurate and constructive feedback. Feedback is most useful when timely, private, specific about the behaviour, linked to its impact on safety, and ends with an agreed plan.

n.0: Delaying until the final report denies Kezia the chance to improve during the placement.
n.1: Public correction can humiliate the student and is not constructive feedback.
n.2: Modelling a good handover helps, but without direct feedback Kezia may not recognise the omission or why blood loss matters.

12.q: On day 15 the community midwife completes postnatal care for Erin, 33, and her baby. Which information about ongoing care is most accurate to give Erin?
o: Her midwife will return at 6 weeks for a final postnatal check
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 6 to 8 weeks
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 2 weeks
Her health visitor will complete her own postnatal check at 6 to 8 weeks
12.w: NG194 1.2.7: the woman should have a GP review of her health 6 to 8 weeks after birth. On completing midwifery care the midwife transfers care to the health visitor and GP (SPM 2.11).

n.0: Midwifery care has ended at transfer; the midwife does not routinely return at 6 weeks.
n.2: 2 weeks is not the routine maternal check; the GP check is at 6 to 8 weeks (NG194 1.2.7).
n.3: The maternal 6 to 8 week check is by the GP; health visitors follow the Healthy Child Programme.

12.q: Tia, 26, is 6 days after a caesarean birth and at home. At a postnatal visit she feels very unwell, with offensive lochia. Her heart rate is 134 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min and blood pressure 108/66 mmHg. What should the community midwife do?
o: Call 999 and pre-alert the hospital
Ask her GP to see her at the surgery later today
Take a high vaginal swab and revisit her tomorrow
Advise paracetamol and phone triage if she worsens
12.w: A heart rate over 130 is a high-risk criterion (NICE NG255 table 1). Outside hospital, a person meeting any high-risk criterion is referred for emergency care, usually by 999 ambulance, and secondary care is pre-alerted (NG255 1.6.1, 1.6.2).

n.1: A GP appointment later delays emergency care for a high-risk woman.
n.2: A swab and revisit delays treatment of possible sepsis with a high-risk criterion.
n.3: Paracetamol can mask fever and delays urgent assessment.

12.q: Zoe, 32, is 38 weeks pregnant and in early labour. Her membranes rupture spontaneously and there is a sudden fresh vaginal bleed of about 100 mL. Within minutes the fetal heart rate falls to 80 beats/min. Zoe is well, with a normal pulse and blood pressure. What should the midwife suspect?
o: Minor placental abruption
Cervical ectropion
A show from cervical change
Ruptured vasa praevia
12.w: RCOG GTG 63: if APH is associated with rupture of the membranes, bleeding from a ruptured vasa praevia should be considered. The bleeding is fetal blood, so the fetus is rapidly compromised while the mother stays well; this needs immediate obstetric help and urgent birth.

n.0: An abruption would usually cause pain and maternal signs; rapid fetal compromise with a well mother at membrane rupture suggests vasa praevia.
n.1: An ectropion does not cause sudden fetal bradycardia at membrane rupture.
n.2: A show is blood-stained mucus, not a 100 mL bleed with fetal bradycardia.

12.q: The labour ward coordinator asks Helen, a midwife, to discharge Mrs Ahmed, 1 day after birth, to free a bed. Helen has just recorded a blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg and Mrs Ahmed has a headache. What should Helen do?
o: Explain why discharge is unsafe and request urgent medical review
Discharge her with advice to see the GP if the headache continues
Recheck the blood pressure in 4 hours before deciding on discharge
Discharge her and arrange a community blood pressure check tomorrow
12.w: SPM 1.18: recognise external pressures that may unduly influence decisions. A blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg with a headache after birth may be postnatal pre-eclampsia and needs urgent medical assessment (NICE NG133). Helen explains her rationale and escalates rather than discharging.

n.1: Discharging with GP advice ignores a possible postnatal pre-eclampsia that needs urgent review now.
n.2: Waiting 4 hours before acting delays the urgent review that hypertension with headache requires.
n.3: A check tomorrow delays assessment of a woman with hypertension and headache today.

12.q: A trust in England has moved from the Serious Incident Framework to the Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF). A midwife asks what has changed. Which description is most accurate?
o: Investigations now identify the individual staff member who is responsible for the harm
System learning and proportionate responses, with compassionate engagement of families
Every incident now has a full root cause analysis completed within 60 working days
Families are no longer involved, so that staff can speak freely
12.w: PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework (2015). Its four aims are compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected, system-based approaches to learning, considered and proportionate responses, and supportive oversight (NHS England PSIRF).

n.0: PSIRF focuses on systems and contributory factors, not on blaming individuals.
n.2: PSIRF moves away from a fixed timescale and investigation for everything towards proportionate responses.
n.3: Compassionate engagement of patients and families is a core PSIRF aim.
